title: 6  Estimation Theory
text:
6.2 Population Parameters

Expected Value and Variance
When we know the theoretical probabilities, the two most basic summaries (center and spread) can be computed exactly rather than estimated.






ImportantKey Definition





The expected value (or population mean) of a random variable \(X_{i}\), written \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), is the probability-weighted average of its values. The population variance, written \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\), is the expected squared deviation from \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\).



These population quantities are useful as targets. Estimators from earlier chapters, like the sample mean, try to recover them. Sampling theory studies how far an estimator can fall from its target. The subsections below show how to compute these for discrete and continuous random variables.


Discrete Random Variables
If the sample space is discrete, we can compute the expected value, or theoretical mean, as \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = \sum_{x} x \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x),
\] where \(\mathbb{E}\) is the expectation function that explicitly uses the population distribution via \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\): the probability the random variable \(X_{i}\) takes the particular value \(x\). Similarly, we can compute the population variance as \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = \mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2] = \sum_{x} \left(x - \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] \right)^2 \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x),
\] where \(\mathbb{V}\) is the variance function which also explicitly uses the population distribution. The population standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}\), which measures the spread of the distribution of individual outcomes around the theoretical mean.






NoteMust Know





For example, consider a five-sided die with equal probability of landing on each side. I.e., \(X_{i}\) is a Discrete Uniform random variable with outcomes \(x~\text{in}~\{1,2,3,4,5\}\). What is the theoretical mean? What is the variance and standard deviation? \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] &= 1\frac{1}{5} + 2\frac{1}{5} + 3\frac{1}{5} + 4\frac{1}{5} + 5\frac{1}{5} = 15/5 = 3 \\
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] &= (1-3)^2\frac{1}{5} +
  (2 - 3)^2\frac{1}{5} +
  (3 - 3)^2\frac{1}{5} +
  (4 - 3)^2\frac{1}{5} +
  (5 - 3)^2\frac{1}{5} \\
&= 2^2 \frac{1}{5} + 1^2\frac{1}{5} + 0^2 \frac{1}{5} + 1^2\frac{1}{5} + 2^2 \frac{1}{5}
  = (4 + 1 + 1 + 4)/5 = 10/5 = 2 \\
\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]} &= \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}\]


Code
# Computerized Way to Compute Mean
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
x_probs <- c(1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5)
population_mean <- sum(x*x_probs)
population_mean
## [1] 3

# Computerized Way to Compute SD
population_var <- sum((x-population_mean)^2*x_probs)
population_var
## [1] 2
population_sd <- sqrt(population_var)
population_sd
## [1] 1.414214

# Verified by simulation
x_sim_hat <- sample(x, prob=x_probs,
          size=10000, replace=TRUE)
mean(x_sim_hat)
## [1] 2.9651
sqrt(mean((x_sim_hat - mean(x_sim_hat))^2)) # divides by n, unlike sd()
## [1] 1.409497





A finite population is also a discrete random variable. In Sampling & Resampling, we pretended the data were the whole population. Drawing one observation at random gives each of the \(N\) observations a probability of \(1/N\), so the population mean and variance follow directly from the formulas above.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Pretend the 3294 workers in Wages1 are the whole population
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_wages <- Wages1[, 'wage'] # hourly wage in 1980 dollars
N <- length(population_wages)
wage_probs <- rep(1/N, N) # each worker equally likely, with probability 1/3294

# Population mean and variance, from the formulas
population_wage_mean <- sum(population_wages * wage_probs)
population_wage_mean
## [1] 5.757585
population_wage_var <- sum((population_wages - population_wage_mean)^2 * wage_probs)
population_wage_var
## [1] 10.68433
sqrt(population_wage_var) ##sd
## [1] 3.26869


With equal probabilities, \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) is just the average over the whole population, which mean() computes. Note that var() would divide by \(N-1\) instead of \(N\), and so differs slightly from \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) when \(N\) is large.






NoteMust Know





For example, an unfair coin with a \(3/4\) probability of heads (\(x=1\)) and a \(1/4\) probability of tails (\(x=0\)) has a theoretical mean of \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 0\frac{1}{4} + 1\frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{4}
\] and a theoretical variance of \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = [0 - \frac{3}{4}]^2 \frac{1}{4} + [1 - \frac{3}{4}]^2 \frac{3}{4}
= \frac{9}{64} + \frac{3}{64}
= \frac{12}{64}
= \frac{3}{16}.
\] Verify both the mean and variance by simulation.


Code
# A simulation of many coin flips
x <- c(0, 1)
x_probs <- c(1/4, 3/4)
x_sim <- sample(x, prob=x_probs, size=1000, replace=TRUE)

round( mean(x_sim), 4)
## [1] 0.737

round( mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2), 4)
## [1] 0.1938











NoteMust Know





Consider a four-sided die with outcomes \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) and corresponding probabilities \(\{1/8, 2/8, 1/8, 4/8\}\). The mean is \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 1 \frac{1}{8} + 2 \frac{2}{8} + 3 \frac{1}{8} + 4 \frac{4}{8} = 3.
\] The variance is the probability-weighted average squared deviation from the mean, \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = (1-3)^2 \frac{1}{8} + (2-3)^2 \frac{2}{8} + (3-3)^2 \frac{1}{8} + (4-3)^2 \frac{4}{8} = \frac{4 + 2 + 0 + 4}{8} = \frac{10}{8} = 1.25.
\]


Code
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
x_probs <- c(1/8, 2/8, 1/8, 4/8)
population_mean <- sum(x * x_probs)
population_mean
## [1] 3

population_var <- sum((x - population_mean)^2 * x_probs)
population_var
## [1] 1.25

# Verify by simulation
x_sim <- sample(x, prob=x_probs, size=10000, replace=TRUE)
round(mean(x_sim), 2)
## [1] 3
round(mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2), 2)
## [1] 1.25











TipTest Yourself





Consider an unfair coin with a \(\theta\) probability of heads (\(x=1\)) and a \(1-\theta\) probability of tails (\(x=0\)), where \(\theta\) is a distribution parameter between \(0\) and \(1\). The theoretical mean is \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 1[\theta] + 0[1-\theta] = \theta
\] and the theoretical variance is \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]
= [1 - \theta]^2 \theta + [0 - \theta]^2 [1-\theta] = [1 - \theta]^2 \theta + \theta^2 [1-\theta]
= [1-\theta]\theta\left( [1-\theta] + \theta\right) = [1-\theta] \theta.
\] So the theoretical standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}=\sqrt{[1-\theta] \theta}\).









TipTest Yourself





Suppose \(X_{i}\) is a discrete random variable with this probability mass function: \[\begin{aligned}
X_{i} &= \begin{cases}
-1 &  \text{ with probability } \frac{1}{2 \lambda^2} \\
0  & \text{ with probability } 1-\frac{1}{\lambda^2} \\
+1 & \text{ with probability } \frac{1}{2\lambda^2}
\end{cases},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\lambda \geq 1\) is a distribution parameter. What is the theoretical standard deviation?









TipTest Yourself





For a discrete uniform random variable with the sample space \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\), calculate the theoretical median and IQR.





Continuous Random Variables
The distribution parameters of a continuous random variable determine its mean and variance. For example, an exponential random variable with rate parameter \(\lambda\) has theoretical mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=1/\lambda\) and variance \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=1/\lambda^2\). For a normal random variable, we can specify its theoretical mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu\) and variance \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=\sigma^2\) directly.






NoteMust Know





An exponential random variable with \(\lambda=2\) has \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=1/2\). R’s rnorm() takes the mean and standard deviation, so the normal draws below have \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=1\) and \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=2^2=4\).


Code
# Exponential Random Variable
x_sim <- rexp(5000, 2)
m_hat <- mean(x_sim)
round(m_hat, 2)
## [1] 0.5

# Normal Random Variable
x_sim <- rnorm(5000, 1, 2)
round(mean(x_sim), 2)
## [1] 1.02
round(mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2), 2)
## [1] 3.98





Data recorded to many decimal places can also be treated as continuous, with a density \(f(x)\) that a histogram approximates. The integral \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\int x f(x) dx\) is then approximated by a sum over the histogram bins: each bin midpoint times the area of its bar.


Code
# Wages are recorded to many decimal places, so treat them as continuous.
f_hat <- hist(population_wages, breaks=seq(0, 40, by=1), plot=FALSE)
bin_areas <- f_hat[['density']] * diff(f_hat[['breaks']]) # f(x) dx

# Mean from the histogram, and the exact population mean
sum(f_hat[['mids']] * bin_areas)
## [1] 5.757134
population_wage_mean
## [1] 5.757585
# The two numbers are close, 5.757 and 5.758.


As the bins get narrower, the sum approaches the exact mean.






TipTest Yourself





If the sample space is continuous, we can compute the theoretical mean (or expected value) as \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = \int x f(x) d x,
\] where \(f(x)\) is the probability density for the particular value \(x\). Note that this is not a probability; probabilities are areas under \(f\).
Similarly, we can compute the theoretical variance as \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]= \int \left(x - \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] \right)^2 f(x) d x.
\]
For example, consider a random variable with a continuous uniform distribution over \([-1, 1]\). In this case, \(f(x)=1/[1 - (-1)]=1/2\) for each \(x~\text{in}~[-1, 1]\) and \[
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{x}{2} d x = \int_{-1}^{0} \frac{x}{2} d x + \int_{0}^{1} \frac{x}{2} d x = 0
\] and \[
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]= \int_{-1}^{1} x^2 \frac{1}{2} d x = \frac{1}{2} \frac{x^3}{3}|_{-1}^{1} = \frac{1}{6}[1 - (-1)] = 2/6 =1/3
\]


Code
# Verify by simulation
x_sim <- runif(100000, -1, 1)
round( mean(x_sim), 2)
## [1] 0
round( mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2), 2)
## [1] 0.33

title: 6  Estimation Theory
text:
6.3 Estimates
Each population formula above has a sample counterpart. Replace \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\) with the sample proportion \(\hat{p}(x)\) from the empirical mass function. The expected value and variance then become the sample mean and the divide-by-\(n\) sample variance from Summary Statistics, \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m} &= \sum_{x} x \hat{p}(x) \\
\hat{v} &= \sum_{x} \left(x - \hat{m}\right)^2 \hat{p}(x).
\end{aligned}\] Building an estimate this way, by putting sample proportions into a population formula, is called the plug-in principle. The same substitution works for other parameters.






NoteMust Know





Suppose we flipped a coin \(100\) times and found that \(75\) were heads and \(25\) were tails. The estimated probabilities are \(\hat{p}(1)=75/100=3/4\) and \(\hat{p}(0)=25/100=1/4\), so \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m} &= 1 \times \frac{3}{4} + 0 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4} \\
\hat{v} &= \left(1-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times \frac{3}{4} + \left(0-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{64} + \frac{9}{64} = \frac{12}{64} = \frac{3}{16}.
\end{aligned}\] These are the plug-in versions of the theoretical coin mean \(\theta\) and variance \([1-\theta]\theta\), with \(\hat{m}\) in place of \(\theta\): \(\hat{m}(1-\hat{m}) = 3/4 \times 1/4 = 3/16\).


Code
x0_hat <- c(rep(1, 75), rep(0, 25)) # 75 heads and 25 tails
p_hat <- table(x0_hat)/length(x0_hat)
x <- as.numeric(names(p_hat))
m_hat <- sum(x * p_hat)
v_hat <- sum((x - m_hat)^2 * p_hat)
c(m_hat, v_hat)
## [1] 0.7500 0.1875





With many unique values, the plug-in mean and variance still match the averages over the observations. To see this, take one sample from the pretend population, as if it were all we observed.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# One sample of 50 workers, as if it were all we observed
x_sim <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)

# Wages have many unique values.
# Plug-in mean and variance, from the estimated probability of each unique value
p_hat <- table(x_sim)/length(x_sim)
x <- as.numeric(names(p_hat))
m_hat <- sum(x * p_hat)
v_hat <- sum((x - m_hat)^2 * p_hat)
round(c(m_hat, v_hat), 4)
## [1]  6.1480 12.7499

# Same numbers, from the observations directly
round(c(mean(x_sim), mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2)), 4)
## [1]  6.1480 12.7499

# Population parameters, which these numbers estimate
round(c(population_wage_mean, population_wage_var), 4)
## [1]  5.7576 10.6843
# The estimates, about 6.15 and 12.75, differ from these parameters.


An estimate can differ from its population parameter because it comes from only one sample.






TipTest Yourself





You can estimate means and variances for continuous random variables with weights, but here we have an additional approximation error due to binning by the histogram.


Code
x_sim <- rnorm(5000, 1, 2) # continuous draws, as in Continuous Random Variables

# values and probabilities
f_hat  <- hist(x_sim, plot=FALSE)
wt <- f_hat[['counts']]/length(x_sim)
xt <- f_hat[['mids']]
# Weighted mean
m_hat <- sum(wt*xt)
m_hat
## [1] 0.9946

# Compare to 'mean(x_sim)'


Try it yourself with


Code
x_sim <- runif(2000, -1, 1)

title: 6  Estimation Theory
text:
6.4 Estimators

Means
The LLN says the sample mean concentrates on the population mean as \(n\) grows. To explain it, we first find where the sampling distribution of \(M\) is centered, using a basic rule about how expectations distribute over sums. Linearity of expectation states that for any random variables \(X_{1}, X_{2}\) and constants \(a, b\), \[\mathbb{E}[a X_{1} + b X_{2}] = a \mathbb{E}[X_{1}] + b \mathbb{E}[X_{2}].\] This is useful because it lets us reason about the mean of any linear combination of random variables without computing a joint distribution.
Applied to the sample mean estimator \(M = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}/n\), with the constants \(1/n\): \[
\mathbb{E}\left[M\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}/n \right] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]/n.
\] Assuming each observation has the same finite expected value, the expected value of the sample average equals this common population mean: \(\mathbb{E}\left[M\right] = \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) for every \(i\). For a detailed treatment, see here.






NoteMust Know





Return to the two fair coin flips in Statistical Theory, where \(\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{2}]=1/2\) and each of the four samples HH, HT, TH, and TT has probability \(1/4\). Weighting the sum \(X_{1}+X_{2}\) and the sample mean \(M\) of each sample by \(1/4\) gives \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X_{1}+X_{2}] &= 2 \times \frac{1}{4} + 1 \times \frac{1}{4} + 1 \times \frac{1}{4} + 0 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1 = \mathbb{E}[X_{1}] + \mathbb{E}[X_{2}] \\
\mathbb{E}[M] &= 1 \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} + 0 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} = \mathbb{E}[X_{i}].
\end{aligned}\]


Code
# The four samples HH, HT, TH, TT, each with probability 1/4
x1 <- c(1, 1, 0, 0) # first flip
x2 <- c(1, 0, 1, 0) # second flip
x_probs <- c(1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)
sum((x1 + x2) * x_probs) # E[X1 + X2]
## [1] 1
sum((x1 + x2)/2 * x_probs) # E[M]
## [1] 0.5

# Verify by simulation
coin_means <- rep(NA, 10000)
for(i in seq_along(coin_means)){
    x_sim <- sample(c(0, 1), size=2, replace=TRUE)
    m_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    coin_means[i] <- m_hat
}
round(mean(coin_means), 2)
## [1] 0.5





The pretend population lets us check this by comparing the average of many sample means with the population mean.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Many samples of 50 workers
wage_means <- rep(NA, 1000)
for(i in seq_along(wage_means)){
    x_sim <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
    m_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    wage_means[i] <- m_hat
}
round(mean(wage_means), 3) # average estimate across samples
## [1] 5.742
round(population_wage_mean, 3) # population mean
## [1] 5.758
# The average estimate, about 5.742, is close to the population mean, 5.758.








TipTest Yourself





Now consider an unfair coin with Heads \(X_{i}=1\) having probability \(\theta\) and Tails \(X_{i}=0\) having probability \(1-\theta\). First notice that \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\theta\). Then notice we can first list the four outcomes, and then separate the first and second flips: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X_{1}+X_{2}]
&= [1+1][\theta \times \theta] + [1+0][\theta \times (1-\theta)] + [0+1][(1-\theta) \times \theta] + [0+0][(1-\theta) \times (1-\theta)] \quad \text{"HH + HT + TH + TT"} \\
&= [1][\theta \times \theta] + [1][\theta \times (1-\theta)] + [0][(1-\theta) \times \theta] + [0][(1-\theta) \times (1-\theta)] \quad \text{first outcomes times prob.} \\
&+ [1][\theta \times \theta] + [0][\theta \times (1-\theta)] + [1][(1-\theta) \times \theta] + [0][(1-\theta) \times (1-\theta)] \quad \text{+second outcomes times prob.} \\
&= [1][\theta \times \theta] + [1][\theta \times (1-\theta)] + [1][\theta \times \theta] + [1][(1-\theta) \times \theta] \quad \text{drop zeros} \\
&= 1\theta (\theta + [1-\theta]) +  1\theta (\theta + [1-\theta]) = \theta+\theta \quad \text{algebra} \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X_{1}] +  \mathbb{E}[X_{2}].
\end{aligned}\] The theoretical mean is \(\mathbb{E}[\frac{X_{1}+X_{2}}{2}]=\frac{\theta+\theta}{2}=\theta\).





Variances
If the observations \(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\) are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) with finite variance, then the standard error of the sample mean decreases at the rate \(1/\sqrt{n}\). The individual observations have a common variance \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\), which is the mean squared deviation from their common mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\). \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{V}\left[ M \right]
&= \mathbb{V}\left[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}}{n} \right]
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{V}\left[\frac{X_{i}}{n}\right]
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}{n^2}
= \mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n \\
\text{SE}\left(M\right) &= \sqrt{\mathbb{V}\left[ M \right] } = \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n} = \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}/\sqrt{n}.
\end{aligned}\]






NoteMust Know





For example, if the population standard deviation is \(10\) and we draw samples of size \(n=4\), then \(\mathbb{V}[M]=\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n=100/4=25\) and \(\text{SE}(M)=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n}=10/2=5\). Quadrupling the sample size to \(n=16\) halves the standard error to \(10/\sqrt{16}=2.5\).



With the pretend population, the formula can be checked against the spread of the sample means computed above.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
round(sqrt(population_wage_var/50), 3) # SE from the formula
## [1] 0.462
round(sd(wage_means), 3) # SE from many samples
## [1] 0.454


The standard error is distinct from the sample standard deviation \(\hat{s}\), which measures spread of observations. The two are easy to confuse. The sample standard deviation \(\hat{s}\) is the variability of individual observations within a single sample, while the standard error is the variability of a statistic across repeated samples. To be clear,

Types of variability







Concept
What varies
Notation




Standard deviation
individual observations within a sample or population
\(\hat{s}\) or \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}\)


Standard error
a statistic across samples
\(\text{SE}(M)\)



Nonetheless, the sample standard deviation can be used to estimate the standard error of the sample mean. Specifically, under the i.i.d. assumptions above, we can estimate the population standard deviation, \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}\), with the sample standard deviation, \(\hat{s}\): \[
\text{SE}(M) = \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n} \approx \hat{s}/\sqrt{n}.
\]
Another data-driven way is to create a bootstrap distribution for the sample mean and then compute the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution \(\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{boot}} \approx \text{SE}(M)\), as shown in Sampling & Resampling. The theory-driven estimate can differ from the bootstrap estimate in a finite sample, although both methods here assume i.i.d. observations. The standard error formula does not require normality. The theory-driven estimate does have some advantages too, but we do not go into that as we would need more advanced mathematics.
To compare the two, take another sample from the pretend population, as if it were all we observed.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# One sample of 50 workers, as if it were all we observed
x_sim <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
n <- length(x_sim)
s_hat <- sqrt(mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2)) # divides by n, unlike sd()
theory_se <- s_hat/sqrt(n)

# Bootstrap estimates
boot_means_wage <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means_wage)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_sim, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means_wage[b] <- m_b_hat
}
boot_se <- sd(boot_means_wage)

# Compare SE's
paste0('Bootstrap SE = ', round(boot_se, 3))
## [1] "Bootstrap SE = 0.458"
paste0('Class SE = ', round(theory_se, 3))
## [1] "Class SE = 0.459"
paste0('True SE = ', round(sqrt(population_wage_var/n), 3))
## [1] "True SE = 0.462"


Both estimates use only the one sample. We can compute the true standard error only because we pretend to know the population.


Shape
Sometimes, the sampling distribution is approximately normal due to the CLT. For a sufficiently large sample of i.i.d. observations with finite positive variance, \(M\) is approximately normal with mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) and standard deviation \(\text{SE}(M)=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n}\). We estimate this standard error with \(\hat{s}/\sqrt{n}\).


Code
# Bootstrap Distribution
hist(boot_means_wage, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 1),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
title('Bootstrap vs Normal Distribution', font.main=1)

# Theoretical Distribution: Normal Approximation with IID SEs
x <- seq(3, 9, by=0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, mean(x_sim), theory_se)
lines(x, fx, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)















TipTest Yourself





Repeat the comparison with murder arrests in USArrests. With no known population, there is no true standard error to compare with.


Code
# These 50 US states are one sample, with no known population.
x2_hat <- USArrests[, 'Murder'] # murder arrests per 100,000
n2 <- length(x2_hat)
s2_hat <- sqrt(mean((x2_hat - mean(x2_hat))^2)) # divides by n, unlike sd()
theory_se2 <- s2_hat/sqrt(n2)

# Bootstrap estimates
boot_means2 <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means2)){
    x_boot <- sample(x2_hat, replace=TRUE)
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means2[b] <- m_b_hat
}
boot_se2 <- sd(boot_means2)

# Compare SE's
paste0('Bootstrap SE = ', round(boot_se2, 3))
## [1] "Bootstrap SE = 0.603"
paste0('Class SE = ', round(theory_se2, 3))
## [1] "Class SE = 0.61"

# Bootstrap Distribution
hist(boot_means2, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 0.7),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
title('Bootstrap vs Normal Distribution', font.main=1)

# Theoretical Distribution: Normal Approximation with IID SEs
x <- seq(5, 10, by=0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, mean(x2_hat), theory_se2)
lines(x, fx, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)














Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)
The variance estimator \(V=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-M)^2/n\) is nearly a sample mean of the squared deviations \(Y_{i}=(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2\). So in large samples, the CLT says \(V\) is approximately normal, with a center and spread set by the mean and variance of \(Y_{i}\). We often care about a transformed quantity like \(Y_{i}\) or \(\log(X_{i})\), and would prefer not to derive its full distribution from scratch just to take its expectation. The Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS) gives the expected value of a function of a random variable without first deriving the distribution of that function. For discrete \(X_{i}\) and any function \(g\), \[\mathbb{E}[g(X_{i})] = \sum_{x} g(x) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x).\] For continuous \(X_{i}\), replace the sum with an integral against \(f(x)\). LOTUS is useful as a shortcut: instead of deriving the distribution of \(g(X_{i})\) and then summing \(y \cdot \text{Prob}(g(X_{i}) = y)\), we sum \(g(x) \cdot \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\) directly using the original distribution of \(X_{i}\). You have already seen the special case \(g(X_{i})=\left(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\right)^2\), which is the population variance. The plug-in principle applies here too: putting \(\hat{p}(x)\) into LOTUS estimates \(\mathbb{E}[g(X_{i})]\) with \(\sum_{x} g(x)\hat{p}(x)\), which is the sample mean of the \(g(\hat{x}_{i})\). With \(g(x)=(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2\), this is the average squared deviation from the population mean, and \(V\) differs from it only by using \(M\) in place of \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\).






TipTest Yourself





Let \(X_{i}\) take values \(\{1,2,3\}\) with \[
\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)=0.2,\quad \text{Prob}(X_{i}=2)=0.5,\quad \text{Prob}(X_{i}=3)=0.3.
\] Let \(g(x)=x^2+1\). Then \(g(1)=1^2+1=2\), \(g(2)=2^2+1=5\), \(g(3)=3^2+1=10\).
Then, by LOTUS, \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[g(X_{i})]=\sum_{x} g(x)\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)
&= g(1)\cdot 0.2 + g(2)\cdot 0.5 + g(3)\cdot 0.3 \\
&= 2 \cdot 0.2 + 5 \cdot 0.5 + 10 \cdot 0.3 \\
&= 0.4 + 2.5 + 3 = 5.9.
\end{aligned}\]


Code
x  <- c(1, 2, 3)
x_probs <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3)
g  <- function(x) x^2 + 1
sum(g(x) * x_probs) 
## [1] 5.9











NoteMust Know





For a fair four-sided die and \(g(x)=x^2+1\), LOTUS gives \(\mathbb{E}[g(X_{i})]\) exactly, and a simulation gives nearly the same number.


Code
g  <- function(x) x^2 + 1

# A theoretical example
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
x_probs <- c(1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)
sum(g(x) * x_probs)
## [1] 8.5

# A simulation example
x_sim <- sample(x, prob=x_probs, size=1000, replace=TRUE)
mean(g(x_sim))
## [1] 8.348





Economists often work with logged data. LOTUS gives the population mean of the logged values directly from the original distribution, with \(g(x)=\log(x)\).


Code
# E[log(X)] by LOTUS
sum(log(population_wages) * wage_probs)
## [1] 1.587268
# The population mean of log wages is 1.59.

# log(E[X]) is a different number
log(population_wage_mean)
## [1] 1.750518
# The log of the population mean wage is 1.75, so the two numbers differ.


In general, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X_{i})] \neq g(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])\), so you cannot compute the expected value first and transform it afterwards.






TipTest Yourself





If \(X_{i}\) is a continuous random variable (a random variable with a continuous sample space) and \(g\) is a function, then \(\mathbb E[g(X_{i})] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)f(x) dx\).


Code
x_sim <- rexp(5e5, rate = 1)           # X ~ Exp(1)
mean(sqrt(x_sim))                      # LOTUS Simulation
## [1] 0.8857528
sqrt(pi) / 2                       # Exact via LOTUS integral
## [1] 0.8862269











TipTest Yourself





The variance estimator \(V=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-M)^2/n\) also has a sampling distribution. Write \(Y_{i}=g(X_{i})=(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2\) for the squared deviation of each observation from the population mean. Expanding the square, and using \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])/n = M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), \[\begin{aligned}
V &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( [X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]] - [M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]] \right)^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_{i} - 2\left(M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\right)^2 + \left(M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\right)^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_{i} - \left(M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\right)^2.
\end{aligned}\] So \(V\) is a sample mean of the \(Y_{i}\) minus a correction term. By LOTUS, each \(Y_{i}\) has mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]=\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) and variance \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]=\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^4]-\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]^2\). The correction term has mean \(\mathbb{E}[(M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2]=\mathbb{V}[M]=\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n\), so \(\mathbb{E}[V]=\frac{n-1}{n}\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\). The correction term shrinks like \(1/n\), faster than the \(1/\sqrt{n}\) standard error of the sample mean of the \(Y_{i}\). So the CLT applied to the \(Y_{i}\) says that, in large samples, \(V\) is approximately normal with mean \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) and standard error \(\text{SE}(V)=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]/n}\).
For the five-sided die, LOTUS gives \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=2\) and \(\mathbb{E}[(X_{i}-3)^4]=(16+1+0+1+16)/5=34/5\), so \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]=34/5-2^2=14/5\). With \(n=100\) rolls, \(\mathbb{E}[V]=\frac{99}{100} \times 2=\frac{99}{50}\) and \(\text{SE}(V)=\sqrt{\frac{14/5}{100}}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{250}}\approx 0.167\).


Code
# Five-sided die: population moments by LOTUS
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
x_probs <- rep(1/5, 5)
population_mean <- sum(x * x_probs)
population_var <- sum((x - population_mean)^2 * x_probs) # E[Y_i]
population_m4 <- sum((x - population_mean)^4 * x_probs) # E[(X_i - E[X_i])^4]
y_var <- population_m4 - population_var^2 # V[Y_i]

# Sampling distribution of V across many samples of n rolls
n <- 100
sample_vars <- rep(NA, 2000)
for(i in seq_along(sample_vars)){
    x_sim <- sample(x, prob=x_probs, size=n, replace=TRUE)
    v_hat <- mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2) # divide-by-n variance
    sample_vars[i] <- v_hat
}
round(mean(sample_vars), 3) # near (n-1)/n * 2 = 1.98
## [1] 1.986
round(sd(sample_vars), 3) # near sqrt(2.8/n) = 0.167
## [1] 0.17

hist(sample_vars, breaks=25,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 2.6),
    xlab=expression(hat(v)),
    main=NA)
title('Sampling Distribution of the Variance', font.main=1)

# CLT approximation, with the SE from LOTUS
v <- seq(1, 3, by=0.01)
fv <- dnorm(v, population_var, sqrt(y_var/n))
lines(v, fv, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Try it yourself with \(n=10\) rolls. Is the normal approximation still good?

title: 6  Estimation Theory
text:
6.5 Bias and Consistency
Knowing an estimator’s sampling distribution lets us judge how good the estimator is.

Bias
A natural first question is whether an estimator is right on average. The bias of an estimator is its expected value minus the parameter it targets. For the sample mean, \(\text{Bias}(M) = \mathbb{E}[M] - \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\). An estimator is unbiased if its bias is zero.
Bias is useful for separating two reasons an estimate can miss its target: bad luck in one sample, which averages out across samples, and a systematic error, which does not. From Means, \(\mathbb{E}[M]=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), so the sample mean is unbiased.
The variance estimator \(V=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-M)^2/n\) is biased, because \(\mathbb{E}[V]=\frac{n-1}{n}\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\). So we often use the adjusted sample standard deviation in theoretical calculations, \[
\hat{s}_{\text{adj}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m})^2}{n-1}},
\] which divides by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\). R’s sd() computes \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\), and var() computes its square.






TipTest Yourself





The variance estimator is \(V=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{i}-M)^2/n\), which is biased; \(\text{Bias}(V) = \mathbb{E}[V] - \mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\). On average, it is too small by a factor of \(\frac{n-1}{n}\), \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[V] &= \frac{n-1}{n}\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] \\
\text{Bias}(V) &= -\frac{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}{n}.
\end{aligned}\] The reason is that \(V\) measures deviations from the sample mean, which sits at the center of its own sample. In total, the observations are closer to it than to the population mean, so the squared deviations come out too small. This is why the adjusted version in Summary Statistics, which divides by \(n-1\), is called unbiased. The Test Yourself in LOTUS derives the formula. The bias shrinks as \(n\) grows.
The pretend population lets us check this with samples of \(n=10\) observations, where the bias is a tenth of the population variance.


Code
# Many samples of 10 workers
n <- 10
wage_vars <- rep(NA, 10000)
for(i in seq_along(wage_vars)){
    x_sim <- sample(population_wages, n, replace=FALSE)
    v_hat <- mean((x_sim - mean(x_sim))^2) # divide-by-n variance
    wage_vars[i] <- v_hat
}
round(mean(wage_vars), 2) # average estimate across samples
## [1] 9.6
round((n-1)/n*population_wage_var, 2) # E[V] from the formula
## [1] 9.62
round(population_wage_var, 2) # population variance
## [1] 10.68
# The average estimate, about 9.6, is close to E[V] from the formula, 9.62.
# It is not close to the population variance, 10.68.


Now return to the two fair coin flips in Statistical Theory, where \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}\). In each of the four samples, compute \(V=[(X_{1}-M)^2+(X_{2}-M)^2]/2\): \[\begin{aligned}
\text{HH}: \quad V &= [(1-1)^2+(1-1)^2]/2 = 0 \\
\text{HT}: \quad V &= [(1-\frac{1}{2})^2+(0-\frac{1}{2})^2]/2 = 1/4 \\
\text{TH}: \quad V &= [(0-\frac{1}{2})^2+(1-\frac{1}{2})^2]/2 = 1/4 \\
\text{TT}: \quad V &= [(0-0)^2+(0-0)^2]/2 = 0.
\end{aligned}\] Each sample has probability \(1/4\), so \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[V] &= 0 \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} + 0 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8} \\
\text{Bias}(V) &= \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{4} = -\frac{1}{8},
\end{aligned}\] which matches \(-\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n = -\frac{1}{4}/2 = -\frac{1}{8}\).


Code
# The four samples HH, HT, TH, TT, each with probability 1/4
x1 <- c(1, 1, 0, 0) # first flip
x2 <- c(1, 0, 1, 0) # second flip
x_probs <- c(1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)
m_samples <- (x1 + x2)/2
v_samples <- ((x1 - m_samples)^2 + (x2 - m_samples)^2)/2
v_samples
## [1] 0.00 0.25 0.25 0.00

sum(v_samples * x_probs) # E[V]
## [1] 0.125
sum(v_samples * x_probs) - 1/4 # Bias(V)
## [1] -0.125







Consistency
Bias describes an estimator at one sample size, so a natural next question is what happens as we collect more data. An estimator is consistent if its estimates get closer and closer to the parameter it targets as the sample grows. With enough data, nearly every sample gives an estimate close to the parameter.
Consistency is useful as a minimum requirement: an estimator that is not consistent can stay wrong no matter how much data we collect. The Law of Large Numbers says that the sample mean is consistent. The reason is the shrinking standard error from Variances. As \(\text{SE}(M)=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n}\) falls toward zero, the sampling distribution of \(M\) piles up around \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\).
Note that each additional data point you have provides more information, which ultimately decreases the standard error of your estimates. This is why statisticians will often recommend that you get more data. However, the \(1/\sqrt{n}\) rate means each additional data point lowers the standard error by less than the one before. In economics, this is known as diminishing returns, and it is why economists may recommend you do not get more data.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# One sample of 50 workers, as if it were all we observed
x_sim <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)

n_boot <- 999 # number of bootstrap samples
sample_sizes <- seq(1, length(x_sim), by=1) # different resample sizes

## For each sample size, compute the bootstrap SE
se_by_n <- rep(NA, length(sample_sizes))
for(n in seq_along(sample_sizes)){
    boot_means_n <- rep(NA, n_boot)
    for(b in seq(1, n_boot)){
        x_boot <- sample(x_sim, size=n, replace=TRUE)
        m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot) # statistic of interest
        boot_means_n[b] <- m_b_hat
    }
    se_n <- sd(boot_means_n) # How much the statistic varies across samples
    se_by_n[n] <- se_n
}

# Theory-driven standard error at each sample size, with s_adj in place of the population SD
se_theory_n <- sd(x_sim)/sqrt(sample_sizes)

plot(sample_sizes, se_by_n, pch=16, col=grey(0, 0.5),
    ylim=range(c(se_by_n, se_theory_n)),
    ylab='standard error', xlab='sample size', main=NA)
lines(sample_sizes, se_theory_n, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=1, lty=2)















TipTest Yourself





With the pretend population, we can watch this happen. The chunk below records how often the sample mean misses the population mean by a fixed amount.


Code
# Share of 2000 samples whose mean misses by one dollar or more
n_values <- c(10, 50, 250)
miss_share <- rep(NA, length(n_values))
for(ni in seq_along(n_values)){
    wage_means_n <- rep(NA, 2000)
    for(i in seq_along(wage_means_n)){
        x_sim <- sample(population_wages, n_values[ni], replace=FALSE)
        wage_means_n[i] <- mean(x_sim)
    }
    miss_share[ni] <- mean(abs(wage_means_n - population_wage_mean) >= 1)
}
round(cbind(n=n_values, share=miss_share), 3)
##        n share
## [1,]  10 0.314
## [2,]  50 0.024
## [3,] 250 0.000
# The share of samples that miss falls toward zero as n grows.
# It is about 31% with n=10, about 2% with n=50, and about 0% with n=250.





Consistency does not require an unbiased estimator. The variance estimator \(V\) is biased, but both its bias and its spread shrink as \(n\) grows, so \(V\) is consistent too. The reverse also happens. The first observation \(X_{1}\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), but it is not consistent, because its distribution does not change as \(n\) grows.

title: 6  Estimation Theory
text:
6.6 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain in your own words the difference between an estimate \(\hat{m}\), an estimator \(M\), and a population parameter \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\). Why is it important to distinguish between these three concepts?
Suppose \(X_{i}\) is a discrete random variable with outcomes \(\{1, 3, 5, 7\}\) and corresponding probabilities \(\{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.3\}\). Compute the theoretical mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), variance \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\), and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}\) by hand. Verify your answers using R.
Using the USArrests dataset in R, compute the sample mean and the bootstrap standard error of the mean for the Assault variable. Then compute the theory-driven standard error \(\hat{s}/\sqrt{n}\) and compare the two estimates.
Using the Wages1 population, draw many samples of \(n=5\) workers and compute the bias of the variance estimator \(V\). Compare it with the formula \(-\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]/n\). Repeat with \(n=50\).


Further Reading

https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/probability-library/basic-theoretical-probability/a/probability-the-basics – Refresher on the basics of probability theory.
https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/2.1-random-variables-and-probability-distributions.html – Expected value, variance, and population parameters in an econometrics setting.
https://dlsun.github.io/probability/linearity.html – Detailed explanation of the linearity of expectation and rules for computing expected values.



Recall
We defined population parameters, \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) and \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\), and their estimators, \(M\) and \(V\). We also covered linearity of expectation and LOTUS. The standard error of the sample mean shrinks at the \(1/\sqrt{n}\) rate. The five-sided die computation made the parameters concrete: with outcomes \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\) each having probability \(1/5\), the population mean is \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 15/5 = 3\) and the variance is \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = (4+1+0+1+4)/5 = 2\). The \(1/\sqrt{n}\) rule then says that if a population has standard deviation \(10\), samples of size \(n=4\) have \(\text{SE}(M) = 5\) but quadrupling the sample size to \(n=16\) halves the standard error to \(2.5\). An estimator’s bias is its expected value minus its target. For two fair coin flips, the divide-by-\(n\) variance has \(\mathbb{E}[V]=1/8\) against a target of \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=1/4\), so its bias is \(-1/8\). An estimator is consistent if its estimates get closer and closer to the parameter it targets as the sample grows. In the wage population, the share of samples whose mean missed by a dollar or more fell from about 31% with \(10\) workers to almost none with \(250\).

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
7.1 Resampling Intervals
The sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies across samples; the confidence interval turns knowledge about that sampling distribution into a statement about the unknown parameter.
This chapter asks three questions.
Confidence intervals are useful for reporting uncertainty alongside an estimate. Along with the estimate \(\hat{m}\), we report a range and a coverage level. The range shows how much sampling noise could plausibly move the estimate. The width depends on the sample size, the spread of the data, and the coverage level \(1-\alpha\) that the user chooses.
If we have a sampling distribution for a statistic, the simplest way to read off a confidence interval is to take its middle quantiles.
Critical values are useful because they translate any coverage level into a pair of numbers that can be looked up or simulated, without committing to a parametric model for the sampling distribution. Often, we have only one sample, in which case we can construct a bootstrap or jackknife sampling distribution (as in Sampling & Resampling) and compute the critical values directly from it:
The histogram below shows the bootstrap distribution of the mean with the \(95\%\) interval marked.
Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Pretend these 3294 hourly wages are the whole population
# Source: US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_wages <- Wages1[, 'wage']

# Lab data: one random sample of 50 workers, as if it were all we observed
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
x_hat <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
m_hat <- mean(x_hat)
m_hat
## [1] 5.708014
# The sample mean is about 5.71 dollars an hour.

# Bootstrap Distribution
boot_means <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means[b] <-m_b_hat
}

# 95% CI
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
boot_ci
##    2.5%   97.5% 
## 4.96511 6.46076
# The interval runs from about 4.97 to 6.46 dollars.
# We are 95% confident it contains the population mean wage.
# The pretend population mean is about 5.76, so this interval does contain it.

# Visualize
hist(boot_means, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    border=NA, breaks=50,
    xlab='Bootstrap means of hourly wages (1980 dollars)')
title('Bootstrap CI', font.main=1)
abline(v=boot_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
This approach can be easily extended to other statistics. For example, a \(Z\%\) confidence interval for the median is an interval where \(Z\%\) of those generated will contain the population median.

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
ImportantKey Definition





The critical values of a sampling distribution are the lower and upper quantiles that bracket the middle \(Z\%\) of the distribution. For a \(95\%\) confidence interval, the critical values are the \(2.5\)th and \(97.5\)th percentiles.





The \(5^{\text{th}}\) and \(95^{\text{th}}\) percentiles are the critical values for the \(90\%\) confidence interval.
The \(2.5^{\text{th}}\) and \(97.5^{\text{th}}\) percentiles are the critical values for the \(95\%\) confidence interval.
The \(0.5^{\text{th}}\) and \(99.5^{\text{th}}\) percentiles are the critical values for the \(99\%\) confidence interval.









NoteMust Know





Using the bootstrap distribution above, here are the \(90\%\) and \(99\%\) confidence intervals.


Code
# 90% CI: 5th and 95th percentiles
quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.05, .95), na.rm=TRUE)
##       5%      95% 
## 5.086016 6.335946

# 99% CI: 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles
quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.005, .995), na.rm=TRUE)
##     0.5%    99.5% 
## 4.758652 6.695011


The \(99\%\) interval is wider than the \(90\%\) interval: demanding higher coverage forces a longer interval.









NoteMust Know





Here is the same bootstrap \(95\%\) confidence interval for a second sample, x2_hat.


Code
# Hourly wages of the 1569 women in Wages1 (1980 dollars)
# Wages1 is really a sample of US workers, so these women are a sample too.
x2_hat <- Wages1[Wages1[, 'sex']=='female', 'wage']
m2_hat <- mean(x2_hat)
m2_hat
## [1] 5.146924

# Bootstrap Distribution
boot_means2 <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means2)){
    x_boot <- sample(x2_hat, replace=TRUE)
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means2[b] <- m_b_hat
}

# 95% CI
boot_ci2 <- quantile(boot_means2, probs=c(.025, .975))
boot_ci2
##     2.5%    97.5% 
## 5.007022 5.289265
# The interval runs from about 5.01 to 5.29 dollars.
# We are 95% confident it contains the population mean wage for women.

# Visualize
hist(boot_means2, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    border=NA, breaks=50,
    xlab='Bootstrap means of hourly wages (1980 dollars)')
title('Bootstrap CI', font.main=1)
abline(v=boot_ci2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
7.2 Normal Approximation
When the sampling distribution is well approximated by a Normal curve, the confidence interval has a simple closed form built from the standard error.






ImportantKey Definition





The margin of error \(E\) is the half-width of a Normal-approximation confidence interval, so the interval is \(\hat{m} \pm E\). It equals the critical value times the standard error, \(E = q(\alpha/2) \cdot \text{SE}(M)\), and shrinks as \(n\) grows.



The Normal-approximation interval is useful because it requires only an estimate \(\hat{m}\), a standard error \(\text{SE}(M)\), and a single Normal quantile (no resampling loop, no full sampling distribution). The \(95\%\) interval is the most common and uses critical value \(q=1.96\) (the \(97.5\)th percentile of the standard Normal); the \(90\%\) interval uses \(q=1.645\). \(\text{SE}(M)\) can come from the classical formula \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}/\sqrt{n}\), the bootstrap, or the jackknife. The classical formula uses the adjusted sample standard deviation \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\).
A coverage level of \(1-\alpha\) means that if the same sampling procedure were repeated \(100\) times from the same population, approximately \(100(1-\alpha)\) percent of the intervals are expected to contain the true population mean. 1






NoteMust Know





For example, suppose we sample \(n=36\) monthly electricity bills (in dollars) and find \(\hat{m}=142\) and \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}=30\). The classical standard error is \(\text{SE}(M) \approx \hat{s}_{\text{adj}}/\sqrt{n} = 30/\sqrt{36} = 5\). From theory, we also know that \(95\%\) confidence interval has upper and lower critical value of \[\begin{aligned}
F^{-1}_{\text{Normal}}\left(0.975, \text{SE}(M) \right) &= +1.96 \cdot \text{SE}(M) \\
F^{-1}_{\text{Normal}}\left(0.025, \text{SE}(M) \right) &= -1.96 \cdot \text{SE}(M)
\end{aligned}\] Together, we can calculate \[\begin{aligned}
E &= q(\alpha/2) \cdot \text{SE}(M) = 1.96 \cdot 5 = 9.8 \\
[\hat{m} - E, \hat{m} + E] &= [142 - 9.8, 142 + 9.8] = [132.2,~ 151.8].
\end{aligned}\] We are \(95\%\) confident that the population mean electricity bill is between \(\$132.20\) and \(\$151.80\).


Code
m_bill_hat <- 142
s_bill_adj_hat <- 30
n <- 36
SE <- s_bill_adj_hat / sqrt(n)
SE
## [1] 5

# 95% CI Manual Calculation
m_bill_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * SE
## [1] 132.2 151.8

## 95% CI Intuition
qnorm( c(0.025, 0.975), m_bill_hat, SE)
## [1] 132.2002 151.7998





The main advantages of the Normal approximation are that it

can be computed formulaically as above
works well for estimating extreme probabilities, where resampling methods tend to be worse.

The main disadvantage is that

the sampling distribution might be far from normal.

The Normal approximation is least reliable when the sample is small or the data are strongly skewed: the sampling distribution is then asymmetric, and a symmetric \(\hat{m}\pm E\) interval cannot capture that. The percentile bootstrap interval reads quantiles directly off the resampling distribution, so it can be lopsided when the data call for it. The figure below compares the percentile and Normal intervals, which are not always similar.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Bootstrap Distribution with Percentile CI
hist(boot_means, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 1.2),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
title('Percentile vs Normal 95% CIs', font.main=1)
boot_ci_percentile <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

# Normal Approximation with IID Theory SEs
classic_se <- sd(x_hat)/sqrt(length(x_hat))
x <- seq(3, 9, by=0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, m_hat, classic_se)
lines(x, fx, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)
ci_normal <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), m_hat, classic_se)
#ci_normal <- m_hat+c(-1.96, +1.96)*classic_se
abline(v=ci_normal, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Percentile', 'Normal'),
    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')









Code
# The percentile and Normal intervals are quite similar for this sample.








NoteMust Know





Here is the same comparison for the second sample, x2_hat.


Code
# x2_hat (hourly wages of the 1569 women), m2_hat, and boot_means2 defined above
c(mean=m2_hat, median=median(x2_hat))
##     mean   median 
## 5.146924 4.693262
# Hourly wages are strongly right-skewed: the median is well below the mean.

# Bootstrap Distribution with Percentile CI
hist(boot_means2, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 5.5),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
title('Percentile vs Normal 95% CIs', font.main=1)
boot_ci2_percentile <- quantile(boot_means2, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=boot_ci2_percentile, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

# Normal Approximation with IID Theory SEs
classic_se2 <- sd(x2_hat)/sqrt(length(x2_hat))
x <- seq(4.5, 5.8, by=0.005)
fx2 <- dnorm(x, m2_hat, classic_se2)
lines(x, fx2, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)
ci2_normal <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), m2_hat, classic_se2)
abline(v=ci2_normal, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Percentile', 'Normal'),
    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')









Code

# Compare the two intervals
rbind(percentile=boot_ci2_percentile, normal=ci2_normal)
##                2.5%    97.5%
## percentile 5.007022 5.289265
## normal     5.004605 5.289242
# With 1569 women, the bootstrap distribution of the mean is close to Normal.
# So the two intervals nearly coincide, even though wages are skewed.


The Normal approximation needs the sampling distribution of the mean to be close to Normal, not the data themselves. Skewed data are mainly a problem when the sample is also small.

Note that you can also plug in Bootstrap or Jackknife SEs to the Normal Approximation.


Code
## Bootstrap Distribution

    main=NA, border=NA,

    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')









Update the example to use se_boot <- sd(boot_means) in place of se_jack

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
7.3 Theoretical Properties
A \(Z\%\) confidence interval for the mean is an interval where \(Z\%\) of the intervals generated on different samples will contain the population mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\). As in Sampling, pretend the full dataset that the lab sample came from is the whole population, so we know the population mean. We draw \(100\) samples of \(n=30\) observations, compute a \(90\%\) Normal confidence interval for each, and check which intervals contain the population mean.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# population_wages, the pretend population, defined above
population_wage_mean <- mean(population_wages)

n <- 30
n_samples <- 100
sample_CIs <- matrix(nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
for(i in seq(1, n_samples)){
    # Random sample of workers
    x_sim <- sample(population_wages, n, replace=FALSE)
    # Confidence Interval for each sample
    m_sim_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    SE <- sd(x_sim)/sqrt(n)
    CI <- qnorm( c(0.05, 0.95), m_sim_hat, SE)
    sample_CIs[i, ] <- CI
}

# Explicit calculation: whether the population mean is in each CI
covered <- population_wage_mean >= sample_CIs[, 1] & population_wage_mean <= sample_CIs[, 2]
sum(covered) # number of intervals that contain the population mean
## [1] 89
# The count is typically a bit below 90.
# Wages are right-skewed, so with n=30 the Normal approximation is not exact.
# The long-run coverage of this procedure is about 88%, not 90%.

# Visualize confidence intervals
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = range(sample_CIs), ylim = c(0, n_samples))
for(i in seq(1, n_samples) ) {
  col_i <- if (covered[i]) rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3) else rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5)
  segments(
    sample_CIs[i, 1], i,
    sample_CIs[i, 2], i,
    col = col_i, lwd = 2)
}
abline(v = population_wage_mean, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 2)
axis(1)
title('90% Coverage (Red = Missed)', font.main=1)









When the data are skewed and the sample is small, the Normal approximation is not exact, so the long-run coverage can fall below the chosen level.






NoteMust Know





Here is the same coverage check for uniform random data, where the true mean is \(0.5\).


Code
n <- 30
n_samples <- 100
sample_CIs <- matrix(nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
for(i in seq(1, n_samples)){
    # Random Sample
    x_sim <- runif(n)
    # Confidence Interval for each sample
    m_sim_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    SE <- sd(x_sim)/sqrt(n)
    CI <- qnorm( c(0.05, 0.95), m_sim_hat, SE)
    sample_CIs[i, ] <- CI
}


# Explicit calculation: whether the true mean is in each CI
true_mean <- 0.5 # theoretical result for uniform samples
covered <- true_mean >= sample_CIs[, 1] & true_mean <= sample_CIs[, 2]

# Visualize confidence intervals
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = range(sample_CIs), ylim = c(0, n_samples))
for(i in seq(1, n_samples) ) {
  col_i <- if (covered[i]) rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3) else rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5)
  segments(
    sample_CIs[i, 1], i,
    sample_CIs[i, 2], i,
    col = col_i, lwd = 2)
}
abline(v = true_mean, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 2)
axis(1)
title('90% Coverage (Red = Missed)', font.main=1)












We typically have only one sample and compute a single confidence interval with the data we have. The interval you computed either contains the true mean or it does not. 2 So “\(Z\%\) confident” translates to “\(Z\%\) of intervals constructed on different samples will contain \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\)”.






NoteMust Know





A confidence interval contains many values, and every one of them is a hypothesis the data cannot rule out. Suppose a \(95\%\) confidence interval for a population mean comes out as \([6.6, 9.0]\). The data are consistent with \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=7\), and also with \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=8\), and also with \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=8.9\): none of these competing values can be ruled out at the \(5\%\) level. You would, however, rule out \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=5\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=10\), since they fall outside the interval. “Failing to reject” a value is therefore a weak statement: it says only that the value is one of many still compatible with the data, not that it is correct.




Sampling Distribution Quantiles
To better understand the link between our theoretical interpretation and our calculations, we will compute the quantiles of the sampling distribution. E.g., We construct a \(90\%\) confidence interval of the mean by taking the \(5^{\text{th}}\) and \(95^{\text{th}}\) percentiles of the sampling distribution of the mean. We draw \(300\) samples of \(n=50\) observations from the population, and then construct a confidence interval using quantiles.


Code
# Create 300 samples, each with 50 workers
wage_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=50)
for(i in seq(1, nrow(wage_samples))){
    wage_samples[i, ] <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
}
wage_means <- apply(wage_samples, 1, mean) # mean for each sample (row)

# Middle 90%
mq <- quantile(wage_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the mean is between ', 
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the mean is between 5.07 and 6.5"

hist(wage_means,
    breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.1),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=population_wage_mean, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)















NoteMust Know





Here is the same calculation for \(300\) uniform random samples of size \(n=1000\).


Code
# Create 300 samples, each with 1000 random uniform variables
X_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=1000)
for(i in seq(1, nrow(X_samples))){
    X_samples[i, ] <- runif(1000)
}
sample_means <- apply(X_samples, 1, mean) # mean for each sample (row)

# Middle 90%
mq <- quantile(sample_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the mean is between ',
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the mean is between 0.49 and 0.51"
# The interval runs from about 0.486 to 0.515, a width of about 0.03.

hist(sample_means,
    breaks=seq(.4, .6, by=.001),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)


















TipTest Yourself





For another example, consider the median. We now repeat the above process to estimate the median for each sample, instead of the mean.


Code
## Sample Quantiles (medians)
sample_quants <- apply(wage_samples, 1, quantile, probs=0.5) #quantile for each sample (row)

# Middle 90% of estimates
mq <- quantile(sample_quants, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the median is between ', 
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the median is between 4.56 and 6.11"

hist(sample_quants,
    breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.1),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Median', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)














Interval Size
Confidence intervals shrink with more data, as averaging washes out random fluctuations.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Create 300 samples of workers, each of size n
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for(n in c(25, 100, 250)){
    # Draw 300 samples
    wage_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=n)
    for(i in seq(1, nrow(wage_samples))){
        wage_samples[i, ] <- sample(population_wages, n, replace=FALSE)
    }

    # Compute means for each sample (row)
    wage_means <- apply(wage_samples, 1, mean)
    # 90% Confidence Interval
    mq <- quantile(wage_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
    hist(wage_means,
        breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.05),
        border=NA, freq=FALSE,
        main=NA)
    title(paste0('n=', n), font.main=1)
    abline(v=mq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
}















NoteMust Know





Here is the same comparison for uniform random samples.


Code
# Create 300 samples, each of size n
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for(n in c(25, 100, 250)){
    # Simulate 300 samples
    X_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=n)
    for(i in seq(1, nrow(X_samples))){
        X_samples[i, ] <- runif(n)
    }

    # Compute means for each sample (row)
    sample_means <- apply(X_samples, 1, mean)
    # 90% Confidence Interval
    mq <- quantile(sample_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
    hist(sample_means,
        breaks=seq(.1, .9, by=.005),
        border=NA, freq=FALSE,
        main=NA)
    title(paste0('n=', n), font.main=1)
    abline(v=mq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
}












Confidence intervals also shrink with lower probabilities of containing the theoretical value. For a fixed sample size \(n\), there is a trade-off between precision: the width of a confidence interval, and accuracy: the probability that a confidence interval contains the theoretical value.






TipTest Yourself





Here is an example showing what a Normal CI estimates. Theoretically, \(\pm 1 \cdot \text{SE}(M)\) has 2/3 coverage. Change to \(\pm 2 \cdot \text{SE}(M)\) to see Precision-Accuracy tradeoff.


Code
# Normal CI for each sample
# Uses the last wage_samples above (n=250)
xq <- apply(wage_samples, 1, function(x_row_hat){ #theoretical se's
    mean(x_row_hat) + c(-1, 1)*sd(x_row_hat)/sqrt(length(x_row_hat))
})
# First 3 interval estimates
xq[, c(1, 2, 3)]
##          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
## [1,] 5.386284 5.803504 5.227066
## [2,] 5.762652 6.249468 5.671207

# Explicit calculation
# Logical vector: whether the population mean is in each CI
covered <- population_wage_mean >= xq[1, ] & population_wage_mean <= xq[2, ]
# Empirical coverage rate
coverage_rate <- mean(covered)
cat(sprintf('Estimated coverage probability: %.2f%%\n', 100 * coverage_rate))
## Estimated coverage probability: 72.00%

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
7.4 Misc. Topics

Prediction Intervals
Sometimes we want to know what range a single new observation will likely fall in.






ImportantKey Definition





A prediction interval is a range that aims to contain a future single observation, not a statistic. We compute it from the lower and upper quantiles of the data themselves, so its width reflects the spread of individual observations rather than the spread of a sampling distribution.



Prediction intervals are useful when a decision depends on individual outcomes. For example, a firm may want to forecast whether a single warranty claim will fall in a tolerable range. Note that \(Z\%\) confidence intervals do not generally cover \(Z\%\) of the data. Compare the \(90\%\) bootstrap confidence interval for the mean with the middle \(90\%\) of the observations themselves.


Code
# 90% CI for the mean, from the bootstrap distribution above
boot_ci_90 <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
boot_ci_90
##       5%      95% 
## 5.086016 6.335946
# Share of sampled workers with a wage inside the CI for the mean
mean(x_hat >= boot_ci_90[1] & x_hat <= boot_ci_90[2])
## [1] 0.14
# Only about 14% of these workers have a wage in the CI, roughly [5.09, 6.34].

# Middle 90% of values: prediction interval
xq <- quantile(x_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between ',
    round(xq[1], 2), ' and ', round(xq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between 1.79 and 10.75"
# The prediction interval, roughly [1.79, 10.75], is much wider than that CI.

hist(x_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 16, by=1), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
rug(x_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
title('Prediction Interval vs CI for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=boot_ci_90, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Prediction interval', 'CI for the mean'),
    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')









The prediction interval is much wider because it reflects the spread of individual observations rather than the spread of the sample mean.






NoteMust Know





Here is the same comparison for the second sample, x2_hat.


Code
# x2_hat (hourly wages of the 1569 women), m2_hat, and boot_means2 defined above
# 90% CI for the mean
boot_ci2_90 <- quantile(boot_means2, probs=c(.05, .95))
boot_ci2_90
##       5%      95% 
## 5.027807 5.263843
# Share of women with a wage inside the CI for the mean
mean(x2_hat >= boot_ci2_90[1] & x2_hat <= boot_ci2_90[2])
## [1] 0.03696622
# Only about 4% of women earn a wage inside the CI, roughly [5.03, 5.26].

# Middle 90% of values: prediction interval
xq2 <- quantile(x2_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
xq2
##        5%       95% 
##  1.508883 10.105341
# The prediction interval is roughly [1.51, 10.11].

# Distance from the mean to each end of the prediction interval
c(below=m2_hat - xq2[[1]], above=xq2[[2]] - m2_hat)
##    below    above 
## 3.638041 4.958417
# It reaches about 3.64 dollars below the mean but 4.96 above it.
# It is not centered on the mean because wages are right-skewed.

hist(x2_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 40, by=.5), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
title('Prediction Interval vs CI for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=boot_ci2_90, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Prediction interval', 'CI for the mean'),
    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')









When the data are skewed, a prediction interval is also not centered on the mean.









TipTest Yourself





Repeat the comparison with the murder arrest rates in x3_hat.


Code
# x3_hat and boot_means3 defined above
# 90% CI for the mean, from the bootstrap distribution above
boot_ci3_90 <- quantile(boot_means3, probs=c(.05, .95))
boot_ci3_90
##     5%    95% 
## 6.8098 8.7760
# Share of states with a murder rate inside the CI for the mean
mean(x3_hat >= boot_ci3_90[1] & x3_hat <= boot_ci3_90[2])
## [1] 0.12
# Only about 12% of states have a murder rate inside the CI, roughly [6.8, 8.8].

# Middle 90% of values: prediction interval
xq3 <- quantile(x3_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between ',
    round(xq3[1], 2), ' and ', round(xq3[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between 2.14 and 15.4"
# The prediction interval, roughly [2.1, 15.4], is much wider than that CI.
# It reflects the spread of individual states, not of the sample mean.

hist(x3_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 20, by=1), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Murder arrests per 100,000')
rug(x3_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
title('Prediction Interval vs CI for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq3, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=boot_ci3_90, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Prediction interval', 'CI for the mean'),
    lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), bty='n')


















NoteMust Know





For uniform random data, the \(90\%\) confidence interval for the mean from the quantile example above theoretically covers far less than \(0.9\) of the data.


Code
x_future_hat <- runif(1000)
# Middle 90% of values
xq0 <- quantile(x_future_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that a future data point will be between ',
    round(xq0[1], 2), ' and ', round(xq0[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that a future data point will be between 0.04 and 0.96"
# By contrast, the 90% CI for the mean above has a width of about 0.03.
# So it theoretically covers only about 0.03 of the data.

hist(x_future_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 1, by=.05), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA)
rug(x_future_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
title('Prediction Interval', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq0, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)














One-Sided Intervals
Above, our confidence intervals were two-sided: they contained the middle \(Z\%\) of the sampling distribution. We can also construct one-sided intervals that extend to infinity in one direction.
A one-sided interval is shifted to one side, containing one tail rather than the middle. For example, an upper-bounded interval uses \((-\infty, q_{0.95}]\), where \(q_{0.95}\) is the \(95^{\text{th}}\) percentile of the bootstrap distribution: we are \(95\%\) confident the true value is at most \(q_{0.95}\). A lower-bounded interval uses \([q_{0.05}, \infty)\), where \(q_{0.05}\) is the \(5^{\text{th}}\) percentile of the bootstrap distribution: we are \(95\%\) confident the true value is at least \(q_{0.05}\).






TipTest Yourself





For the electricity bill example above with \(\hat{m}=142\) and \(\text{SE}=5\), a one-sided \(95\%\) upper-bounded confidence interval is \[(-\infty,~ \hat{m} + 1.645 \times \text{SE}] = (-\infty,~ 142 + 1.645 \times 5] = (-\infty,~ 150.2].\] We are \(95\%\) confident the population mean bill is at most \(\$150.20\). Note that \(1.645\) is the \(95^{\text{th}}\) percentile of the standard normal (compared to \(1.96\) for the two-sided case).


Code
m_bill_hat <- 142
SE <- 5
# One-sided 95% upper bound
m_bill_hat + qnorm(0.95) * SE
## [1] 150.2243











TipTest Yourself





Here is a bootstrap right-tail example


Code
# Bootstrap Distribution
boot_means <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means[b] <-m_b_hat
}

# One-sided 95% lower bound
# We are 95% confident the mean is at least q_05
hist(boot_means, border=NA, breaks=50,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap')
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(0.05, 1) )
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

7.5 Exercises

Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.

Compute the 90% and 99% Normal-approximation confidence intervals for the population mean lifetime. Which interval is wider, and why?
