Further Reading

https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/estimation.html#interval-estimates – Confidence intervals explained with intuition and R code.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/confidence-intervals-one-sample – Video walkthroughs of confidence interval construction and interpretation.
https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/3.1-hypothesis-tests-and-confidence-intervals-in-the-simple-linear-regression-model.html – Confidence intervals applied to regression, bridging descriptive and inferential statistics.



Recall
We built confidence intervals in two ways, with the bootstrap percentile method and the Normal approximation. Being “\(Z\%\) confident” means that \(Z\%\) of intervals built on different samples will contain the true value. For a fixed sample size, there is a trade-off between precision and accuracy. In the electricity-bill example, \(\hat{m}=142\), \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}=30\), and \(n=36\). The classical standard error is \(\text{SE}(M) = 30/\sqrt{36} = 5\). The \(95\%\) margin of error is \(E = 1.96 \times 5 = 9.8\), giving a confidence interval of \([\$132.20, \$151.80]\).

title: 7  Confidence Intervals
text:
Generally, a coverage level of \(1-\alpha\) means \(\text{Prob}( M - E < \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] < M + E)=1-\alpha\). Notice that \(\text{Prob}( M - E < \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] < M + E) = \text{Prob}( - E < \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] - M < + E) = \text{Prob}( \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] + E > M > \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] - E)\). So if the interval \([\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] - 10, \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] + 10]\) contains \(95\%\) of all \(M\), then the interval \([M-10, M+10]\) will also contain \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) in \(95\%\) of the samples. This is because whenever \(M\) is within \(10\) of \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), the value \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) is also within \(10\) of \(M\). But for any particular sample, the interval \([\hat{m}-10, \hat{m}+10]\) either does or does not contain \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\). Similarly, if you compute \(\hat{m}=9\) for your particular sample, a coverage level of \(1-\alpha=95\%\) does not mean \(\text{Prob}(9 - E < \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] < 9 + E)=95\%\).↩︎
As such, a \(Z\%\) confidence interval does not imply a \(Z\%\) probability that the true parameter lies within a particular calculated interval. In practice, people often interpret confidence intervals informally as “showing the uncertainty around our estimate”: wider intervals correspond to higher sampling variability and less precise information about \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\).↩︎

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
8.1 Testing Methods
A hypothesis test turns a question about the population into a decision: given the data, do we have enough evidence to reject a specific value for the parameter?
This chapter asks three questions.
In this chapter, we test hypotheses using data-driven methods that assume much less about the data generating process. There are two main ways to conduct a hypothesis test: inverting a confidence interval and imposing the null. The first treats the distribution of estimates directly; the second explicitly enforces the null hypothesis to evaluate how unusual the observed statistic is. Both approaches rely on the bootstrap to approximate sampling variability.
Before either test can run, we have to name the claim being tested and the alternative we would favor if the data spoke against it (Neyman and Pearson 1933).
This setup is useful because the test only ever asks about \(H_{0}\). Either the data contradict \(H_{0}\) enough to reject it, or they do not. The data never “prove” \(H_{A}\). The most common test concerns the mean, \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0}\), where \(m_{0}\) is a hypothesized value. The two-sided alternative is \(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] \neq m_{0}\). E.g., you hypothesize your stock returns have earnings \(m_{0}=0\) and consider that the returns could truly be either positive or negative.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
ImportantKey Definition





The null hypothesis \(H_{0}\) is the specific claim about the parameter that we will test.
The alternative hypothesis \(H_{A}\) is the competing claim.
A two-sided hypothesis test covers deviations from the null in either direction (alternative values are higher or lower than the null).





Choosing a Null
Where does a hypothesized value like \(m_{0}\) come from? It comes from outside the sample, and it is best written down before looking at the data. Common sources include

a claim someone else makes that you want to check, such as a firm’s advertised battery life
an economic theory, such as the efficient markets hypothesis, which predicts that the average return of a trading strategy, minus the market’s return, is zero
a policy target or legal standard, such as a central bank’s \(2\%\) inflation target
an earlier value, such as last year’s average wage
“no effect” or “no change”, such as a mean change in store sales of zero after a new layout, which is the most common null in practice

For example, Adamson and Kimbrough (2023) and Adamson and Wilson (2024) test whether the estimates from their laboratory experiments equal the values an economic model predicts, rather than zero (Lehmann and Romano 2005).
A null chosen after seeing the data is circular: you could always pick a value that the data already contradict and then reject it.
Whatever its source, the null makes a specific claim, such as a single value for the mean. Because the claim is specific, we can compute how the statistic would vary if the null were true. The alternative covers a whole range of values, so there is no single sampling distribution to compute under it. This is also why the claim you hope to support usually goes in \(H_{A}\): the only strong conclusion a test can deliver is to reject \(H_{0}\).


Invert a CI
One way to test a hypothesis is to look at whether a confidence interval contains the hypothesized value: if the value lies outside the interval, sampling variability alone cannot easily explain the gap.






ImportantKey Definition





The rejection region is the set of values for the test statistic (or hypothesized parameter) that lead us to reject \(H_{0}\). For a two-sided test at level \(\alpha=0.05\), the rejection region is the two tails outside the central \(95\%\) of the null distribution.



The rejection region is useful as a decision rule that mirrors how we read a confidence interval:

reject \(H_{0}\) if the hypothesized value falls outside the interval (it is in the rejection region)
fail to reject \(H_{0}\) if it falls inside

A \(95\%\) confidence interval corresponds to a \(5\%\) rejection region split between the two tails. So a test at level \(\alpha\) uses an interval with coverage \(1-\alpha\). See the previous Confidence Intervals chapter for how the interval is computed.
For example, suppose you hypothesize the mean equals \(m_{0}\). You then construct a bootstrap distribution with \(95\%\) confidence interval, and find your hypothesized value falls outside of the confidence interval. Then, after accounting for sampling variability (which you estimate), it still seems extremely unlikely that the theoretical mean actually equals \(m_{0}\), so you reject that hypothesis. (If the theoretical value landed in the interval, you would “fail to reject” the theoretical mean equals \(m_{0}\).)


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Pretend these 3294 hourly wages are the whole population
# Source: US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_wages <- Wages1[, 'wage']

# Lab data: one random sample of 50 workers, as if it were all we observed
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
x_hat <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
m_hat <- mean(x_hat)
m_hat
## [1] 5.708014
# The sample mean is about 5.71 dollars an hour.

# Bootstrap Distribution
n <- length(x_hat)
boot_means <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means[b] <- m_b_hat
}

hist(boot_means, breaks=25,
    border=NA,
    freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Bootstrap Samples')
# CI
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
# H0: mean=6.5
abline(v=6.5, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The 95% interval runs from about 4.93 to 6.47 dollars an hour.
# The hypothesized 6.5 falls just above it, so we reject this null.
# The population mean is about 5.76, so this null is in fact false.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat this test with the murder arrest rates in USArrests, for the hypothesized mean of \(9\) arrests per \(100{,}000\).


Code
x2_hat <- USArrests[, 'Murder'] # murder arrests per 100,000
m2_hat <- mean(x2_hat)
m2_hat
## [1] 7.788

# Bootstrap Distribution
n2 <- length(x2_hat)
boot_means2 <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means2)){
    x_boot <- sample(x2_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means2[b] <- m_b_hat
}

hist(boot_means2, breaks=25,
    border=NA,
    freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Bootstrap Samples')
# CI
ci2_95 <- quantile(boot_means2, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=ci2_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
# H0: mean=9
abline(v=9, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The hypothesized 9 falls just above the 95% interval, so we reject it.











TipTest Yourself





The above procedure also generalizes to many other statistics. Perhaps the most informative are those for spread or shape. E.g., you can conduct hypothesis tests for sd and IQR, or skew and kurtosis.


Code
# Bootstrap Distribution for SD
s_adj_hat <- sd(x_hat)
boot_sds <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_sds)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
    s_adj_b_hat <- sd(x_boot)
    boot_sds[b] <- s_adj_b_hat
}

# Test for SD Differences (Invert CI)
sd_null <- 2.2
hist(boot_sds, freq=FALSE, breaks=50,
    border=NA, xlab='Bootstrap',
    main=NA)
title('Standard Deviations (Invert CI)', font.main=1)
sd_ci <- quantile(boot_sds, probs=c(0.025, .975) )
abline(v=sd_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=sd_null, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The hypothesized 2.2 falls just below the 95% interval, so we reject it.


To better your understanding, try redoing the above for any function (such as IQR(x_boot)/median(x_boot))









NoteMust Know





Suppose a student scores \(77\%\) on a \(44\)-question multiple-choice exam but believes they are really an \(85\%\) student who had a bad day. The professor is skeptical: “where’s your evidence?” The student bootstraps a confidence interval for their “true” proportion correct, resampling from the \(44\) right/wrong answers on that one exam.
This creates a conundrum. If the confidence interval comes out narrow, it may exclude \(85\%\), and the \(85\%\) hypothesis is rejected. But an interval wide enough to contain \(85\%\) is also wide enough to contain \(70\%\), so the same evidence fails to rule out a worse student who simply got lucky. A single exam cannot easily distinguish the two stories.
We compute the student’s interval and mark both \(70\%\) and \(85\%\) on it.


Code
# One exam: 34 correct out of 44 questions
n_questions <- 44
n_correct <- 34
outcomes <- c(rep(1, n_correct), rep(0, n_questions - n_correct)) # 1=correct, 0=incorrect

# Bootstrap Distribution for the proportion correct
boot_props <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_props)){
    x_boot <- sample(outcomes, replace=TRUE)
    boot_props[b] <- mean(x_boot)
}

hist(boot_props, breaks=25,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap Proportion Correct')
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_props, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=c(.70, .85), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The 95% interval runs from about 0.64 to 0.89.
# It comfortably contains both 0.70 and 0.85.
# So the student can reject neither story.


The deeper issue is what the bootstrap resample actually represents. Resampling only reshuffles the same \(44\) questions, so it approximates how the score would vary if the student retook that exact exam. It says nothing about how the student would do on a different exam with different questions. The student needs that sampling distribution to make their case. Estimating that sampling distribution properly needs new, independent samples: more exams, not more resamples of one exam, and that is a cost the student is unlikely to accept for the rest of the semester.





Impose the Null
We can also compute a null distribution: the sampling distribution of the statistic under the null hypothesis (assuming your null hypothesis was true). We use the bootstrap to loop through a large number of “resamples”. In each iteration of the loop, we impose the null hypothesis and re-estimate the statistic of interest. We then calculate the range of the statistic across all resamples and compare how extreme the original value we observed is.
For example, suppose you again hypothesize the mean equals \(m_{0}\). You then construct a \(95\%\) confidence interval around the null bootstrap distribution (resamples centered around \(m_{0}\)). Suppose your sample mean falls outside of that interval. Then even after accounting for sampling variability (which you estimate), it seems extremely unlikely that the theoretical mean actually equals \(m_{0}\), so you reject that hypothesis. (If the sample mean landed in the interval, you would “fail to reject” the theoretical mean equals \(m_{0}\).)


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
m_hat <- mean(x_hat)

# Bootstrap NULL: mean=6.5
# Bootstrap shift: center each bootstrap resample so that the distribution satisfies the null hypothesis on average.
null_mean <- 6.5
boot_means_null <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means_null)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot) + (null_mean - m_hat) # impose the null via Bootstrap shift
    boot_means_null[b] <- m_b_hat
}
hist(boot_means_null, breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Null Bootstrap Samples')
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_means_null, probs=c(.025, .975)) # critical region
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=m_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code
# The middle 95% of the null distribution runs from about 5.79 to 7.23.
# The sample mean of about 5.71 falls just below it, so we reject this null.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat this test with the murder arrest rates in USArrests, again for the hypothesized mean of \(9\).


Code
x2_hat <- USArrests[, 'Murder'] # murder arrests per 100,000
m2_hat <- mean(x2_hat)

# Bootstrap NULL: mean=9
# Bootstrap shift: center each bootstrap resample so that the distribution satisfies the null hypothesis on average.
null_mean2 <- 9
boot_means_null2 <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means_null2)){
    x_boot <- sample(x2_hat, replace=TRUE)
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot) + (null_mean2 - m2_hat) # impose the null via Bootstrap shift
    boot_means_null2[b] <- m_b_hat
}
hist(boot_means_null2, breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Null Bootstrap Samples')
ci2_95 <- quantile(boot_means_null2, probs=c(.025, .975)) # critical region
abline(v=ci2_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=m2_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code
# The sample mean falls just below the middle 95%, so we reject a mean of 9.











NoteMust Know





Why does adding \((m_{0} - \hat{m})\) impose the null? A bootstrap resample of the data has a mean that varies around the sample mean \(\hat{m}\), not around the hypothesized \(m_{0}\). Adding the constant \((m_{0} - \hat{m})\) slides the whole resampling distribution over so it is centered at \(m_{0}\) instead. A shift moves the center but leaves the spread and shape unchanged, so the result is a sampling distribution with the null mean and the same variability as the data.
For example, take the three observations \(\{2, 4, 9\}\), which have mean \(\hat{m}=5\), and the null \(m_{0}=6\). Adding \(m_{0}-\hat{m}=1\) to every observation gives \(\{3, 5, 10\}\), which has mean \(6\) and the same spread.


Code
x0_hat <- c(2, 4, 9)
m0_hat <- mean(x0_hat)
x0_null <- x0_hat + (6 - m0_hat) # shift so the mean equals 6
x0_null
## [1]  3  5 10
c(mean(x0_null), sd(x0_hat), sd(x0_null))
## [1] 6.000000 3.605551 3.605551





The Normal approximation from the previous chapter can also impose the null: center the interval at the hypothesized value \(m_{0}\) and use \(m_{0} \pm q(\alpha/2) \cdot \text{SE}(M)\), where \(\text{SE}(M)\) is estimated via bootstrap or classical formulas. (While we could also use a Null Jackknife distribution, that is rarely done in practice.) Altogether, there are two different types of confidence intervals that “impose the null”. Until you know more, a conservative rule-of-thumb is to take the larger estimate.

Types of Confidence Interval Estimates that “impose the null”






Interval
Mechanism




Bootstrap (Percentile)
randomly resample \(n\) observations with replacement and shift


Normal
assume sampling distribution is Normal and use formula \(\pm q(\alpha/2) \cdot \text{SE}\)

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
8.2 \(p\)-values
Reading a hypothesis test off a confidence interval is binary (reject or not); often we also want a number that describes how extreme the observed statistic is relative to the null.






ImportantKey Definition





The \(p\)-value is the probability, under the null hypothesis, of seeing a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. Small \(p\)-values give evidence against the null; the threshold \(p \leq 0.05\) is a convention, not a law of nature. The \(p\)-value is not the probability that the null is true.



The \(p\)-value is useful as a continuous summary of how strongly the data oppose the null, whereas a confidence interval gives only a yes/no answer at a fixed coverage level. For the running mean example, we want the probability that the random variable \(M\) is at least as extreme (far from the null mean \(m_{0}\)) as our observed sample mean \(\hat{m}\).
Recall that we used the bootstrap to estimate the distribution of the sample statistic like the mean, and the null-bootstrap shifted the bootstrap to be centered at a hypothesized value. The bootstrap idea here is to approximate \(M-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), the difference between the sample mean \(M\) and the unknown theoretical mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), with \(M^{\text{boot}}-\hat{m}\). To test \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=m_{0}\), we recenter the bootstrap mean as \(M^{\text{boot}}_{0}=M^{\text{boot}}+(m_{0}-\hat{m})\), so \(M^{\text{boot}}_{0}-m_{0}=M^{\text{boot}}-\hat{m}\). The two-sided \(p\)-value is then \[\begin{aligned}
&  \text{Prob}( |M - m_{0}| \geq |\hat{m} - m_{0}| \mid \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0} ) \\
&  \approx \text{Prob}( |M^{\text{boot}}_{0}- m_{0}| \geq |\hat{m}- m_{0}| ) \\
&  = 1-\hat{F}^{|\text{boot}|}_{0}(|\hat{m}-m_{0}|),
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{F}^{|\text{boot}|}_{0}\) is the ECDF of \(|M^{\text{boot}}_{0}- m_{0}|\).
Using the null bootstrap distribution boot_means_null from above, we compute the two-sided \(p\)-value for the lab data.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Two-Sided Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean < 6.5 or mean > 6.5
# Visualize Two Sided Prob. & reject region boundary
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(boot_means_null-null_mean,
    freq=FALSE, breaks=25,
    border=NA,
    main=NA,
    xlab=expression('Null Bootstrap for M - '~m[0]))
abline(v=m_hat-null_mean, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_means_null-null_mean, probs=c(0.025, .975))
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

# Equivalent Visualization
boot_absval <- abs(boot_means_null-null_mean)
F_hat <- ecdf(boot_absval)
plot(F_hat,
    main=NA,
    xlab=expression('Null Bootstrap for |M - '~m[0]~'|'))
abline(v=abs(m_hat-null_mean), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
# with Two Sided Probability
p2 <- 1 - F_hat( abs(m_hat-null_mean) )
title( paste0('p=', round(p2, 3)), font.main=1)









Code
# The two-sided p-value is about 0.03, below the 5% level.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the two-sided \(p\)-value with the murder arrest rates, using boot_means_null2 from the Test Yourself in Impose the Null.


Code
# Two-Sided Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean < 9 or mean > 9
# Visualize Two Sided Prob. & reject region boundary
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(boot_means_null2-null_mean2,
    freq=FALSE, breaks=25,
    border=NA,
    main=NA,
    xlab=expression('Null Bootstrap for M - '~m[0]))
abline(v=m2_hat-null_mean2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
ci2_95 <- quantile(boot_means_null2-null_mean2, probs=c(0.025, .975))
abline(v=ci2_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

# Equivalent Visualization
boot_absval2 <- abs(boot_means_null2-null_mean2)
F2_hat <- ecdf(boot_absval2)
plot(F2_hat,
    main=NA,
    xlab=expression('Null Bootstrap for |M - '~m[0]~'|'))
abline(v=abs(m2_hat-null_mean2), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
# with Two Sided Probability
p2_2 <- 1 - F2_hat( abs(m2_hat-null_mean2) )
title( paste0('p=', round(p2_2, 3)), font.main=1)









Code
# The two-sided p-value is about 0.045, just below the 5% level.











NoteMust Know





Continuing the exam example from above: the student scored \(\hat{p}=34/44 \approx 77\%\) and wants to test \(H_{0}: p=0.85\). Imposing the null shifts the bootstrap distribution of the proportion correct so that it is centered at \(0.85\) instead of at \(\hat{p}\), exactly as was done for the mean.


Code
n_questions <- 44
n_correct <- 34
outcomes <- c(rep(1, n_correct), rep(0, n_questions - n_correct))
p_hat <- mean(outcomes)

# Bootstrap NULL: p=0.85
# Bootstrap shift: center each bootstrap resample so that the distribution satisfies the null hypothesis on average.
p0 <- 0.85
boot_props_null <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_props_null)){
    x_boot <- sample(outcomes, replace=TRUE)
    boot_props_null[b] <- mean(x_boot) + (p0 - p_hat) # impose the null via Bootstrap shift
}

# Two-Sided p-value
boot_absval <- abs(boot_props_null - p0)
F_hat <- ecdf(boot_absval)
p2_exam <- 1 - F_hat( abs(p_hat - p0) )

hist(boot_props_null, breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Null Bootstrap Proportion (H0: p=0.85)')
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_props_null, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=p_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
title( paste0('p=', round(p2_exam, 3)), font.main=1)









Code
# The two-sided p-value is about 0.20, far above the 5% level.
# So we fail to reject p=0.85, which matches the interval above.


Compared with an interval, the \(p\)-value adds a precise number for how strong or weak the evidence against the null is, rather than just a reject/fail-to-reject label.
The other story, \(H_{0}: p=0.70\), can be tested the same way.


Code
# Impose p=0.70 instead, by shifting the same resamples
p0_low <- 0.70
boot_props_null_low <- boot_props_null + (p0_low - p0)

# Two-Sided p-value
1 - ecdf( abs(boot_props_null_low-p0_low) )( abs(p_hat-p0_low) )
## [1] 0.2012012
# The p-value is again about 0.20, so we also fail to reject p=0.70.
# The two nulls are nearly equally far from p_hat, so their p-values match.
# The p-value is large in both directions, so neither story is ruled out.


A single \(44\)-question exam simply cannot pin down the student’s true ability closely enough to rule out either story.



You can conduct a hypothesis test using \(p\)-values instead of confidence intervals. It is common to use this decision rule:

reject the null at the \(5\%\) level if \(p \leq 0.05\)
fail to reject the null at the \(5\%\) level if \(p > 0.05\)


Caveats
Beware of a common misreading of the \(p\)-value as “the probability the null is true”. That is false. A \(p\)-value is the frequency you see something at least as extreme as your statistic under the null hypothesis.
Failing to reject \(H_{0}\) does not show that \(H_{0}\) is true (Altman and Bland 1995; Abadie 2020). The exam example above is a case in point, because the student’s true score cannot be both \(70\%\) and \(85\%\). A large \(p\)-value can simply mean that the sample is too small to tell nearby values apart. This is one reason why we say “fail to reject” rather than “accept”. Another reason is that we can “fail to reject” multiple different hypotheses, and “accepting” them all would be nonsense. E.g., we cannot accept the mean is both \(4\) and \(2\) even if both fall inside of a confidence interval. Adamson (2025) makes this point about earlier work that “ruled out” trade because a proxy for trade was statistically insignificant. As the paper puts it, “the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.”
Often, one may also see or hear “\(p<.05\): statistically significant” and “\(p>.05\): not statistically significant”. That is decision making on purely statistical grounds, and it may or may not be suitable for your context. You simply need to know that whoever says those things is using \(5\%\) as a critical value to reject a null hypothesis.
A rejection also does not mean the null is far from the truth (McCloskey and Ziliak 1996; Wasserstein and Lazar 2016; Imbens 2021).
Running many hypothesis tests inflates the chance of a false rejection. At the \(5\%\) level, you expect roughly \(1\) in \(20\) true nulls to be rejected by chance alone, so if you test \(20\) independent nulls and find \(1\) “significant” result, that result is what you would expect even when every null is true. The fix is to correct the level (e.g., Bonferroni (1936): use \(0.05/k\) when running \(k\) tests) or to pre-specify a small set of hypotheses before looking at the data.


Code
# Purely-Statistical Decision Making
# via Two Sided Test
if(p2 >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=6.5, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of either <6.5 or >6.5, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of either <6.5 or >6.5, at the 5% level"


Also note that the \(p\)-value is itself a function of data, and hence a random variable that changes from sample to sample. To see this, return to the pretend population from Sampling. We know its mean, so we can draw many samples and test the null that is actually true.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Known population mean, from the pretend population defined above
population_wage_mean <- mean(population_wages)

# 300 samples, each tested against the true mean
p_values <- rep(NA, 300)
for(s in seq_along(p_values)){
    x_sim <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
    m_sim <- mean(x_sim)
    boot_means_null_sim <- rep(NA, 999)
    for(b in seq_along(boot_means_null_sim)){
        x_boot <- sample(x_sim, replace=TRUE)
        boot_means_null_sim[b] <- mean(x_boot) + (population_wage_mean - m_sim) # impose the (true) null
    }
    F_hat <- ecdf( abs(boot_means_null_sim-population_wage_mean) )
    p_values[s] <- 1 - F_hat( abs(m_sim-population_wage_mean) )
}

hist(p_values, breaks=seq(0, 1, by=.05),
    freq=FALSE, border=NA, main=NA,
    xlab='p-values when the null is true')
abline(v=.05, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# Share of samples that falsely reject at the 5% level
mean(p_values <= .05)
## [1] 0.05333333
# About 5% of these samples still reject at the 5% level.
# These are the false rejections described above.


The null is true in every one of these samples, yet the \(p\)-values spread across the whole range from \(0\) to \(1\). Given that the \(5\%\) level is somewhat arbitrary, and that the \(p\)-value both varies from sample to sample and is often misunderstood, it makes sense to give specific \(p\)-values a limited role in decision making.






NoteMust Know





The \(p\)-value also varies a little each time you rerun the bootstrap on the same data, because each run draws different resamples. This variation comes from the computer, not from the sample, and it shrinks as you use more resamples. Here we repeat the two-sided test \(300\) times on the one sample we have.


Code
p_values_boot <- rep(NA, 300)
for(b2 in seq(p_values_boot)){
    boot_means_null_p <- rep(NA, 999)
    for(b in seq_along(boot_means_null_p)){
        x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
        m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot) + (null_mean - m_hat) # impose the null
        boot_means_null_p[b] <- m_b_hat
    }
    F_hat <- ecdf( abs(boot_means_null_p-null_mean) )
    p_values_boot[b2] <- 1- F_hat( abs(m_hat-null_mean) )
}

hist(p_values_boot, freq=FALSE, breaks=50,
    border=NA, main=NA)
abline(v=.05, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code
# The p-values run from about 0.02 to 0.06, so they land on both sides of 0.05.
# Rerunning the bootstrap alone could flip this decision.


When the \(p\)-value is close to the cutoff, rerunning the bootstrap alone could flip the decision. This is one more reason not to lean on the exact \(5\%\) cutoff.

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
8.3 Other Statistics

\(t\)-values
Different studies have different \(\text{SE}(M)\), so the raw difference \(\hat{m} - m_{0}\) is hard to compare across studies; we need to express the deviation in standard-error units.






ImportantKey Definition





The \(t\)-value (or \(t\)-statistic) standardizes the deviation of \(\hat{m}\) from the hypothesized \(m_{0}\) by the standard error, \[t = \frac{M - m_{0}}{\text{SE}(M)}.\] Using a standardized statistic makes results comparable across studies and connects to a well-studied reference distribution (Normal in large samples, Student’s \(t\) in small).



The \(t\)-value is useful as a test statistic that does not depend on units. The units cancel between the numerator and the denominator. So a given \(t\)-value means roughly the same thing whether the data are measured in dollars or hours. For any specific sample we must approximate the standard error. Using the theory-driven approach, we compute \(\hat{t}=(\hat{m}-m_{0})/(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}/\sqrt{n})\), with the adjusted sample standard deviation \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\). Using the data-driven approach, we compute \(\hat{t}=(\hat{m}-m_{0})/(\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{jack}})\) or \(\hat{t}=(\hat{m}-m_{0})/(\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{boot}})\). In any case, we can use bootstrapping to estimate the variability of the \(t\) statistic, just like we did with the mean.






NoteMust Know





Take the four observations \(\{3, 5, 7, 9\}\) and the null \(m_{0}=4\). The sample mean is \(\hat{m}=6\) and the adjusted sample standard deviation is \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\approx 2.58\). The theory-driven standard error is \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}/\sqrt{4} \approx 1.29\), so \(\hat{t} \approx (6-4)/1.29 \approx 1.55\). The sample mean is about one and a half standard errors above the null.


Code
x0_hat <- c(3, 5, 7, 9)
se0_hat <- sd(x0_hat)/sqrt(length(x0_hat))
t0_hat <- (mean(x0_hat) - 4)/se0_hat
c(se0_hat, t0_hat)
## [1] 1.290994 1.549193





For the lab data, we compute \(\hat{t}\) with jackknife standard errors and then bootstrap its null distribution.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
#null hypothesis
null_mean <- 6.5

# t statistic
jack_means <- rep(NA, length(x_hat))
for(i in seq_along(jack_means)){
    x_jack <- x_hat[-i]
    jack_means[i] <- mean(x_jack)
}
jackknife_se <- sd(jack_means)*sqrt(length(x_hat))
t_hat <- (m_hat - null_mean)/jackknife_se

# Bootstrap Null Distribution
boot_t_null <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_t_null)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot) + (null_mean - m_hat) # impose the null by recentering
    # Compute t stat using jackknife ses (same as above)
    jack_means_b <- rep(NA, length(x_boot))
    for(i in seq_along(jack_means_b)){
        jack_means_b[i] <- mean(x_boot[-i])
    }
    jackknife_se_b <- sd(jack_means_b)*sqrt(length(x_boot))
    t_b_hat <- (m_b_hat - null_mean)/jackknife_se_b
    boot_t_null[b] <- t_b_hat
}

# Plot the null distribution and CI
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(boot_t_null, border=NA, breaks=50,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Null Bootstrap for t')
abline(v=t_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_t_null, probs=c(0.025, 0.975) )
abline(v=ci_95, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

# Compute the p-value for two-sided test
F_hat <- ecdf(abs(boot_t_null))
plot(F_hat,
    xlim=range(boot_t_null, t_hat),
    xlab='Null Bootstrap for |t|',
    main=NA)
abline(v=abs(t_hat), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
p <- 1 - F_hat( abs(t_hat) )
title( paste0('p=', round(p, 3)), font.main=1)









Code

if(p >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=6.5, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of either <6.5 or >6.5, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of either <6.5 or >6.5, at the 5% level"
# The observed t is about -1.99, just inside the middle 95% of its null distribution.
# Its two-sided p-value, about 0.045, is just below 0.05, so this test also rejects.
# The interval and the p-value can disagree this close to the cutoff.


There are several benefits to this statistic:

uses the same statistic for different hypothesis tests
makes the statistic comparable across different studies
removes dependence on unknown parameters by normalizing with a standard error
makes the null distribution theoretically known asymptotically (approximately)

The last point implies we are typically dealing with a normal distribution that is well-studied, or another well-studied distribution derived from it. Because \(\hat{t}\) is comparable across tests, many null distributions can share one figure. For example, Adamson (2022) summarizes many simulated null distributions of \(t\)-values (Hope 1968; Besag and Diggle 1977; Baddeley et al. 2015) with “spreadplots”. Each spreadplot draws the range as a black line, the middle \(95\%\) between the \(0.025\) and \(0.975\) quantiles as a thick grey bar, and the median as a white line. The observed \(t\)-values appear as points, with reference lines at \(0\) and \(\pm 1.96\).






TipTest Yourself





Make a spreadplot for three tests at once. In USArrests, test the nulls \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=9\) for Murder, \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=150\) for Assault, and \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=70\) for UrbanPop. For each variable, compute \(\hat{t}\) and bootstrap its null distribution as above. Then draw one spreadplot per variable and add each observed \(\hat{t}\) as a point. Which nulls would you reject at the \(5\%\) level? Does the answer change if you use \(\pm 1.96\) instead of the bootstrap bands?


Code
# t-statistic with a jackknife standard error, as above
t_jack <- function(x_hat, null_mean) {
    jack_means <- rep(NA, length(x_hat))
    for (i in seq_along(jack_means)) {
        jack_means[i] <- mean(x_hat[-i])
    }
    jackknife_se <- sd(jack_means) * sqrt(length(x_hat))
    t_hat <- (mean(x_hat) - null_mean) / jackknife_se
    return(t_hat)
}

# One null for each variable, on very different scales
null_means2 <- c(Murder=9, Assault=150, UrbanPop=70)

# Observed t and its bootstrap null distribution for each variable
n_boot <- 999
t2_hats <- rep(NA, length(null_means2))
boot_t_nulls2 <- matrix(NA, nrow=n_boot, ncol=length(null_means2))
for (k in seq_along(null_means2)) {
    x2_k_hat <- USArrests[, names(null_means2)[k]]
    t2_hats[k] <- t_jack(x2_k_hat, null_means2[k])
    for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
        x_boot <- sample(x2_k_hat, replace=TRUE)
        x_boot <- x_boot + (null_means2[k] - mean(x2_k_hat)) # impose the null by recentering
        boot_t_nulls2[b, k] <- t_jack(x_boot, null_means2[k])
    }
}

# Spreadplot: range as a black line, middle 95% as a grey bar, median as a white line
plot(NA, xlim=c(0.5, length(null_means2) + 0.5), ylim=range(boot_t_nulls2, t2_hats),
    xaxt='n', xlab=NA, ylab=expression(hat(t)), main=NA)
axis(1, at=seq_along(null_means2), labels=names(null_means2))
abline(h=0, col=grey(.5), lty=3)                   # zero line
abline(h=c(-1.96, 1.96), col=grey(0.5), lty=3)     # Normal critical values
for (k in seq_along(null_means2)) {
    t_q <- quantile(boot_t_nulls2[, k], probs=c(0, 0.025, 0.5, 0.975, 1))
    segments(k, t_q[1], k, t_q[5], col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8))
    rect(k - 0.1, t_q[2], k + 0.1, t_q[4], col=grey(0.6), border=NA)
    segments(k - 0.1, t_q[3], k + 0.1, t_q[3], col='white', lwd=2)
}
points(seq_along(null_means2), t2_hats, pch=16, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)) # observed t









Code
# The three means, about 7.8, 170.8, and 65.5, are on very different scales.
# Their observed t-values, about -1.93, 1.73, and -2.14, are not.







Quantiles and Shape Statistics
Bootstrap allows hypothesis tests for any statistic, not just the mean, without relying on parametric theory. For example, the above procedures generalize from means to quantile statistics like medians.


Code
# Test for Median Differences (Impose the Null)
# Bootstrap Null Distribution for the median
# Each Bootstrap shifts medians so that median = null_median

med_hat <- quantile(x_hat, probs=.5)
null_median <- 5.7
boot_medians_null <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_medians_null)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) #bootstrap sample
    med_b_hat <- quantile(x_boot, probs=.5) # median
    med_null_b_hat <- med_b_hat + (null_median - med_hat) # impose the null
    boot_medians_null[b] <- med_null_b_hat
}

# 2-Sided Test for Medians
hist(boot_medians_null-null_median, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab='Null Bootstrap',
    main=NA)
title('Medians (Impose Null)', font.main=1)
median_ci <- quantile(boot_medians_null-null_median, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=median_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=med_hat-null_median, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# 2-Sided Test for Median Difference
## Null: No Median Difference
1 - ecdf( abs(boot_medians_null-null_median))( abs(med_hat-null_median) )
## [1] 0.5755756
# The p-value is about 0.58, so we fail to reject a median of 5.7.
# The population median is about 5.21, so this unrejected null is still false.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the median test with the murder arrest rates in USArrests, for the hypothesized median of \(7.8\).


Code
x2_hat <- USArrests[, 'Murder'] # murder arrests per 100,000

# Test for Median Differences (Impose the Null)
# Bootstrap Null Distribution for the median
# Each Bootstrap shifts medians so that median = null_median2

med2_hat <- quantile(x2_hat, probs=.5)
null_median2 <- 7.8
boot_medians_null2 <- rep(NA, 999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_medians_null2)){
    x_boot <- sample(x2_hat, replace=TRUE) #bootstrap sample
    med_b_hat <- quantile(x_boot, probs=.5) # median
    med_null_b_hat <- med_b_hat + (null_median2 - med2_hat) # impose the null
    boot_medians_null2[b] <- med_null_b_hat
}

# 2-Sided Test for Medians
hist(boot_medians_null2-null_median2, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE, xlab='Null Bootstrap',
    main=NA)
title('Medians (Impose Null)', font.main=1)
median_ci2 <- quantile(boot_medians_null2-null_median2, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=median_ci2, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=med2_hat-null_median2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# 2-Sided Test for Median Difference
## Null: No Median Difference
1 - ecdf( abs(boot_medians_null2-null_median2))( abs(med2_hat-null_median2) )
## [1] 0.5845846
# The p-value is about 0.58, so we fail to reject a median of 7.8.











TipTest Yourself





Conduct a hypothesis test for whether the upper quartile is statistically different from \(8\).


Code
q_hat <- quantile(x_hat, probs=.75)

title: 8  Hypothesis Testing
text:
8.4 One-Sided Tests
Above, we tested whether the observed statistic is either extremely high or low. This is known as a two-sided test. There are also two one-sided tests (left tail: observed statistic is extremely low, right tail: observed statistic is extremely high). For example, consider whether the mean statistic, \(M\), is centered on a theoretical value of \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=m_{0}\) for the population. If your null hypothesis is that the theoretical mean is \(m_{0}\), \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0}\), and you calculated the mean for your sample as \(\hat{m}\), then you can consider any one of these three alternative hypotheses:

\(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] \neq m_{0}\), a two-tail test
\(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] < m_{0}\), a left-tail test
\(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] > m_{0}\), a right-tail test







TipTest Yourself





A fitness tracker manufacturer claims that users take more than \(8{,}000\) steps per day on average. A sample of \(25\) users has \(\hat{m}=8{,}492\) steps and \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}=1{,}200\) steps. Test at the \(5\%\) level using theory-based intervals.
(a) Hypotheses. The claim is a right-tail alternative: \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 8000\) versus \(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] > 8000\).
(b) Test statistic. The classical standard error is \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}/\sqrt{n} = 1200/\sqrt{25} = 240\), so \(t = (8492 - 8000)/240 \approx 2.05\).
(c) Decision. The right-tail critical value at \(5\%\) is \(q_{0.95} \approx 1.645\) from the Normal. Since \(t = 2.05 > 1.645\), we reject \(H_{0}\).
(d) Conclusion. At the \(5\%\) level, the data are consistent with the manufacturer’s claim: there is evidence the population mean exceeds \(8{,}000\) steps per day.


Code
m_steps_hat <- 8492
s_steps_adj_hat <- 1200
n <- 25
steps_null_mean <- 8000
SE <- s_steps_adj_hat / sqrt(n)
t_stat <- (m_steps_hat - steps_null_mean) / SE
t_stat
## [1] 2.05

# Right-tail p-value from the standard Normal approximation
1 - pnorm(t_stat)
## [1] 0.02018222





One-sided hypothesis tests can be conducted by inverting a one-sided confidence interval (covered in the previous chapter) or by computing a one-sided \(p\)-value.

One-Sided \(p\)-values
The \(p\)-value for a one-sided test is more straightforward to implement via a bootstrap null distribution.
For a left-tail test, we examine \[\begin{aligned}
p = \text{Prob}( M < \hat{m} \mid \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0} )
    &\approx \text{Prob}( M^{\text{boot}}_{0} < \hat{m} ) = \hat{F}^{\text{boot}}_{0}(\hat{m}),
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{F}^{\text{boot}}_{0}\) is the ECDF of the bootstrap null distribution. We reject the null if \(p < 0.05\) at the \(5\%\) level, and otherwise fail to reject.
For a right-tail test, we examine \(p=\text{Prob}( M > \hat{m} \mid \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0} ) \approx 1-\hat{F}^{\text{boot}}_{0}(\hat{m})\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Right-tail Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean > 6.5
# Equivalent Visualization with p-value
F_hat <- ecdf(boot_means_null) # Look at right tail
plot(F_hat,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Null Bootstrap')
abline(v=m_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
p1 <- 1- F_hat(m_hat) #Compute right tail prob: 0.99
title( paste0('p=', round(p1, 3)), font.main=1)









Code

if(p1 >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=6.5, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of >6.5, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "fail to reject the null that mean=6.5, at the 5% level"
# The sample mean is below 6.5, so it gives no evidence for a mean above 6.5.


The left-tail test uses the other side of the same null distribution.


Code
# Left-tail Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean < 6.5
# Compute left-tail prob: p = F(m_hat)
p_left <- F_hat(m_hat)
p_left
## [1] 0.01001001

if(p_left >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=6.5, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of <6.5, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "reject the null that mean=6.5 in favor of <6.5, at the 5% level"
# The left-tail p-value is about 0.01, so we favor a mean below 6.5.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat both one-sided tests with the murder arrest rates, using boot_means_null2 from the Test Yourself in Impose the Null.


Code
# Right-tail Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean > 9
# Equivalent Visualization with p-value
F2_hat <- ecdf(boot_means_null2) # Look at right tail
plot(F2_hat,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Null Bootstrap')
abline(v=m2_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
p1_2 <- 1- F2_hat(m2_hat) #Compute right tail prob
title( paste0('p=', round(p1_2, 3)), font.main=1)









Code

if(p1_2 >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=9, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=9 in favor of >9, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "fail to reject the null that mean=9, at the 5% level"
# The sample mean is below 9, so it gives no evidence for a mean above 9.

# Left-tail Test, ALTERNATIVE: mean < 9
# Compute left-tail prob: p = F(m_hat)
p_left2 <- F2_hat(m2_hat)
p_left2
## [1] 0.02402402

if(p_left2 >.05){
    print('fail to reject the null that mean=9, at the 5% level')
} else {
    print('reject the null that mean=9 in favor of <9, at the 5% level')
}
## [1] "reject the null that mean=9 in favor of <9, at the 5% level"
# The left-tail p-value is about 0.02, so we favor a mean below 9.











TipTest Yourself





For two-sided tests, measure distance from \(m_{0}\) by subtracting it before taking absolute values. For one-sided tests, subtracting \(m_{0}\) from both the null-bootstrap statistic and the observed statistic leaves their ordering unchanged. Specifically, \(p = \text{Prob}( M < \hat{m} \mid \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0} ) = \text{Prob}( M - m_{0} < \hat{m} - m_{0} \mid \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = m_{0} )\). That is intuitively also why the \(t\)-value can be used for both one and two-sided hypothesis tests.


Code
# See that the 'recentering' matters for two-sided tests
ecdf( abs(boot_means_null-null_mean) )( abs(m_hat-null_mean) )
## [1] 0.970971
ecdf( abs(boot_means_null) )( abs(m_hat) )
## [1] 0.01001001

# See that the 'recentering' doesn't matter for one-sided ones
ecdf( boot_means_null-null_mean)( m_hat-null_mean)
## [1] 0.01001001
ecdf( boot_means_null )( m_hat)
## [1] 0.01001001

8.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain the difference between “rejecting the null hypothesis” and “proving the alternative hypothesis is true.” Why is the phrase “fail to reject” used instead of “accept the null”?
Suppose you collect a sample of \(n = 50\) observations with \(\hat{m} = 22.4\) and \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}} = 6.0\). You want to test \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 20\) against \(H_{A}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] \neq 20\) at the \(5\%\) level. Compute the \(t\)-value using theory-driven standard errors and determine whether you reject or fail to reject.
Using the USArrests dataset in R, test the hypothesis that the population mean of Assault equals \(150\) by constructing a bootstrap null distribution. Compute the two-sided \(p\)-value and state whether you reject or fail to reject at the \(5\%\) level.


Further Reading

https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/hypothesistesting.html – Comprehensive chapter on null hypotheses, p-values, and test decisions with R examples.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/significance-tests-one-sample – Step-by-step video lessons on hypothesis testing for one-sample means and proportions.



Recall
We built hypothesis tests in two ways, invert a CI and impose the null. We also summarized the evidence with the \(p\)-value and the \(t\)-value. Running many tests inflates the chance of a false rejection. The fitness-tracker example tied these ideas together: with \(\hat{m}=8492\), \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}=1200\), and \(n=25\), the standard error is \(\text{SE} = 1200/\sqrt{25} = 240\) and the \(t\)-value for \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 8000\) is \((8492 - 8000)/240 \approx 2.05\), which exceeds the right-tail critical value \(1.645\) at the \(5\%\) level and so rejects the null.
