The base-rate fallacy often shows up as reading a large count as a high rate. A common category can have the most cases even when its rate per case is the lowest.






TipTest Yourself





The most-stolen car. Suppose you read that the Honda Civic is the most-stolen car in a city. Does that mean a Civic is more likely to be stolen than other cars? Not necessarily.
Imagine a city with \(100{,}000\) cars: \(70{,}000\) Civics and \(30{,}000\) of other models. Let \(\hat{x}_{i}\) be the model and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) whether car \(i\) was stolen. The counts are
\[\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
& \text{not stolen} & \text{stolen} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{Civic} & 69300 & 700 & 70000\\
\text{other} & 29460 & 540 & 30000\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 98760 & 1240 & 100000
\end{array}\]
More Civics are stolen than other cars (\(700 > 540\)), so the Civic is the “most-stolen” model. But the conditional distributions tell two different stories:

\(\hat{p}(\text{stolen}\mid\text{Civic}) = \frac{700}{70000} = 0.010\) is the theft rate for a Civic.
\(\hat{p}(\text{stolen}\mid\text{other}) = \frac{540}{30000} = 0.018\) is the theft rate for other cars.
\(\hat{p}(\text{Civic}\mid\text{stolen}) = \frac{700}{1240} \approx 0.565\) is the share of stolen cars that are Civics.

A Civic is less likely to be stolen (\(1.0\%\) vs \(1.8\%\)), yet most stolen cars are Civics. The reason is the base rate: \(\hat{p}(\text{Civic}) = 0.70\) of all cars are Civics. “Most-stolen” is a statement about \(\hat{p}(x\mid y)\) (the model given theft), while car-theft risk is a statement about \(\hat{p}(y\mid x)\) (theft given the model).


Code
# Count table: rows = model, columns = stolen
counts <- rbind(
    Civic = c(not=69300, stolen=700),
    other = c(not=29460, stolen=540))

# Theft rate by model: p(stolen | model)
counts[, 'stolen'] / rowSums(counts)
## Civic other 
## 0.010 0.018

# Share of stolen cars by model: p(model | stolen)
counts[, 'stolen'] / sum(counts[, 'stolen'])
##     Civic     other 
## 0.5645161 0.4354839





How far a signal moves \(\hat{p}(y\mid x)\) away from \(\hat{p}(y)\) depends on the base rate \(\hat{p}(y)\) itself. The fraud-detection example below applies one screen to a rare outcome and then to a common one.






TipTest Yourself





Fraud detection. A bank’s model flags \(99\%\) of fraudulent transactions and \(1\%\) of legitimate ones. What is the chance that a flagged transaction is fraud? The answer depends on the base rate \(\hat{p}(y)\): the share of all transactions that are fraud.
Let \(\hat{x}_{i}\) be whether the model flags transaction \(i\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) be whether the transaction is fraud. Suppose fraud is rare, \(100\) of \(100{,}000\) transactions, so \(\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 0.001\). The counts are
\[\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
& \text{legitimate} & \text{fraud} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{not flagged} & 98901 & 1 & 98902\\
\text{flagged} & 999 & 99 & 1098\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 99900 & 100 & 100000
\end{array}\]
Before seeing the model’s output, the chance that a transaction is fraud is the base rate, \(\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 100/100000 = 0.001\). After seeing a flag, it is the conditional, \(\hat{p}(\text{fraud}\mid\text{flagged}) = 99/1098 \approx 0.09\). The flag matters: it raises the chance of fraud \(90\)-fold. But \(91\%\) of flags are still false alarms, because the \(1\%\) false alarm rate applies to \(99{,}900\) legitimate transactions, which swamps the \(99\) true detections.
Now suppose fraud is common, \(10{,}000\) of \(100{,}000\) transactions, so \(\hat{p}(\text{fraud}) = 0.10\). The model is unchanged, but the counts become
\[\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
& \text{legitimate} & \text{fraud} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{not flagged} & 89100 & 100 & 89200\\
\text{flagged} & 900 & 9900 & 10800\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 90000 & 10000 & 100000
\end{array}\]
and \(\hat{p}(\text{fraud}\mid\text{flagged}) = 9900/10800 \approx 0.92\). The same flag from the same model means fraud is unlikely in one setting and likely in the other. The only thing that changed is the base rate.
The base-rate fallacy is to judge the flag by the model’s accuracy alone, as if \(\hat{p}(y\mid x)\) did not depend on \(\hat{p}(y)\). When the outcome is rare, even an accurate screen produces mostly false positives. The same arithmetic applies to medical tests for rare diseases, polygraph screening of employees, and airport security checks.


Code
# Rare fraud: rows = model output, columns = transaction type
counts_rare <- rbind(
    not_flagged = c(legitimate=98901, fraud=1),
    flagged = c(legitimate=999, fraud=99))
colSums(counts_rare) / sum(counts_rare)      # base rate p(y)
## legitimate      fraud 
##      0.999      0.001
round(prop.table(counts_rare, 1), 3)         # conditional p(y | x)
##             legitimate fraud
## not_flagged       1.00  0.00
## flagged           0.91  0.09

# Common fraud: same model, base rate 100 times higher
counts_common <- rbind(
    not_flagged = c(legitimate=89100, fraud=100),
    flagged = c(legitimate=900, fraud=9900))
colSums(counts_common) / sum(counts_common)
## legitimate      fraud 
##        0.9        0.1
round(prop.table(counts_common, 1), 3)
##             legitimate fraud
## not_flagged      0.999 0.001
## flagged          0.083 0.917







Continuous Data
Conditional distributions describe the relationship between \(\hat{y}_{i}\) and \(\hat{x}_{i}\). We show how \(\hat{y}\) changes according to \(\hat{x}\) using a histogram or bar plot. When \(\hat{x}\) is continuous, as it often is, or takes many values, we split it into distinct bins and convert it to a factor variable. E.g.,


Code

m_x_hat

NoteMust Know





You can also split data into more than two groups. Here we cut \(\hat{x}\) into \(K=4\) bins and draw one boxplot per bin. It helps to check how many observations fall in each bin, since evenly spaced bins can be nearly empty.


Code

# K Groups with even spacing (not even counts)

table(cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], K))

11.3 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain the difference between a joint distribution, a marginal distribution, and a conditional distribution. Using the schooling-and-sex example from this chapter, describe in words what \(\hat{p}(y=\text{female} \mid x=13)\) tells you and how it differs from \(\hat{p}(x=13 \mid y=\text{female})\).
Suppose you observe a sample of \(n=20\) people with two discrete variables: \(\hat{x}_{i}\) takes values in \(\{A, B\}\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) takes values in \(\{1, 2\}\). The counts are: \((A,1)=6\), \((A,2)=4\), \((B,1)=3\), \((B,2)=7\). Compute the joint distribution \(\hat{p}(x,y)\), both marginal distributions, and the conditional distribution \(\hat{p}(y \mid x)\).
Using the USArrests dataset, split the variable Assault into two groups based on whether UrbanPop is above or below its median. Plot overlapping histograms of Assault for both groups with semi-transparent colors. Then plot the ECDF for each group on the same axes with a legend.


Further Reading

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/2-1-random-variables-and-probability-distributions.html – joint, marginal, and conditional distributions in an econometrics context.
https://r-graph-gallery.com/histogram.html – gallery of histogram styles in R, useful for building marginal-distribution plots.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/random-variables-stats-library/random-variables-discrete/v/valid-discrete-probability-distribution-examples – short video introduction to discrete probability distributions and joint tables.



Recall
We summarized two variables with joint, marginal, and conditional distributions. In the Wages1 schooling-and-sex table, \(\hat{p}(y=\text{female}\mid x=13)\approx 0.56\) is the share of female workers within the 13-years-of-school subgroup. We then saw how the base-rate fallacy reads a large count as a high rate (the “most-stolen car” calculation, where Civics are the most-stolen model but the least likely to be stolen per car).

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
12.1 Discrete Data
We now compare two groups: how the distribution of one variable changes across the categories of another. We begin with discrete data and then turn to continuous data. In both cases, a cardinal outcome \(\hat{y}_{i}\) is split into groups by a factor \(\hat{x}_{i}\).
This chapter asks three questions.
When both variables are factors, a natural way to summarize their association is to look at how the average of one (treated as cardinal) changes across categories of the other. When its categories are ordered, we can also look at how its quantiles change.
Comparing \(\hat{m}_{Y}(x)\) across values of \(x\) is useful as the simplest summary of association between a cardinal outcome and a factor. One number per subgroup shows whether \(\hat{y}\) tends to be higher in one category. The calculation breaks into two steps: column-by-column, compute the conditional distribution \(\hat{p}(y\mid x)\), then take its weighted average using the values of \(y\).
For example, the code below treats a discrete \(\hat{y}\) as cardinal and compares it across the categories of \(\hat{x}\). We first split \(\hat{y}\) into one group per category, and then average within each group.
Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Lab data: 3294 US workers from the Ecdat package
# school is years of schooling, treated here as cardinal
# sex is a factor with levels female and male
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# Years of schooling within each sex
D_female <- Wages1[, 'sex'] == 'female'
y1_hat <- Wages1[D_female, 'school']
y2_hat <- Wages1[!D_female, 'school']

# Conditional mean of schooling within each sex
m1_hat <- mean(y1_hat)
m2_hat <- mean(y2_hat)
c(m1_hat=m1_hat, m2_hat=m2_hat)
##   m1_hat   m2_hat 
## 11.83748 11.44232
# Women in this sample average about 11.8 years and men about 11.4 years.
Alternatively, aggregate computes the conditional mean for every group at once. To see the two steps in the definition, we first compute the conditional distribution of \(\hat{y}\) within each category of \(\hat{x}\), so that each column sums to 1. We then take the weighted average of the values of \(y\) within each column.
Code
# Mean years of school by sex
aggregate(school ~ sex, Wages1, mean)
##      sex   school
## 1 female 11.83748
## 2   male 11.44232

## Breakdown
# Counts of years of schooling (rows) by sex (columns)
school_sex <- table(Wages1[, 'school'], Wages1[, 'sex'])

# Conditional distribution p(y|x): each column sums to 1
p_school_sex <- prop.table(school_sex, 2)
round(p_school_sex, 3)
##     
##      female  male
##   3   0.000 0.001
##   4   0.000 0.001
##   5   0.001 0.002
##   6   0.002 0.006
##   7   0.005 0.009
##   8   0.014 0.037
##   9   0.038 0.059
##   10  0.106 0.135
##   11  0.196 0.205
##   12  0.379 0.344
##   13  0.120 0.087
##   14  0.089 0.072
##   15  0.043 0.038
##   16  0.007 0.003
# Men are more common at 10 years or fewer.
# Women are more common at 12 years or more.

# Conditional mean of schooling within each sex
school_values <- as.numeric(rownames(p_school_sex))
m_school_sex <- colSums(school_values * p_school_sex)
m_school_sex
##   female     male 
## 11.83748 11.44232
The conditional mean summarizes each subgroup with one number, but we can also ask where the lower, middle, and upper parts of each subgroup lie.
Conditional quantiles are useful when \(\hat{y}\) is ordered but not cardinal: unlike the conditional mean, they only use the ordering of the categories, as with ordered factors. In R, quantile with type=1 inverts the ECDF within each group, so it returns an observed value.
Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Conditional medians within each sex
med1_hat <- median(y1_hat)
med2_hat <- median(y2_hat)
c(med1_hat=med1_hat, med2_hat=med2_hat)
## med1_hat med2_hat 
##       12       12
# The medians are both 12 years.
# That is because over a third of each group stopped at exactly 12 years.

# Conditional quartiles within each sex
q1_hat <- quantile(y1_hat, probs=c(.25, .5, .75), type=1)
q2_hat <- quantile(y2_hat, probs=c(.25, .5, .75), type=1)
rbind(q1_hat, q2_hat)
##        25% 50% 75%
## q1_hat  11  12  13
## q2_hat  10  12  12
# The quartiles still show a difference.
# The middle half of women have between 11 and 13 years.
# The middle half of men have between 10 and 12 years.
With lumpy discrete data, a single median can hide a difference that several quantiles reveal.
Alternatively, aggregate computes the conditional quantiles for every group at once. To see where these quantiles come from, cumsum down each column of the conditional distribution gives \(\hat{F}_{Y}(y \mid x)\) for each group. Each quartile is the first row where its column reaches \(p\).
Code
# Conditional Quantiles
aggregate(school ~ sex, Wages1, median)
##      sex school
## 1 female     12
## 2   male     12
aggregate(school ~ sex, Wages1, quantile, probs=c(.25, .5, .75), type=1)
##      sex school.25% school.50% school.75%
## 1 female         11         12         13
## 2   male         10         12         12

## Breakdown
# Conditional ECDF within each sex: cumulative proportions down each column
F_school_sex <- apply(p_school_sex, 2, cumsum)
round(F_school_sex, 3)
##     
##      female  male
##   3   0.000 0.001
##   4   0.000 0.002
##   5   0.001 0.004
##   6   0.003 0.010
##   7   0.008 0.020
##   8   0.022 0.057
##   9   0.060 0.115
##   10  0.166 0.250
##   11  0.361 0.456
##   12  0.740 0.800
##   13  0.860 0.887
##   14  0.950 0.959
##   15  0.993 0.997
##   16  1.000 1.000

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
ImportantKey Definition





The conditional mean \(\hat{m}_{Y}(x)\) is the average value of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) inside the subgroup where \(\hat{x}_{i}=x\): \[\hat{m}_{Y}(x)=\sum_{y} y\,\hat{p}(y\mid x).\]














NoteMust Know





Suppose our data is given in the table shown below.

Counts of \(y\) by \(x\)



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)




\(y=1\)
\(12\)
\(8\)


\(y=2\)
\(18\)
\(6\)


\(y=3\)
\(10\)
\(16\)



First, we compute conditional probabilities to examine how the distribution changes.

Conditional Proportions of \(y\) Given \(x\)



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)




\(y=1\)
\(12/40\)
\(8/30\)


\(y=2\)
\(18/40\)
\(6/30\)


\(y=3\)
\(10/40\)
\(16/30\)



\(40/40\)
\(30/30\)



Second, we apply the conditional-mean formula column by column: \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m}_{Y}(x=0) &= 1 \frac{12}{40} + 2 \frac{18}{40} + 3 \frac{10}{40} = \frac{12+36+30}{40} = \frac{78}{40} \\
\hat{m}_{Y}(x=1) &= 1 \frac{8}{30} + 2 \frac{6}{30} + 3 \frac{16}{30} = \frac{8+12+48}{30} = \frac{68}{30}
\end{aligned}\] Notice that \(\hat{m}_{Y}(x=0) < \hat{m}_{Y}(x=1)\), which shows that the mean value of \(\hat{y}\) is higher when \(\hat{x}\) is higher. I.e., there is a positive association.
We can also compare conditional medians by adding up the conditional proportions down each column. When \(x=0\), the running total is \(12/40\) at \(y=1\) and \(30/40\) at \(y=2\), so \(\hat{F}_{Y}^{-1}(0.5 \mid x=0) = 2\). When \(x=1\), the running total is \(8/30\) at \(y=1\), \(14/30\) at \(y=2\), and \(30/30\) at \(y=3\), so \(\hat{F}_{Y}^{-1}(0.5 \mid x=1) = 3\). The median value of \(\hat{y}\) is also higher when \(\hat{x}\) is higher.









TipTest Yourself





We can compute the mean \(\hat{m}_{Y}\) using the marginal distributions, as already shown in the last chapter. To compute the mean, \(\hat{m}_{Y}\), we first compute the joint distribution by dividing each cell with \(12+8+18+6+10+16 = 70\) so that all cells sum to 1. We then sum up proportions along each row and column to compute the marginals.

Joint and Marginal Proportions



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
Marginal y 




\(y=1\)
\(12/70\)
\(8/70\)
\(20/70\)


\(y=2\)
\(18/70\)
\(6/70\)
\(24/70\)


\(y=3\)
\(10/70\)
\(16/70\)
\(26/70\)


Marginal x 
\(40/70\)
\(30/70\)
\(70/70\)



Second, we compute the overall mean using the marginals \[
\hat{m}_{Y} = 1 \frac{20}{70} + 2 \frac{24}{70} + 3 \frac{26}{70} = \frac{20 + 48 + 78}{70} = {146/70}
\]
Third, we compare \(\hat{m}_{Y}\) to the conditional means from the Must Know box. The overall mean is a weighted average of the two conditional means, where each weight is the marginal proportion \(\hat{p}(x)\): \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m}_{Y} &= \hat{p}(x=0) \hat{m}_{Y}(x=0) + \hat{p}(x=1) \hat{m}_{Y}(x=1) \\
&= \frac{40}{70} \frac{78}{40} + \frac{30}{70} \frac{68}{30} = \frac{78 + 68}{70} = \frac{146}{70}
\end{aligned}\] A weighted average always lies between the values being averaged, so \(\hat{m}_{Y}(x=0) < \hat{m}_{Y} < \hat{m}_{Y}(x=1)\). In numbers, \(78/40 = 1.95\), \(146/70 \approx 2.09\), and \(68/30 \approx 2.27\).










ImportantKey Definition





The conditional quantile is the \(p\)th quantile of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) inside the subgroup where \(\hat{x}_{i}=x\). It inverts the conditional ECDF and is written \(\hat{F}_{Y}^{-1}(p \mid x)\). For discrete \(\hat{y}\), \(\hat{F}_{Y}^{-1}(p \mid x)\) is the smallest \(y\) where \(\hat{F}_{Y}(y \mid x) \geq p\).

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
12.2 Continuous Data
Consider a mixed dataset where \(\hat{y}_{i}\) is a continuous cardinal variable and \(\hat{x}_{i}\) is a factor variable (typically unordered). For such “grouped data”, we analyze associations via group comparisons. The basic idea is best seen in a comparison of two samples, which corresponds to an \(\hat{x}_{i}\) with two categories. For example, we might compare the heights of men and women in Canada or the homicide rates in two different American states.
To compare two groups, we start by making a histogram for each.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Compare wages for people who did and did not complete a degree
# Workers with 12 or 16 years of schooling, and which of them are high school only
xy_hat <- Wages1[Wages1[, 'school'] %in% c(12, 16), c('school', 'wage')]
D_hs <- xy_hat[, 'school'] == 12

# Hourly wages within each level of schooling
y1_hat <- xy_hat[D_hs, 'wage'] # high school only
y2_hat <- xy_hat[!D_hs, 'wage'] # university graduates

# Initial summary figure: two overlaid histograms on a common grid
bks <- seq(0, 34, by=1)             # shared bin edges
dlim <- c(0, .2)                    # shared y limit
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5)) # semi-transparent fill

hist(y1_hat, breaks=bks, ylim=dlim,
     col=cols[1], xlab='Wages',
     freq=FALSE, border=NA, main=NA)
rug(y1_hat, col=cols[1])
hist(y2_hat, breaks=bks, ylim=dlim,
     col=cols[2],
     freq=FALSE, border=NA, add=TRUE)
rug(y2_hat, col=cols[2])
legend('topright',
       col=cols, pch=15,
       legend=c('12 Years (High School)', '16 Years (University)'),
       title='School Completed')









The histogram may show several differences between groups or none at all. In general, we test whether the difference in some statistic \(\hat{g}\) equals \(0\). As in LOTUS and Data Transformations, \(g\) denotes a function, but here \(\hat{g}\) is a function of a group’s whole sample rather than of a single observation. Often, the first statistic we investigate for hypothesis testing is the mean, \(\hat{m}\).






ImportantKey Definition





The difference statistic is the sample-statistic in group 1 minus the sample-statistic in group 2: \[\hat{d} = \hat{g}_{1} - \hat{g}_{2},\] where \(\hat{g}_{1}\) and \(\hat{g}_{2}\) are the statistic computed from the group 1 data and the group 2 data, such as the means \(\hat{m}_{1}\) and \(\hat{m}_{2}\) or the medians \(\tilde{m}_{1}\) and \(\tilde{m}_{2}\). A positive value says the statistic is higher in group 1, zero means no difference between groups, and a negative value says the statistic is higher in group 2.




Mean Differences
The mean difference is useful for summarizing how different two groups are on average. It is on the same scale as the outcome. Its null hypothesis is no difference in population means, \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i2}]\). We can test that hypothesis by inverting a confidence interval. The code below computes \(\hat{m}_{1}\) and \(\hat{m}_{2}\) and reports \(\hat{d}\). Is the gap bigger than we would expect from sampling noise? To answer that, we resample each group separately and recompute \(\hat{d}\) each time.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Difference between means
m1_hat <- mean(y1_hat)
m2_hat <- mean(y2_hat)
d_hat <- m1_hat - m2_hat
round(c(m1_hat=m1_hat, m2_hat=m2_hat, d_hat=d_hat), 2)
## m1_hat m2_hat  d_hat 
##   5.67   7.54  -1.87
# The university group has the higher mean wage, so d_hat is negative.

# Bootstrap Distribution
bootstrap_diff <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(bootstrap_diff) ){
    # keep each worker's group fixed and resample wages within each group
    y1_boot <- sample(xy_hat[D_hs, 'wage'], replace=TRUE)
    y2_boot <- sample(xy_hat[!D_hs, 'wage'], replace=TRUE)
    m1_b_hat <- mean(y1_boot)
    m2_b_hat <- mean(y2_boot)
    d_b <- m1_b_hat - m2_b_hat
    bootstrap_diff[b] <- d_b
}
hist(bootstrap_diff, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Means')
title('Bootstrapped Difference in Means', font.main=1)

# 2-Sided Test via Confidence Interval
boot_ci <- quantile(bootstrap_diff, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=boot_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Such tests make purely statistical statements that only speak to how frequently differences are generated by random chance. They do not say why there are any differences or how large they are. Even on purely statistical grounds, however, we would want to be cautious about making data-driven decisions when

the significance level is somewhat arbitrary (what if we reject at the \(5\%\) level but not \(10\%\) level?)
the test statistic is somewhat arbitrary (what if we reject for means but not medians?)
there are multiple differences

For such reasons, applied statisticians consider many statistics.


Quantile Differences
The above procedure generalizes from differences in means to differences in medians. To start, we plot the ECDF’s for both groups.


Code
# Quantile Comparison

## Distribution 1
F1_hat <- ecdf(y1_hat)
plot(F1_hat, col=cols[1],
     pch=16, xlab='Wages', xlim=c(0, 24),
     main=NA, bty='n')
title('Comparing Medians', font.main=1)
## Median 1
med1_hat <- median(y1_hat) # equivalently, quantile(F1_hat, probs=0.5)
segments(med1_hat, 0, med1_hat, 0.5, col=cols[1], lty=2)
abline(h=0.5, col=grey(.5), lty=3)

## Distribution 2
F2_hat <- ecdf(y2_hat)
plot(F2_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2], pch=16)
## Median 2
med2_hat <- median(y2_hat) # equivalently, quantile(F2_hat, probs=0.5)
segments(med2_hat, 0, med2_hat, 0.5, col=cols[2], lty=2)

## Legend
legend('bottomright',
       col=cols, pch=15,
       legend=c('12 Years (High School)', '16 Years (University)'),
       title='School Completed')















NoteMust Know







Code
# Bootstrap Distribution Function
boot_quant <- function(y_hat, D_group, n_boot=9999, probs=0.5, ...){
    bootstrap_diff <- rep(NA, n_boot)
    for(b in seq(bootstrap_diff)){
        y1_boot <- sample(y_hat[D_group], replace=TRUE)
        y2_boot <- sample(y_hat[!D_group], replace=TRUE)
        q1_b <- quantile(y1_boot, probs=probs, ...)
        q2_b <- quantile(y2_boot, probs=probs, ...)
        d_b <- q1_b - q2_b
        bootstrap_diff[b] <- d_b
    }
    return(bootstrap_diff)
}

# 2-Sided Test for Median Differences
d_med <- med1_hat - med2_hat
d_med
## [1] -2.489273
boot_d <- boot_quant(xy_hat[, 'wage'], D_hs, n_boot=9999, probs=0.5)
hist(boot_d, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Medians')
title('Bootstrap Difference in Medians', font.main=1)
abline(v=quantile(boot_d, probs=c(.025, .975)), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)












Changing probs in boot_quant tests other quantiles, such as the quartiles. Note that bootstrap tests can perform poorly with highly unequal variances or skewed data. To see this yourself, make a simulation with skewed data and unequal variances.


Other Statistics
In principle, we can also examine whether there are differences in spread (sd or IQR) or shape (skew or kurtosis). We use the same hypothesis testing procedure as above.






TipTest Yourself





Here is an example to look at differences in “spread”


Code
boot_fun <- function( fun, n_boot=9999, ...){
    bootstrap_diff <- rep(NA, n_boot)
    for(b in seq(bootstrap_diff)){
        y1_boot <- sample(xy_hat[D_hs, 'wage'], replace=TRUE)
        y2_boot <- sample(xy_hat[!D_hs, 'wage'], replace=TRUE)
        f1_b <- fun(y1_boot, ...)
        f2_b <- fun(y2_boot, ...)
        d_b <- f1_b - f2_b
        bootstrap_diff[b] <- d_b
    }
    return(bootstrap_diff)
}

# 2-Sided Test for SD Differences
d_sd <- sd(y1_hat) - sd(y2_hat)
d_sd
boot_d <- boot_fun(sd)
hist(boot_d, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Standard Deviations')
title('Bootstrap Difference in Standard Deviations', font.main=1)
abline(v=quantile(boot_d, probs=c(.025, .975)), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)

# Try any function!
# boot_fun( function(xs) { IQR(xs)/median(xs) } )

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
12.3 Distributional Comparisons
We can also examine whether there are any differences between the entire distributions. We typically start by plotting the two ECDF’s, and then calculate a statistic for hypothesis testing. A quantile-quantile plot is another way to compare the two distributions visually.

KS and CVM Statistics
To go from a picture of two distributions to a single-number summary of how different they are, we measure the gap between their ECDFs.






ImportantKey Definition





The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) (Kolmogorov 1933; Smirnov 1948) summarizes the difference between two ECDFs by their single biggest vertical gap, evaluated over the pooled sample \(y~\text{in}~\{\hat{y}_{i1}\} \cup \{\hat{y}_{i2}\}\): \[\hat{\text{KS}} = \max_{y} |\hat{F}_{1}(y)- \hat{F}_{2}(y)|^{p}.\]
The Cramer-von Mises statistic \(\hat{\text{CVM}}\) (Cramér 1928; von Mises 1928; Anderson 1962) instead sums the vertical gaps at every pooled sample point: \[\hat{\text{CVM}} = \sum_{y} | \hat{F}_{1}(y)- \hat{F}_{2}(y)|^{p}.\]
The integer \(p\) is typically \(1\) for \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) and \(2\) for \(\hat{\text{CVM}}\).



\(\hat{\text{KS}}\) is useful when we expect distributions to differ by a shift: the gap piles up at one location and the max catches it. The cost is that \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) uses only the single largest gap, so it can miss many small differences spread across the support. \(\hat{\text{CVM}}\) is useful for accumulated small differences spread across the support, since every pooled sample point contributes to the sum.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# KS and CVM statistics for any two-group split
ks_cvm <- function(y1_hat, y2_hat){
    y_values <- sort(c(y1_hat, y2_hat)) # pooled sample points
    F1_vals <- ecdf(y1_hat)(y_values)
    F2_vals <- ecdf(y2_hat)(y_values)
    gap <- abs(F1_vals - F2_vals)
    # KS: largest vertical gap (p=1); CVM: summed squared gaps (p=2)
    return(c(KS=max(gap), CVM=sum(gap^2)))
}
stat_obs <- ks_cvm(y1_hat, y2_hat)
round(stat_obs, 2)
##    KS   CVM 
##  0.42 76.16

















NoteMust Know





Suppose there are two groups of summer workers, with data on the earnings of each individual. In thousands of Canadian Dollars, specifically, Group \(A\) has earnings \(\{18,20,25,30\}\) and group \(B\) has earnings \(\{19,21,24,35\}\).
We can compute the CVM and KS statistics for further statistical testing. Start by drawing the ECDF’s.


Code
# Earnings of each group, in thousands of Canadian Dollars
yA0_hat <- c(18, 20, 25, 30)
yB0_hat <- c(19, 21, 24, 35)
FA_hat <- ecdf(yA0_hat)
FB_hat <- ecdf(yB0_hat)

# ECDFs as step functions; shape and line type also mark the group
plot(FA_hat, col=cols[1], pch=16, lwd=2,
    xlab='Earnings', ylab='ECDF',
    main=NA, bty='n')
plot(FB_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2], pch=17, lty=2, lwd=2)

# Vertical gaps at the 8 pooled values, one per row of the table below
x_values <- sort(c(yA0_hat, yB0_hat))
segments(x_values, FA_hat(x_values), x_values, FB_hat(x_values),
    lwd=3, col=grey(0, .75), lty=3)
cvm0_hat <- sum((FA_hat(x_values) - FB_hat(x_values))^2)
title(paste0('CVM: ', cvm0_hat), adj=1, font.main=1)

legend('topleft', bty='n', inset=c(0, .1),
    col=cols, pch=c(16, 17), lty=c(1, 2), lwd=2,
    legend=c('Group A', 'Group B'))









Each dotted segment is a gap of \(1/4\), and at the other four pooled values the two ECDFs meet. Then compute \(\hat{F}_{A}(x) - \hat{F}_{B}(x)\) and its square at each of the 8 pooled sorted values:

ECDF Gaps at Each Pooled Value









\(x\)

Quantile-Quantile Plots
Another useful visualization for two groups is to plot the quantiles against one another: a quantile-quantile plot. I.e., the first data point on the bottom left shows the first quantile for both distributions.


Code
# Percentiles of each group's wages
quants <- seq(0, 1, length.out=101)
Q1 <- quantile(y1_hat, probs=quants)
Q2 <- quantile(y2_hat, probs=quants)

ry <- range(c(y1_hat, y2_hat))
plot(Q1, Q2, xlim=ry, ylim=ry,
    xlab=expression(Q[1]),
    ylab=expression(Q[2]),
    main=NA,
    pch=16, col=grey(0, .25))

Code
# Sorting pairs the k-th smallest earnings in group A with the k-th smallest in group B

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
12.4 Permutation Tests
The mean and median tests above invert a bootstrap confidence interval. We can also test by “imposing the null”, where it is more common to use \(p\)-values instead of confidence intervals.






ImportantKey Definition





A permutation test of “no difference between groups” recomputes the test statistic on many random reshufflings of the group labels. Because each reshuffle keeps the pooled data but breaks the link between label and outcome, the resulting distribution shows what differences look like under the null of no association.



The permutation test (also called a randomization test) is useful when the null hypothesis is “no association”. Reshuffling the labels imposes that null, and we do not need to assume a distributional form. Every reshuffle uses the same pooled data, so the only variability comes from re-splitting the labels. If using a hard decision rule, it is most common to reject the null at the \(5\%\) level when \(p<0.05\) and fail to reject when \(p>0.05\). Alternatively, we can reject when the observed statistic falls outside the middle \(95\%\) of the permutation distribution, as with the null bootstrap in Hypothesis Testing.

Permuting Means






NoteMust Know





Consider again the two groups of summer workers, with earnings in thousands of Canadian Dollars. Group \(A\) has earnings \(\{18,20,25,30\}\) and group \(B\) has earnings \(\{19,21,24,35\}\). The observed mean difference is \(\hat{d}=23.25-24.75=-1.5\). A permutation keeps the eight pooled values but reassigns which four belong to group \(A\).


Code
# Pooled earnings and group labels (1=A, 2=B)
y0_hat <- c(yA0_hat, yB0_hat) # group A's four earnings, then group B's
g0 <- c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2)
d0_hat <- mean(y0_hat[g0==1]) - mean(y0_hat[g0==2])
d0_hat
## [1] -1.5

# A few reshuffled labels, written out by hand
g0_perm1 <- c(2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
g0_perm2 <- c(1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2)
g0_perm3 <- c(2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1)
mean(y0_hat[g0_perm1==1]) - mean(y0_hat[g0_perm1==2])
## [1] -4
mean(y0_hat[g0_perm2==1]) - mean(y0_hat[g0_perm2==2])
## [1] -2.5
mean(y0_hat[g0_perm3==1]) - mean(y0_hat[g0_perm3==2])
## [1] 6.5

# With 8 values there are only choose(8, 4)=70 ways to pick group A
id_A <- combn(8, 4)
d0_perm <- apply(id_A, 2, function(id){
    yA0_perm <- y0_hat[id]
    yB0_perm <- y0_hat[-id]
    mean(yA0_perm) - mean(yB0_perm)
})
hist(d0_perm, breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Means')

# 2-Sided Test via the middle 95% of the relabelings
perm0_ci <- quantile(d0_perm, probs=c(.025, .975))
perm0_ci
##    2.5%   97.5% 
## -7.1375  7.1375
abline(v=perm0_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=d0_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# Two-sided p-value: share of relabelings at least as extreme as observed
mean(abs(d0_perm) >= abs(d0_hat))
## [1] 0.7714286


About \(77\%\) of the \(70\) relabelings produce a gap at least as large as \(1.5\), so this small difference is easy to explain by chance. Likewise, \(\hat{d}=-1.5\) sits well inside the middle \(95\%\) of relabelings, from about \(-7.1\) to \(7.1\).



With larger samples, there are far too many relabelings to list, so we draw many of them at random.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Permutation Distribution: re-split the pooled wages of the two groups
permute_diff <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(permute_diff) ){
    #randomize data
    D_hs0 <- sample(D_hs)
    y1_perm <- xy_hat[D_hs0, 'wage']
    y2_perm <- xy_hat[!D_hs0, 'wage']
    # recompute statistic
    m1_perm_hat <- mean(y1_perm)
    m2_perm_hat <- mean(y2_perm)
    d_b <- m1_perm_hat - m2_perm_hat
    permute_diff[b] <- d_b
}
hist(permute_diff, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Means')
title('Permuted Difference in Means', font.main=1)

# 2-Sided Test via the middle 95% of the permutation distribution
perm_ci <- quantile(permute_diff, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=perm_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=d_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# Two-sided p-value: share of permutations at least as extreme as observed
p <- mean(abs(permute_diff) >= abs(d_hat))
p
## [1] 0.02060206




Permuting Quantiles
The same reshuffling works for medians: only the statistic that we recompute on each permutation changes. We pool the outcomes of the two groups, randomly pick which of them belong to group 1, and compute the difference in medians.


Code
# Observed difference in medians
d_med <- med1_hat - med2_hat

# Permutation Distribution: same re-split as for means, recomputing medians
permute_med_diff <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq(permute_med_diff) ){
    D_hs0 <- sample(D_hs)
    y1_perm <- xy_hat[D_hs0, 'wage']
    y2_perm <- xy_hat[!D_hs0, 'wage']
    permute_med_diff[b] <- median(y1_perm) - median(y2_perm)
}
hist(permute_med_diff, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Difference in Medians')
title('Permuted Difference in Medians', font.main=1)

# 2-Sided Test via the middle 95% of the permutation distribution
perm_med_ci <- quantile(permute_med_diff, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=perm_med_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=d_med, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# Two-sided p-value: share of permutations at least as extreme as observed
p_med <- mean(abs(permute_med_diff) >= abs(d_med))
p_med
## [1] 0.00350035


The \(p\)-value is the share of permutations with a median gap at least as large as the observed one. A small \(p\)-value means the observed gap in medians is hard to explain by chance.






TipTest Yourself





Return to the summer workers from the Must Know above, with group \(A\) earning \(\{18,20,25,30\}\) and group \(B\) earning \(\{19,21,24,35\}\). Both groups have the same median, \((20+25)/2 = 22.5\) and \((21+24)/2 = 22.5\), so the observed median difference is \(0\). Every relabeling has a median gap at least as large as \(0\), so the permutation \(p\)-value is \(1\).


Code
# Median difference for all 70 ways to pick group A
d0_med <- median(y0_hat[g0==1]) - median(y0_hat[g0==2])
d0_med_perm <- apply(id_A, 2, function(id){
    yA0_perm <- y0_hat[id]
    yB0_perm <- y0_hat[-id]
    median(yA0_perm) - median(yB0_perm)
})
mean(abs(d0_med_perm) >= abs(d0_med))
## [1] 1


The means differ by \(1.5\), but the medians do not differ at all. A permutation test only looks for differences in the statistic it recomputes, so the choice of statistic matters.





Permuting Distributions
The same reshuffling tests whether the \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) and \(\hat{\text{CVM}}\) statistics from Distributional Comparisons are bigger than chance alone would produce. To impose the null hypothesis of identical distributions, we permute the group labels: each resample keeps the pooled data but randomly re-splits it into two groups of the original sizes. Some permutations produce a statistic at least as large as the observed one. In those cases, random label-shuffling alone created a gap this big. The \(p\)-value is the fraction of such permutations. A small \(p\)-value means the observed gap is hard to explain by chance. Both statistics are never negative, and only large values count against the null. So we use a one-sided interval. We reject at the \(5\%\) level when the observed statistic exceeds the \(95\)th percentile of its permutation distribution.


Code
# ks_cvm() and the observed statistics stat_obs come from Distributional Comparisons

# Permutation null distribution: reshuffle group labels
perm_stats <- matrix(NA, nrow=999, ncol=2,
    dimnames=list(NULL, c('KS', 'CVM')))
for(b in seq(nrow(perm_stats))){
    D_hs0 <- sample(D_hs)
    y1_perm <- xy_hat[D_hs0, 'wage']
    y2_perm <- xy_hat[!D_hs0, 'wage']
    perm_stats[b, ] <- ks_cvm(y1_perm, y2_perm)
}

# Permutation p-values
p_ks  <- mean(perm_stats[, 'KS']  >= stat_obs['KS'])
p_cvm <- mean(perm_stats[, 'CVM'] >= stat_obs['CVM'])

# One-sided critical values: 95th percentile of each permutation distribution
perm_crit <- apply(perm_stats, 2, quantile, probs=.95)
round(c(KS_stat=stat_obs[['KS']], KS_crit=perm_crit[['KS']], KS_pval=p_ks,
    CVM_stat=stat_obs[['CVM']], CVM_crit=perm_crit[['CVM']], CVM_pval=p_cvm), 3)
##  KS_stat  KS_crit  KS_pval CVM_stat CVM_crit CVM_pval 
##    0.418    0.330    0.007   76.164   34.893    0.003

title: 12  Comparing Two Groups
text:
12.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
A permutation test shuffles the group labels to build a null distribution, while a bootstrap test resamples with replacement from each group separately. Explain why permutation is appropriate for testing “no difference between groups” and when you might prefer the bootstrap instead.
Using the Wages1 data from the Ecdat package, compute the difference in mean wages \(\hat{d} = \hat{m}_{1} - \hat{m}_{2}\) between men and women (the sex variable). Then compute the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) between the two wage distributions by hand (i.e., find the maximum absolute difference between the two ECDF’s evaluated at the pooled sorted data).
Using the mtcars dataset, split cars into two groups based on transmission type (am: 0 = automatic, 1 = manual). Write a permutation test with \(B = 9999\) iterations to test whether the difference in mean mpg between automatic and manual cars is statistically different from zero. Report the \(p\)-value.


Further Reading

https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/ttest.html – comparing two groups with t-tests and effect sizes, with R examples.
https://www.jwilber.me/permutationtest/ – interactive visual explanation of how permutation tests build a null distribution.
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/qualvar/vignettes/wilcox1973.html – the qualitative variation index for comparing categorical distributions across groups.



Recall
This chapter compared two groups by their means, their quantiles, and their whole distributions using \(\hat{\text{KS}}\) and \(\hat{\text{CVM}}\). The main example compared wages in Wages1 for workers with 12 and 16 years of schooling, with permutation tests for \(p\)-values. A small example used summer earnings \(A=\{18,20,25,30\}\) and \(B=\{19,21,24,35\}\). By hand, we found \(\hat{d}=-1.5\) with a permutation \(p\)-value of about \(0.77\), and computed \(\hat{\text{CVM}}=1/4\) cell by cell.

Cramér, Harald. 1928. “On the Composition of Elementary Errors.” Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 1928 (1): 13–74. https://doi.org/10.1080/03461238.1928.10416862.


Kolmogorov, A. N. 1933. “Sulla determinazione empirica di una legge di distribuzione.” Giornale dell’Istituto Italiano degli Attuari 4: 83–91. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-2260-3_15.


Smirnov, N. 1948. “Table for Estimating the Goodness of Fit of Empirical Distributions.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 19 (2): 279–81. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177730256.


von Mises, Richard. 1928. Wahrscheinlichkeit, Statistik und Wahrheit. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-36230-3.

title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
13.1 Describing Groups
Comparing Two Groups split a cardinal outcome by a two-level factor and tested whether the two groups differed. We now extend that idea to \(G\) groups.
This chapter asks three questions.
A cardinal variable can be grouped into a factor with \(G\) levels. We pair these groups with a cardinal outcome.
Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Load the data: 3294 US workers
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# Outcome: hourly wage in 1980 dollars, one value per worker
y_hat <- Wages1[, 'wage']
# Group: years of schooling, cut into three levels (G=3).
# Its levels are the values the categorical variable can take.
# Here they are fewer than 12 years, exactly 12 years, and more than 12 years.
school_g <- cut(Wages1[, 'school'], breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 16),
    labels=c('<12', '12', '>12'))
levels(school_g)
## [1] "<12" "12"  ">12"
table(school_g)
## school_g
##  <12   12  >12 
## 1353 1188  753

title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
Group Summaries
A factor with \(G\) levels splits a cardinal variable into \(G\) conditional distributions, one per group. The group summaries from Bivariate Distributions apply directly. The ECDF shows every observation, and drawing one per group on the same axes compares the whole distributions at once: a curve further to the right has higher values at every quantile. Each line’s thickness scales with its group size.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# One ECDF per schooling group, on the same axes
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, .8, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
n_g <- table(school_g)
lwd_g <- 1.5 + 2.5 * (n_g - min(n_g)) / (max(n_g) - min(n_g))

# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn
plot(NULL, xlim=c(0, 20), ylim=c(0, 1),
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers', main=NA)
for (g in seq_along(levels(school_g))) {
    F_g_hat <- ecdf(y_hat[school_g == levels(school_g)[g]])
    plot(F_g_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[g], lwd=lwd_g[g],
        verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
}
legend('bottomright', bty='n',
    legend=paste0(levels(school_g), ' years (n=', n_g, ')'), col=cols, lty=1, lwd=lwd_g)









Code
# The curve for more than 12 years sits to the right of the other two.
# That holds over the whole range shown.
# So its higher wages are not driven by a few workers.


A table of group sizes and centers puts numbers on the figure. The conditional mean \(\hat{m}_{Y}(g)\) is the average of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) among the \(n_{g}\) observations in group \(g\), and aggregate() computes it for every group at once.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Group size, mean, and median of the hourly wage by schooling group
summary_fun <- function(y_hat) {
    out <- c(n=length(y_hat), mean=mean(y_hat), median=median(y_hat))
    return(out)
}
aggregate(y_hat ~ school_g, FUN=summary_fun)
##   school_g     y_hat.n  y_hat.mean y_hat.median
## 1      <12 1353.000000    4.990937     4.593337
## 2       12 1188.000000    5.668354     5.166288
## 3      >12  753.000000    7.275887     6.736894
# Workers with more than 12 years of schooling have the highest center.
# Those with fewer than 12 years have the lowest.


Are the differences between group centers larger than we would expect by chance?






TipTest Yourself





Here is another example, with murder arrest rates across the four census regions, an unordered factor with \(G=4\) levels. To make the bootstrap intervals in the later callouts meaningful, pretend we observed only a random sample of \(35\) states, as we did with workers in Sampling.


Code
# USArrests covers all 50 states, so it is the whole population of states.
# Draw one random sample of 35 of the 50 states, and use only it from here on
set.seed(111)
state_id <- sample(nrow(USArrests), 35)

# Outcome: murder arrests per 100K, one value per sampled state
murder_hat <- USArrests[state_id, 'Murder']
# Group: the four-level region factor, for the same sampled states.
# Its levels are the values the categorical variable can take.
# The built-in state.region lists them in the same state order as USArrests.
# So it can be paired directly with the murder rates.
region <- state.region[state_id]
levels(region)
## [1] "Northeast"     "South"         "North Central" "West"
table(region)
## region
##     Northeast         South North Central          West 
##             5            14             8             8


The regions are ordered by median murder rate from lowest to highest, and each line’s thickness scales with its group size.


Code
# Order regions by their median murder rate, lowest to highest
region_order <- names(sort(tapply(murder_hat, region, median)))
region <- factor(region, levels=region_order)

# One ECDF per region, on the same axes
line_cols <- hcl.colors(4)
n_g <- table(region)
lwd_g <- 1.5 + 2.5 * (n_g - min(n_g)) / (max(n_g) - min(n_g))

par(mar=c(4, 4, 4.5, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim=range(murder_hat), ylim=c(0, 1),
    xlab='Murder arrests (per 100,000)', ylab='Proportion of states', main=NA)
for (g in seq_along(levels(region))) {
    F_g_hat <- ecdf(murder_hat[region == levels(region)[g]])
    plot(F_g_hat, add=TRUE, col=line_cols[g], lwd=lwd_g[g],
        verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
}
legend('topleft', inset=c(0, -.2), xpd=TRUE, ncol=2, bty='n',
    legend=paste0(levels(region), ' (n=', n_g, ')'), col=line_cols, lty=1, lwd=lwd_g)









Code
# The South has the highest median, so it is last in the legend.
# Its curve sits to the right of the others over its whole range.
# So its higher values are not driven by a few states.


A table of group sizes and centers puts numbers on the figure.


Code
# Group size, mean, and median of the murder rate by region
aggregate(murder_hat ~ region, FUN=summary_fun)
##          region murder_hat.n murder_hat.mean murder_hat.median
## 1     Northeast      5.00000         3.08000           3.30000
## 2 North Central      8.00000         5.48750           4.95000
## 3          West      8.00000         7.15000           7.35000
## 4         South     14.00000        11.58571          12.85000
# The South has the highest center and the Northeast the lowest.

title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
13.2 Equal Medians
In Comparing Two Groups, we bootstrapped a confidence interval for the difference between two medians; with \(G\) groups, we can instead bootstrap one interval per group and compare them all on one figure.






ImportantKey Definition





A notched boxplot draws one box per group \(g=1,\dots,G\) from the group’s lower to upper quartile. Each box has a line at the group median \(\tilde{m}_{Y}(g)\). A notch cut into each side of the box spans a confidence interval for that median (McGill et al. 1978). With a \(95\%\) bootstrap percentile interval, the notch for group \(g\) spans the \(2.5\)th to \(97.5\)th percentiles of the \(B\) bootstrap medians \(\tilde{m}_{Y}^{(b)}(g)\). Each bootstrap median is the median of a resample of the \(n_{g}\) observations in group \(g\).



Notched boxplots are useful for comparing medians across many groups at a glance: if two notches do not overlap, that is strong evidence the two medians differ. Overlapping notches do not show that the medians are equal, because comparing two separate \(95\%\) intervals is stricter than a \(95\%\) test of their difference. Unlike R’s built-in notches, the bootstrap interval needs no normal-theory formula.1


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Bootstrap the median within each schooling group, keeping each group's size
n_boot <- 999
boot_medians <- matrix(NA, n_boot, nlevels(school_g))
colnames(boot_medians) <- levels(school_g)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    for (g in levels(school_g)) {
        y_boot <- sample(y_hat[school_g == g], replace=TRUE)
        boot_medians[b, g] <- median(y_boot)
    }
}

# 95% bootstrap percentile intervals: one column per schooling group
med_ci <- apply(boot_medians, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
round(med_ci, 2)
##        <12   12  >12
## 2.5%  4.39 4.97 6.37
## 97.5% 4.68 5.37 7.10

# Boxplot statistics, with the bootstrap intervals as the notches
bx <- boxplot(y_hat ~ school_g, plot=FALSE)
bx[['conf']] <- med_ci

# One notched box per schooling group, box width scaled to group size
# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn
bxp(bx, notch=TRUE, varwidth=TRUE,
    boxfill=cols, ylim=c(0, 20),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outpch=NA,
    ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', xlab='Years of schooling', main=NA)
title('Wages by years of schooling', font.main=1)
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(y_hat ~ school_g,
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .2), cex=1,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)









Code
# With 753 to 1353 workers per group, every interval is narrow.
# Each one stays well inside its box.
# No two notches overlap.
# That is strong evidence that all three medians differ.


Each box shows the median and the two quartiles, and each dash is one observation. varwidth=TRUE also scales each box’s width to \(\sqrt{n_{g}}\), so a group with more observations draws a wider box.
Researchers use the same displays (Tukey 1977) to compare treatments in experiments.






TipTest Yourself





Here are the notched boxplots for the sampled states from Describing Groups.


Code
# Bootstrap the median within each region, keeping each region's size
n_boot <- 999
boot_medians <- matrix(NA, n_boot, nlevels(region))
colnames(boot_medians) <- levels(region)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    for (g in levels(region)) {
        y_boot <- sample(murder_hat[region == g], replace=TRUE)
        boot_medians[b, g] <- median(y_boot)
    }
}

# 95% bootstrap percentile intervals: one column per region
med_ci <- apply(boot_medians, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
round(med_ci, 2)
##       Northeast North Central West South
## 2.5%        2.1           2.2    4  8.65
## 97.5%       4.4           9.0    9 14.06

# Boxplot statistics, with the bootstrap intervals as the notches
bx <- boxplot(murder_hat ~ region, plot=FALSE)
bx[['conf']] <- med_ci

# One notched box per region, box width scaled to group size
bxp(bx, notch=TRUE, varwidth=TRUE,
    boxfill=hcl.colors(4, alpha=.45),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outpch=NA,
    ylab='Murder arrests (per 100,000)', xlab='Region', main=NA)
title('Murder rates by region', font.main=1)
# Raw Observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(murder_hat ~ region,
    pch='-', col=grey(0, .5), cex=2,
    vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)









Code
# Each dash is one state's murder rate.
# There are only 5 to 14 sampled states per region.
# So three of the four intervals are wider than the box itself.
# Only the South, with the most states, has an interval inside its box.
# The South's notch lies above the Northeast's, so the South's median is higher.


When an interval reaches past a quartile, the notch folds back outside the box. Besides the South and the Northeast, do any other pairs of regions have notches that do not overlap?









TipTest Yourself





Here is another example, with monthly earnings by years of education.


Code
# Monthly earnings of 935 US working men in 1980
data(wage2, package='wooldridge')
wage_hat <- wage2[, 'wage']
educ <- wage2[, 'educ']
# Group years of schooling: dropout, high school, some college, BA, graduate.
educ_g <- cut(educ, breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 15, 16, 18),
    labels=c('<12', '12', '13-15', '16', '17-18'))
n_g <- table(educ_g)
n_g
## educ_g
##   <12    12 13-15    16 17-18 
##    88   393   207   150    97

# Bootstrap the median within each education group, keeping each group's size.
n_boot <- 999
boot_med_g <- matrix(NA, n_boot, nlevels(educ_g))
colnames(boot_med_g) <- levels(educ_g)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    for (g in levels(educ_g)) {
        wage_boot <- sample(wage_hat[educ_g == g], replace=TRUE)
        boot_med_g[b, g] <- median(wage_boot)
    }
}
# 95% bootstrap percentile intervals: one column per education group.
med_ci <- apply(boot_med_g, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
round(med_ci)
##       <12  12 13-15   16 17-18
## 2.5%  625 800   900  981  1000
## 97.5% 800 881  1000 1133  1304




Code
educ_cols <- hcl.colors(nlevels(educ_g))
lwd_g <- 1.5 + 2.5 * (n_g - min(n_g)) / (max(n_g) - min(n_g))
educ_par <- par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4.5, 4.2, 1, 1))

### One ECDF per education group on the same axes, line width scaled to group size

    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers')
for (g in seq_along(levels(educ_g))) {
    plot(ecdf(wage_hat[educ_g == levels(educ_g)[g]]), add=TRUE,
        col=educ_cols[g], lwd=lwd_g[g],
        verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
}
legend('bottomright', legend=paste0(levels(educ_g), ' years (n=', n_g, ')'),
    col=educ_cols, lty=1, lwd=lwd_g, bty='n', cex=.8)

### Boxplots with the bootstrap intervals as notches, box width scaled to group size
bx <- boxplot(wage_hat ~ educ_g, plot=FALSE)
bx[['conf']] <- med_ci
bxp(bx, notch=TRUE, varwidth=TRUE, boxfill=hcl.colors(nlevels(educ_g), alpha=.45),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outpch=NA, main=NA,
    xlab='Years of education', ylab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)')
# Raw observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
