title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
13.3 Equal Means (ANOVA)
In Comparing Two Groups, we tested whether two groups had the same mean. We now extend this to \(G\) groups. The Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) approach asks: are the observed differences in group means larger than we would expect from random variation alone?

Decomposition
If group means differ, some of the spread in \(\hat{y}\) must come from differences between groups rather than within them. We can split each piece out.






ImportantKey Definition





Label each observation \(\hat{y}_{ig}\) for individual \(i\) in group \(g\), where group \(g=1,\dots,G\) has \(n_{g}\) observations with group mean \(\hat{m}_{Y}(g)\), and the grand mean across all \(n=\sum_{g} n_{g}\) observations is \(\hat{m}_{Y}\). The ANOVA decomposition splits the total sum of squares into between-group and within-group pieces: \[\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}(\hat{y}_{ig}-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\hat{\text{TSS}}}
&=
\underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} n_{g} (\hat{m}_{Y}(g)-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\hat{\text{BSS}}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}(\hat{y}_{ig}-\hat{m}_{Y}(g))^2}_{\hat{\text{WSS}}},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\) measures variation in group means around the grand mean and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}\) measures variation of observations around their own group mean.



The decomposition is useful for testing whether group means differ. If they do not, \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\) should be small relative to \(\hat{\text{WSS}}\). The equality holds exactly because the cross-term \(\sum_{g,i}(\hat{y}_{ig}-\hat{m}_{Y}(g))(\hat{m}_{Y}(g)-\hat{m}_{Y})\) vanishes, since the within-group deviations sum to zero around their own group mean.
In R, aov() fits the ANOVA model and summary() returns the standard ANOVA table. The ANOVA table reports \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\) (“Sum Sq” for the group factor) and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}\) (“Sum Sq” for Residuals).


Code
# Fit ANOVA
reg_aov <- aov(y_hat ~ school_g)
summary(reg_aov)
##               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## school_g       2   2541  1270.3     128 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   3291  32654     9.9                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








NoteMust Know





For example, suppose we have \(G=3\) groups with the following data:

Data for Three Groups


Group A
Group B
Group C




4
8
5


5
7
6


6
9
7



Group means: \(\hat{m}_{Y}(A) = 5\), \(\hat{m}_{Y}(B) = 8\), \(\hat{m}_{Y}(C) = 6\). Grand mean: \(\hat{m}_{Y} = (5+8+6)/3 = 19/3 \approx 6.33\). Each group has \(n_{g} = 3\).
Between-group sum of squares: \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{BSS}} &= 3(5-19/3)^2 + 3(8-19/3)^2 + 3(6-19/3)^2 \\
&= 3(16/9) + 3(25/9) + 3(1/9) = 48/9 + 75/9 + 3/9 = 14
\end{aligned}\] Within-group sum of squares: \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{WSS}} &= [(4-5)^2+(5-5)^2+(6-5)^2] + [(8-8)^2+(7-8)^2+(9-8)^2] \\
& + [(5-6)^2+(6-6)^2+(7-6)^2] = 2+2+2 = 6
\end{aligned}\]


Code
# Data
y0_hat <- c(4, 5, 6, 8, 7, 9, 5, 6, 7)
g0 <- factor(c('A', 'A', 'A', 'B', 'B', 'B', 'C', 'C', 'C'))

# Verify by hand
m0_hat <- mean(y0_hat)
m0_g_hat <- aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), mean)$x
n0_g <- aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), length)$x

BSS <- sum(n0_g * (m0_g_hat - m0_hat)^2)
WSS <- sum(aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), function(y_hat) sum((y_hat - mean(y_hat))^2))$x)
cbind(BSS, WSS)
##      BSS WSS
## [1,]  14   6







The F-statistic
We have the decomposition; now we need a single number that tells us when the between-group piece is “large” relative to the within-group piece.






ImportantKey Definition





The ANOVA \(F\)-statistic is the ratio of average between-group variation to average within-group variation: \[\hat{F} = \frac{\hat{\text{BSS}}/(G-1)}{\hat{\text{WSS}}/(n-G)}.\] Writing \(Y_{ig}\) for the random outcome of individual \(i\) in group \(g\), the null is \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i2}]=\dots=\mathbb{E}[Y_{iG}]\).



The ANOVA F-statistic is useful as the global “do any means differ?” test: one number and one \(p\)-value, regardless of how many groups you have. A large \(\hat{F}\) means the group means are more spread out than individual-level noise would predict.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
F_fun <- function(y_hat,g){
    m_y_hat <- mean(y_hat)
    m_g_hat <- aggregate(y_hat, list(g), mean)$x
    n_g <- aggregate(y_hat, list(g), length)$x

    BSS <- sum(n_g * (m_g_hat - m_y_hat)^2)
    WSS <- sum(aggregate(y_hat, list(g), function(y_hat) sum((y_hat - mean(y_hat))^2))$x)

    n <- length(y_hat)
    G <- nlevels(g)
    F_obs <- (BSS/(G-1)) / (WSS/(n-G))
    return(F_obs)
}
F_obs <- F_fun(y_hat=y_hat, g=school_g)
F_obs
## [1] 128.0237


To compute a \(p\)-value, we use a permutation test: shuffle the group labels, which keeps each group’s number of observations fixed, and recompute \(\hat{F}\) each time. Only large values of \(\hat{F}\) count against the null. As with KS and CVM in Comparing Two Groups, we reject at the \(5\%\) level when \(\hat{F}\) exceeds the \(95\)th percentile of the permutation distribution.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Null distribution: shuffle schooling labels to break the Y--group pairing
F_perm <- vector(length=999)
for( b in seq_along(F_perm)){
    g_perm <- sample(school_g, replace=FALSE)
    F_perm[b] <- F_fun(y_hat=y_hat, g=g_perm)
}

# Permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(F_perm >= F_obs)
p_perm
## [1] 0

# One-sided critical value: 95th percentile of the permutation distribution
F_crit <- quantile(F_perm, probs=.95)

hist(F_perm, breaks = 40,
    border = NA,
    freq = FALSE, main = NA, xlab = 'Null Permutation F-statistic',
    xlim = range(c(0, F_perm, F_obs)))
title('Null Permutation F-test', font.main = 1)
abline(v = F_crit, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2)
abline(v = F_obs, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2)
legend('top', legend = c('Observed F', '95th percentile'),
    col = c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)), lwd = 2, bty='n')









Code
# No shuffle comes close to the observed F of about 128.
# So the permutation p-value is zero.








NoteMust Know





Pairing the observed outcomes y_hat with a shuffled vector of group labels breaks the link between outcome and group: under the null, group labels are exchangeable, so this approximates the distribution of \(\hat{F}\) when no group effect exists.



Under the null and additional parametric assumptions, \(\hat{F}\) follows an \(F_{G-1,\;n-G}\) distribution. The parametric \(F_{G-1,\;n-G}\) null distribution requires three assumptions: independent observations, normal errors within each group, and equal variances across groups (homoscedasticity). R reports \(p\)-values from this theoretical distribution by default.






TipTest Yourself





Here is the same test for the sampled states from Describing Groups.


Code
# Fit ANOVA
summary(aov(murder_hat ~ region))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
## region       3  357.3  119.09   10.07 8.64e-05 ***
## Residuals   31  366.5   11.82                     
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# F-statistic
F_obs <- F_fun(y_hat=murder_hat, g=region)
F_obs
## [1] 10.0743

# Null distribution: shuffle region labels to break the Y--group pairing
F_perm <- vector(length=999)
for( b in seq_along(F_perm)){
    g_perm <- sample(region, replace=FALSE)
    F_perm[b] <- F_fun(y_hat=murder_hat, g=g_perm)
}

# Permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(F_perm >= F_obs)
p_perm
## [1] 0

# One-sided critical value: 95th percentile of the permutation distribution
F_crit <- quantile(F_perm, probs=.95)

hist(F_perm, breaks = 40,
    border = NA,
    freq = FALSE, main = NA, xlab = 'Null Permutation F-statistic',
    xlim = range(c(0, F_perm, F_obs)))
title('Null Permutation F-test', font.main = 1)
abline(v = F_crit, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2)
abline(v = F_obs, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2)
legend('top', legend = c('Observed F', '95th percentile'),
    col = c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)), lwd = 2, bty='n')


















TipTest Yourself





The figure below draws the theoretical \(F_{G-1,\;n-G}\) density over the permutation distribution for the sampled states, from the callout above.


Code
# Degrees of freedom for the regional data
n <- length(murder_hat)
G <- nlevels(region)
p_param <- 1 - pf(F_obs, G-1, n-G)

# Compare parametric and permutation p-values
cbind(F_obs, p_param, p_perm)
##        F_obs      p_param p_perm
## [1,] 10.0743 8.639652e-05      0

# Overlay: permutation histogram vs. theoretical F density
hist(F_perm, breaks = 40,
    border = NA,
    freq = FALSE, main = NA, xlab = 'Null F-statistic',
    xlim = range(c(0, F_perm, F_obs)))
title('Permutation vs. Theoretical Null Distribution', font.main = 1)
F_grid <- seq(0, max(c(F_perm, F_obs)), length = 200)
lines(F_grid, df(F_grid, G-1, n-G), col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd = 1, lty = 2)
abline(v = F_obs, col = rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2)
legend('top', legend = c('Null permutation', paste0('F(', G-1, ', ', n-G, ')'), 'Observed F'),
    fill = c(grey(.83), NA, NA), border = NA, # grey(.83) matches the default histogram fill
    lwd = c(NA, 1, 2), lty = c(NA, 2, 1), col = c(NA, rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)), bty = 'n')









If these assumptions are doubtful, the Kruskal-Wallis test below is a safer alternative. As a quick check, compare side-by-side boxplots: if the spread differs across groups or the distributions show strong skewness or kurtosis, be cautious with the parametric test.
For the three-group example above, \(\hat{F}=(14/2)/(6/6)=7\). With \(G-1=2\) and \(n-G=6\) degrees of freedom, we compare it to an \(F_{2,6}\) distribution: \(p = 1 - F_{2,6}(7) \approx 0.027\).


Code
# Data (the three-group example from the decomposition above)
y0_hat <- c(4, 5, 6, 8, 7, 9, 5, 6, 7)
g0 <- factor(c('A', 'A', 'A', 'B', 'B', 'B', 'C', 'C', 'C'))

# Computation
summary(aov(y0_hat ~ g0))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
## g0           2     14       7       7  0.027 *
## Residuals    6      6       1                 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Verify by hand
n0 <- length(y0_hat)
G0 <- nlevels(g0)
m0_hat <- mean(y0_hat)
m0_g_hat <- aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), mean)$x
n0_g <- aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), length)$x
BSS <- sum(n0_g * (m0_g_hat - m0_hat)^2)
WSS <- sum(aggregate(y0_hat, list(g0), function(y_hat) sum((y_hat - mean(y_hat))^2))$x)
Fstat <- (BSS/(G0-1)) / (WSS/(n0-G0))
pval  <- 1 - pf(Fstat, G0-1, n0-G0)
cbind(BSS, WSS, Fstat, pval)
##      BSS WSS Fstat  pval
## [1,]  14   6     7 0.027

title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
13.4 Equal Distributions
ANOVA tests whether group means differ; sometimes the entire distributions differ in ways the mean would miss.

Kruskal-Wallis Test
When data are skewed, heavy-tailed, or only ordinal, a test built on means may overlook differences that show up in the rank order.






ImportantKey Definition





The Kruskal-Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) is a nonparametric test for equal distributions across \(G\) groups, testing \(H_{0}: F_{1} = F_{2} = \dots = F_{G}\) against \(H_{A}:\) at least one \(F_{g}\) differs (where \(F_{g}\) is the continuous distribution of group \(g=1,...G\)). It uses the average ranks within each group rather than the raw observations, so it only requires the data to be ordinal. With two groups it reduces to the Mann-Whitney U (equivalently Wilcoxon rank-sum) test (Wilcoxon 1945; Mann and Whitney 1947).



The Kruskal-Wallis test is useful when the equal-variance normal-error assumption is implausible, as with income, response times, or other heavy-tailed outcomes. Rank-based tests need only the orderings of the data. A significant result tells us that some distribution differs, but not which one; the global rejection has to be followed up with pairwise tests.
To conduct the test, first denote individuals \(i=1,...n\) with overall ranks \(\hat{r}_{1},....\hat{r}_{n}\). Each individual belongs to group \(g=1,...G\), and each group \(g\) has \(n_{g}\) individuals with average rank \(\bar{r}_{g} = \sum_{i} \hat{r}_{i} /n_{g}\). The Kruskal Wallis statistic is \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{KW}} &= (n-1) \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{G} n_{g}( \bar{r}_{g} - \bar{r}  )^2  }{\sum_{i=1}^{n} ( \hat{r}_{i} - \bar{r}  )^2},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\bar{r} = \frac{n+1}{2}\) is the grand mean rank.
In the special case with only two groups, the Kruskal Wallis test reduces to the Mann–Whitney U test (also known as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test). In this case, we can write the hypotheses in terms of individual outcomes in each group, \(Y_{i}\) in one group and \(Y_{j}\) in the other: \(H_{0}: \text{Prob}(Y_{i} > Y_{j})=\text{Prob}(Y_{j} > Y_{i})\) versus \(H_{A}: \text{Prob}(Y_{i} > Y_{j}) \neq \text{Prob}(Y_{j} > Y_{i})\). The corresponding test statistic is \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{U}   &= \min(\hat{U}_{1}, \hat{U}_{2}) \\
\hat{U}_{g} &= \sum_{i~\text{in}~g}\sum_{j~\text{in}~-g}
           \Bigl[\mathbf 1( \hat{y}_{i} > \hat{y}_{j}) + \tfrac12\mathbf 1(\hat{y}_{i} = \hat{y}_{j})\Bigr].
\end{aligned}\]
Interpretation template:

If the Kruskal-Wallis p-value is large, keep the global null and stop.
If the p-value is small, report that at least one group differs.
Report both statistical and practical importance (distribution plots + effect size summaries), not only p-values.



Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
kw <- kruskal.test(y_hat ~ school_g)
kw
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  y_hat by school_g
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 259.3, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16


The test above does not tell us which groups differ. To answer which, use a post-hoc pairwise test together with a multiple-comparisons correction. Here, pairwise.wilcox.test() runs a Mann-Whitney test on each pair of groups, and the Holm correction (Holm 1979) adjusts the \(p\)-values for the number of pairs tested.


Code
pairwise.wilcox.test(y_hat, school_g, p.adjust.method='holm')
## 
##  Pairwise comparisons using Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction 
## 
## data:  y_hat and school_g 
## 
##     <12     12     
## 12  2.6e-10 -      
## >12 < 2e-16 < 2e-16
## 
## P value adjustment method: holm
# All three adjusted p-values are tiny, so every pair of groups differs.


Looking back at the boxplot in Equal Medians, which two groups are closest?






TipTest Yourself





Here are the same tests for the sampled states from Describing Groups.


Code
kw <- kruskal.test(murder_hat ~ region)
kw
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  murder_hat by region
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 16.394, df = 3, p-value = 0.0009415

pairwise.wilcox.test(murder_hat, region, p.adjust.method='holm')
## 
##  Pairwise comparisons using Wilcoxon rank sum exact test 
## 
## data:  murder_hat and region 
## 
##               Northeast North Central West 
## North Central 0.582     -             -    
## West          0.075     0.582         -    
## South         0.001     0.031         0.075
## 
## P value adjustment method: holm


Looking back at the boxplot in the Equal Medians callout, which region stands out?









NoteMust Know





Worked example: \(G=3\) groups with values \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), \(B=\{4,5,6\}\), \(C=\{7,8,9\}\).
Pooling and ranking gives the ranks \(1,\ldots,9\) in order. Group rank averages: \(\bar{r}_{A}=2\), \(\bar{r}_{B}=5\), \(\bar{r}_{C}=8\). Grand mean rank: \(\bar{r}=(n+1)/2=5\). Plug into \(\hat{\text{KW}}\) with \(n=9\), \(n_{g}=3\): \[
\hat{\text{KW}} = (n-1) \cdot \frac{3(2-5)^2 + 3(5-5)^2 + 3(8-5)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{9}(\hat{r}_{i} - 5)^2}
        = 8 \cdot \frac{27 + 0 + 27}{60} = 7.2.
\]


Code
y0_hat <- c(1,2,3, 4,5,6, 7,8,9)
g0 <- factor(rep(c('A','B','C'), each=3))
kruskal.test(y0_hat ~ g0)
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  y0_hat by g0
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 7.2, df = 2, p-value = 0.02732


For the two-group case, the Mann-Whitney statistic counts pairwise wins. Compare \(A=\{1,3,5\}\) to \(B=\{2,4,6\}\): out of \(3\times 3 = 9\) pairs, \(A\) wins three (\((3,2), (5,2), (5,4)\)), so \(\hat{U}_{A}=3\), \(\hat{U}_{B}=6\), giving \(\hat{U}=\min(3,6)=3\).


Code
a0_hat <- c(1,3,5); b0_hat <- c(2,4,6)
wilcox.test(a0_hat, b0_hat)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum exact test
## 
## data:  a0_hat and b0_hat
## W = 3, p-value = 0.7
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0





The Mann-Whitney test compares medians when the two groups have the same shape, so that one distribution is a shifted copy of the other. Otherwise, it tests whether a draw from one group is as likely to exceed a draw from the other as the reverse, and it can reject even when the two medians are equal.






TipTest Yourself





Same shape. Suppose hourly wages in two labor markets have the same right-skewed shape, but every wage in the second market is \(2\) dollars higher. The population medians are \(15\) and \(17\). Consider the probability that a worker drawn from the second market earns more than a worker drawn from the first. Its sample analog is the share of pairs that the second group wins, \(\hat{U}_{2}/(n_{1}n_{2})\) in the notation above. With conf.int=TRUE, wilcox.test also reports a shift estimate, the median of all differences \(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{y}_{j}\) between a worker \(i\) in the second group and a worker \(j\) in the first. Because the shapes match, the shift estimate and the difference in sample medians both estimate the \(2\) dollar gap. So here, a Mann-Whitney rejection is evidence that the medians differ.


Code
# Same right-skewed shape, with every wage in market 2 shifted up by 2 dollars
n_g <- 2000
y1_sim <- 15 + 3 * (rexp(n_g) - log(2)) # population median 15
y2_sim <- 17 + 3 * (rexp(n_g) - log(2)) # population median 17

# Difference in sample medians
median(y2_sim) - median(y1_sim)
## [1] 1.934255

# Share of pairs that market 2 wins
mean(outer(y2_sim, y1_sim, '>'))
## [1] 0.7364205
# A market 2 worker earns more than a market 1 worker about 74% of the time.

# Mann-Whitney test and its shift estimate
mw <- wilcox.test(y2_sim, y1_sim, conf.int=TRUE)
c(shift=unname(mw[['estimate']]), p_value=mw[['p.value']])
##    shift  p_value 
## 1.930319 0.000000

# The market 2 ECDF is the market 1 ECDF moved right by 2
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
F1_hat <- ecdf(y1_sim)
F2_hat <- ecdf(y2_sim)
plot(F1_hat, col=cols[1], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA,
    xlim=c(5, 35), main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage', ylab='Proportion of workers')
plot(F2_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
abline(h=.5, col=grey(.5), lty=3) # each curve crosses this line at its median
legend('bottomright', legend=c('Market 1', 'Market 2'),
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols, bty='n')


















TipTest Yourself





Different shapes. Now suppose wages in the first market are symmetric around \(15\), while the second market keeps the right-skewed shape from above, also with median \(15\). The medians are equal, but the second market has no wages below about \(12.92\), while the first market has a long left tail. When both workers earn less than \(15\), the worker from the second market earns more about \(70\%\) of the time. Overall, the second market wins more than half of all pairs. So the Mann-Whitney test can reject, with a shift estimate above zero, even though the medians are equal.


Code
# Same population median of 15, different shapes
y1_sim <- 15 + 3 * rnorm(n_g)             # symmetric
y2_sim <- 15 + 3 * (rexp(n_g) - log(2))   # right-skewed, no wages below 12.92

# Difference in sample medians is close to zero
median(y2_sim) - median(y1_sim)
## [1] -0.1661474

# Yet market 2 wins more than half of the pairs
mean(outer(y2_sim, y1_sim, '>'))
## [1] 0.5432795
# The sample share is about 54%, and the population share is about 56%.

# So the Mann-Whitney test rejects
mw <- wilcox.test(y2_sim, y1_sim, conf.int=TRUE)
c(shift=unname(mw[['estimate']]), p_value=mw[['p.value']])
##        shift      p_value 
## 4.178188e-01 2.132699e-06
# The shift estimate is about 0.42, and the population shift is about 0.55.
# Both are well above zero, even though the medians are equal.

# The ECDFs cross at the median but differ below it
F1_hat <- ecdf(y1_sim)
F2_hat <- ecdf(y2_sim)
plot(F1_hat, col=cols[1], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA,
    xlim=c(5, 35), main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage', ylab='Proportion of workers')
plot(F2_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
abline(h=.5, col=grey(.5), lty=3) # both curves cross this line at 15
legend('bottomright', legend=c('Market 1', 'Market 2'),
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols, bty='n')














Categorical ANOVA
When the outcome is a factor, we can still ask whether the groups spread their observations across the categories in the same proportions. Let \(\hat{p}(y)\) be the proportion of all \(n\) observations in category \(y\), and \(\hat{p}(y \mid g)\) the proportion of the \(n_{g}\) observations in group \(g\). The categorical ANOVA measures variation with one minus the Herfindahl index, and splits it into between-group and within-group pieces: \[\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\frac{n}{2}\left(1-\hat{H}\right)}_{\hat{\text{TSS}}}
&=
\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{g=1}^{G} n_{g} \sum_{y}\left(\hat{p}(y \mid g)-\hat{p}(y)\right)^2}_{\hat{\text{BSS}}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} \frac{n_{g}}{2}\left(1-\hat{H}(g)\right)}_{\hat{\text{WSS}}},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{H}=\sum_{y}\hat{p}(y)^2\) is the Herfindahl index of the pooled data and \(\hat{H}(g)=\sum_{y}\hat{p}(y \mid g)^2\) is the Herfindahl index within group \(g\).
The categorical ANOVA is useful when the outcome is an unordered factor, such as occupation, brand, or vote choice, where there are no means to compare and no ranks to sort. Recall that \(1-\hat{H}\) is zero when every observation falls in one category and grows as the categories become equally common, so it plays the role of the variance. The pieces are also ordinary ANOVA sums of squares. Make one 0/1 indicator for each category and compute its \(\hat{\text{TSS}}\), \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\), and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}\) as in the decomposition above. Adding each piece up across the categories and halving it gives the three pieces here. With a binary outcome, the two indicators have the same sums of squares, so the categorical ANOVA is exactly the ANOVA of a single 0/1 variable. The share \(\hat{\text{BSS}}/\hat{\text{TSS}}\) reports the fraction of the variation in \(\hat{y}\) that lies between groups.2
For example, cut a cardinal outcome into brackets and sort each group’s observations into them. The brackets are an ordered factor, but the categorical ANOVA ignores that order, so it treats them as it would any unordered factor.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Outcome: hourly wage in four brackets, an ordered factor
# The brackets are up to 4 dollars an hour, 4 to 6, 6 to 8, and above 8.
wage_bracket <- cut(y_hat, breaks=c(0, 4, 6, 8, Inf), ordered_result=TRUE)
tab <- table(school_g, wage_bracket)
tab
##         wage_bracket
## school_g (0,4] (4,6] (6,8] (8,Inf]
##      <12   542   430   236     145
##      12    365   375   251     197
##      >12   126   177   194     256

# Proportions within each schooling group: each bar sums to 1
p_bracket_school <- prop.table(tab, 1)
cols <- hcl.colors(4, alpha=.45)
par(mar=c(4, 4, 3.5, 1))
barplot(t(p_bracket_school), col=cols, border=NA,
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Proportion of workers', main=NA)
legend('top', inset=c(0, -.15), xpd=TRUE, ncol=4, bty='n',
    fill=cols, border=NA, legend=levels(wage_bracket))









Code
# Workers with more schooling are less often in the lowest bracket.
# They are more often in the highest.


The function below computes the three pieces and the between-group share.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Categorical ANOVA: variation is measured by one minus the Herfindahl index
cat_anova <- function(y_hat, g) {
    # Total variation, from the pooled proportions
    n <- length(y_hat)
    p_hat <- table(y_hat) / n
    TSS <- n / 2 * (1 - sum(p_hat^2))
    # Within-group variation, from each group's own proportions
    WSS_g <- tapply(y_hat, g, function(y_g) {
        p_g_hat <- table(y_g) / length(y_g)
        return(length(y_g) / 2 * (1 - sum(p_g_hat^2)))
    })
    WSS <- sum(WSS_g)
    # Between-group variation, from the decomposition
    BSS <- TSS - WSS
    return(c(BSS=BSS, WSS=WSS, TSS=TSS, share=BSS / TSS))
}
cat_anova(wage_bracket, school_g)
##          BSS          WSS          TSS        share 
## 3.017363e+01 1.183800e+03 1.213974e+03 2.485526e-02
# About 2.5% of the variation in wage brackets lies between schooling groups.








TipTest Yourself





Suppose we record how \(n=8\) workers commute, \(n_{g}=4\) from each of two neighborhoods. Neighborhood \(A\) has car, car, car, bus, and neighborhood \(B\) has car, bus, bike, bike.
Pooled, the proportions are \(\hat{p}(\text{car})=4/8\), \(\hat{p}(\text{bus})=2/8\), and \(\hat{p}(\text{bike})=2/8\), so \(\hat{H}=1/4+1/16+1/16=3/8\) and \(\hat{\text{TSS}}=\frac{8}{2}(1-3/8)=5/2\). Within \(A\), \(\hat{H}(A)=(3/4)^2+(1/4)^2=5/8\), and within \(B\), \(\hat{H}(B)=(1/4)^2+(1/4)^2+(2/4)^2=3/8\). So \(\hat{\text{WSS}}=\frac{4}{2}(1-5/8)+\frac{4}{2}(1-3/8)=3/4+5/4=2\). For \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\), each neighborhood’s proportions differ from the pooled ones by \(1/4\) in two categories and by \(0\) in the third, so \(\hat{\text{BSS}}=\frac{1}{2}[4(1/16+0+1/16)+4(1/16+0+1/16)]=1/2\). The pieces add up, \(5/2=1/2+2\), and the between-group share is \(\hat{\text{BSS}}/\hat{\text{TSS}}=1/5\).


Code
# Commute mode of 8 workers, 4 from each neighborhood
y0_hat <- factor(c('car', 'car', 'car', 'bus', 'car', 'bus', 'bike', 'bike'))
g0 <- factor(c('A', 'A', 'A', 'A', 'B', 'B', 'B', 'B'))
table(g0, y0_hat)
##    y0_hat
## g0  bike bus car
##   A    0   1   3
##   B    2   1   1
cat_anova(y0_hat, g0)
##   BSS   WSS   TSS share 
##   0.5   2.0   2.5   0.2





As with the ANOVA \(F\)-statistic, we get a \(p\)-value by shuffling the group labels and recomputing the share each time.


Code
# Observed between-group share
share_obs <- cat_anova(wage_bracket, school_g)[['share']]

# Null distribution: shuffle schooling labels to break the outcome--group pairing
share_perm <- rep(NA, 999)
for (b in seq_along(share_perm)) {
    g_perm <- sample(school_g, replace=FALSE)
    share_perm[b] <- cat_anova(wage_bracket, g_perm)[['share']]
}

# Permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(share_perm >= share_obs)
p_perm
## [1] 0

# One-sided critical value: 95th percentile of the permutation distribution
share_crit <- quantile(share_perm, probs=.95)

hist(share_perm, breaks=40,
    border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Null Permutation Between-Group Share',
    xlim=range(c(0, share_perm, share_obs)))
title('Null Permutation Categorical ANOVA', font.main=1)
abline(v=share_crit, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=share_obs, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
legend('top', legend=c('Observed share', '95th percentile'),
    col=c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)), lwd=2, bty='n')









Because the brackets are ordered, the Kruskal-Wallis test also applies.


Code
# Kruskal-Wallis ranks the brackets, so it uses their order
kruskal.test(wage_bracket ~ school_g)
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  wage_bracket by school_g
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 241.42, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16
# Both this test and the categorical ANOVA reject.
# The schooling groups differ along one direction, from low to high brackets.


Ranks concentrate on differences along one direction, from low to high brackets. The categorical ANOVA spreads its attention over every way the proportions could differ, so a rank test is usually more powerful when the categories are ordered. The categorical ANOVA can still detect differences that ranks miss, such as one group concentrated in the middle brackets and another split between the two extremes.






TipTest Yourself





Here is the same analysis for the sampled states from Describing Groups. The urban population bands from Ordered Factors sort each region’s states into mostly rural, mixed, and mostly urban.


Code
# Outcome: urban population in three bands, an ordered factor, for the sampled states
urban_band <- cut(USArrests[state_id, 'UrbanPop'], breaks=c(0, 50, 75, 100),
    labels=c('mostly rural', 'mixed', 'mostly urban'), ordered_result=TRUE)
tab <- table(region, urban_band)
tab
##                urban_band
## region          mostly rural mixed mostly urban
##   Northeast                1     1            3
##   North Central            1     7            0
##   West                     0     3            5
##   South                    5     7            2

# Proportions within each region: each bar sums to 1
p_band_region <- prop.table(tab, 1)
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, .8, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
par(mar=c(4, 4, 3.5, 1))
barplot(t(p_band_region), col=cols, border=NA,
    xlab='Region', ylab='Proportion of states', main=NA)
legend('top', inset=c(0, -.15), xpd=TRUE, ncol=3, bty='n',
    fill=cols, border=NA, legend=levels(urban_band))









Code
# The South and North Central lean rural.
# The Northeast and West lean urban.


The function from above computes the three pieces and the between-group share.


Code
cat_anova(urban_band, region)
##        BSS        WSS        TSS      share 
##  2.3785714  8.3642857 10.7428571  0.2214096
# About 22% of the variation in urban bands lies between regions.


As above, we get a \(p\)-value by shuffling the group labels and recomputing the share each time.


Code
# Observed between-group share
share_obs <- cat_anova(urban_band, region)[['share']]

# Null distribution: shuffle region labels to break the outcome--group pairing
share_perm <- rep(NA, 999)
for (b in seq_along(share_perm)) {
    g_perm <- sample(region, replace=FALSE)
    share_perm[b] <- cat_anova(urban_band, g_perm)[['share']]
}

# Permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(share_perm >= share_obs)
p_perm
## [1] 0.01801802

# One-sided critical value: 95th percentile of the permutation distribution
share_crit <- quantile(share_perm, probs=.95)

hist(share_perm, breaks=40,
    border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Null Permutation Between-Group Share',
    xlim=range(c(0, share_perm, share_obs)))
title('Null Permutation Categorical ANOVA', font.main=1)
abline(v=share_crit, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=share_obs, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Observed share', '95th percentile'),
    col=c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)), lwd=2, bty='n')









Because the bands are ordered, the Kruskal-Wallis test also applies.


Code
# Kruskal-Wallis ranks the bands, so it uses their order
kruskal.test(urban_band ~ region)
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  urban_band by region
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 9.284, df = 3, p-value = 0.02574
# The categorical ANOVA gives the smaller p-value, about 0.018 against 0.026.
# The regions differ partly along one direction, from rural to urban.
# Ranks concentrate on that direction.
# In this sample, 7 of North Central's 8 states are in the middle band.
# That pattern contributes more to the categorical ANOVA than any other region.
# It contributes the least to the Kruskal-Wallis statistic.











TipTest Yourself





For the sampled states in the callout above, make a binary outcome that marks the mostly urban states. Check that the categorical ANOVA of this outcome gives the same \(\hat{\text{BSS}}\) and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}\) as the ordinary ANOVA of the 0/1 variable.


Code
# 1 for mostly urban states, 0 otherwise
d_hat <- as.numeric(urban_band == 'mostly urban')
cat_anova(factor(d_hat), region)
##      BSS      WSS      TSS    share 
## 2.353571 4.789286 7.142857 0.329500
summary(aov(d_hat ~ region))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
## region       3  2.354  0.7845   5.078 0.00563 **
## Residuals   31  4.789  0.1545                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: 13  Comparing Multiple Groups
text:
13.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Load Wages1 from the Ecdat package. Draw a boxplot of wage by sex, then add an ECDF of wage for each sex on the same axes. Compute the mean and median wage for each sex with aggregate(). Does one sex’s ECDF sit to the right of the other’s over the whole range, or do the curves cross?
An ANOVA \(F\)-test rejects the null that all group means are equal. Does this tell you which group is different, or only that at least one differs?
Using the USArrests dataset with state.region as the grouping variable, compute the between-group sum of squares (\(\hat{\text{BSS}}\)) and within-group sum of squares (\(\hat{\text{WSS}}\)) for Assault by hand (using aggregate()). Verify your \(\hat{F}\) statistic matches the output of summary(aov(Assault ~ state.region, data = ...)).


Further Reading

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/7-htaciimr.html – hypothesis tests for comparing groups in a regression framework, including F-tests and joint restrictions.
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat462/node/137/ – ANOVA as a special case of regression, with examples of multiple group comparisons.



Recall
This chapter described several groups with ECDFs and a table of group means. We compared their medians with bootstrap notches on boxplots. We then tested whether the differences reflected more than chance. ANOVA splits variation into between-group and within-group pieces and combines them into an \(F\)-statistic. In the three-group example with \(A=\{4,5,6\}, B=\{8,7,9\}, C=\{5,6,7\}\), we found \(\hat{\text{BSS}}=14\) and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}=6\) by hand. The function aov(y0_hat ~ g0) gives the same numbers. The Kruskal-Wallis test replaced outcomes with ranks when the equal-variance normal-error assumptions were doubtful. The categorical ANOVA measured the variation of a factor outcome with one minus the Herfindahl index; for the commutes in two neighborhoods it gave \(\hat{\text{TSS}}=5/2\), \(\hat{\text{BSS}}=1/2\), and \(\hat{\text{WSS}}=2\) by hand.




Holm, Sture. 1979. “A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure.” Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6: 65–70. https://www.jstor.org/stable/4615733.


Kruskal, William H., and W. Allen Wallis. 1952. “Use of Ranks in One-Criterion Variance Analysis.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 47 (260): 583–621. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1952.10483441.


Mann, H. B., and D. R. Whitney. 1947. “On a Test of Whether One of Two Random Variables Is Stochastically Larger Than the Other.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 18 (1): 50–60. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177730491.


McGill, Robert, John W. Tukey, and Wayne A. Larsen. 1978. “Variations of Box Plots.” The American Statistician 32 (1): 12–16. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1978.10479236.


Tukey, John Wilder. 1977. Exploratory Data Analysis. Vol. 2. Springer.


Wilcoxon, Frank. 1945. “Individual Comparisons by Ranking Methods.” Biometrics Bulletin 1 (6): 80–83. https://doi.org/10.2307/3001968.

title: 14  Statistics of Association
text:
14.1 Cardinal Data
There are several ways to statistically assess the relationship between two variables. The major differences surround whether the data are cardinal or an ordered/unordered factor. In all cases, these statistics measure association, not causation.
This chapter asks three questions.

title: 14  Statistics of Association
text:
Pearson (Linear) Correlation
When two variables are cardinal, the foundational measure of how they move together is the covariance.






ImportantKey Definition





The covariance \(\hat{c}_{XY}\) is the average product of paired deviations from each variable’s mean (where \(\hat{m}_{X}\) and \(\hat{m}_{Y}\) are the sample means): \[\hat{c}_{XY} =  \sum_{i=1}^{n} [\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}] [\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}] / n.\]



The covariance is useful as a building block for other linear two-variable statistics. It is positive when \(\hat{x}_{i}\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) tend to be above or below their means together. It is negative when they tend to move apart, and zero when there is no linear co-movement. Its units are the units of \(\hat{x}_{i}\) times the units of \(\hat{y}_{i}\), which makes raw values hard to compare across datasets. Note that the covariance of \(\hat{x}\) with itself is just its variance, \(\hat{c}_{XX}=\hat{v}_{X}\), and the standard deviation is \(\hat{s}_{X}=\sqrt{\hat{v}_{X}}\).
For an interpretable, unit-free measure that is comparable across datasets, we rescale the covariance.






ImportantKey Definition





The Pearson correlation \(\hat{r}_{XY}\) (Pearson 1896) rescales the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations: \[\hat{r}_{XY} = \frac{ \hat{c}_{XY} }{ \hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y}}.\]



The Pearson correlation is useful as the standard unit-free summary of linear association. It is constrained to \([-1, 1]\), with \(+1\) for a perfect rising line, \(-1\) for a perfect falling line, and \(0\) for no linear association. Because the bounds are the same in every dataset, it lets us compare the strength of two-variable associations across studies.






NoteMust Know





What is the correlation for the dataset \(\{ (0,0.1) , (1, 0.3), (2, 0.2) \}\)? Find the answer both mathematically and computationally.
Mathematically, there are five steps.
Step 1: Compute the means \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m}_{X} &= \frac{0+1+2}{3} = 1 \\
\hat{m}_{Y} &= \frac{0.1+0.3+0.2}{3} = 0.2
\end{aligned}\]
Step 2: Compute the deviances \[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\hat{x}_{i}   & 0   & 1 & 2 \\
\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X} & -1  & 0 & 1 \\
\hat{y}_{i}   & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\
\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y}   & -0.1 & 0.1 & 0
\end{array}
\]
Step 3: Compute the Covariance \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{c}_{XY} &=
\sum  (\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})/n
= \left[ (-1)(-0.1) + 0(0.1) + 1(0) \right] \frac{1}{3}
=  (0.1) \frac{1}{3}
= 1/30
\end{aligned}\]
Step 4: Compute Standard Deviations \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{v}_{X} &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X}\right)^2 / n
= \left[(-1)^2+0^2+1^2 \right]/3
= 2/3 \\
\hat{s}_{X} &= \sqrt{2/3} \\
\hat{v}_{Y} &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y} \right)^2 / n
= \left[ (-0.1)^2+(0.1)^2+0^2 \right]/3
= \left[0.01+0.01\right]/3
= \frac{2}{100} \frac{1}{3} = 2/300 \\
\hat{s}_{Y} &= \sqrt{2/300}
\end{aligned}\]
Step 5: Compute the Correlation \[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{s}_{X} \hat{s}_{Y}}
&= \frac{1/30}{ \sqrt{2/3}  \sqrt{2/300}}
= \frac{1/30}{ 2 /\sqrt{900}}
= \frac{1/30}{2/30} = 1/2
\end{aligned}\]
Note that this value suggests a positive relationship between the variables.
Computationally, we do the same steps


Code
# Create the Data
x0_hat <- c(0, 1, 2)
x0_hat
## [1] 0 1 2
y0_hat <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2)
y0_hat
## [1] 0.1 0.3 0.2

# Compute the Means
m_x_hat <- mean(x0_hat)
m_y_hat <- mean(y0_hat)

# Compute the Deviances
dev_X <- x0_hat - m_x_hat
dev_Y <- y0_hat - m_y_hat

# Compute the Covariance
cov_manual <-  sum(dev_X * dev_Y) / length(x0_hat)

# Compute the Standard Deviations
v_x_hat <- sum(dev_X^2) / length(x0_hat)
s_x_hat <- sqrt(v_x_hat)
v_y_hat <- sum(dev_Y^2) / length(y0_hat)
s_y_hat <- sqrt(v_y_hat)

# Compute the Correlation
cor_manual <- cov_manual / (s_x_hat * s_y_hat)
cor_manual
## [1] 0.5

# Verify with the built-in function
cor(x0_hat, y0_hat)
## [1] 0.5





For example, the code below draws a scatterplot of two cardinal variables and computes their covariance and correlation.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Load the Data: 3294 US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage

# Scatterplot
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')









Code
# Workers with more schooling tend to earn more.
# Wages vary a lot at every level of schooling.

# Covariance: cov() divides by n-1 rather than n, which barely matters with n=3294
cov(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
## [1] 1.530776
# The covariance is positive.
# Its units (years times dollars per hour) are hard to judge.

# Correlation
xy_cor <- cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
xy_cor
## [1] 0.2824925
# The correlation of about 0.28 suggests a positive but weak linear association.




Hypothesis Testing
You can conduct hypothesis tests for these statistics using the same procedures we learned for univariate data, Intervals. For example, you can do so by inverting a confidence interval. The histogram below shows the bootstrap distribution of the correlation, with the interval and \(0\) marked.






NoteMust Know







Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# xy_hat and xy_cor defined above
# Bootstrap Distribution of Correlation
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
bootstrap_cor <- rep(NA, 9999)

    xy_cor_b <- cor(xy_boot[, 'x_hat'], xy_boot[, 'y_hat'])

Importantly, we can also impose the null hypothesis of no association by reshuffling the data. If we resample without replacement, this is known as a permutation test.

Drawing \(\hat{x}\) with replacement also breaks the pairing, which gives the Null Bootstrap row of the table. Compare this distribution to the permutation distribution above.





Robust Correlation
When the data contain outliers, the mean-based covariance can be misleading and a robust alternative is needed. The Falk codeviance \(\tilde{c}_{XY}\) (Falk 1997) replaces the mean-based average in the covariance with the median of paired deviations from each variable’s median (where \(\tilde{m}_{X}\) and \(\tilde{m}_{Y}\) are the sample medians): \[\tilde{c}_{XY} = \text{Med}\left\{ (\hat{x}_{i} - \tilde{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \tilde{m}_{Y}) \right\}.\]
Falk’s median correlation \(\tilde{r}_{XY}\) rescales the codeviance by the product of the two median absolute deviations: \[\tilde{r}_{XY} = \frac{ \tilde{c}_{XY} }{ \hat{\text{MAD}}_{X} \hat{\text{MAD}}_{Y}}.\]
The Falk codeviance is useful for cardinal data with outliers or heavy tails, such as income and prices. One extreme observation can move \(\hat{c}_{XY}\) by a lot but \(\tilde{c}_{XY}\) by very little. The median, \(\hat{\text{IQR}}\), and \(\hat{\text{MAD}}\) from Part 1 are robust for the same reason.1 Falk’s median correlation \(\tilde{r}_{XY}\) typically lies in \([-1,1]\) but, unlike the Pearson correlation, not always. Ties can be a problem, however. Every observation tied at a median has a product of \(0\), so with enough ties the median product is also \(0\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
codev <- function(xy) {
  # Compute medians for each column
  med_hat <- apply(xy, 2, median)
  # Subtract the medians from each column
  xm <- sweep(xy, 2, med_hat, '-')
  # Return the median of the paired products
  CoDev <- median(xm[, 1] * xm[, 2])
  return(CoDev)
}
med_cor <- function(xy) {
  # Compute the medians of absolute deviation
  med_hat <- apply(xy, 2, median)
  xm <- sweep(xy, 2, med_hat, '-')
  MadProd <- prod( apply(abs(xm), 2, median) )
  # Return the robust correlation measure
  return( codev(xy) / MadProd)
}
# xy_hat defined above
xy_codev <- codev(xy_hat)
xy_codev
## [1] 0
xy_med_cor <- med_cor(xy_hat)
xy_med_cor
## [1] 0
# Both are exactly 0, although the Pearson correlation is about 0.28.
# The median worker has 12 years of schooling, and so do 36% of all workers.
# Their products are all 0, and the median product falls among them.








TipTest Yourself





Compute the Codeviance for the dataset \(\{(1,2),(2,1),(3,4),(4,3),(5,6)\}\).
The medians are \(\tilde{m}_{X}=3\) and \(\tilde{m}_{Y}=3\), giving signed deviations and products
\[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
\hat{x}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{X} & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\
\hat{y}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{Y} & -1 & -2 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\
(\hat{x}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\tilde{m}_{Y}) & 2 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 6
\end{array}\]
The Codeviance is the median of those products: \(\tilde{c}_{XY}=\text{Med}\{0,0,2,2,6\}=2\). The median absolute deviations are \(\hat{\text{MAD}}_{X}=\text{Med}\{0,1,1,2,2\}=1\) and \(\hat{\text{MAD}}_{Y}=\text{Med}\{0,1,1,2,3\}=1\), so Falk’s median correlation is \(\tilde{r}_{XY}=2/(1\cdot1)=2\). Here \(\tilde{r}_{XY}\) exceeds \(1\): unlike Pearson’s correlation, Falk’s median correlation is not confined to \([-1,1]\).

title: 14  Statistics of Association
text:
14.2 Factor Data

Two Ordered Factors
When the data are ordered (rankings or ordered categories), we can summarize association by counting which pairs of observations agree in direction.






ImportantKey Definition





Kendall’s rank correlation \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) (Kendall 1938) is the share of variable-pairs that agree in direction (concordant) minus the share that disagree (discordant): \[\hat{\text{KT}} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i} \sum_{j > i} \text{sgn} \Bigl( (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{x}_{j})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{j}) \Bigr),\] where the sign function is \[\text{sgn}(z) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } z > 0\\ 0  & \text{if } z = 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } z < 0 \end{cases}.\]



Kendall’s \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) is useful for any monotone relationship: the values do not have to fall on a straight line, only have consistent ordering. Because it only uses signs, it works for any ordinal data (rankings, ordered categories) where arithmetic averages are not meaningful. The bounds \([-1, 1]\) make it directly comparable to the Pearson correlation: a value closer to \(+1\) suggests positive association in rankings, \(-1\) negative, and \(0\) no association in the ordering. For example, the table below cross-classifies two ordered variables, and \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) summarizes it.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Load the Data
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# Group hourly wages into four ordered brackets
wage_bracket <- cut(Wages1[, 'wage'], breaks=c(0, 4, 6, 8, Inf), ordered_result=TRUE)
xy_ord_hat <- data.frame(x_hat=Wages1[, 'school'], y_hat=wage_bracket) # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=wage bracket
table(xy_ord_hat)
##      y_hat
## x_hat (0,4] (4,6] (6,8] (8,Inf]
##    3      0     1     0       0
##    4      1     0     0       1
##    5      2     2     1       0
##    6      4     7     3       0
##    7     11     9     3       1
##    8     51    22     9       4
##    9     90    52    13       6
##    10   169   119    78      33
##    11   214   218   129     100
##    12   365   375   251     197
##    13    63    93    93      90
##    14    50    55    59     100
##    15    13    23    40      58
##    16     0     6     2       8
# Both are ordered categories: 12 years is more than 10.
# The top bracket pays more than the bottom one.

# Kendall's rank correlation uses only the order of the categories
KT <- cor(xy_ord_hat[, 'x_hat'], as.integer(xy_ord_hat[, 'y_hat']), method='kendall')
round(KT, 3)
## [1] 0.236
# The value is positive.
# So workers with more schooling tend to be in higher wage brackets.








NoteMust Know





Kendall’s \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) also applies to cardinal data, because it only uses the ordering of the values. Converting each variable to ranks first does not change the statistic.


Code
# xy_hat defined above
# Convert each variable to ranks
xy_rank_hat <- xy_hat
xy_rank_hat[, 'x_hat'] <- rank(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
xy_rank_hat[, 'y_hat'] <- rank(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
# plot(xy_rank_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1))
KT_rank <- cor(xy_rank_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_rank_hat[, 'y_hat'], method = 'kendall')
round(KT_rank, 3)
## [1] 0.219
# Same value using the raw data
round(cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], method='kendall'), 3)
## [1] 0.219











NoteMust Know





Compute Kendall’s \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) for the dataset \(\{(1,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,4)\}\).
With \(n=4\) there are \(n(n-1)/2=6\) pairs. For each pair we take the sign of \((\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{x}_{j})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{y}_{j})\): a pair is concordant (\(+1\)) if both variables move the same way, discordant (\(-1\)) if they move oppositely.

\hat{\text{KT}} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}\text{sgn}(\cdots) = \frac{2}{4\cdot3}(5-1) = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67.
\]


Code
cor(c(1,2,3,4), c(1,3,2,4), method='kendall')
## [1] 0.6666667





You construct sampling distributions and conduct hypothesis tests for Kendall’s rank correlation statistic in the same way you do for Pearson’s Correlation statistic and Falk’s Codeviance statistic.






TipTest Yourself





Test whether Kendall’s correlation statistic is statistically different from \(0\). Expand on the example below to use bootstrapping.


Code

KT <- cor(xy_ord_hat[, 'x_hat'], as.integer(xy_ord_hat[, 'y_hat']), method='kendall')





Kendall’s rank correlation coefficient can also be used for non-linear relationships, where Pearson’s correlation coefficient often falls short. It almost always helps to visualize your data first before summarizing it with a statistic.











Two Unordered Factors
When neither variable has a meaningful order, we organize the data as a contingency table and summarize the strength of association with a single bounded score. Cramer’s V \(\hat{\text{CramV}}\) (Cramér 1946) rescales the chi-squared statistic \(\hat{\chi}^{2}\) into a \([0, 1]\) score for the strength of association between two categorical variables in a \(K\times J\) contingency table: \[\hat{\chi}^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \frac{(\hat{o}_{kj} - \hat{e}_{kj})^2}{\hat{e}_{kj}}, \qquad \hat{\text{CramV}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\chi}^2 / n}{\min(J - 1, \, K - 1)}},\] where \(\hat{o}_{kj}\) is the observed frequency in cell \((k, j)\), \(\hat{e}_{kj} = \hat{\text{RF}}_{k} \cdot \hat{\text{CF}}_{j} / n\) is the expected frequency under independence, and \(\hat{\text{RF}}_{k}=\sum_{j} \hat{o}_{kj}\), \(\hat{\text{CF}}_{j}=\sum_{k} \hat{o}_{kj}\) are the row and column totals.
Cramer’s V is useful for two unordered categorical variables, such as occupation and region. Reordering the rows or columns of the table does not change it. The chi-squared piece measures how far observed counts are from what we would expect if \(\hat{x}\) and \(\hat{y}\) were independent. Dividing by \(n \cdot \min(J - 1, K - 1)\) rescales it into a bounded score, so different tables are comparable. A value of \(0\) suggests no association, and a value closer to \(1\) suggests a strong association.
For example, the table below cross-classifies two categorical variables, and the function below computes their Cramer’s V.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Pair each worker's sex with a schooling group, as in Comparing Multiple Groups
# The schooling groups have an order, but Cramer's V ignores it.
# So we treat both variables as unordered.
school_g <- cut(Wages1[, 'school'], breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 16), labels=c('<12', '12', '>12'))
xy_cat_hat <- data.frame(x_hat=Wages1[, 'sex'], y_hat=school_g) # x_hat=sex, y_hat=schooling group
table(xy_cat_hat)
##         y_hat
## x_hat    <12  12 >12
##   female 567 594 408
##   male   786 594 345
# Men are more likely than women to have fewer than 12 years of schooling.

CV <- function(xy){
    # Create a contingency table from the categorical variables
    tbl <- table(xy)
    # Compute the chi-square statistic (without Yates' continuity correction)
    chi2 <- chisq.test(tbl, correct=FALSE)[['statistic']]
    # Total sample size
    n <- sum(tbl)
    # Compute the minimum degrees of freedom (min(rows-1, columns-1))
    df_min <- min(nrow(tbl) - 1, ncol(tbl) - 1)
    # Calculate Cramer's V
    V <- sqrt((chi2 / n) / df_min)
    return(V)
}
CV(xy_cat_hat)
## X-squared 
## 0.1007045
# Cramer's V of about 0.10 suggests a weak association.

# DescTools::CramerV( table(xy_cat_hat) )

Here is the same calculation for a second table, UCBAdmissions.

# CV defined above
# Built-in: 4526 applications to six graduate departments at Berkeley in 1973
# One row per (Admit, Gender, Dept) cell, with the number of applicants in Freq

## x_hat Admitted Rejected

##     B      370      215

CV(xy_cat2_hat)
## X-squared 
## 0.4148446
# Cramer's V is about 0.41.
# This reflects a strong association between department and admission.

##   West            5      4    2
CV(xy_cat3_hat)
## X-squared 
## 0.4085406











TipTest Yourself





You can also apply Cramer’s V to cardinal data after cutting each variable into bins. This throws away the ordering of the bins, so Kendall’s \(\hat{\text{KT}}\) or Pearson’s \(\hat{r}_{XY}\) usually make better use of the data.


Code
# xy_hat and CV defined above
# Cut each variable into bins: years of schooling into 3, hourly wages into 4
# Wages have a long right tail, so use the brackets above, not equal widths
xy_bin_hat <- xy_hat
xy_bin_hat[, 'x_hat'] <- cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], 3)
xy_bin_hat[, 'y_hat'] <- cut(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'], breaks=c(0, 4, 6, 8, Inf))
table(xy_bin_hat)
##              y_hat
## x_hat         (0,4] (4,6] (6,8] (8,Inf]
##   (2.99,7.33]    18    19     7       2
##   (7.33,11.7]   524   411   229     143
##   (11.7,16]     491   552   445     453
CV(xy_bin_hat)
## X-squared 
## 0.1471187











TipTest Yourself





Compute Cramer’s V for this \(2\times2\) table of \(100\) workers, cross-classifying a college degree against employment.
\[\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
& \text{employed} & \text{unemployed} & \text{Row total}\\
\hline
\text{degree}    & 30 & 10 & 40\\
\text{no degree} & 20 & 40 & 60\\
\hline
\text{Column total} & 50 & 50 & 100
\end{array}\]
If degree and employment were independent, the expected count in each cell is \(\hat{e}_{kj}=\hat{\text{RF}}_{k}\hat{\text{CF}}_{j}/n\). For the top-left cell, \(\hat{e}_{11}=40\cdot50/100=20\); all four expected counts are \((20,20,30,30)\). \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\chi}^2 &= \frac{(30-20)^2}{20}+\frac{(10-20)^2}{20}+\frac{(20-30)^2}{30}+\frac{(40-30)^2}{30} = 5+5+\frac{10}{3}+\frac{10}{3} = \frac{50}{3} \approx 16.67.
\end{aligned}\] With \(K=2\) rows and \(J=2\) columns, \(\min(J-1,K-1)=1\), so \[
\hat{\text{CramV}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\chi}^2/n}{\min(J-1,K-1)}} = \sqrt{\frac{(50/3)/100}{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{6}} \approx 0.41.
\]


Code
# Observed 2x2 table
O <- rbind(degree    = c(employed=30, unemployed=10),
           no_degree = c(20, 40))
n0 <- sum(O)

# Expected counts under independence
E <- outer(rowSums(O), colSums(O)) / n0

# Chi-square statistic and Cramer's V
chi2 <- sum((O - E)^2 / E)
df_min <- min(nrow(O)-1, ncol(O)-1)
c(chi2=chi2, CramerV=sqrt((chi2/n0)/df_min))
##       chi2    CramerV 
## 16.6666667  0.4082483





You construct sampling distributions and conduct hypothesis tests for Cramer’s V statistic in the same way you do for the other statistics.

title: 14  Statistics of Association
text:
14.3 Association is not Causation
None of the tools in this chapter alone identifies what would happen to \(Y_{i}\) if we intervened and changed \(X_{i}\) (Holland 1986). Sampling variability is one problem: relationships in the population may not appear in a sample, and apparent sample relationships may not exist in the population. Hypothesis tests help quantify that uncertainty, but statistical significance does not distinguish association from causation. Two other problems remain: real relationships can average out, and random data can acquire mechanically induced relationships. To make both problems concrete, we focus on the Pearson correlation from Cardinal Data and examine

Causation without correlation
Correlation without causation


Causation without correlation
Examples of the first problem include nonlinear effects and heterogeneous effects that average out. For example, wages tend to rise with age early in a career and then flatten or fall, and a minimum wage increase can raise pay for some workers while others lose their jobs.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
n <- 10000

# X causes Y via Y = X^2 + noise
x_sim <- runif(n, min = -1, max = 1)
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.1)
y_sim <- x_sim^2 + epsilon  # clear causal effect of X on Y
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')

# Correlation over the entire range
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)











Code
# Heterogeneous Effects
x_sim <- rnorm(n) # Randomized 'treatment'

# Heterogeneous effects based on group
group <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.5)
epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_sim <- ifelse(group == 1,
            x_sim + epsilon,   # positive effect
            -x_sim + epsilon)  # negative effect
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')

# Correlation in the pooled sample
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)











Correlation without causation
Examples of the second problem include shared denominators and selection bias that induce correlations.
Consider three completely random variables. We can induce a mechanical relationship between the first two variables by dividing them both by the third variable. Per-capita statistics are a common real case, such as crimes per resident and police officers per resident across cities, which share population as the denominator.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
n <- 20000

# Independent components
A <- runif(n)
B <- runif(n)
C <- runif(n)
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(A, B, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='A', ylab='B')
cor_ab <- round(cor(A, B), 2)
title(paste0('Independent Variables\nCor: ', cor_ab), font.main=1)

# Ratios with a shared denominator
x_sim <- A / C
y_sim <- B / C
plot(x_sim, y_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')
cor_sim <- round(cor(x_sim, y_sim), 2)
title(paste0('With Common Divisor\nCor: ', cor_sim), font.main=1)









Code

# Correlation
cor(x_sim, y_sim)
## [1] 0.8094966


Consider an admissions rule into university: applicants are accepted if they have either high test scores or strong extracurriculars. Even if there is no general relationship between test scores and extracurriculars, you will see one amongst university students. Real datasets are often selected in a similar way, so their relationships describe the selected group rather than everyone.


Code

# Independent traits in the population
test_score        <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
extracurriculars  <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Selection above thresholds
threshold <- 1.0
admitted <- (test_score > threshold) | (extracurriculars > threshold)
mean(admitted)  # admission rate
## [1] 0.294

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
# Full population
plot(test_score, extracurriculars,
     pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
     main=NA, xlab='Test Score', ylab='Extracurriculars')
cor_all <- round(cor(test_score, extracurriculars), 2)
title(paste0('General Sample\nCor: ', cor_all), font.main=1)
# Admitted only
plot(test_score[admitted], extracurriculars[admitted],
     pch=16, col=grey(0, .05),
     main=NA, xlab='Test Score', ylab='Extracurriculars')
cor_adm <- round(cor(test_score[admitted], extracurriculars[admitted]), 2)
title(paste0('University Sample\nCor: ', cor_adm), font.main=1)









Code
# Correlation among admitted applicants only
cor(test_score[admitted], extracurriculars[admitted])
## [1] -0.5570494


Real data often mix several of these issues. Two variables can also move together because both respond to common factors. The scatterplot below shows one correlation that need not be causal.


Code
# xy_hat defined above: years of schooling and hourly wages of 3294 workers
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
cor_wages <- round(cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat']), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_wages), font.main=1)









Code

# Correlation across workers
cor(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
## [1] 0.2824925
# The correlation is about 0.28.
# This alone does not show that schooling raises wages.
# Both likely respond to common factors, such as ability or family background.
# Wages1 also only includes people with observed wages.
# So its relationships describe workers, not everyone who could have worked.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat this for murder and assault arrests across US states in USArrests.


Code
# Arrests per 100,000 residents in each US state in 1973
plot(Murder ~ Assault, USArrests, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    main=NA, xlab='Assault Arrests', ylab='Murder Arrests')
cor_arrests <- round(cor(USArrests$Murder, USArrests$Assault), 2)
title(paste0('Cor: ', cor_arrests), font.main=1)









Code
# States with more assault arrests also tend to have more murder arrests.

# Correlation across states
cor(USArrests$Murder, USArrests$Assault)
## [1] 0.8018733
# The correlation is about 0.8.
# This does not mean that assaults cause murders.
# Both variables are divided by the same state population.
# Both also likely respond to common factors.
# Examples are policing practices or local economic conditions.





Note that the examples above are not the only examples of “correlation does not mean causation” (Freedman 1991). Many real datasets have temporal and spatial interdependence that create additional issues. Many real datasets also have economic interdependence, which also creates additional issues (Adamson and Stephenson 2026).

title: 14  Statistics of Association
text:
14.4 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
For the dataset \(\{(1, 5),\ (2, 3),\ (3, 4),\ (4, 2),\ (5, 1)\}\), compute the Pearson correlation \(\hat{r}_{XY}\) by hand. Show all five steps: means, deviances, covariance \(\hat{c}_{XY}\), standard deviations \(\hat{s}_{X}\) and \(\hat{s}_{Y}\), and the final correlation.
Using the \(35\) sampled states in state_id, compute both the Pearson correlation and Kendall’s rank correlation between Murder and Assault in USArrests. Then write a bootstrap with \(B = 9999\) iterations to construct a \(95\%\) confidence interval for the Pearson correlation. Does the interval contain zero?
Give an example of a dataset where Pearson’s correlation \(\hat{r}_{XY}\) is close to zero but there is a clear causal relationship between \(X_{i}\) and \(Y_{i}\). What feature of the relationship causes the correlation to miss it, and which alternative statistic from this chapter might detect it?


Further Reading

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/2-2-an-application-to-the-gender-gap-of-earnings.html – worked example of computing and interpreting correlation in an economics setting.
https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/regression.html#correlations – clear introduction to Pearson, Spearman, and other correlation measures with R code.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/describing-relationships-quantitative-data/scatterplots-and-correlation/v/correlation-and-causality – short video on why correlation does not imply causation.



Recall
The right statistic of association depends on the type of data. For cardinal data, we computed the Pearson correlation by hand for \(\{(0, 0.1), (1, 0.3), (2, 0.2)\}\) and found \(\hat{r}_{XY}=1/2\). For cardinal data with outliers, the Falk codeviance \(\tilde{c}_{XY}\) is a robust alternative. For ordered factors, the six pairs of \(\{(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 4)\}\) gave Kendall’s \(\hat{\text{KT}}=2/3\). For unordered factors, the \(2\times 2\) table of degree and employment gave Cramer’s V \(\hat{\text{CramV}}=\sqrt{1/6}\approx 0.41\). These statistics describe association rather than causation.

title: 15  Simple Regression
text:
15.1 Simple Linear Regression
Suppose we have some bivariate data: \(\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i}\). In the previous chapter, we summarized the strength of association between two variables using correlation. Correlation tells us how strongly \(\hat{x}\) and \(\hat{y}\) move together, but not by how much \(\hat{y}\) changes per unit change in \(\hat{x}\). Regression answers that question by fitting a line through the data.
This chapter asks two questions.
We square the residuals so that positive and negative errors do not cancel, and so that big misses are penalized more than small ones.
This refers to fitting a linear model to bivariate data.

title: 15  Simple Regression
text:
Model and Objective
A regression line goes through the cloud of points. To calculate it, we need some definitions first.






ImportantKey Definition





Our simple linear model is \[
\hat{y}_{i}=b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}+\hat{e}_{i},
\] where \(b_{0}\) and \(b_{1}\) are the coefficients, and \(\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i}\) are the data for observation \(i\).



The residual \(\hat{e}_{i}\) is the vertical gap between observation \(i\)’s actual value of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) and the model’s prediction for that observation: \[\hat{e}_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-(b_{0}+b_{1}\hat{x}_{i}).\] During minimization, \(\hat{e}_{i}\) depends on the trial coefficients \(b_{0}, b_{1}\); the final residuals use the fitted coefficients \(\hat{b}_{0}, \hat{b}_{1}\). For the linear model, the OLS problem is \[\begin{aligned}
\min_{b_{0}, b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{e}_{i} \right)^2 &= \min_{b_{0}, b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2.
\end{aligned}\] We could find the best-fitting coefficients numerically, by trying out different combinations of \((b_{0}, b_{1})\). You can do that in this example, which can help you understand what is happening. This problem has an analytic solution, however, which means we know that the optimal OLS slope and intercept are \[\hat{b}_{1} = \frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{v}_{X}}, \qquad \hat{b}_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1} \hat{m}_{X}.\] The computer uses this math to find the coefficients quickly. For example, the code below fits a line to two cardinal variables and checks the coefficients with these formulas.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Lab data: 3294 US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
# Pull two columns from Wages1 and rename for compact code below
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage

# Run a Simple Regression
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)
coef(reg)
## (Intercept)       x_hat 
##  -0.7225066   0.5571617
# The intercept of about -0.72 is a negative hourly wage.

# Manual verification
x_hat <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat']
y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'y_hat']
b1 <- cov( x_hat, y_hat)/var(x_hat)
b1
## [1] 0.5571617
b0 <- mean(y_hat) - b1*mean(x_hat)
b0
## [1] -0.7225066


The least-squares slope \(\hat{b}_{1}\) seeks to answer “how much does the fitted value \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}\) change per one-unit change in \(\hat{x}\)?” When the data are not known to be linearly related, the formula shows the slope is generally just the covariance divided by the variance of \(\hat{x}\). As such, \(\hat{b}_{1}\) is generally interpreted as a summary statistic for associations, just like the correlation. In fact, \(\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{r}_{XY} \cdot \hat{s}_{Y}/\hat{s}_{X}\), so the simple regression slope is a rescaled version of the Pearson correlation statistic.


Code
# Slope
coef(reg)[2]
##     x_hat 
## 0.5571617
# Pearson Correlation
cor(xy_hat$x_hat, xy_hat$y_hat)
## [1] 0.2824925
# Slope from correlation: R_{XY} * S_Y / S_X
cor(xy_hat$x_hat, xy_hat$y_hat) * sd(xy_hat$y_hat)/sd(xy_hat$x_hat)
## [1] 0.5571617


The intercept guarantees the fitted line passes through the point of means \((\hat{m}_{X}, \hat{m}_{Y})\). To see why, add \(\hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}\) to both sides of the intercept formula to get \(\hat{m}_{Y} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}\). This says that the line’s height at \(\hat{m}_{X}\) is exactly \(\hat{m}_{Y}\).






TipTest Yourself





Derive the OLS intercept and slope by taking the partial derivative of the objective with respect to each coefficient and setting it to zero.
Start with the intercept. By the chain rule, the derivative of each squared term with respect to \(b_{0}\) is \(-2\) times the residual: \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\partial}{\partial b_{0}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} -2\left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right).
\end{aligned}\] Divide both sides by \(-2n\), and use the means \(\hat{m}_{X} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{x}_{i}/n\) and \(\hat{m}_{Y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{y}_{i}/n\): \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{y}_{i} - b_{0} - b_{1} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i} \\
&= \hat{m}_{Y} - b_{0} - b_{1} \hat{m}_{X} \\
\Rightarrow \hat{b}_{0} &= \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1}\hat{m}_{X}.
\end{aligned}\]
Now the slope. The derivative of each squared term with respect to \(b_{1}\) is \(-2 \hat{x}_{i}\) times the residual: \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\partial}{\partial b_{1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right)^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} -2\left( \hat{y}_{i} - [b_{0}+b_{1} \hat{x}_{i}] \right) \hat{x}_{i}.
\end{aligned}\] Divide both sides by \(-2\), substitute the intercept \(b_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - b_{1}\hat{m}_{X}\), and split the sum in two: \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( [\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}] - b_{1} [\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}] \right) \hat{x}_{i} \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) \hat{x}_{i} - b_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) \hat{x}_{i}.
\end{aligned}\] Deviations from the mean sum to zero, so \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) \hat{m}_{X} = 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) \hat{m}_{X} = 0\). Subtracting these from the two sums replaces each trailing \(\hat{x}_{i}\) with \(\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}\): \[\begin{aligned}
0 &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) - b_{1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 \\
\Rightarrow \hat{b}_{1} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{m}_{X})^2}.
\end{aligned}\] Dividing the top and bottom by \(n\) gives \(\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}\). This point is a minimum and not a maximum because each squared residual is U-shaped in the coefficients, so their sum is bowl-shaped in \((b_{0}, b_{1})\) and the only point where both derivatives are zero is the bottom of the bowl.





Predictions
Plugging the coefficients into the line gives the fitted value for observation \(i\). A prediction uses the same line at any design point \(x\). A fitted value is thus the prediction at a sample point. \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x) &= \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} x \\
\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} &= \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(\hat{x}_{i}) = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i}.
\end{aligned}\]
Fitted values are useful for in-sample diagnostics: comparing \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\) to \(\hat{y}_{i}\) shows where the model fits well and where it misses (these are the residuals \(\hat{e}_{i}\) we minimized). Predictions at new values are useful for out-of-sample questions like “what hourly wage would the model predict for a worker with 14 years of schooling?”. Making predictions far away from your observations is risky, with no nearby data to anchor its prediction. Also note that a model can predict well and still not tell us what would happen. For example, a store’s daily umbrella sales predict its raincoat sales well, yet a discount that raises umbrella sales need not raise raincoat sales.


Code
# Find predicted values and residuals
predict(reg)
resid(reg)

# Manual verification
y_fit <- b0+b1*x_hat
y_fit

e_hat <- y_hat - y_fit
e_hat

















TipTest Yourself





Suppose the intercept is a value the outcome cannot take, such as a negative hourly wage. What went wrong?
Nothing went wrong with the fit. The intercept is the prediction at \(x=0\), \(\hat{b}_{0}=\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(0)\). When no observation has \(\hat{x}_{i}\) near zero, this prediction is far away from the observations. The intercept sets the height of the line so that it passes through the point of means, and need not be a good guess for the outcome at \(x=0\). The code below checks the observed range of \(\hat{x}\) and the predictions at both ends.


Code
# The intercept from above, about -0.72, is a negative hourly wage.
# Range of schooling in the sample
range(x_hat)
## [1]  3 16
# No worker in the sample has fewer than 3 years of schooling.
# So the prediction at zero years is far away from the observations.
# The intercept is not a good guess for the wage of a worker with no schooling.

# Predictions at the lowest and highest observed years of schooling
predict(reg, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=range(x_hat)))
##         1         2 
## 0.9489785 8.1920805
# Over the observed range of 3 to 16 years, every prediction is positive.











NoteMust Know





Suppose we have a dataset with \(n = 3\) observations: \(\{(1,2), (2,2.5), (3,4)\}\).
We can compute the regression coefficients and model predictions in five steps.
Step 1. Sample Means
\[\begin{aligned}
\hat{m}_{X} &= \frac{1+2+3}{3} = 2 \\
\hat{m}_{Y} &= \frac{2 + 2.5 + 4}{3} = \frac{17}{6}.
\end{aligned}\]
Step 2. Covariance and Variance
\[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
i & \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i} & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X}) & (\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) & (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 \\ \hline
1 & 1 & 2 & -1 & -\tfrac{5}{6} & \tfrac{5}{6} & 1 \\
2 & 2 & 2.5 & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 \\
3 & 3 & 4 & 1 & \tfrac{7}{6} & \tfrac{7}{6} & 1 \\
\end{array}\]
\[\begin{aligned}
\hat{c}_{XY} &= \sum_{i=1}^3 (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{m}_{Y}) /3
= [\tfrac{5}{6} + \tfrac{7}{6}]/3 = 2/3 \\
\hat{v}_{X} &= \sum_{i=1}^3 (\hat{x}_{i} - \hat{m}_{X})^2 / 3 = [1 + 1]/3 = 2/3.
\end{aligned}\]
Step 3. Slope and Intercept
\[
\hat{b}_{1} = \frac{\hat{c}_{XY}}{\hat{v}_{X}} = \frac{2/3}{2/3} = 1,
\]
\[
\hat{b}_{0} = \hat{m}_{Y} - \hat{b}_{1} \hat{m}_{X}
= \frac{17}{6} - 2
= \frac{5}{6} \approx 0.83.
\]
\[
\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i}
          = \frac{5}{6} + \hat{x}_{i}.
\]
Step 4. Fitted Values and Residuals
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
i & \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i} & \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \tfrac{5}{6} + \hat{x}_{i} & \hat{e}_{i} = \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} \\ \hline
1 & 1 & 2   & \tfrac{11}{6} & \tfrac{1}{6} \\
2 & 2 & 2.5 & \tfrac{17}{6} & -\tfrac{1}{3} \\
3 & 3 & 4   & \tfrac{23}{6} & \tfrac{1}{6} \\
\end{array}
\]
Step 5: Prediction at chosen design point \(x=2.5\) \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(2.5) &= \frac{5}{6} + 2.5 = \frac{5}{6} + \frac{15}{6} = \frac{20}{6} = \frac{10}{3} \approx 3.3
\end{aligned}\]


Code
## Data
xy0_hat <- data.frame(
    x_hat=c(1, 2, 3),
    y_hat=c(2, 2.5, 4))

## Simple Linear Regression
reg0 <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy0_hat)
coef(reg0)
## (Intercept)       x_hat 
##   0.8333333   1.0000000

## Sample Predictions
predict(reg0)
##        1        2        3 
## 1.833333 2.833333 3.833333
resid(reg0)
##          1          2          3 
##  0.1666667 -0.3333333  0.1666667

## Out-of-Sample predictions
predict(reg0, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=c(2.5)))
##        1 
## 3.333333







Simple Constant Regression
Sometimes we restrict one coefficient of the simple linear model to zero, to get an even simpler model. Setting \(b_{1}=0\) removes \(\hat{x}_{i}\) from the model, so every observation gets the same fitted value. Our simple constant model is \[
\hat{y}_{i}=b_{0}+\hat{e}_{i},
\] where the coefficient \(b_{0}\) is a single number shared by every observation, and \(\hat{y}_{i}\) is the data for observation \(i\).
The constant model is useful as a baseline: it is our best prediction of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) when we ignore \(\hat{x}_{i}\), and other regressions can be judged by how much they improve on it. For the constant model, the OLS problem is \[
\min_{b_{0}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_{i} - b_{0} \right)^2.
\] Setting the derivative to zero shows that the least-squares constant is the sample mean: \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{b}_{0} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{y}_{i}}{n} = \hat{m}_{Y}.
\end{aligned}\] So every fitted value is the same, \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} = \hat{m}_{Y}\).


Code
# Regress on a constant only: '~ 1' means an intercept and no slope
reg_const <- lm(y_hat ~ 1, data=xy_hat)
coef(reg_const)
## (Intercept) 
##    5.757585

# Same as the sample mean
mean(xy_hat[, 'y_hat'])
## [1] 5.757585








TipTest Yourself





Regression Through the Origin
Setting \(b_{0}=0\) instead forces the fitted line through the point \((0, 0)\). Our simple model through the origin is \[
\hat{y}_{i}=b_{1}\hat{x}_{i}+\hat{e}_{i},
\] where the coefficient \(b_{1}\) is a slope with no intercept. This model is useful when theory says \(\hat{y}\) must be zero whenever \(\hat{x}\) is zero, such as a firm’s total cost when it has no fixed costs. Fit this model to the wage data, and compare its slope with the slope of the unrestricted line.
Minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} ( \hat{y}_{i} - b_{1}\hat{x}_{i} )^2\) gives \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{b}_{1} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i}\hat{y}_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{x}_{i}^{2}}.
\end{aligned}\] Unlike \(\hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}\), this slope does not subtract the means \(\hat{m}_{X}\) and \(\hat{m}_{Y}\).


Code
# Regress without an intercept: '0 +' drops b0 from the model
reg_origin <- lm(y_hat ~ 0 + x_hat, data=xy_hat)
coef(reg_origin)
##     x_hat 
## 0.4962765
# The unrestricted line already has an intercept near zero, about -0.72.
# So pinning the line to the origin changes its slope only a little.
# The slope moves from about 0.56 to about 0.50.

# Manual verification
sum(x_hat*y_hat)/sum(x_hat^2)
## [1] 0.4962765

# Scatter with the axes extended to the origin, then add all three fitted lines
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, xy_hat, col=grey(0, .1), pch=16,
    xlim=c(0, max(x_hat)), ylim=c(0, max(y_hat)),
    main=NA,
    xlab='Years of Schooling',
    ylab='Hourly Wage (1980 Dollars)')
abline(reg, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(reg_origin, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
abline(h=coef(reg_const), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
legend('topleft', legend=c('Unrestricted', 'Through origin', 'Constant'),
    col=c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)),
    lwd=2, lty=c(1, 2, 1), bty='n')









When the unrestricted line already has an intercept near zero, pinning the line to the origin changes its slope only a little.

title: 15  Simple Regression
text:
15.2 Goodness of Fit
After fitting the line, the next question is how much of the variation in \(\hat{y}\) the line actually accounts for.






ImportantKey Definition





The R-squared (or coefficient of determination) \(\hat{R}^{2}\) is the share of total variation in \(\hat{y}_{i}\) that the model explains. Using the Total, Explained, and Residual sums of squares, \[\underbrace{\sum_{i}(\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\text{TSS}} = \underbrace{\sum_{i}(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}-\hat{m}_{Y})^2}_{\text{ESS}}+\underbrace{\sum_{i}\hat{e}_{i}^2}_{\text{RSS}},\] \[\hat{R}^{2} = \frac{\hat{\text{ESS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}}=1-\frac{\hat{\text{MSE}}}{\hat{v}_{Y}},\] where \(\hat{\text{MSE}}=\hat{\text{RSS}}/n\) is the mean squared error and \(\hat{v}_{Y}=\hat{\text{TSS}}/n\) is the variance of \(\hat{y}\). Equivalently, \(\hat{R}^{2}\) equals the squared Pearson correlation between the fitted values \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\) and the actual \(\hat{y}_{i}\); \(\hat{r}_{YY^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2}\).
