\end{aligned}\] Here \(|\hat{x}_{i}-x|_{(q)}\) is the \(q^{\text{th}}\) smallest of the distances \(|\hat{x}_{1}-x|, ..., |\hat{x}_{n}-x|\) and \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\) rounds down. The tricube kernel \[\begin{aligned}
k\left(\hat{x}_{i}, x, h(x)\right) &= \left(1 - \frac{|\hat{x}_{i}-x|^{3}}{h(x)^{3}}\right)^{3}
\end{aligned}\] weights observations with \(|\hat{x}_{i}-x| < h(x)\) and gives the rest weight \(0\).



LOESS is useful for smoothing data with uneven \(\hat{x}\). Because the share of points in each neighborhood is fixed, every window reaches the same number of nearest points, even where the data are sparse. The kernel weights still depend on distance, so the effective sample size can differ from window to window. The span argument plays the role \(h\) does for fixed-bandwidth methods, so smaller spans mean narrower neighborhoods, more flexibility, and noisier curves, while larger spans pool more data and smooth more aggressively.
With degree=1, loess() fits a weighted line in each window, as the local linear regression does, so the main difference below is the window. We set span=.4, smaller than the default of \(0.75\), so the windows are narrower where the data are dense.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Loess with a line in each window, so mainly the window differs from the fit above
reg_lo1 <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, degree=1, span=.4)
y_pred_lo1 <- predict(reg_lo1, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_values))

# Every window reaches the same number of nearest workers
floor(reg_lo1$pars$span*nrow(xy_hat))
## [1] 1317
# Each window reaches the 40 percent of workers nearest x, 1317 of the 3294.
# Schooling has ties, and workers exactly at the edge get zero weight.
# So at 3 years, only the 692 workers with under 11 years get positive weight.
# At 11, 12, and 13 years, only the workers at that level get positive weight.
# A line cannot be fit to one level, so loess() warns and its fit there is that level's mean.

# Compare the two fits
lo_col <- rgb(0, .7, .7, .8) # teal, the color of every LOESS fit
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    ylim=c(0, 15), # zoom in on the fits
    main=NA, xlab='School', ylab='Wage')
lines(x_values, y_pred_fixed, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, type='o')
lines(x_values, y_pred_lo1, col=lo_col, lwd=2, type='o')
points(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=school_means, pch=24, col='white', bg=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), cex=1.3) # grouped means
legend('topleft', legend=c('Grouped mean', 'Local line, h=1', 'Loess, span=.4'),
    pch=c(24, 1, 1), lty=c(NA, 1, 1), lwd=c(NA, 2, 2), pt.bg=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8),
    col=c('white', rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lo_col), cex=.8, bty='n')









Code
# From 8 to 15 years, where workers are plentiful, the two fits differ by at most 20 cents.
# The loess fit does not follow the 3 workers with 3 or 4 years of schooling.
# It also does not follow the 16 workers with 16 years.
# The price is a much wider window: at 3 years, it reaches out to 11 years.


With span=.4, every LOESS window includes the \(40\) percent of observations nearest the design point. So the LOESS fit does not follow the few observations where the data are sparse. The price is a much wider window there.
By default, loess() fits a local quadratic (degree=2) instead of a line, so the fitted curve can bend within each window. The rest of this chapter uses the default.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Fit loess with the default span and degree
reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)








TipTest Yourself





A local quadratic adds the term \(b_{2}(x)\hat{x}_{i}^{2}\) in each window, so the coefficients at \(x\) solve \(\min_{b_{0}(x), b_{1}(x), b_{2}(x)} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat{y}_{i} - b_{0}(x) - b_{1}(x) \hat{x}_{i} - b_{2}(x)\hat{x}_{i}^{2} \right]^{2} k\left(\hat{x}_{i}, x, h(x)\right)\).


Code
# reg_lo defined above
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1), data=xy_hat,
    main=NA, xlab='School', ylab='Wage')
lines(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], predict(reg_lo),
    col=lo_col, lwd=2)

legend('topleft',
    legend=sprintf('Loess (span = %.2f)', reg_lo$pars$span),
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=lo_col, cex=.8)

title: 17  Local Regression II
text:
17.2 Model Fit
Each model produces fitted values \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\) and residuals \(\hat{e}_{i} = \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\). To compare models, we often summarize the residuals with a single number.
The mean squared error averages the squared residuals, \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{MSE}} &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{e}_{i}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}\] Squaring penalizes large misses heavily, and the units are the square of the units of \(\hat{y}_{i}\).
The R-squared rescales \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\) by the variance of \(\hat{y}\), \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{R}^{2} &= 1 - \frac{\hat{\text{RSS}}}{\hat{\text{TSS}}} = 1 - \frac{\hat{\text{MSE}}}{\hat{v}_{Y}}.
\end{aligned}\] It is unit-free and applies to any model with fitted values. On the same data, it ranks models exactly as \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\) does. For least squares fits with an intercept, it also equals the squared correlation between \(\hat{y}_{i}\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\). For any model, this squared correlation is the generalized \(R^{2}\) statistic, \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen}} &= \hat{r}_{YY^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2} = \frac{\hat{c}_{YY^{\mathrm{fit}}}^{2}}{\hat{v}_{Y} \hat{v}_{Y^{\mathrm{fit}}}},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{c}_{YY^{\mathrm{fit}}}\) is the covariance of \(\hat{y}\) and \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}\), and \(\hat{v}_{Y^{\mathrm{fit}}}\) is the variance of \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}\). For other fits, such as LOESS, the two versions can differ, and only \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen}}\) is guaranteed to lie between \(0\) and \(1\). Both estimate the share of the variation in \(Y_{i}\) that \(X_{i}\) explains (Doksum and Samarov 1995).






NoteMust Know





Suppose three workers have wages \(\hat{y}=(8, 10, 15)\) and a model predicts \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}=(9, 9, 14)\). The residuals are \(\hat{e}=(-1, 1, 1)\), so \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{MSE}} &= \frac{(-1)^2 + 1^2 + 1^2}{3} = \frac{3}{3} = 1.
\end{aligned}\] The model misses by \(1\) squared-dollar on average.


Code
y0_hat <- c(8, 10, 15)
y0_fit <- c(9, 9, 14)
e0_hat <- y0_hat - y0_fit
mean(e0_hat^2) # MSE
## [1] 1





We can compute these for the linear model, the regressogram with three bins, and LOESS.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# xy_hat and reg_lo defined above

# Two more models for wage on schooling
reg_lin <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)        # globally linear
xy_hat[, 'xcf'] <- cut(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'], 3)
reg_rgram <- lm(y_hat ~ xcf, data=xy_hat)         # regressogram, 3 bins

# Mean squared error and both R-squared statistics
fit_stats <- function(model){
    e_hat <- resid(model)
    y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'y_hat']
    c(MSE=mean(e_hat^2),
        R2=1 - mean(e_hat^2)/mean((y_hat-mean(y_hat))^2),
        R2_gen=cor(y_hat, y_hat-e_hat)^2)
}
fit_table <- rbind(
    Linear       = fit_stats(reg_lin),
    Regressogram = fit_stats(reg_rgram),
    LOESS        = fit_stats(reg_lo))
round(fit_table, 3)
##                 MSE    R2 R2_gen
## Linear        9.832 0.080  0.080
## Regressogram 10.270 0.039  0.039
## LOESS         9.721 0.090  0.090
# MSE is in squared dollars.
# LOESS has the smallest MSE, and the regressogram has the largest.
# Every R-squared is below 0.1.
# So each model leaves over 90 percent of the variation in wages unexplained.


A smaller error on the data used to fit a model does not guarantee smaller errors on new data, since a flexible enough model also fits the noise in the sample.






TipTest Yourself





The mean absolute percentage error averages each residual relative to its observed value, \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{MAPE}} &= \frac{100}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left| \frac{\hat{e}_{i}}{\hat{y}_{i}} \right|.
\end{aligned}\] MAPE is unit-free, which makes it easy to communicate, but it is undefined when \(\hat{y}_{i}=0\) and over-weights observations with small \(\hat{y}_{i}\). MSE is easier to analyze theoretically.
Compute \(\hat{\text{MAPE}}\) for the three workers with wages \(\hat{y}=(8, 10, 15)\) and predictions \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}=(9, 9, 14)\). Then compute it for the line, the regressogram, and LOESS, and check whether it ranks the models as \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\) does.
For the three workers, the residuals are \(\hat{e}=(-1, 1, 1)\), so \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\text{MAPE}} &= \frac{100}{3}\left( \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15} \right) = \frac{100}{3}\left( \frac{15}{120} + \frac{12}{120} + \frac{8}{120} \right) \\
&= \frac{100}{3} \times \frac{35}{120} = \frac{175}{18} \approx 9.7.
\end{aligned}\] The model misses by about \(10\%\) of each wage.


Code
# y0_hat and e0_hat defined above
100*mean(abs(e0_hat/y0_hat))
## [1] 9.722222

# reg_lin, reg_rgram, and reg_lo defined above
mape <- function(model){
    100*mean(abs(resid(model)/xy_hat[, 'y_hat']))
}
round(c(Linear=mape(reg_lin), Regressogram=mape(reg_rgram), LOESS=mape(reg_lo)), 3)
##       Linear Regressogram        LOESS 
##       73.275       75.879       72.952
# LOESS has the smallest MAPE and the regressogram the largest, as with MSE.
# Every model misses by over 70 percent on average.
# Partly that is because a few workers earn less than 20 cents an hour.
# Their percentage errors are huge.


The two measures can rank models differently, because MAPE weights observations with low \(\hat{y}_{i}\) more heavily.



Adamson (2025) tests whether a more flexible model’s gain in fit is larger than chance, using a loss-in-fit statistic (Härdle and Mammen 1993; Henderson and Parmeter 2015). The statistic is the rise in the residual sum of squares from an unrestricted to a restricted model, divided by the unrestricted residual sum of squares. It is a nonparametric analog of the \(F\)-statistic, and the paper computes its \(p\)-values with a bootstrap.

Cross-Validation
To measure out-of-sample fit, we use the leave-one-out cross-validation error \(\hat{\text{CV}}\), the \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\) of predictions for held-out observations. A model that fits the noise in the sample predicts held-out observations poorly, so its \(\hat{\text{CV}}\) rises above its \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\).
The code below refits each model \(n\) times, each time without one observation, and predicts that observation’s \(\hat{y}_{i}\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# xy_hat defined above, including the bins xcf

# Leave-one-out prediction errors, one column per model
loo_errors <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(xy_hat), ncol=3)
colnames(loo_errors) <- c('Linear', 'Regressogram', 'LOESS')
loo_errors_mean <- rep(NA, nrow(xy_hat))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(xy_hat))) {
    xy_i <- xy_hat[-i, ] # drop worker i
    reg_lin_i   <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_i)
    reg_rgram_i <- lm(y_hat ~ xcf, data=xy_i)
    reg_lo_i    <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_i)
    # Predict worker i from the fits without worker i
    y_pred_i <- c(
        predict(reg_lin_i, newdata=xy_hat[i, ]),
        predict(reg_rgram_i, newdata=xy_hat[i, ]),
        predict(reg_lo_i, newdata=xy_hat[i, ]))
    loo_errors[i, ] <- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'] - y_pred_i
    # Compare worker i with the mean wage of the other workers
    loo_errors_mean[i] <- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'] - mean(xy_i[, 'y_hat'])
}

# LOESS does not extrapolate, so it cannot predict the only worker with 3 years of schooling
# Compare all models on the workers every model can predict
loo_ok <- complete.cases(loo_errors)
cv_hat <- colMeans(loo_errors[loo_ok, ]^2)

# Out-of-sample R-squared rescales CV by the leave-one-out version of the variance, for the same workers
v_cv_hat <- mean(loo_errors_mean[loo_ok]^2)
r2_cv <- 1 - cv_hat/v_cv_hat

# Out-of-sample generalized R-squared squares the correlation of wages and held-out predictions
y_ok <- xy_hat[loo_ok, 'y_hat']
y_pred_cv <- y_ok - loo_errors[loo_ok, ]
r2_gen_cv <- cor(y_ok, y_pred_cv)[1, ]^2
round(cbind(fit_table, CV=cv_hat, R2_CV=r2_cv, R2_gen_CV=r2_gen_cv), 3)
##                 MSE    R2 R2_gen     CV R2_CV R2_gen_CV
## Linear        9.832 0.080  0.080  9.840 0.080     0.079
## Regressogram 10.270 0.039  0.039 10.288 0.038     0.037
## LOESS         9.721 0.090  0.090  9.762 0.087     0.087
# Every model predicts held-out workers a little worse than those it was fit to.
# The gap between CV and MSE grows with flexibility.
# It runs from about 0.01 for the line to about 0.04 for LOESS.
# LOESS still predicts held-out workers best.
# Its lead over the line shrinks from about 0.11 in sample to about 0.08.
# R2_gen_CV falls below its in-sample version for every model.
# R2_CV also falls, except that the line's rounds to its in-sample R-squared.
# That is because R2_CV omits the one worker LOESS cannot predict.
# R2_CV and R2_gen_CV are within about 0.001 of each other.
# They differ more for the USArrests line in Simple Regression (not run here).
# Its R2_CV is negative, about -0.04, yet its R2_gen_CV is about 0.22.
# That is above its in-sample R-squared of about 0.005.
# Squaring hides the sign of the correlation, which is about -0.47.


The gap between \(\hat{\text{CV}}\) and \(\hat{\text{MSE}}\) tends to grow with a model’s flexibility. The out-of-sample generalized \(R^{2}\) replaces the fitted values in \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen}}\) with the held-out predictions \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})\), \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen,CV}} &= \hat{r}_{YY^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}}^{2},
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{r}_{YY^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}}\) is the correlation between \(\hat{y}_{i}\) and \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})\). The out-of-sample R-squared \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}\) is negative when a model predicts held-out observations worse than the mean of the other observations would, but \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen,CV}}\) always lies between \(0\) and \(1\). The two can differ, since a squared correlation ignores whether the predictions are shifted or scaled away from the observed \(\hat{y}_{i}\). Squaring also hides a negative correlation, so a model can have an \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{gen,CV}}\) above its in-sample \(\hat{R}^{2}\) even when its \(\hat{R}^{2}_{\text{CV}}\) is negative, as a Test Yourself in Cross-Validation shows.
Adamson (2025) compares a local constant regression with a linear model using both in-sample and out-of-sample errors (Mullainathan and Spiess 2017). It notes that fitting simple models to complex relationships is believed to be a major source of false positives (Henderson and Parmeter 2015; Racine 2019; Hansen 2022).

title: 17  Local Regression II
text:
17.3 Gradients
Once the fitted curve can bend, “the slope” is no longer a single number; we want the slope locally at each \(x\).






ImportantKey Definition





A gradient \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) at the design point \(x\) is the rate of change of the prediction \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\) with respect to \(x\) in a neighborhood of \(x\).
The mean of the gradients (sometimes called the average effect or mean marginal effect) averages \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) across every observation in the dataset: \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{b}_{1}(x=\hat{x}_{i}).\]



The gradient is useful as the local analog of the simple-regression slope. For a globally linear model, it equals the single coefficient \(\hat{b}_{1}\) everywhere. For a local model, it varies with \(x\) and shows how the marginal relationship changes across the range of \(\hat{x}\). Three common ways to estimate gradients are:

For all methods, including regressograms, you can approximate gradients with small finite differences. For some small difference \(d\), we can manually compute \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{b}_{1}(x) &= \frac{ \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x+\frac{d}{2}) - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x-\frac{d}{2})}{d},
\end{aligned}\]
When using split-sample regressions or local linear regressions, you can use the estimated slope coefficients \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) as a gradient estimate.
More sophisticated methods that are beyond the scope of this book.







NoteMust Know





Suppose a local model predicts wages near \(x=12\) years of schooling: \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(11.5)=9.2\) and \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(12.5)=10.4\) (dollars per hour). With step \(d=1\), the finite-difference gradient at \(x=12\) is \[
\hat{b}_{1}(12) = \frac{\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(12.5) - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(11.5)}{d} = \frac{10.4 - 9.2}{1} = 1.2.
\] Near \(12\) years of schooling, each extra year is associated with about \(\$1.20\) more per hour.


Code
d <- 1
y_pred_hi <- 10.4  # prediction at x + d/2
y_pred_lo <- 9.2   # prediction at x - d/2
(y_pred_hi - y_pred_lo) / d
## [1] 1.2





After computing gradients, you can summarize them in various plots, such as histograms and scatterplots. These plots show how the gradient varies within the sample. You can also plot all gradients with their confidence intervals (Chaudhuri and Marron 1999; Henderson et al. 2012).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Gradient at each observation, as a centered finite difference with d=1
## Many workers share a schooling level, so compute it once per level
grad_by_obs <- function(xy, reg, d=1) {
    x_levels <- sort(unique(xy[, 'x_hat']))
    # loess does not extrapolate, so the step is cut short at the edges of the data
    x_lo <- pmax(x_levels - d/2, min(x_levels))
    x_hi <- pmin(x_levels + d/2, max(x_levels))
    y_pred_lo <- predict(reg, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_lo))
    y_pred_hi <- predict(reg, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_hi))
    grad_levels <- (y_pred_hi - y_pred_lo)/(x_hi - x_lo)
    grad_obs <- grad_levels[match(xy[, 'x_hat'], x_levels)]
    return(grad_obs)
}
grad_obs <- grad_by_obs(xy_hat, reg_lo)

## Visual Summary
f_grad <- hist(grad_obs, breaks=20, plot=FALSE)
layout(matrix(1:2, ncol=2), widths=c(4/5, 1/5))

# One point per schooling level, since all workers at a level share one gradient
x_levels <- sort(unique(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))
grad_levels <- grad_obs[match(x_levels, xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])]
n_levels <- as.numeric(table(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))

# Point area scales with the number of workers
sizes <- sqrt(n_levels / max(n_levels)) * 4

# Scatterplot, with limits that line up with the marginal bars below
par(mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(x_levels, grad_levels, cex=sizes,
    xlab='x', ylab=expression(d~hat(y)^plain(pred)/dx),
    mgp=c(2.5, 1, 0),
    ylim=range(f_grad[['breaks']]),
    col=lo_col, pch=16, main=NA) ## Diminishing Returns?
legend('bottomright', bty='n', y.intersp=1.6, x.intersp=1.4,
    legend=c('10 workers', '100 workers', '1000 workers'),
    pch=16, col=lo_col, pt.cex=sqrt(c(10, 100, 1000) / max(n_levels)) * 4)

# Add Marginal
par(mar=c(4, 0, 1, 1))
barplot(f_grad[['density']], axes=FALSE, space=0, horiz=TRUE, border=NA,
    col=lo_col) ## Distributional Summary









Code
# The largest point is at 12 years, where 1188 workers share one gradient.
# The longest bar, gradients from 0.6 to 0.7, holds the 1851 workers with 10, 12, or 14 years.
# Only the 46 workers with under 8 years of schooling have negative gradients.


A different kind of summary collapses the whole gradient curve into a single number for tabular reporting. The mean of the gradients answers “what is the average slope across the sample?”. This generally differs from the gradient at the mean (sometimes called the marginal effect at the mean) which evaluates the gradient at a single design point: \(\hat{b}_{1}(x=\hat{m}_{X})\) and answers “what is the slope at a typical \(\hat{x}_{i}\)?” The two coincide for a globally linear model but can differ for any other, sometimes substantially when the relationship bends (Henderson et al. 2012; Adamson 2021). You may also be interested in the median of the gradients, or in measures of effect heterogeneity like the interquartile range or standard deviation of the gradients. Such statistics can be presented in tabular form with estimates of sampling variability.






TipTest Yourself





These two summaries usually differ. Suppose a local model has gradients \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) at schooling levels \(x=(8,10,12,14,16)\) equal to \((0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 0.3)\), and the sample mean schooling is \(\hat{m}_{X}=12\).

The gradient at the mean is the single gradient at \(x=\hat{m}_{X}\): \(\hat{b}_{1}(12) = 1.2\).
The mean of the gradients averages over all five points: \(\frac{0.4+0.8+1.2+0.9+0.3}{5} = \frac{3.6}{5} = 0.72\).

They differ because the gradient is not constant: here the relationship is steepest near the mean and flatter at the extremes.


Code
grads <- c(0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 0.3)
grads[3]      # gradient at the mean (x = 12)
## [1] 1.2
mean(grads)   # mean of the gradients
## [1] 0.72





The code below computes the gradient at the mean, along with the mean and the standard deviation of the gradients.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Gradient at the mean, as a centered finite difference with d=1 around the mean schooling
grad_at_mean <- function(xy, reg, d=1) {
    m_hat <- mean(xy[, 'x_hat'])
    y_pred_d <- predict(reg, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=c(m_hat-d/2, m_hat+d/2)))
    grad_m <- (y_pred_d[2] - y_pred_d[1])/d
    return(unname(grad_m))
}

## Tabular Summary
## grad_obs defined above
tab_stats <- c(
    'At the mean'=grad_at_mean(xy_hat, reg_lo),
    Mean=mean(grad_obs),
    SD=sd(grad_obs))
round(tab_stats, 3)
## At the mean        Mean          SD 
##       0.239       0.583       0.220
# The gradient at the mean, about 0.24, is much smaller than the mean gradient.
# The mean of the gradients is about 0.58.
# The mean schooling, about 11.6 years, falls between 11 and 12 years.
# The loess curve is flatter there than at the neighboring levels.

title: 17  Local Regression II
text:
17.4 Variability Estimates

Confidence Bands
A single fitted curve does not show how much that curve would change in another sample, so we draw a region around it.






ImportantKey Definition





A confidence band is a confidence interval drawn at every design point: a region around the fitted curve that captures sample-to-sample variability. A bootstrap confidence band collects the predictions from many resamples and reads off pointwise quantiles at each \(x\).



Confidence bands are useful for showing where a fitted curve is well-supported by the data and where another sample could move it. The width is typically wider at the edges of \(\hat{x}\) (few neighbors) and narrower in the dense middle, which is itself a quick visual diagnostic. The same bootstrap that produces the band also produces standard errors for any single design point and for the gradient summaries below. The band shows variability across samples, whereas the gradient plots show variability within the sample.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Same loess fit as above (default span)
pred_design <- data.frame(x_hat=unique(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))
y_pred <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=pred_design)

plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1), data=xy_hat,
    main=NA, xlab='School', ylab='Wage')
lines(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], y_pred,
    col=lo_col, lwd=2, type='o')

# Boot CI with the same default-span loess
boot_lo <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=399)
for (b in 1:399) {
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[sample(nrow(xy_hat), replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot)
    boot_lo[, b] <- predict(reg_b, newdata=pred_design)
}
boot_cb <- apply(boot_lo, 1, quantile,
    probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)

# Plot CI
polygon(
    c(pred_design[[1]], rev(pred_design[[1]])),
    c(boot_cb[1, ], rev(boot_cb[2, ])),
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .3),
    border=NA)















TipTest Yourself





Construct a bootstrap confidence band for the following loess regression


Code
# Adaptive-width subsamples with non-uniform weights
xy2_hat <- USArrests[, c('UrbanPop', 'Murder')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=urban population share, y_hat=murder arrests per 100K
xy2_ord_hat <- xy2_hat[order(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat']), ]

plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5), data=xy2_ord_hat,
    main=NA, xlab='Urban Population', ylab='Murder Arrests')
reg_lo_usa <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_ord_hat, span=.6)

lines(xy2_ord_hat[, 'x_hat'], predict(reg_lo_usa),
    col=lo_col, lwd=2)














Gradient Standard Errors
Repeating the gradient summaries on each bootstrap resample gives their standard errors and confidence intervals.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Use bootstrap to approximate sampling dist
boot_stats <- matrix(NA, nrow=299, ncol=3)
colnames(boot_stats) <- c('At the mean', 'Mean', 'SD')
for(b in 1:nrow(boot_stats)){
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[sample(1:nrow(xy_hat), replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_lo_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot)
    grad_m_b_hat <- grad_at_mean(xy_boot, reg_lo_b)
    grad_obs_b <- grad_by_obs(xy_boot, reg_lo_b)
    m_grad_b_hat <- mean(grad_obs_b)
    s_grad_b_hat <- sd(grad_obs_b)
    boot_stats[b, 1] <- grad_m_b_hat
    boot_stats[b, 2] <- m_grad_b_hat
    boot_stats[b, 3] <- s_grad_b_hat
}
## SEs and CIs
boot_se <- apply(boot_stats, 2, sd)
boot_quants <- apply(boot_stats, 2, quantile, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))
boot_quants <- apply( round(boot_quants, 3), 2, paste0, collapse=', ')

## Printing
tab_regstyle <- data.frame(
  Estimate  = round(tab_stats, 3),
  SE = paste0('(', round(boot_se, 3), ')'),
  CI_95 = paste0('[', boot_quants, ']')
)
tab_regstyle
##             Estimate      SE          CI_95
## At the mean    0.239  (0.15) [-0.046, 0.53]
## Mean           0.583 (0.047)  [0.49, 0.667]
## SD             0.220 (0.045) [0.176, 0.363]
# The gradient at the mean varies more across samples: its SE is about 0.15.
# The SE of the mean of the gradients is about 0.047.
# The interval for the gradient at the mean includes zero.
# The interval for the mean of the gradients does not.



Summary of Local Gradients



Estimate
Bootstrap SE
Bootstrap 95% CI




At the mean

The gradient at the mean depends on the fit near a single design point, so it tends to vary more across samples than the mean of the gradients, which averages over all observations.

title: 17  Local Regression II
text:
17.5 Hypothesis Testing
We can test whether the mean gradient is statistically different from zero. The first way is to invert a confidence interval. A \(95\%\) confidence interval gives a test at the \(5\%\) level: reject a hypothesized value if it falls outside the interval, and fail to reject it if it falls inside. So we need no new resampling to test \(H_{0}\): the mean gradient equals zero. We only check whether the bootstrap interval from Gradient Standard Errors contains \(0\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Bootstrap distribution of the mean gradient, with its 95% CI and zero marked
## boot_stats defined above
boot_ci_mean <- quantile(boot_stats[, 'Mean'], probs=c(.025, .975))

hist(boot_stats[, 'Mean'], breaks=25,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlim=range(c(0, boot_stats[, 'Mean'])),
    xlab='Mean of the Gradients',
    main=NA)
title('Bootstrap Distribution with 95% CI', font.main=1)
abline(v=boot_ci_mean, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) # 95% CI
abline(v=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)            # H0: mean gradient=0









Code

## Does the 95% interval contain zero?
boot_ci_mean
##      2.5%     97.5% 
## 0.4902400 0.6667944
unname(boot_ci_mean[1] <= 0 & boot_ci_mean[2] >= 0)
## [1] FALSE
# The interval, about 0.49 to 0.67, does not contain 0.
# So we reject the null that the mean gradient is zero at the 5% level.
# The interval for the gradient at the mean, about -0.05 to 0.53, does contain 0.
# So we fail to reject the same null for that statistic.


We can also compute the p-value directly from the same bootstrap distribution. Under \(H_{0}\), the mean gradient equals zero, so we center the bootstrap distribution at zero, as in Impose the Null, and ask how often it produces values as extreme as the observed mean gradient.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## P-value via null bootstrap ECDF
## Center bootstrap means at zero (impose H0)
boot_centered <- boot_stats[, 'Mean'] - mean(boot_stats[, 'Mean'])

## ECDF of centered bootstrap distribution
F_hat <- ecdf(boot_centered)

## Two-sided p-value: P(|centered mean| >= |observed mean|)
p_boot <- 1 - F_hat(abs(tab_stats['Mean'])) +
              F_hat(-abs(tab_stats['Mean']))

cat('Bootstrap p-value (ECDF):', p_boot, '\n')
## Bootstrap p-value (ECDF): 0
# The observed mean gradient is farther from zero than all 299 centered means.
# So the p-value is 0.
# That means only that it is below 1/299, about 0.003.
# The mean gradient is statistically distinguishable from zero.
# On average, wages increase with schooling.


With \(B\) resamples, a p-value of \(0\) means only that the p-value is below \(1/B\). A small p-value indicates that the mean gradient is statistically distinguishable from zero.
We can also use a normal approximation. Under the null hypothesis \(H_{0}\): the mean gradient equals zero, we use the test statistic \[\hat{t} = \frac{\text{mean gradient}}{\hat{\text{SE}}(\text{mean gradient})}\] and the p-value comes from the standard normal distribution.


Code
## P-value for mean gradient
## Standard Normal Approximation
t_stat <- tab_stats['Mean'] / boot_se['Mean']
p_val  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(t_stat))

cat('Mean gradient:', round(tab_stats['Mean'], 3), '\n')
## Mean gradient: 0.583
cat('Bootstrap SE: ', round(boot_se['Mean'], 3), '\n')
## Bootstrap SE:  0.047
cat('t-statistic:  ', round(t_stat, 3), '\n')
## t-statistic:   12.372
cat('p-value:      ', format.pval(p_val, digits=3), '\n')
## p-value:       <2e-16








TipTest Yourself





Compute the t-statistic and p-value using jackknife standard errors instead of the bootstrap.


Code
## Jackknife SE for mean gradient
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
jack_means <- numeric(n)
for (i in 1:n) {
    xy_i  <- xy_hat[-i, ]
    reg_i  <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_i)
    grad_i <- grad_by_obs(xy_i, reg_i)
    jack_means[i] <- mean(grad_i)
}

## Jackknife SE
jack_se <- sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((jack_means - mean(jack_means))^2))

## t-statistic and p-value
t_jack <- tab_stats['Mean'] / jack_se
p_jack <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(t_jack))

cat('Jackknife SE: ', round(jack_se, 3), '\n')
## Jackknife SE:  0.046
cat('t-statistic:  ', round(t_jack, 3), '\n')
## t-statistic:   12.59
cat('p-value:      ', format.pval(p_jack, digits=3), '\n')
## p-value:       <2e-16






All Gradients
The mean gradient can be near zero even when the gradients are not, because positive and negative gradients cancel. To test whether all gradients equal zero, Racine (1997) squares them so they cannot cancel.
Racine’s statistic is the mean of the squared gradients: \[\hat{G}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{b}_{1}(x=\hat{x}_{i})^{2}.\] It tests the null hypothesis that the population gradient is zero at every design point, \(H_{0}\): \(m_{Y}'(x)=0\) for all \(x\).
The statistic \(\hat{G}^2\) is zero only when every gradient is zero, so only large values count against \(H_{0}\).






TipTest Yourself





Suppose wages rise with age early in a career and fall near retirement. A local model has gradients \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) at ages \(x=(20, 30, 40, 50, 60)\) equal to \((0.6, 0.3, 0, -0.3, -0.6)\). Compute the mean of the gradients and \(\hat{G}^2\).

The mean of the gradients is \(\frac{0.6+0.3+0-0.3-0.6}{5} = 0\).
Racine’s statistic is \(\frac{0.36+0.09+0+0.09+0.36}{5} = \frac{0.9}{5} = 0.18\).

The mean of the gradients misses the relationship because the rising and falling parts cancel, while \(\hat{G}^2\) does not.


Code
grads_age <- c(0.6, 0.3, 0, -0.3, -0.6)
mean(grads_age)   # mean of the gradients
## [1] 0
mean(grads_age^2) # Racine's statistic
## [1] 0.18





To impose \(H_{0}\), we shuffle \(\hat{x}_{i}\) across observations, as in the permutation test for correlation. Each permutation refits LOESS and recomputes \(\hat{G}^2\). The p-value is the share of permuted \(\hat{G}^2\) at least as large as the observed one. Shuffling makes \(\hat{y}\) unrelated to \(\hat{x}\) in every respect, such as its spread, so it imposes slightly more than \(H_{0}\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Racine's statistic: mean of the squared gradients
## grad_obs defined above
racine_hat <- mean(grad_obs^2)

## Null permutation distribution: shuffle schooling across workers
null_racine <- rep(NA, 299)
for(b in seq_along(null_racine)){
    xy_perm <- xy_hat
    xy_perm[, 'x_hat'] <- sample(xy_perm[, 'x_hat'], replace=FALSE) ## Reshuffle X
    reg_lo_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_perm)
    grad_obs_b <- grad_by_obs(xy_perm, reg_lo_b)
    null_racine[b] <- mean(grad_obs_b^2)
}
perm_cut <- quantile(null_racine, probs=0.95)

## Plot the null distribution, extending the axis to the observed statistic
hist(null_racine, breaks=50,
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlim=range(c(null_racine, racine_hat)),
    xlab=expression(hat(G)^2),
    main=NA)
title('Null Permutation Distribution', font.main=1)
abline(v=racine_hat, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) # observed statistic
abline(v=perm_cut, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)   # 95% permutation cutoff









Code

## One-sided p-value: P(permuted statistic >= observed statistic)
F_racine <- ecdf(null_racine)
p_racine <- 1 - F_racine(racine_hat)

cat('Observed statistic: ', round(racine_hat, 3), '\n')
## Observed statistic:  0.388
cat('95% cutoff:         ', round(perm_cut, 3), '\n')
## 95% cutoff:          0.052
cat('Permutation p-value:', p_racine, '\n')
## Permutation p-value: 0
# The observed statistic, about 0.39, is far above the 95% cutoff of about 0.05.
# None of the 299 permuted values is as large, so the p-value is 0.
# That means only that it is below 1/299, about 0.003.
# Both tests reject: about 99 percent of workers have a positive gradient.
# So little cancels.


If most gradients share a sign, little cancels, so this test and the test of the mean gradient tend to agree.

title: 17  Local Regression II
text:
17.6 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Using the USArrests dataset, fit a loess regression of Murder on UrbanPop with span = 0.6. Compute the finite-difference gradients \(\hat{b}_{1}(x)\) and report their mean and standard deviation. Compare these to the OLS slope \(\hat{b}_{1}\) from a simple linear regression.
Explain the difference between the gradient at the mean and the mean of the gradients. Why are the two equal for a simple linear regression? Describe a relationship between wages and schooling for which the mean of the gradients is larger than the gradient at the mean.
Using the Wages1 dataset and the default-span loess fit from this chapter, recompute the gradient at the mean, \(\hat{b}_{1}(x=\hat{m}_{X})\), as a finite difference with \(d=0.2\) and with \(d=2\) instead of \(d=1\). How much does it change, and how does the fitted curve near \(\hat{m}_{X}\) explain the change?
Using the loess fit from Exercise 2, compute the gradient at each observation with grad_by_obs(), and bootstrap the standard error of the mean gradient with \(B = 299\) replicates. Test whether the mean gradient differs from zero.


Further Reading

https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/loess.html – R’s help page for loess(), including the span and degree arguments.
https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/5.1-testing-two-sided-hypotheses-concerning-the-slope-coefficient.html – testing whether a regression slope differs from zero, with worked R examples.



Recall
We used LOESS to reduce bias at the edges of the data and to avoid small samples where the data are sparse. We compared its fit with the line and the regressogram, both in sample and with cross-validation. We then summarized and tested the gradients of a LOESS fit to the Wages1 data. At \(x=15\), the locally constant window mean of about \(6.29\) fell far below the grouped mean of \(8.38\), while a line through the same window predicted about \(8.24\). The small worked example with \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(11.5)=9.2\) and \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(12.5)=10.4\) gave a finite-difference gradient \(\hat{b}_{1}(12)=1.2\) dollars per year of schooling, and the gradient-vector example \((0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 0.3)\) at \(x=(8, 10, 12, 14, 16)\) showed the gradient at the mean (\(1.2\)) and the mean of the gradients (\(0.72\)) diverging when the relationship bends. The mean gradient of the LOESS fit, about \(0.58\) dollars per year of schooling, had a bootstrap standard error of about \(0.047\) and a \(\hat{t}\)-statistic of about \(12\), while the gradient at the mean, about \(0.24\), had a 95% confidence interval that included zero. Racine’s statistic \(\hat{G}^2\), about \(0.39\), was far above the \(95\%\) permutation cutoff of about \(0.05\), so we rejected that all gradients are zero.

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
text:
18.1 Theoretical Distributions
The previous chapters summarized bivariate data that we observed. Just as a single random variable has a theoretical mean and variance, a pair \((X_{i}, Y_{i})\) has a theoretical covariance, correlation, and regression coefficient.
This chapter asks three questions.
To talk about what sample statistics estimate, we need a theoretical counterpart to the bivariate observations of the previous chapters.
The random vector is useful as the formal object that the empirical pair \((\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i})\) samples from. For example, if we are going to flip two coins, then \((X_{i}, Y_{i})\) corresponds to the unflipped coins and \((\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i})\) to the concrete outcomes once they are flipped. Each sample-level object from earlier chapters (\(\hat{p}(x,y)\), \(\hat{c}_{XY}\), \(\hat{r}_{XY}\), \(\hat{b}_{1}\)) has a population counterpart defined at the level of the random vector.

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
text:
ImportantKey Definition





A random vector \((X_{i}, Y_{i})\) is a pair of random variables drawn together. It is the population analog of one paired observation \((\hat{x}_{i}, \hat{y}_{i})\), described before the data exist.





Definitions for Discrete Data
For discrete random variables, the starting point is the table of probabilities for every possible pair of values.






ImportantKey Definition





The joint probability of two discrete random variables is the probability that both events \(X_{i}=x\) and \(Y_{i}=y\) occur: \[\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y).\] The joint distribution is the table of these probabilities over all pairs \((x, y)\), summing to one.



The joint probability is useful as the theoretical version of the empirical joint distribution \(\hat{p}(x,y)\) from Bivariate Distributions: the same table structure, but with population probabilities in place of sample proportions. With enough draws, \(\hat{p}(x,y)\) approaches the joint distribution.
A particularly simple special case is when the two variables carry no information about each other.






ImportantKey Definition





Two random variables are statistically independent when the joint probability factors as the product of the marginals: \[\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x, Y_{i}=y)=\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y) \quad \text{for every } (x, y).\] Equivalently, knowing \(Y_{i}\) tells you nothing about the distribution of \(X_{i}\).



Independence is useful as the cleanest baseline against which to compare real data: most of the dependence statistics in Statistics of Association take value zero when the variables are independent. Independence is sometimes assumed for mathematical simplicity, not because it generally fits data well.1
The marginal distributions are then defined as \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x) &= \sum_{y} \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x | Y_{i} = y) \text{Prob}( Y_{i} = y ) \\
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y) &= \sum_{x} \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y | X_{i} = x) \text{Prob}( X_{i} = x ),
\end{aligned}\] which is also known as the law of total probability.
The conditional distributions are defined as \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x | Y_{i} = y) &= \frac{ \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y)}{ \text{Prob}( Y_{i} = y )} \\
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y | X_{i} = x) &= \frac{ \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y)}{ \text{Prob}( X_{i} = x )}
\end{aligned}\]


Coin Flips Example
For one example, consider flipping two coins, where we mark whether “heads” is face up with a \(1\) and “tail” with a \(0\). E.g., the first coin has a value of \(x=1\) if it shows heads and \(x=0\) if it shows tails. This table shows both the joint distribution and also each marginal distribution.

Joint and Marginal Distributions of Two Coins









\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
Marginal




\(y=0\)
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=0,Y_{i}=0)\)
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1,Y_{i}=0)\)
\(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=0)\)


\(y=1\)
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=0,Y_{i}=1)\)
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1,Y_{i}=1)\)
\(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1)\)


Marginal
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=0)\)
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)\)
\(1\)



Note that different joint distributions can have the same marginal distributions.






NoteMust Know





Suppose both coins are “fair”: \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)= 1/2\) and \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1|X_{i}=x)=1/2\) for either \(x=1\) or \(x=0\), then the four potential outcomes have equal probabilities. \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0, Y_{i} = 0) &= 1/2 \times 1/2 = 1/4 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0, Y_{i} = 1) &= 1/4 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1, Y_{i} = 0) &= 1/4 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1, Y_{i} = 1) &= 1/4 .
\end{aligned}\] The joint distribution is written generally as \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y) &= \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x) \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y).
\end{aligned}\]


Code
# Create a 2x2 matrix for the joint distribution.
# Rows correspond to X (coin 1), and columns correspond to Y (coin 2).
probs <- c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) # Fair coin
P_xy <- matrix( probs, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
rownames(P_xy) <- c('Y=0', 'Y=1')
colnames(P_xy) <- c('X=0', 'X=1')
P_xy
##      X=0  X=1
## Y=0 0.25 0.25
## Y=1 0.25 0.25

# Draw N bivariate observations
N <- 500
xy_vals <- expand.grid(y = 0:1, x = 0:1)
draws <- sample(nrow(xy_vals), N, replace = TRUE, prob = P_xy)
x_sim <- xy_vals[draws, 'x']
y_sim <- xy_vals[draws, 'y']

# With enough draws, empirical frequencies approach the true probabilities
table(y_sim, x_sim) / N
##      x_sim
## y_sim     0     1
##     0 0.242 0.298
##     1 0.242 0.218
P_xy
##      X=0  X=1
## Y=0 0.25 0.25
## Y=1 0.25 0.25


The marginal distribution of the second coin is \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0) &= \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0 | X_{i} = 0) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=0) + \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0 | X_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=1) \\
&= 1/2 (1/2) + 1/2 (1/2) = 1/2 \\
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1) &= \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1 | X_{i} = 0) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=0) + \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1 | X_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=1) \\
&= 1/2 (1/2) + 1/2 (1/2) = 1/2
\end{aligned}\]
The marginal distribution of the first coin is found in the exact same way \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0) &= \text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0 | Y_{i} = 0) \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=0) + \text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0 | Y_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1) \\
&= 1/2 (1/2) + 1/2 (1/2) = 1/2 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1) &= \text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1 | Y_{i} = 0) \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=0) + \text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1 | Y_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1) \\
&= 1/2 (1/2) + 1/2 (1/2) = 1/2
\end{aligned}\]
Altogether, we find

Two Fair Coins



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
Marginal




\(y=0\)
\(1/4\)
\(1/4\)
\(1/2\)


\(y=1\)
\(1/4\)
\(1/4\)
\(1/2\)


Marginal
\(1/2\)
\(1/2\)
\(1\)





Code
# Compute the marginal distributions.
# Marginal for X: sum across columns.
P_x <- colSums(P_xy)
P_x
## X=0 X=1 
## 0.5 0.5
# Marginal for Y: sum across rows.
P_y <- rowSums(P_xy)
P_y
## Y=0 Y=1 
## 0.5 0.5

# Compute the conditional probabilities Prob(Y | X).
PY_x <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
for (j in c(1, 2)) {
  PY_x[, j] <- P_xy[, j] / P_x[j]
}
rownames(PY_x) <- c('Y=0', 'Y=1')
colnames(PY_x) <- c('given X=0', 'given X=1')
PY_x
##     given X=0 given X=1
## Y=0       0.5       0.5
## Y=1       0.5       0.5


Are the coins statistically independent?









NoteMust Know





Now consider a second example, where the second coin is “Completely Unfair”, so that it is always the same as the first. The outcomes generated with a Completely Unfair coin are the same as if we only flipped one coin. \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0, Y_{i} = 0) &= 1/2 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 0, Y_{i} = 1) &= 0 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1, Y_{i} = 0) &= 0 \\
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1, Y_{i} = 1) &= 1/2 .
\end{aligned}\] The joint distribution is written generally as \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y) &= \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x) \mathbf{1}( x=y ),
\end{aligned}\] where \(\mathbf{1}(x=y)\) equals \(1\) when \(x=y\) and \(0\) otherwise. The marginal distribution of the second coin is \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0)
&= \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0 | X_{i} = 0) \text{Prob}(X_{i}=0) + \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 0 | X_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}(X_{i} = 1) \\
&= 1 (1/2) + 0(1/2) = 1/2 . \\
\text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1)
&= \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1 | X_{i} =0) \text{Prob}( X_{i} = 0) + \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = 1 | X_{i} = 1) \text{Prob}( X_{i} = 1) \\
&= 0 (1/2) + 1 (1/2) = 1/2 .
\end{aligned}\] which is the same marginal as in the first example!
The marginal distribution of the first coin is found in the exact same way (show this yourself).
Altogether, we find

A Fair Coin and a Completely Unfair Coin



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
Marginal




\(y=0\)
\(1/2\)
\(0\)
\(1/2\)


\(y=1\)
\(0\)
\(1/2\)
\(1/2\)


Marginal
\(1/2\)
\(1/2\)
\(1\)





Code
# Create the joint distribution matrix for the unfair coin case.
probs <- c(0.5, 0, 0, 0.5) # unfair coin

P_xy <- matrix( probs, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
rownames(P_xy) <- c('Y=0', 'Y=1')
colnames(P_xy) <- c('X=0', 'X=1')
P_xy
##     X=0 X=1
## Y=0 0.5 0.0
## Y=1 0.0 0.5


# Compute the marginal distributions.
# Marginal for X: sum across columns.
P_x <- colSums(P_xy)
P_x
## X=0 X=1 
## 0.5 0.5
# Marginal for Y: sum across rows.
P_y <- rowSums(P_xy)
P_y
## Y=0 Y=1 
## 0.5 0.5

# Compute the conditional probabilities Prob(Y | X).
PY_x <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
for (j in c(1, 2)) {
  PY_x[, j] <- P_xy[, j] / P_x[j]
}
rownames(PY_x) <- c('Y=0', 'Y=1')
colnames(PY_x) <- c('given X=0', 'given X=1')
PY_x
##     given X=0 given X=1
## Y=0         1         0
## Y=1         0         1


Are the coins statistically independent?









TipTest Yourself





Try computing conditional probabilities for another unfair set of coins below. Explain why the marginal distribution of the second coin is balanced.


Code
probs <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3)
P_xy <- matrix(probs, nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(c('Y=0', 'Y=1'), c('X=0', 'X=1')))

# Draw N bivariate observations
xy_vals <- expand.grid(y = 0:1, x = 0:1)
N <- 500
draws <- sample(nrow(xy_vals), N, replace = TRUE, prob = P_xy)
x_sim <- xy_vals[draws, 'x']
y_sim <- xy_vals[draws, 'y']

table(y_sim, x_sim) / N
##      x_sim
## y_sim     0     1
##     0 0.398 0.116
##     1 0.202 0.284
P_xy
##     X=0 X=1
## Y=0 0.4 0.1
## Y=1 0.2 0.3





Sometimes we observe one variable and want to learn about the other, which reverses the direction of conditioning.






ImportantKey Definition





Bayes’ theorem (Bayes 1763) relates the two conditional directions: \[\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x \mid Y_{i}=y) = \frac{\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y \mid X_{i}=x)\,\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)}{\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y)}.\]



Bayes’ theorem is useful because it is exactly how an observation updates a prior belief. It applies the event version of Bayes’ theorem to random variables. Building on the coin-flip examples above, suppose we observe the outcome of the second coin (\(Y_{i}\)) and want to update our belief about the first coin (\(X_{i}\)).






NoteMust Know





Unfair coins. Now consider the joint distribution from the Test Yourself above, with probs <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3):

\(0.4\)
\(1\)



The prior is \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)=0.4\). The conditional probabilities of heads on the second coin are \[
\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1|X_{i}=1) = \frac{0.3}{0.4} = 0.75,\quad
\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1|X_{i}=0) = \frac{0.2}{0.6} = \frac{1}{3}.
\] Applying Bayes’ theorem, \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1|Y_{i}=1)
&= \frac{0.75 \times 0.4}{0.75 \times 0.4 + \frac{1}{3}\times 0.6}
= \frac{0.3}{0.3+0.2} = 0.6.
\end{aligned}\] The prior probability of heads on the first coin was \(0.4\), but after seeing heads on the second coin, it increases to \(0.6\). The coins are not independent: when the second coin shows heads, it is more likely that the first coin also shows heads.


Code
# Unfair coins
probs <- c(0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3)
P_xy <- matrix(probs, nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(c('Y=0', 'Y=1'), c('X=0', 'X=1')))
P_xy
##     X=0 X=1
## Y=0 0.4 0.1
## Y=1 0.2 0.3

# Marginals
P_x <- colSums(P_xy)
P_y <- rowSums(P_xy)

# Prob(Y=1 | X=x)
PY1_x <- P_xy['Y=1', ] / P_x
PY1_x
##       X=0       X=1 
## 0.3333333 0.7500000

# Posterior: Prob(X=1 | Y=1)
posterior_x1 <- (PY1_x['X=1'] * P_x['X=1']) / P_y['Y=1']
posterior_x1  # prior was 0.4, posterior is 0.6
## X=1 
## 0.6

# Also compute Prob(X=1 | Y=0)
PY0_x <- P_xy['Y=0', ] / P_x
posterior_x1_y0 <- (PY0_x['X=1'] * P_x['X=1']) / P_y['Y=0']
posterior_x1_y0  # seeing tails lowers belief to 0.2
## X=1 
## 0.2


Are the coins statistically independent?





Definitions for Continuous Data
The joint distribution is defined as \[\begin{aligned}
F(x, y) &= \text{Prob}(X_{i} \leq x, Y_{i} \leq y)
\end{aligned}\] The marginal distributions are then defined as \[\begin{aligned}
F_{X}(x) &= F(x, \infty) \\
F_{Y}(y) &= F(\infty, y).
\end{aligned}\] which is called marginalizing (an application of the law of total probability). Variables are statistically independent if \(F(x, y) = F_{X}(x)F_{Y}(y)\) for all \(x, y\).
The most-used parametric joint distribution on continuous data is the bivariate analog of the Normal.






ImportantKey Definition





A bivariate normal distribution describes a random vector \((X_{i}, Y_{i})\) whose joint density is the multivariate normal with mean vector \((\mathbb{E}[X_{i}], \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}])\), variances \((\mathbb{V}[X_{i}], \mathbb{V}[Y_{i}])\), and correlation \(\rho\).



The bivariate normal is useful for analytical work on multivariate random variables. Both marginals are normal, and every conditional \(Y_{i} \mid X_{i} = x\) is also normal with a linear conditional mean. Many results for one Normal random variable therefore extend to the pair.


Code
library('mvtnorm')

# Simulate Bivariate Data
N <- 10000
Mu <- c(2, 2) ## Means

Sigma1 <- matrix(c(2, -.8, -.8, 1), 2, 2) ## CoVariance Matrix 1
xy1_sim <- rmvnorm(N, Mu, Sigma1)
colnames(xy1_sim) <- c('x_sim', 'y_sim')

Sigma2 <- matrix(c(2, .4, .4, 1), 2, 2) ## CoVariance Matrix 2
xy2_sim <- rmvnorm(N, Mu, Sigma2)
colnames(xy2_sim) <- c('x_sim', 'y_sim')

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
## Different diagonals
plot(xy2_sim, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.02), pch=16,
    main=NA,
    ylim=c(-4, 8), xlim=c(-4, 8),
    xlab='X', ylab='Y')
title('Joint Distributions', font.main=1)
points(xy1_sim, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.02), pch=16)
## Same marginal distributions
xbks <- seq(-4, 8, by=.2)
hist(xy2_sim[, 2], col=rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5),
    breaks=xbks, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    xlab='Y',
    main=NA)
title('Marginal Distributions', font.main=1)
hist(xy1_sim[, 2], col=rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.5),
    add=TRUE, breaks=xbks, border=NA, freq=FALSE)















NoteMust Know





Independent normal random variables are a special case of the bivariate normal. With both variances equal to \(1\) and \(\rho=0\), drawing \(X_{i}\) and \(Y_{i}\) separately gives the same joint distribution as one draw from the bivariate normal.


Code
# Two independent standard normal random variables
n <- 2e4
xy_iid_sim <- cbind(rnorm(n), rnorm(n))

# One joint draw from a bivariate normal with zero correlation
xy_joint_sim <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(n, c(0, 0))

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(xy_iid_sim, col=grey(0, .05), pch=16,
    xlim=c(-5, 5), ylim=c(-5, 5),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')
title('Two Independent Draws', font.main=1)
plot(xy_joint_sim, col=grey(0, .05), pch=16,
    xlim=c(-5, 5), ylim=c(-5, 5),
    main=NA, xlab='X', ylab='Y')
title('One Joint Draw', font.main=1)









Code

# The joint density equals the product of the two marginal densities
d1 <- dnorm(xy_iid_sim[, 1])*dnorm(xy_iid_sim[, 2])
d2 <- mvtnorm::dmvnorm(xy_iid_sim, c(0, 0))
head(cbind(product=d1, joint=d2))
##         product      joint
## [1,] 0.04924204 0.04924204
## [2,] 0.07451359 0.07451359
## [3,] 0.14921940 0.14921940
## [4,] 0.06446184 0.06446184
## [5,] 0.03244693 0.03244693
## [6,] 0.15220066 0.15220066





Other joint distributions exist; see e.g., https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/NonNorMvtDist/NonNorMvtDist.pdf.

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
text:
18.2 Statistics

Conditional Expectation
The natural population object that regression tries to estimate is the average of \(Y_{i}\) within each subpopulation defined by \(X_{i}\).






ImportantKey Definition





The conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]\) is the population mean of \(Y_{i}\) inside the subpopulation where \(X_{i}=x\): \[\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]=\sum_{y} y\,\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y\mid X_{i}=x).\]



The conditional expectation is useful as the population target for regression. The sample conditional means \(\hat{m}_{Y}(x)\) from Two Groups estimate \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]\). The fitted line from Simple Regression estimates its best linear approximation. The formula above sums over conditional probabilities for discrete \(X_{i}\); for continuous \(X_{i}\) the conditional expectation function traces a smooth curve indexed by \(x\) (the integral version replaces the sum).
For example, consider a bivariate random vector with three outcomes for \(X_{i}\) and three outcomes for \(Y_{i}\).

Joint Distribution with Three Outcomes Each



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
\(x=2\)




\(y=0\)
\(0.0\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.0\)


\(y=10\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.3\)
\(0.1\)


\(y=20\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.2\)



The plot below shows each outcome \((x,y)\) with deeper colors reflecting higher probability events.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Make a Probability Table
x <- c(0, 1, 2)
y <- c(0, 10, 20)
P_xy <- matrix(c(
    0.0, 0.1, 0.0,
    0.1, 0.3, 0.1,
    0.1, 0.1, 0.2
), nrow=3, ncol=3, byrow=TRUE)
rownames(P_xy) <- paste0('y=', y)
colnames(P_xy) <-  paste0('x=', x)
P_xy
##      x=0 x=1 x=2
## y=0  0.0 0.1 0.0
## y=10 0.1 0.3 0.1
## y=20 0.1 0.1 0.2

# Plot joint distribution
prob_table <- expand.grid(x=x, y=y)
prob_table[, 'probabilities'] <- as.vector(t(P_xy))
plot(prob_table[, 'x'], prob_table[, 'y'],
     xlim=c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim=c(-5, 25),
     pch=21, cex=8, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8),
     bg=rgb(0, 0, 1, prob_table[, 'probabilities']),
     main=NA, xlab='x', ylab='y')









We can compute marginals from the table, \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i}=0)=0.2,\quad & \text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)=0.5 ,\quad \text{Prob}(X_{i}=2) = 0.3 \\
\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=0)=0.1,\quad & \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=10)=0.5 ,\quad \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=20) = 0.4
\end{aligned}\]
This gives us conditional probabilities and hence also conditional expectations; \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=0] &= 0\frac{0}{0.2} + 10\frac{0.1}{0.2} + 20\frac{0.1}{0.2} = 0 + \frac{10}{2} + \frac{20}{2} = 15, \\
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=1] &= 0\frac{0.1}{0.5} + 10\frac{0.3}{0.5} + 20\frac{0.1}{0.5} = 0 + \frac{30}{5} + \frac{20}{5} = 10, \\
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=2] &= 0\frac{0}{0.3} + 10\frac{0.1}{0.3} + 20\frac{0.2}{0.3} = 0 + \frac{10}{3} + \frac{40}{3} = \frac{50}{3} \approx 16.67.
\end{aligned}\] Note that the conditional mean is non-monotonic: \[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=0]}{1-0} &= \frac{10 - 15}{1} = -5, \\
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=2] - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=1]}{2-1} &= \frac{\frac{50}{3} - 10}{1} = \frac{20}{3} \approx 6.67.
\end{aligned}\] It decreases from \(x=0\) to \(x=1\) and then increases from \(x=1\) to \(x=2\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Compute Marginals
P_x <- colSums(P_xy) #Prob(X_i=x)
P_y <- rowSums(P_xy) #Prob(Y_i=y)

# Compute the conditional probabilities Prob(Y_i=y | X_i=x).
PY_x <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
for (j in seq(ncol(P_xy)) ) {
  PY_x[, j] <- P_xy[, j] / P_x[j]
}
rownames(PY_x) <- paste0('Y=', y)
colnames(PY_x) <- paste0('given X=', x)
PY_x
##      given X=0 given X=1 given X=2
## Y=0        0.0       0.2 0.0000000
## Y=10       0.5       0.6 0.3333333
## Y=20       0.5       0.2 0.6666667

# Computational Shortcut: PY_x <- t( t(P_xy) / P_x )

# Conditional expectation E[Y_i|X_i=x]
EY_x <- colSums(PY_x * y)
EY_x
## given X=0 given X=1 given X=2 
##  15.00000  10.00000  16.66667

# Contrast with Grand Means
EX <- sum(x * P_x)
EY <- sum(y * P_y)
EY
## [1] 13

# E[X_i|Y_i=y]
# PX_y <- P_xy / P_y  #Prob(X_i=x | Y_i=y)
# EX_y <- colSums(PX_y * x)




Covariance
We can also dig a little deeper into the other bivariate statistics we compute. When we know how the data are generated, we can often compute the foundational covariance statistic. The covariance is the expected product of deviations from the population means: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]
&= \mathbb{E}\left[(X_{i} - \mathbb{E}[X_{i}])(Y_{i} - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}])\right] \\
&= \sum_{x}\sum_{y} (x - \mathbb{E}[X_{i}])(y - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]) \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y)
\end{aligned}\]
Using the marginal distributions from before allows us to compute the means: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] &= 0(0.2)+1(0.5)+2(0.3) = 1.1 \\
\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}] &= 0(0.1)+10(0.5)+20(0.4) = 13
\end{aligned}\] We can then compute the cell-by-cell contributions: \(\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y) (x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])(y-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}])\), which plug in to the covariance formula; \[
\begin{array}{l l r r r r r}
\hline
x & y & \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x, Y_{i}=y) & x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] & y-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}] & (x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])(y-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]) & \text{Contribution}\\
\hline
0 & 0  & 0.0 & -1.1 & -13 & 14.3  & 0\\
0 & 10 & 0.1 & -1.1 & -3  & 3.3   & 0.330\\
0 & 20 & 0.1 & -1.1 & 7   & -7.7  & -0.770\\
1 & 0  & 0.1 & -0.1 & -13 & 1.3   & 0.130\\
1 & 10 & 0.3 & -0.1 & -3  & 0.3   & 0.090\\
1 & 20 & 0.1 & -0.1 & 7   & -0.7  & -0.070\\
2 & 0  & 0.0 & 0.9  & -13 & -11.7 & 0\\
2 & 10 & 0.1 & 0.9  & -3  & -2.7  & -0.270\\
2 & 20 & 0.2 & 0.9  & 7   & 6.3   & 1.260\\
\hline
\end{array}
\] \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{C}[X_{i},Y_{i}] &= \sum_{x} \sum_{y} \left(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\right)\left(y-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]\right) \text{Prob}\left(X_{i} = x, Y_{i} = y\right) \\
&= 0 + 0.330 -0.770 + 0.130 + 0.090  -0.070 +0 -0.270 + 1.260
= 0.7
\end{aligned}\]
Note that you can do the above calculations using the computer instead of by hand.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Compute Covariance
dxy_grid <- expand.grid(dy=y-EY, dx=x-EX)[, c(2, 1)]
dxy_grid[, 'p'] <- as.vector(P_xy)
dxy_grid[, 'contribution'] <- dxy_grid[, 'dx'] * dxy_grid[, 'dy'] * dxy_grid[, 'p']
CovXY <- sum(dxy_grid[, 'contribution'])
CovXY
## [1] 0.7


We can now use the covariance to compute the often-used Pearson correlation.






NoteMust Know





The Pearson correlation (Pearson 1896) divides the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations: \[
\frac{\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}] }{ \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]} \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]} }
\]
To compute this statistic in the previous example, we first need the variances \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] &= \sum_{x} (x-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2 \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x) \\
&= (0-1.1)^2(0.2)+(1-1.1)^2(0.5)+(2-1.1)^2(0.3)=0.49 \\
\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}] &= \sum_{y}  (y-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}])^2 \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y) \\
&= (0-13)^2(0.1)+(10-13)^2(0.5)+(20-13)^2(0.4)=41
\end{aligned}\] Then we can find the correlation as \[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathbb{C}[X_{i},Y_{i}]}{ \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]} \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]} }
&= \frac{0.7}{\sqrt{0.49} \sqrt{41}} = \frac{0.7}{0.7 \sqrt{41}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{41}} \approx 0.156,
\end{aligned}\] which suggests a weak positive association between the variables.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# CovXY defined above
# Compute Variances
VX <- sum( (x-EX)^2 * P_x)
SX <- sqrt(VX)
VY <- sum( (y-EY)^2 * P_y)
SY <- sqrt(VY)

# Compute Correlation
CorXY <- CovXY / (SX * SY)
CorXY
## [1] 0.1561738











NoteMust Know





Compute the correlation for bivariate data with these probabilities, using both math (first) and the computer (second)

Joint Distribution C

\(x=10\)

\(0.05\)
