Explain intuitively when the correlation equals \(0\) and when it does not.





Regression Coefficient
Just as the sample slope \(\hat{b}_{1}\) summarized a sample, its population counterpart describes how the data are generated.






ImportantKey Definition





A linear data generating process is \[Y_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X_{i} + \epsilon_{i}, \quad \mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i} \mid X_{i}=x] = 0 \text{ for every } x,\] where the fixed numbers \(\beta_{0}\) and \(\beta_{1}\) are the (theoretical) regression coefficients and \(\epsilon_{i}\) is the population error term. In this model, the slope equals the covariance over the variance of \(X_{i}\): \[\beta_{1} = \frac{\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}] }{ \mathbb{V}[X_{i}] }.\]



To see why, note that the error has mean zero at every \(x\), so it also has mean zero overall, and \(Y_{i} - \mathbb{E}[Y_{i}] = \beta_{1}(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]) + \epsilon_{i}\). Then \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]
&= \mathbb{E}\left[(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])\left(\beta_{1}(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]) + \epsilon_{i}\right)\right] \\
&= \beta_{1}\mathbb{E}\left[(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])^2\right] + \mathbb{E}\left[(X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i}])\epsilon_{i}\right] \\
&= \beta_{1}\mathbb{V}[X_{i}],
\end{aligned}\] where the last term is zero because \(\epsilon_{i}\) averages to zero at each value of \(X_{i}\). Dividing both sides by \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) gives the formula in the definition.
\(\beta_{1}\) is useful as the population target of the sample slope \(\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}\) from Simple Regression: when the data come from a linear data generating process, OLS estimates \(\beta_{1}\) from a finite sample. In that case, the conditional expectation is itself a straight line, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x] = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x\), because the error averages to zero at every \(x\). However, the ratio \(\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]/\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) can be computed for any joint distribution, even when no linear data generating process exists.






NoteMust Know





For the \(3\times3\) table above, the conditional expectation computed earlier is not a straight line (it falls from \(x=0\) to \(x=1\), then rises), so the data are not generated by a linear model and there is no true \(\beta_{1}\). We already found \(\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}] = 0.7\) and \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = 0.49\), so the ratio is still \[
\frac{\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]}{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]} = \frac{0.7}{0.49} = \frac{70}{49} = \frac{10}{7} \approx 1.43.
\] This is the slope of the best straight-line approximation to the conditional expectation. The line is “best” in the sense that it minimizes mean squared error among all linear approximations to the conditional expectation function. OLS estimates this slope from samples of the table, and it is positive because the line captures the overall upward tendency. But when the conditional expectation bends, the best line still misses: here it misses the dip at \(x=1\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# CovXY and VX defined above
# Slope of the best linear approximation: covariance over variance of X
CovXY / VX
## [1] 1.428571

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
section: 18.3 Type I and Type II Errors
text:
18.3 Type I and Type II Errors
A hypothesis test starts with a null \(H_{0}\) and an alternative \(H_{A}\), and produces a decision (reject or fail-to-reject) from finite sample data. Because the data have variability, the decision can be wrong in two ways (Neyman and Pearson 1933).






ImportantKey Definition





A Type I error is rejecting \(H_{0}\) when \(H_{0}\) is true (a false positive). A Type II error is failing to reject \(H_{0}\) when \(H_{0}\) is false (a false negative).



This distinction is useful because the two error types are managed by different levers: we control Type I error by setting the significance level \(\alpha=\text{Prob}(\text{Type I})\) before looking at the data, while Type II error is harder to control directly and depends on the sample size and the true effect size. Reducing one error rate usually raises the other for a fixed sample.

Type I and Type II Errors







True Situation
Decision: Fail to Reject \(H_{0}\)
Decision: Reject \(H_{0}\)




\(H_{0}\) is True
Correct (no detection)
Type I Error (False Positive)


\(H_{0}\) is False
Type II Error (False Negative; missed detection)
Correct (effect detected)









TipTest Yourself





Here is a Courtroom example: Someone suspected of committing a crime is at trial, and they are either guilty or not (a Bernoulli random variable). You hypothesize that the suspect is innocent, and a jury can either convict them (decide guilty) or free them (decide not-guilty). Recall that fail-to-reject a hypothesis does not mean accepting it, so deciding not-guilty does not necessarily mean innocent.

Courtroom Decisions


True Situation
Decision: Free
Decision: Convict




Suspect Innocent
Correctly Freed
Falsely Convicted


Suspect Guilty
Falsely Freed
Correctly Convicted






Adamson and Rentschler (2025) build a similar “truth table of criminal justice” for policing. Each civilian either steals or produces, and each can be punished or not, which gives true and false positives and negatives.

Statistical Power
The complement of Type II error has its own name because it is what we actually want from the test.






ImportantKey Definition





Statistical power \(1-\beta\) is the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_{0}\) when \(H_{0}\) is false: \[\text{Power} = 1 - \beta = 1 - \text{Prob}(\text{Type II Error}).\] (Here \(\beta\) is the Type II error probability, not the regression coefficient \(\beta_{1}\).)



Power is useful as the probability that a true effect of a given size will actually show up as a rejection in our data: it rises with the sample size \(n\), the true effect size, and the significance level \(\alpha\). The complementary error rate, the significance level \(\alpha = \text{Prob}(\text{Type I Error})\), is something we choose in advance (commonly \(\alpha=0.05\)). Power is less often chosen directly; it follows from the chosen sample size and the assumed effect size, and lets us judge whether a study is well-powered to detect what we care about (Cohen 1988; Ioannidis et al. 2017).






TipTest Yourself





The code below runs a small simulation using a shifted, nonparametric bootstrap. It uses a two-sided test with a studentized statistic for \(H_{0}: \mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 0\).


Code
# Power for Two-sided test;
# nonparametric bootstrap, studentized statistic
n <- 25
null_mean <- 0
alpha <- 0.05
n_boot <- 299

sim_reps <- 100

p_values <- rep(NA, sim_reps)
for (i in seq(p_values)) {
    # Generate data
    x_sim <- rnorm(n, mean=0.2, sd=1)
    # Observed statistic
    m_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    T_obs <-  (m_hat - null_mean) / (sd(x_sim)/ sqrt(n)) ##studentized
    # Bootstrap null distribution of the statistic
    T_boot <- rep(NA, n_boot)
    x_null_sim <- x_sim - m_hat + null_mean # Impose the null by recentering
    for (b in seq(T_boot)) {
      x_boot <- sample(x_null_sim, size = n, replace = TRUE)
      T_b <- (mean(x_boot) - null_mean) / (sd(x_boot)/sqrt(n))
      T_boot[b] <- T_b
    }
    # Two-sided bootstrap p-value
    pval <- mean(abs(T_boot) >= abs(T_obs))
    p_values[i] <- pval
    }
power <- mean(p_values < alpha)
power





There is an important Trade-off for fixed sample sizes: Increasing significance (fewer false positives) often lowers power (more false negatives). Generally, power depends on the effect size and sample size: bigger true effects and larger \(n\) make it easier to detect real differences (higher power, lower \(\beta\)).
Power also depends on the test. A rank test uses only the order of the data. It usually has a little less power than a test of means when the data are normal, but it can have much more when the tails are heavy (Hodges and Lehmann 1956). With ordered categories, a rank test usually has more power than the categorical ANOVA against differences along the ordering, because it concentrates on that one direction. The categorical ANOVA has more power against other differences, such as one group concentrated in the middle categories and another split between the extremes.


Regression Slope Example
Consider testing \(H_{0}: \beta_{1} = 0\) for a simple regression. As in Sampling, pretend the data are the whole population, so we know the true slope and whether the null is true. When the true slope is nonzero (null is false), failing to reject is a Type II Error, and the share of samples that reject estimates the power. Each sample is tested with the permutation test from Simple Regression, which shuffles the outcome across observations.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Test the slope from a regression of hourly wage on years of schooling
# Pretend these 3294 workers are the whole population
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_xy <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(population_xy) <- c('x', 'y') # x=years of schooling, y=hourly wage
population_slope <- coef(lm(y ~ x, data=population_xy))[2]
population_slope
##         x 
## 0.5571617
# The population slope is about 0.557, so the null is false.

# Function: draw one sample of n workers, return the permutation p-value for the slope
sample_pval <- function(n, population, n_perm=199) {
    s_id <- sample(nrow(population), n, replace=FALSE)
    x_sim <- population[s_id, 'x']
    y_sim <- population[s_id, 'y']
    # Slope as covariance over variance, which is much faster than lm() inside a loop
    b1_hat <- cov(x_sim, y_sim) / var(x_sim)
    b1_perm <- rep(NA, n_perm)
    for (b in seq_along(b1_perm)) {
        y_perm <- sample(y_sim, replace=FALSE) # breaks any link with schooling, imposing the null
        b1_perm[b] <- cov(x_sim, y_perm) / var(x_sim)
    }
    # Two-sided p-value: share of permuted slopes at least as far from zero
    p_value <- mean(abs(b1_perm) >= abs(b1_hat))
    return(p_value)
}

sim_reps <- 300
alpha <- 0.05
n_grid <- c(10, 20, 50, 100, 200)

# Power: share of samples that reject, for each sample size
power_by_n <- rep(NA, length(n_grid))
for (k in seq_along(n_grid)) {
    p_values <- replicate(sim_reps, sample_pval(n_grid[k], population_xy))
    power_by_n[k] <- mean(p_values < alpha)
}
names(power_by_n) <- n_grid
power_by_n
##        10        20        50       100       200 
## 0.1500000 0.2533333 0.5433333 0.8433333 0.9733333

# Power with samples of 50 workers
power_est <- power_by_n['50']


To study Type I errors, we need a population where the null is true. Shuffling the outcome once breaks the link between the two variables. By chance, the shuffled population still has a small slope, so we subtract it to make the population slope exactly \(0\). When the true slope is \(0\) (null is true), rejecting is a Type I Error. The share of samples that reject should be near \(\alpha=0.05\) for every sample size.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# A population where schooling and wages are unrelated
population_null <- population_xy
population_null[, 'y'] <- sample(population_xy[, 'y'])

# Remove the small slope left over by chance
slope_left <- coef(lm(y ~ x, data=population_null))[2]
x_centered <- population_null[, 'x'] - mean(population_null[, 'x'])
population_null[, 'y'] <- population_null[, 'y'] - slope_left * x_centered
coef(lm(y ~ x, data=population_null))[2] # zero, up to rounding
##            x 
## 1.209224e-17

# Type I Error rate: share of samples that reject, for each sample size
type1_by_n <- rep(NA, length(n_grid))
for (k in seq_along(n_grid)) {
    p_values_null <- replicate(sim_reps, sample_pval(n_grid[k], population_null))
    type1_by_n[k] <- mean(p_values_null < alpha)
}
names(type1_by_n) <- n_grid
type1_by_n
##         10         20         50        100        200 
## 0.05333333 0.04333333 0.04666667 0.03333333 0.05666667


Power rises with the sample size, while the Type I Error rate stays near \(\alpha\).


Code
# Rejection rates by sample size
plot(n_grid, power_by_n, type = 'b', pch = 16,
    xlab = 'Sample size (n)', ylab = 'Share of samples that reject',
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    main = NA)
abline(h = alpha, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd = 2) # drawn first, so the Type I Error series stays visible on top
lines(n_grid, type1_by_n, type = 'b', pch = 16, col = grey(0.5, 0.8))
title('Rejection Rates for Regression Slope', font.main = 1)
legend('right', legend = c('Power (true slope 0.557)', 'Type I Error (true slope 0)', expression(alpha)),
    col = c(1, grey(0.5, 0.8), rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)),
    lty = 1, lwd = c(1, 1, 2), pch = c(16, 16, NA), bty = 'n')

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
text:
18.4 Bayesian Updating
The coin flips example used Bayes’ theorem to update a prior belief about one coin after seeing the other. The same formula turns a test result into an updated belief about whether a hypothesis is true.
Each term in the formula has a name:

\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\) is the prior probability for \(X_{i}=x\).
\(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y|X_{i}=x)\) is the likelihood of seeing \(Y_{i}=y\) if \(X_{i}=x\) is true.
\(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x|Y_{i}=y)\) is the posterior, your updated probability after seeing \(Y_{i}=y\).

A useful way to remember the structure is “Posterior \(\propto\) Likelihood \(\times\) Prior”. For two states, the posterior odds equal the prior odds times a likelihood ratio.

Bayesian Screening
A common application of Bayes’ theorem is interpreting a positive result from a diagnostic test.






ImportantKey Definition





For a binary screening test where \(X_{i}=1\) means “condition present” and \(Y_{i}=1\) means “test positive”:
Prevalence \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1)\) is the base rate of the condition in the population.
Sensitivity \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=1)\) is the probability of a positive result when the condition is present.
False positive rate \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=0)\) is the probability of a positive result when it is absent.



Screening is useful for converting test accuracy and base rates into the quantity an individual actually cares about: the posterior \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1\mid Y_{i}=1)\), the probability of having the condition given a positive result. The three inputs play different roles: sensitivity and the false positive rate describe the test, while prevalence describes the population. Suppose a screening test has sensitivity \(0.90\), false positive rate \(0.08\), and prevalence \(0.12\). Applying Bayes’ theorem, \[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1|Y_{i}=1)
&=
\frac{0.90\times0.12}{0.90\times0.12 + 0.08\times0.88}
\approx 0.605.
\end{aligned}\] Even with a good test, the posterior depends strongly on prevalence: rare conditions produce many false alarms even when the test is accurate. The fraud-detection example in Bivariate Distributions showed the same pattern with counts: the same flag meant fraud was unlikely when fraud was rare and likely when it was common.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# States: X in {0, 1}, signal Y in {0, 1}
# Prior Prob(X_i=1)
p_x1 <- 0.12

# Test characteristics
p_y1_x1 <- 0.90
p_y1_x0 <- 0.08

# Law of total probability for Prob(Y_i=1)
p_y1 <- p_y1_x1 * p_x1 + p_y1_x0 * (1 - p_x1)

# Bayes posterior Prob(X_i=1 | Y_i=1)
p_x1_y1 <- (p_y1_x1 * p_x1) / p_y1
p_x1_y1
## [1] 0.6053812

# Also compute Prob(X_i=1 | Y_i=0)
p_y0_x1 <- 1 - p_y1_x1
p_y0_x0 <- 1 - p_y1_x0
p_y0 <- p_y0_x1 * p_x1 + p_y0_x0 * (1 - p_x1)
p_x1_y0 <- (p_y0_x1 * p_x1) / p_y0
p_x1_y0
## [1] 0.01460565








TipTest Yourself





Notice that a positive test result raises the probability of having the condition from \(12\%\) (prior) to about \(60\%\) (posterior). A negative test result lowers it from \(12\%\) to about \(1.5\%\). If prevalence were higher, say \(50\%\), the posterior after a positive test would be \(\frac{0.90 \times 0.50}{0.90 \times 0.50 + 0.08 \times 0.50} = \frac{0.45}{0.49} \approx 0.92\). The same test is far more informative when prevalence is higher.





Posterior for a Regression Slope
The screening test has the same structure as testing a regression slope. Let \(X_{i}=1\) mean “slope is truly nonzero” and \(Y_{i}=1\) mean “the test rejects \(H_{0}\).” Then sensitivity equals power, the false positive rate equals \(\alpha\), and prevalence is your prior belief that the slope is nonzero. Using the simulation results from the previous section:


Code
# Prior: 50-50 chance the slope is nonzero
prior_nonzero <- 0.5

# 'Sensitivity' = power, 'False positive rate' = alpha
p_reject <- power_est * prior_nonzero + alpha * (1 - prior_nonzero)

# Posterior: Prob(slope nonzero | test rejects)
post_nonzero <- (power_est * prior_nonzero) / p_reject
post_nonzero
##        50 
## 0.9157303


Even with moderate power, a rejection substantially updates the posterior probability that the slope is nonzero. A weaker prior (e.g., \(\text{Prob}(\beta_{1} \neq 0) = 0.1\)) would require stronger evidence to reach the same posterior.


Code
# How the posterior changes with different priors
prior_grid <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
post_grid <- (power_est * prior_grid) /
    (power_est * prior_grid + alpha * (1 - prior_grid))

plot(prior_grid, post_grid, type = 'l', lwd = 2,
    xlab = 'Prior Prob(slope nonzero)',
    ylab = 'Posterior Prob(slope nonzero | reject)',
    main = NA)
title('Bayesian Interpretation of Rejection', font.main = 1)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 2)

title: 18  Bivariate Theory
text:
18.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Two joint distributions can have identical marginal distributions but different conditional distributions. Construct a \(2 \times 2\) probability table where \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=0) = \text{Prob}(X_{i}=1) = 1/2\) and \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=0) = \text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1) = 1/2\), but the variables are not independent. Verify by checking whether \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x, Y_{i}=y) = \text{Prob}(X_{i}=x)\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=y)\) holds.
Consider a bivariate random vector with the following joint distribution:

Joint Distribution of \(X_{i}\) and \(Y_{i}\)



\(x=0\)
\(x=1\)
\(x=2\)




\(y=0\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.2\)
\(0.1\)


\(y=5\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.2\)


\(y=10\)
\(0.0\)
\(0.1\)
\(0.1\)



Compute \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=x]\) for each value of \(x\). Then compute \(\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]\) and the Pearson correlation.
Write R code to simulate \(N = 5000\) draws from a bivariate normal distribution with means \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}] = 0\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}] = 5\), variances \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}] = 4\), \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}] = 1\), and correlation \(\rho = 0.6\). Plot the draws as a scatterplot and verify that the sample correlation is close to \(0.6\).
Explain the difference between a Type I Error and a Type II Error in the context of testing \(H_{0}: \beta_{1} = 0\) for a regression slope. Why does increasing the sample size \(n\) improve power without changing the significance level \(\alpha\)?
A screening test has sensitivity \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1|X_{i}=1) = 0.95\), false positive rate \(\text{Prob}(Y_{i}=1|X_{i}=0) = 0.10\), and prevalence \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1) = 0.05\). Use Bayes’ theorem to compute the posterior probability \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=1|Y_{i}=1)\). Explain why the posterior is much lower than the sensitivity.


Further Reading

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/2-1-random-variables-and-probability-distributions.html – formal treatment of joint distributions, expectations, and covariance for econometrics.
https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/probability.html – probability rules, conditional probability, and independence explained with intuitive examples.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/random-variables-stats-library/covariance-correlation/v/covariance – short video deriving covariance from joint distributions.
https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/hypothesisTesting.html – accessible treatment of null distributions, significance levels, and Bayesian interpretation.



Recall
This chapter defined joint, marginal, and conditional distributions for a random vector, and the bivariate normal. It also defined the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]\), the theoretical covariance \(\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]\) and correlation, and the regression coefficient \(\beta_{1}\) of a linear data generating process. It then used conditional probabilities for the Type I / Type II error distinction with statistical power, and Bayes’ theorem for converting a test rejection into a posterior. The \(3\times 3\) worked example with \(\text{Prob}(X_{i}=x, Y_{i}=y)\) across \(x~\text{in}~\{0, 1, 2\}\) and \(y~\text{in}~\{0, 10, 20\}\) produced a non-monotonic conditional expectation. It fell from \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=0]=15\) to \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=1]=10\) and rose to \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}|X_{i}=2]=50/3\), so there is no true \(\beta_{1}\). But the ratio \(\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]/\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=10/7\) still gives an upward best-fitting slope. The example shows the gap between \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]\) and its best linear approximation. The unfair-coin example showed Bayes’ theorem at work: heads on the second coin raised the probability of heads on the first from \(0.4\) to \(0.6\). Treating the Wages1 workers as a population showed both error rates. Samples from the real population estimated power across sample sizes \(n~\text{in}~\{10, 20, 50, 100, 200\}\). Samples from the shuffled population rejected at a rate near \(\alpha\).

Bayes, Thomas. 1763. “An Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 53: 370–418. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1763.0053.


Cohen, Jacob. 1988. Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences. 2nd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203771587.


Hodges, J. L., and E. L. Lehmann. 1956. “The Efficiency of Some Nonparametric Competitors of the \(t\)-Test.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 27 (2): 324–35. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177728261.


Ioannidis, John P. A., T. D. Stanley, and Hristos Doucouliagos. 2017. “The Power of Bias in Economics Research.” The Economic Journal 127 (605): F236–65. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12461.

title: 19  Classical Tests and Bias-Variance
text:
19.1 Classical Tests
Earlier chapters tested hypotheses with resampling.
This chapter asks two questions.
Just as with one sample tests, we can compute standardized differences. The observed difference is converted into a \(t\)-statistic by dividing by an estimated standard error. Note, however, that we have to compute the standard error for the difference statistic, which is a bit more complicated than for a single sample. Under the assumption that both populations are independently distributed, we can analytically derive the sampling distribution for the differences between two groups.

title: 19  Classical Tests and Bias-Variance
text:
Differences in Means
Let \(Y_{ig}\) denote the random outcome for individual \(i\) in group \(g\). To compare two group means, we standardize the observed difference by its estimated standard error.






ImportantKey Definition





The two-sample t-statistic divides the observed mean difference by its estimated standard error: \[\hat{t} = \frac{\hat{m}_{1} - \hat{m}_{2}}{\sqrt{\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}/n_{1}+\hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}/n_{2}}},\] where \(\hat{s}^2_{g,\text{adj}}\) is the adjusted sample variance and \(n_{g}\) is the sample size for group \(g\).
Welch’s t-test (Welch 1947) modifies the two-sample \(\hat{t}\) above to account for unequal variances or unequal sample sizes. The modifications use the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation.



The two-sample \(\hat{t}\) is useful as a standardized test statistic for comparing two means. Dividing by the standard error puts the gap in standard-error units. So the same numerator can be large or small in \(\hat{t}\) units, depending on \(n_{1}, n_{2}\) and the within-group variances. With normally distributed group means, this statistic follows Student’s t-distribution (Student 1908), so we can read a \(p\)-value from a formula rather than from resampling. When the two groups have unequal variances or sample sizes, a small adjustment to the degrees of freedom keeps the \(t\)-distribution approximation accurate.
The \(t\)-distribution result needs normal data, but in large samples the central limit theorem makes the difference in means approximately normal whatever the shape of the data.






ImportantKey Definition





The \(z\)-statistic standardizes an estimate by its estimated standard error, as \(\hat{t}\) does, but compares the result to the standard normal rather than to a \(t\)-distribution. For the difference statistic \(\hat{d}\) and the null of no difference, \[\hat{z} = \frac{\hat{d}}{\hat{\text{SE}}(D)}.\]



The \(z\)-statistic is useful because it only needs the estimate to be approximately normal, which holds in large samples for many statistics besides the mean. For means, \(\hat{d}=\hat{m}_{1}-\hat{m}_{2}\) and \(\hat{\text{SE}}(D)=\sqrt{\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}/n_{1}+\hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}/n_{2}}\), so \(\hat{z}\) is the same number as the two-sample \(\hat{t}\); only the reference distribution changes. The two-sided \(p\)-value is the probability that a standard normal draw lands at least \(|\hat{z}|\) from zero, which R computes as 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_hat)). The standard normal has thinner tails than any \(t\)-distribution, so the \(z\) \(p\)-value is smaller, but the gap shrinks as the groups grow.
For example, the code below compares two group means with Welch’s \(t\)-test.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Hourly wages in 1980 dollars for 3294 US workers
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# The levels are in this order, so the reported difference is female minus male
levels(Wages1[, 'sex'])
## [1] "female" "male"

# Welch's t-test (the default for t.test)
t.test(wage ~ sex, data=Wages1)
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  wage by sex
## t = -10.485, df = 3259.3, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -1.384162 -0.948033
## sample estimates:
## mean in group female   mean in group male 
##             5.146924             6.313021
# The female mean is about 1.17 dollars below the male mean.
# The reported t is also the z-statistic, about -10.5.
# With more than 1500 workers per group, both p-values are essentially zero.








NoteMust Know





The same test works on simulated data, where we choose the group means ourselves. Here the two groups have different means and different variances.


Code
# Sample 1
n1 <- 100
y1_sim <- rnorm(n1, 0, 2)
#hist(y1_sim, freq=FALSE, main='Sample 1')

# Sample 2
n2 <- 80
y2_sim <- rnorm(n2, 1, 1)
#hist(y2_sim, freq=FALSE, main='Sample 2')

t.test(y1_sim, y2_sim, var.equal=FALSE)
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  y1_sim and y2_sim
## t = -3.6939, df = 158.27, p-value = 0.0003037
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -1.190604 -0.360992
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y 
## 0.2177747 0.9935727





Welch’s \(t\)-test is useful as the default for comparing two means without assuming equal variances. Unequal variances are common in applied work, for example when comparing two job markets or two countries. With the variance-and-normality assumptions in place, the test can be conducted entirely with formulas (no bootstrap resampling required). Compare the bootstrap test of a mean difference in Two Groups, which needed neither assumption.






NoteMust Know





The Welch-Satterthwaite equation (Satterthwaite 1946; Welch 1947) approximates the degrees of freedom when the two groups have unequal variances: \[
\text{df} = \frac{\left(\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}/n_{1} + \hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}/n_{2}\right)^2}{\frac{(\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}/n_{1})^2}{n_{1}-1} + \frac{(\hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}/n_{2})^2}{n_{2}-1}}.
\] For example, suppose both groups have \(n_{1}=n_{2}=10\), with adjusted sample variances \(\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}=4\) and \(\hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}=1\). Writing \(v_{g}=\hat{s}^2_{g,\text{adj}}/n_{g}\), we have \(v_{1}=0.4\) and \(v_{2}=0.1\), so \[
\text{df} = \frac{(0.4+0.1)^2}{0.4^2/9 + 0.1^2/9} = \frac{0.25}{0.17/9} \approx 13.2.
\] This is below the equal-variance value \(n_{1}+n_{2}-2=18\): unequal variances cost degrees of freedom, which widens the \(t\)-distribution and makes the test more conservative.


Code
n01 <- 10; n02 <- 10
v01_hat <- 4/n01
v02_hat <- 1/n02
(v01_hat + v02_hat)^2 / (v01_hat^2/(n01-1) + v02_hat^2/(n02-1))
## [1] 13.23529











NoteMust Know





Continue the Welch-Satterthwaite example, with \(n_{1}=n_{2}=10\), \(\hat{s}^2_{1,\text{adj}}=4\), and \(\hat{s}^2_{2,\text{adj}}=1\), and suppose \(\hat{d}=\hat{m}_{1}-\hat{m}_{2}=1.5\). Then \(\hat{\text{SE}}(D)=\sqrt{0.4+0.1}=\sqrt{0.5}\approx 0.71\), so \(\hat{z}=\hat{t}=1.5/\sqrt{0.5}\approx 2.12\). The standard normal gives a \(p\)-value of about \(0.034\), while the \(t\)-distribution with \(13.2\) degrees of freedom gives about \(0.053\). With only \(10\) observations per group, the two reference distributions disagree about rejecting at the \(5\%\) level.


Code
# The two groups from the Welch-Satterthwaite example, with a mean difference of 1.5
d0_hat <- 1.5
se0_hat <- sqrt(v01_hat + v02_hat)
z0_hat <- d0_hat / se0_hat # the same number as the two-sample t-statistic
df0 <- (v01_hat + v02_hat)^2 / (v01_hat^2/(n01 - 1) + v02_hat^2/(n02 - 1))

# Same statistic, two reference distributions
c(z=z0_hat,
    p_normal=2 * pnorm(-abs(z0_hat)),
    p_t=2 * pt(-abs(z0_hat), df=df0))
##          z   p_normal        p_t 
## 2.12132034 0.03389485 0.05332678





We can visualize this by simulating many samples under the null (\(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i2}]\)) and comparing the distribution of \(\hat{t}\) with the theoretical \(t\)-distribution (dashed curve) and the standard normal used for \(\hat{z}\) (dotted curve). As in Sampling, pretend the data are the whole population. If we draw both groups from the same population, then the null of equal means holds exactly.


Code
# Pretend these 3294 workers are the whole population
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_xy <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(population_xy) <- c('x', 'y') # x=years of schooling, y=hourly wage
population_wages <- population_xy[, 'y']

# Simulate the t-statistic under the null (both groups from the same population)
n1 <- 100
n2 <- 80
n_sim <- 399
t_sim <- vector(length = n_sim)
for (b in seq(n_sim)) {
    y1_sim_b <- population_wages[sample(length(population_wages), n1, replace=FALSE)]
    y2_sim_b <- population_wages[sample(length(population_wages), n2, replace=FALSE)]
    t_sim[b] <- t.test(y1_sim_b, y2_sim_b, var.equal = FALSE)$statistic
}

# Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
# (use the population variance for both groups)
v1 <- var(population_wages) / n1
v2 <- var(population_wages) / n2
df_ws <- (v1 + v2)^2 / (v1^2 / (n1 - 1) + v2^2 / (n2 - 1))

# Overlay: simulated histogram vs. theoretical t-distribution
t_range <- range(c(t_sim, -4, 4))
hist(t_sim, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, border = NA,
    xlim = t_range,
    xlab = expression(hat(t)),
    main = NA)
title('Simulated vs. Theoretical Distributions', font.main = 1)

lines(t_grid, dt(t_grid, df = df_ws), col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 2)

Code
# Wages are right-skewed, so the group means are not exactly normal.
# With groups of 100 and 80, the histogram is typically close to both curves.

When the data are skewed, the group means are not exactly normal and the \(t\)-distribution is only an approximation. With small groups, the approximation can be noticeably worse, and the fatter tails of the \(t\)-distribution pull away from the standard normal.






NoteMust Know





We can also simulate under the null with normally distributed data, where the \(t\)-distribution result applies more directly. Here the two groups have the same mean but different variances.


Code
# Simulate the t-statistic under the null (both groups same mean)

for (b in seq(n_sim)) {
    y1_sim_b <- rnorm(n1, 0, 2)
    y2_sim_b <- rnorm(n2, 0, 1)
    t_sim_norm[b] <- t.test(y1_sim_b, y2_sim_b, var.equal = FALSE)$statistic
}

v2_norm <- 1^2 / n2

    xlim = t_range,
    xlab = expression(hat(t)),
    main = NA)

Regression Slope
The same ideas apply to regression coefficients. Recall that the OLS slope \(\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}\) is a statistic computed from the data. In the Simple Regression chapter, we estimated variability using data-driven methods (jackknife and bootstrap). Under standard assumptions, we can instead derive the sampling distribution analytically: the \(t\)-statistic \[
\hat{t} = \frac{\hat{b}_{1}}{\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})}
\] follows a \(t\)-distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom, where \(\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})\) is the classical estimated standard error of the slope. This allows us to test \(H_{0}: \beta_{1} = 0\) using math alone. In large samples, the OLS slope is approximately normal even when the errors are not, so the same ratio can also be read as a \(z\)-statistic, \(\hat{z}=\hat{b}_{1}/\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{1})\), and compared to the standard normal.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Wages1 data (same as Simple Regression chapter)
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data = xy_hat)

# The summary reports theoretical t-statistics and p-values
summary(reg)$coefficients
##               Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) -0.7225066 0.38739136 -1.865056 6.226247e-02
## x_hat        0.5571617 0.03297502 16.896478 1.734818e-61
# Each extra year of schooling goes with about 0.56 more dollars per hour.
# The t-statistic of about 16.9 makes the test of no slope decisive.








NoteMust Know





Manual verification of the theoretical \(t\)-statistic for the slope:


Code

b1_hat <- coef(reg)[2]
e_hat <- resid(reg)
s_adj_hat <- sqrt(sum(e_hat^2) / (n - 2)) # root of the adjusted MSE; summary() prints it as the residual standard error
s_b1 <- s_adj_hat / sqrt(sum((xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] - mean(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']))^2)) # SE of slope
t_stat <- b1_hat / s_b1

# Compare with summary output
c(manual = t_stat, summary = summary(reg)$coefficients[2, 3])
## manual.x_hat      summary 
##     16.89648     16.89648





We can compare the bootstrap sampling distribution of \(\hat{t}\) (histogram) with the theoretical \(t_{n-2}\) distribution (dashed curve) and the standard normal (dotted curve). Each bootstrap \(\hat{t}\) is centered at the original slope estimate, which plays the role of the true slope in the bootstrap world. So the histogram approximates the distribution of \(\hat{t}\) when the null is true. They should be similar, but are not identical because the theoretical result assumes normally distributed errors.


Code
# Bootstrap distribution of the t-statistic
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
b1_hat <- coef(reg)[2]
n_boot <- 399
boot_t <- vector(length = n_boot)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    b_id <- sample(nrow(xy_hat), replace = TRUE)
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[b_id, ]
    reg_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data = xy_boot)
    # Center at the original estimate and use the theoretical SE from summary
    coef_b <- summary(reg_b)$coefficients[2, ]
    boot_t[b] <- (coef_b[1] - b1_hat) / coef_b[2]
}

# Overlay: bootstrap histogram vs. theoretical t-distribution
t_range <- range(c(boot_t, -4, 4))
hist(boot_t, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, border = NA,
    xlim = t_range,
    xlab = expression(hat(t)),
    main = NA)
title('Bootstrap vs. Theoretical Distributions', font.main = 1)
# Theoretical t(n-2) density, and the standard normal for z
t_grid <- seq(t_range[1], t_range[2], length = 200)
lines(t_grid, dt(t_grid, df = n - 2), col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 2)
lines(t_grid, dnorm(t_grid), col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty = 3)
legend('topright', legend = c('Bootstrap', 't(n-2)', 'Standard normal'),
    fill = c(grey(.83), NA, NA), border = NA, # grey(.83) matches the default histogram fill
    lwd = c(NA, 1, 1), lty = c(NA, 2, 3), col = c(NA, rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)), bty = 'n')









Code
# The histogram roughly follows the two curves, which lie on top of each other.
# Wage errors are right-skewed, but with 3294 workers the slope is near normal.
# The observed t of about 16.9 is far off this axis.


We can compute the \(p\)-value for \(H_{0}: \beta_{1} = 0\) three ways: from the theoretical \(t\)-distribution, from the standard normal, and from the bootstrap distribution. All three ask how extreme the observed \(\hat{t}\) is under the null.


Code
t_obs <- summary(reg)$coefficients[2, 3]

# Theoretical p-value: Prob(|t| >= |t_obs|) under t(n-2)
p_theory <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), df = n - 2)

# Normal p-value: the same ratio read as a z-statistic
p_normal <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(t_obs))

# Bootstrap p-value: fraction of bootstrap |t|'s >= |t_obs|
p_boot <- mean(abs(boot_t) >= abs(t_obs))

c(t=p_theory, z=p_normal, bootstrap=p_boot)
##            t            z    bootstrap 
## 1.734818e-61 4.775986e-64 0.000000e+00
# All three are essentially zero, because the observed t is about 16.9.
# The t and z values differ by a large ratio only this far into the tails.
# No bootstrap t came close, so the bootstrap p-value prints as exactly 0.
# With 399 resamples, that only says the p-value is below about 1/399.


The \(t_{n-2}\) distribution gets closer to the standard normal as \(n\) grows, so the \(t\) and \(z\) \(p\)-values differ less in larger samples.

We check the coverage of both intervals from Simple Regression: the jackknife Normal interval and the bootstrap percentile interval. Inside the resampling loops, we compute each slope as \(\hat{c}_{XY}/\hat{v}_{X}\), which gives the same number as lm but runs faster.


Code
# Jackknife Normal CI and bootstrap percentile CI for each sample
n_samples <- 300
jack_cis <- matrix(NA, nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
boot_cis <- matrix(NA, nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
for(s in seq(n_samples)){
    s_id <- sample(nrow(population_xy), n, replace=FALSE)
    x_sim <- population_xy[s_id, 'x']
    y_sim <- population_xy[s_id, 'y']
    slope_s <- cov(x_sim, y_sim)/var(x_sim)
    # Jackknife SE and Normal CI
    jack_coefs_s <- rep(NA, n)
    for(i in seq_along(jack_coefs_s)){
        x_sim_i <- x_sim[-i]
        y_sim_i <- y_sim[-i]
        jack_coefs_s[i] <- cov(x_sim_i, y_sim_i)/var(x_sim_i)
    }
    jack_se_s <- sqrt((n - 1)/n * sum((jack_coefs_s - mean(jack_coefs_s))^2))
    jack_cis[s, ] <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), slope_s, jack_se_s)
    # Bootstrap percentile CI
    boot_coefs_s <- rep(NA, 399)
    for(b in seq_along(boot_coefs_s)){
        b_id <- sample(n, replace=TRUE)
        x_sim_boot <- x_sim[b_id]
        y_sim_boot <- y_sim[b_id]
        boot_coefs_s[b] <- cov(x_sim_boot, y_sim_boot)/var(x_sim_boot)
    }
    boot_cis[s, ] <- quantile(boot_coefs_s, probs=c(.025, .975))
}

# Percent of intervals that contain the population slope
jack_covered <- population_slope >= jack_cis[, 1] & population_slope <= jack_cis[, 2]
boot_covered <- population_slope >= boot_cis[, 1] & population_slope <= boot_cis[, 2]
c(jackknife_normal=mean(jack_covered), bootstrap_percentile=mean(boot_covered))*100
##     jackknife_normal bootstrap_percentile 
##                   94                   91
# Both percents are typically a little below 95%, the bootstrap more so.
# Wages are right-skewed, so neither interval is exact with n=100.

ci_xlim <- range(jack_cis[1:100, ], boot_cis[1:100, ])
par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for(method in names(cis_list)){

    plot.new()
    plot.window(xlim=ci_xlim, ylim=c(0, 100))

}

beta1_true <- coef(reg)[2]

# Function: simulate data, return theoretical p-value for slope
sim_pval <- function(n, beta1) {
    x_sim <- rnorm(n, mean = m_x_hat, sd = s_x_hat)
    y_sim <- beta0 + beta1 * x_sim + rnorm(n, 0, s_adj_hat)
    summary(lm(y_sim ~ x_sim))$coefficients[2, 4]
}

type1_rate_dgp  # should be close to alpha

pvals_alt <- replicate(sim_reps_dgp, sim_pval(n = 50, beta1 = beta1_true))
power_dgp <- mean(pvals_alt < alpha)
power_dgp
