Differences in Medians
If we want to test for the differences in medians across groups with independent observations, we can also use notches in the boxplot, as in Multiple Groups. R’s default notches (notch=TRUE) come from a normal-theory approximation. Let each group \(g\) have median \(\tilde{m}_{Y}(g)\), interquartile range \(\hat{\text{IQR}}_{Y}(g)\), observations \(n_{g}\). We can compute standard deviation of the median as \(\tilde{S}_{Y}(g)= \frac{1.25 \hat{\text{IQR}}_{Y}(g)}{1.35 \sqrt{n_{g}}}\). As a rough guess, the interval \(\tilde{m}_{Y}(g) \pm 1.7 \tilde{S}_{Y}(g)\) is the historical default and displayed as a notch in the boxplot (McGill et al. 1978).
The same standard errors give a \(z\)-statistic for the difference in medians, \[\hat{z} = \frac{\tilde{m}_{Y}(1)-\tilde{m}_{Y}(2)}{\sqrt{\tilde{S}_{Y}(1)^2+\tilde{S}_{Y}(2)^2}}.\] Unlike \(\hat{t}\) for means, this ratio has no \(t\)-distribution result, even when the data are normal, so we compare it to the standard normal, which is accurate only in large samples. The standard error of a median depends on how dense the data are near the median, and \(\tilde{S}_{Y}(g)\) fills that in by assuming normality. Specifically, \(\hat{\text{IQR}}_{Y}(g)/1.35\) estimates the standard deviation of normal data, and \(1.25\approx\sqrt{\pi/2}\) is how much more variable a sample median is than a sample mean when the data are normal. Two notches do not overlap when \(|\tilde{m}_{Y}(1)-\tilde{m}_{Y}(2)| > 1.7[\tilde{S}_{Y}(1)+\tilde{S}_{Y}(2)]\). With equal standard errors, that is the same as \(|\hat{z}| > 1.7\sqrt{2} \approx 2.4\), a stricter cutoff than \(1.96\), which is why overlapping notches do not show that the medians are equal.






NoteMust Know





Suppose two groups of \(n_{1}=n_{2}=100\) workers have median wages \(\tilde{m}_{Y}(1)=17\) and \(\tilde{m}_{Y}(2)=15\), and both have an interquartile range of \(7\). Each standard error is \(\tilde{S}_{Y}(g)=1.25\times 7/(1.35\times 10)\approx 0.648\), so \[\hat{z} = \frac{17-15}{\sqrt{0.648^2+0.648^2}} \approx \frac{2}{0.917} \approx 2.18,\] with a \(p\)-value of about \(0.029\). Each notch extends \(1.7\times 0.648\approx 1.10\) from its median, so the notches \([15.90, 18.10]\) and \([13.90, 16.10]\) overlap. So the \(z\)-statistic rejects at the \(5\%\) level even though the notches overlap.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Two groups of 100 workers with the same interquartile range
n0 <- 100
med01_hat <- 17
med02_hat <- 15
iqr0_hat <- 7

# Normal-theory standard error of each median
se0_hat <- 1.25 * iqr0_hat / (1.35 * sqrt(n0))

# z-statistic and its two-sided p-value
z0_hat <- (med01_hat - med02_hat) / sqrt(se0_hat^2 + se0_hat^2)
c(se=se0_hat, z=z0_hat, p_value=2 * pnorm(-abs(z0_hat)))
##         se          z    p_value 
## 0.64814815 2.18192950 0.02911474

# Notches: each median plus or minus 1.7 standard errors
rbind(group1=med01_hat + c(-1.7, 1.7) * se0_hat,
    group2=med02_hat + c(-1.7, 1.7) * se0_hat)
##            [,1]     [,2]
## group1 15.89815 18.10185
## group2 13.89815 16.10185











TipTest Yourself





Check how well the standard normal describes \(\hat{z}\) when the null is true. As in the simulation for means above, draw both groups from the pretend population of Wages1 workers, so the two population medians are equal. With \(50\) workers per group, about \(5\%\) of the samples should have \(|\hat{z}|>1.96\). The standard normal is only a large-sample approximation, so repeat the check with n_g at \(10\).


Code
# Draw both groups from the same pretend population, so the medians are equal
n_g <- 50
n_sim <- 999
z_sim <- rep(NA, n_sim)
for (b in seq(n_sim)) {
    y1_sim_b <- sample(population_wages, n_g)
    y2_sim_b <- sample(population_wages, n_g)
    se1_b <- 1.25 * IQR(y1_sim_b) / (1.35 * sqrt(n_g)) # normal-theory SE of each median
    se2_b <- 1.25 * IQR(y2_sim_b) / (1.35 * sqrt(n_g))
    z_sim[b] <- (median(y1_sim_b) - median(y2_sim_b)) / sqrt(se1_b^2 + se2_b^2)
}

# Share of samples with |z| > 1.96, near 5% if the standard normal fits
mean(abs(z_sim) > 1.96)
## [1] 0.05105105
# Change n_g to 10 and the share rises.

# Overlay: simulated histogram vs. standard normal
z_range <- range(c(z_sim, -4, 4))
hist(z_sim, breaks=30, freq=FALSE, border=NA,
    xlim=z_range, xlab=expression(hat(z)), main=NA)
title('Simulated vs. Standard Normal', font.main=1)
z_grid <- seq(z_range[1], z_range[2], length=200)
lines(z_grid, dnorm(z_grid), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)
legend('topright', legend=c('Simulated', 'Standard normal'),
    fill=c(grey(.83), NA), border=NA, # grey(.83) matches the default histogram fill
    lwd=c(NA, 1), lty=c(NA, 2), col=c(NA, rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)), bty='n')

title: 19  Classical Tests and Bias-Variance
text:
19.2 Bias-Variance Tradeoff
A better fit on the data you have is not automatically better, because a model can hit every point in the sample and still predict new observations poorly.






ImportantKey Definition





Let \(Y^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\) be a model’s prediction at \(x\) before the sample is drawn, and let \(m_{Y}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid X_{i}=x]\) be the conditional expectation it estimates. The mean squared error of the prediction decomposes into two pieces: \[\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Y^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)-m_{Y}(x)\right)^2\right] = \left(\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\right]-m_{Y}(x)\right)^2 + \mathbb{V}\left[Y^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\right].\] Squared bias, the first piece, is how far the average prediction sits from the truth. Variance, the second piece, is how much the predictions wobble around their own average. The bias-variance tradeoff is that cutting one piece usually raises the other.



The bias-variance tradeoff is useful for thinking about why a tuning parameter matters and how to set it. For local regressions, the bandwidth \(h\) (for LOESS, the span) controls the tradeoff. A large \(h\) lowers variance but raises bias, and a small \(h\) does the opposite. A loess fit narrow enough to interpolate every point has \(\hat{\text{MSE}}=0\) on the fit data, as defined in Model Fit, but generalizes poorly because it has just copied the noise.

Wide window (large span, large \(h\)): each local fit uses many observations, so the fitted curve barely changes from sample to sample (low variance). But a nearly flat fit over a wide region cannot follow a relationship that bends, so it is systematically off (high bias).
Narrow window (small span, small \(h\)): each local fit uses few observations, so the fitted curve chases noise and swings from sample to sample (high variance). But a narrow window can track curvature closely (low bias).

This section fits local linear LOESS (degree=1), which is more stable than the default local quadratic in small samples.


Code
# Lab data from above: wages and schooling for 3294 workers
# Schooling takes only a few distinct values, so all fits here are local linear

# Two-span local linear loess with bootstrap confidence bands on one scatterplot
pred_design <- data.frame(x_hat=sort(unique(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])))
# Schooling is an integer, and about a third of workers have exactly 12 years.
# Spans below about 0.4 leave no other schooling level near 12.
# So loess() breaks down there.
spans <- c(4.0, 0.4)
n_boot <- 399
span_lty <- c(1, 2) # both spans are LOESS, so they share a color and differ by line type

# The axis stops just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    ylim=c(0, 20),
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')

for (s in seq_along(spans)) {
    sp <- spans[s]
    reg_s <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, span=sp, degree=1)
    boot_preds <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=n_boot)
    for (b in 1:n_boot) {
        xy_boot <- xy_hat[sample(nrow(xy_hat), replace=TRUE), ]
        reg_s_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot, span=sp, degree=1)
        boot_preds[, b] <- predict(reg_s_b, newdata=pred_design)
    }
    boot_cb <- apply(boot_preds, 1, quantile,
        probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)

    polygon(c(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], rev(pred_design[, 'x_hat'])),
        c(boot_cb[1, ], rev(boot_cb[2, ])),
        col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .3), border=NA)
    lines(pred_design[, 'x_hat'], predict(reg_s, newdata=pred_design),
        col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lwd=2, lty=span_lty[s], type='o')
}

legend('topleft', title='LOESS span',
    legend=paste0(spans),
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lty=span_lty, lwd=2, pch=1, cex=.8,
    seg.len=4) # long enough that the circle does not hide the dashes









Code
# With span 4.0 the curve is nearly a straight line and very stable.
# With span 0.4 the curve tracks more local variation, and its band fans wider.


A wider span gives a more stable curve and a tighter bootstrap band, while a narrower span tracks more local variation. Following local detail raises the variance.
With local linear fits, a very wide span gives every observation nearly the same weight, so the fit approaches the simple linear regression as \(h \to \infty\). A wide window and a narrow window can therefore also be read as a linear model and a flexible LOESS fit.
The bootstrap bands show variance, but not bias, because we never see the true curve in one sample. As in Sampling, pretend the data are the whole population, so the true curve is known. The population curve is the mean outcome at each value of the explanatory variable, over the whole population. We evaluate it only at values with many observations. The rest of this section compares the linear model, which acts as the widest possible window, with LOESS at span \(0.6\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Wages1 defined above
# Pretend these 3294 workers are the whole population
population_xy <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(population_xy) <- c('x', 'y') # x=years of schooling, y=hourly wage

# Population curve: mean wage at each schooling level
population_curve <- tapply(population_xy[, 'y'], population_xy[, 'x'], mean)

# Evaluate at schooling levels with many workers (8 to 15 years)
# Rare levels are often missing from a sample, and loess does not extrapolate
x_levels <- 8:15
population_levels <- population_curve[as.character(x_levels)]

# Draw a simple random sample of n workers from the population
draw_xy <- function(n=300){
    s_id <- sample(nrow(population_xy), n, replace=FALSE)
    xy_sim <- population_xy[s_id, ]
    colnames(xy_sim) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat')
    return(xy_sim)
}

# Span for all local linear fits in the main text
span_wage <- 0.6



Bias
The plot below shows the average prediction across many samples against the population mean at each value. LOESS can track the population curve closely.1 A linear model can do so only where the population curve is straight.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Shared settings used by Bias, Variance, and the Decomposition
n_rep <- 300
n_seq <- c(50, 100, 200, 400, 800)
n_bias <- 200
x_target <- 12 # high school graduates

## Predictions at x_target: one row per sample, one column per sample size
target_lm_sim <- matrix(NA, nrow=n_rep, ncol=length(n_seq))
target_lo_sim <- matrix(NA, nrow=n_rep, ncol=length(n_seq))

## Predictions at every schooling level when n == n_bias
curves_lm_sim <- matrix(NA, nrow=length(x_levels), ncol=n_rep)
curves_lo_sim <- matrix(NA, nrow=length(x_levels), ncol=n_rep)

## One sweep over sample sizes
for (ni in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[ni]
    for (r in 1:n_rep) {
        xy_sim <- draw_xy(n)
        reg_lm <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sim)
        reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sim, span=span_wage, degree=1)
        y_pred_lm <- predict(reg_lm, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_levels))
        y_pred_lo <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_levels))
        target_lm_sim[r, ni] <- y_pred_lm[x_levels == x_target]
        target_lo_sim[r, ni] <- y_pred_lo[x_levels == x_target]
        if (n == n_bias) {
            curves_lm_sim[, r] <- y_pred_lm
            curves_lo_sim[, r] <- y_pred_lo
        }
    }
}




Code
# Average predictions across the samples of 200 workers
m_lm_hat <- rowMeans(curves_lm_sim, na.rm=TRUE)
m_lo_hat <- rowMeans(curves_lo_sim, na.rm=TRUE)

y_rng <- range(c(population_levels, m_lm_hat, m_lo_hat), na.rm=TRUE)
plot(x_levels, population_levels, type='o', lwd=1, lty=2,
    col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), ylim=y_rng,
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Mean hourly wage (1980 dollars)', main=NA)
lines(x_levels, m_lm_hat, type='o', lwd=2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8))
lines(x_levels, m_lo_hat, type='o', lwd=2, col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8))
legend('topleft', lty=c(2, 1, 1), lwd=c(1, 2, 2), pch=1, bty='n',
    col=c(rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, .7, .7, .8)),
    legend=c('Population mean',
        'Linear',
        paste0('Loess(', span_wage, ')')
))









Code
# LOESS tracks the population curve closely.
# The line is too high at 12 years of schooling and too low at 13 to 15 years.

# reg is the line fit to all 3294 workers, the whole pretend population
y_pred_population <- predict(reg, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_target))
c(line=unname(y_pred_population),
    population_mean=population_curve[[as.character(x_target)]])
##            line population_mean 
##        5.963434        5.668354
# At 12 years, it predicts about 5.96 against a population mean of about 5.67.


The linear bias does not go away with more data. Even the line fit to the whole population is only the best linear approximation to the conditional expectation, so, as in the \(3\times3\) example of Bivariate Theory, it misses wherever the conditional expectation bends.


Variance
The model estimates also vary from sample to sample. The plot below shows the standard error of each model’s prediction at one target point, computed across the repeated samples. A linear prediction generally varies less than a LOESS prediction, even when it is biased.
Also notice that there are diminishing returns to larger sample sizes. Both predictions vary less from sample to sample as \(n\) grows, making confidence intervals narrower and hypothesis tests more accurate.


Code
# Predicted mean wage at 12 years of schooling, across the repeated samples
se_sim <- rbind(
    apply(target_lm_sim, 2, sd, na.rm=TRUE),
    apply(target_lo_sim, 2, sd, na.rm=TRUE))
cols <- c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, .7, .7, .8)) # linear, LOESS
matplot(n_seq, t(se_sim), type='b', pch=16,
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols,
    ylab='standard error', xlab='sample size',
    main=NA)
legend('topright',
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols,
    legend=c('Linear', paste0('Loess(', span_wage, ')')))









Code
# The linear prediction varies less than LOESS at every sample size here.


Bootstrap confidence bands are approximations: they estimate how much predicted values vary from sample to sample. The simulation below compares a bootstrap CI constructed from one sample to the true sampling variation observed across many independent samples from the population.


Code
## Data from one sample of 300 workers
xy_sim <- draw_xy(300)
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    ylim=c(0, 15), # zoom in on the fitted curves
    main=NA, ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', xlab='Years of schooling')

## Plot Bootstrap CI for Single Sample
pred_design <- data.frame(x_hat=x_levels)
boot_lo <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=399)
for (b in 1:399) {
    xy_boot <- xy_sim[sample(nrow(xy_sim), replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot, span=span_wage, degree=1)
    boot_lo[, b] <- predict(reg_b, newdata=pred_design)
}
boot_cb <- apply(boot_lo, 1, quantile,
    probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
polygon(
    c(pred_design[[1]], rev(pred_design[[1]])),
    c(boot_cb[1, ], rev(boot_cb[2, ])),
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .3),
    border=NA)

# Construct CI across Multiple Samples from the population
sample_lo <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(pred_design), ncol=399)
for (b in 1:399) {
    xy_sim_b <- draw_xy(300) # Entirely new sample
    reg_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sim_b, span=span_wage, degree=1)
    sample_lo[, b] <- predict(reg_b, newdata=pred_design)
}
ci_lo <- apply(sample_lo, 1, quantile,
    probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
polygon(
    c(pred_design[[1]], rev(pred_design[[1]])),
    c(ci_lo[1, ], rev(ci_lo[2, ])),
    col=grey(0, alpha=.25),
    border=NA)

# Population curve, in blue as in the Bias plot
points(x_levels, population_levels, pch=16, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
legend('topleft', bty='n', cex=.8,
    legend=c('Bootstrap CI (one sample)', 'CI across samples', 'Population mean'),
    pch=c(15, 15, 16),
    col=c(rgb(0, .7, .7, .5), grey(0, .5), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)))









The two bands typically have a similar width, so the bootstrap from one sample gives a reasonable idea of the variation across samples. The bootstrap band is centered on the one sample we happen to have, however, so it can sit a little above or below the population curve.


Bias-Variance Decomposition
The code below computes the squared bias, the variance, and the mean squared error (MSE) from the definition above, for each model’s prediction at the target point and each sample size.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Squared bias, variance, and MSE for each column (sample size)
truth_target <- population_curve[as.character(x_target)] # 12 years of schooling
mse_parts <- function(P, truth){
    bias2 <- (colMeans(P, na.rm=TRUE) - truth)^2
    variance <- apply(P, 2, var, na.rm=TRUE)
    mse <- colMeans((P - truth)^2, na.rm=TRUE)
    return(cbind(bias2, variance, mse))
}
parts_lm <- mse_parts(target_lm_sim, truth_target)
parts_lo <- mse_parts(target_lo_sim, truth_target)
rownames(parts_lm) <- rownames(parts_lo) <- paste0('n=', n_seq)
round(parts_lm, 3) # Linear
##       bias2 variance   mse
## n=50  0.109    0.215 0.323
## n=100 0.080    0.106 0.186
## n=200 0.089    0.051 0.140
## n=400 0.080    0.023 0.102
## n=800 0.083    0.011 0.093
# The squared bias stays between about 0.08 and 0.11 as n grows.
# The variance falls from about 0.215 with 50 workers to about 0.011 with 800.
round(parts_lo, 3) # Loess
##       bias2 variance   mse
## n=50  0.002    0.480 0.480
## n=100 0.001    0.272 0.272
## n=200 0.000    0.132 0.132
## n=400 0.000    0.052 0.052
## n=800 0.000    0.025 0.025
# The squared bias is at most about 0.002, so the MSE is almost all variance.

# MSE across sample sizes
cols <- c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, .7, .7, .8)) # linear, LOESS
matplot(n_seq, cbind(parts_lm[, 'mse'], parts_lo[, 'mse']),
    type='b', pch=16, lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols,
    ylab='mean squared error', xlab='sample size',
    main=NA)
legend('topright',
    lty=1, lwd=2, col=cols,
    legend=c('Linear', paste0('Loess(', span_wage, ')')))









Code
# The line has the lower MSE with 50 or 100 workers.
# LOESS has the lower MSE with 200 or more workers, narrowly at 200.


For the linear model, the squared bias stays roughly the same as \(n\) grows, while the variance shrinks. For LOESS with a span narrow enough to follow the curve, the squared bias is close to zero, and the MSE is mostly variance. With small samples, the stable linear model typically has the lower MSE. With large samples, the flexible LOESS model typically has the lower MSE.


Consistency
The bias-variance tradeoff raises a question: can both be reduced simultaneously as \(n\) grows? For local regression, the answer is yes, provided we shrink the bandwidth as \(n\) grows. The neighborhood shrinks (reducing bias) while the local sample size still grows (reducing variance). This is often written as bandwidth conditions: \[
h_{n} \to 0
\quad\text{and}\quad
n h_{n} \to \infty.
\] In LOESS language, this corresponds to the span shrinking with \(n\), but not too fast.






NoteMust Know





A common bandwidth rule shrinks \(h\) with the sample size, for example \(h_{n}=n^{-1/5}\). Check the two conditions:

\(h_{n}=n^{-1/5}\to 0\): at \(n=100\) it is about \(0.40\); at \(n=10{,}000\) it is about \(0.16\). The neighborhood shrinks.
\(n h_{n}=n^{4/5}\to\infty\): at \(n=100\) it is about \(40\); at \(n=10{,}000\) it is about \(1585\). The local sample size still grows.

So bias falls (the window narrows) while variance falls (each local fit uses more data).


Code
n <- c(100, 10000)
h_n <- n^(-1/5)
rbind(h_n=round(h_n, 3), n_times_h=round(n*h_n, 1))
##             [,1]     [,2]
## h_n        0.398    0.158
## n_times_h 39.800 1584.900





The simulation below illustrates this at one target point. The span is \(2n^{-1/5}\), which satisfies the same two conditions as \(n^{-1/5}\). The mean absolute error in estimating the population mean tends to decrease with larger \(n\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
x_target <- 12 # high school graduates
n_grid <- c(50, 100, 200, 400, 800)
n_rep <- 200

avg_abs_err <- numeric(length(n_grid))
for (ni in seq_along(n_grid)) {
    n <- n_grid[ni]
    # The factor 2 keeps the span above 0.5 for these sample sizes.
    # About a third of workers have exactly 12 years of schooling.
    # Narrower spans can leave no other schooling level in the neighborhood.
    # Then loess() breaks down.
    span_n <- min(0.9, 2*n^(-1/5)) # shrinks with n
    errs <- replicate(n_rep, {
        xy_sim <- draw_xy(n)
        reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sim, span=span_n, degree=1)
        y_pred <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_target))
        abs(y_pred - population_curve[as.character(x_target)])
    })
    avg_abs_err[ni] <- mean(errs, na.rm=TRUE)
}

plot(n_grid, avg_abs_err, type='b', pch=16,
     xlab='Sample size (n)',
     ylab='Mean Absolute Error',
     main=NA)









Code
# The error falls from about 0.45 with 50 workers to about 0.13 with 800.








NoteMust Know





With a continuous \(\hat{x}\), the span can follow the rule \(h_{n}=n^{-1/5}\) directly, without the factor \(2\). Here yearly productivity depends on age through a smooth true mean, and we check the error at age \(40\).


Code
# True mean productivity at each age
true_m <- function(x){
    m_x <- (1E-10*exp(1.4*x - .015*x^2)*x + 5E5) / 10
    return(m_x)
}

# Simulate n workers with ages evenly spaced from 15 to 70
sim_xy <- function(n){
    x_sim <- seq(15, 70, length.out=n)
    y_sim <- true_m(x_sim) + runif(n, -5E4, 5E4) # true mean plus noise
    return(data.frame(y_sim, x_sim))
}

x_target <- 40  # mid-career age
n_grid <- c(60, 120, 240, 480)
n_rep <- 120

avg_abs_err <- numeric(length(n_grid))
for (ni in seq_along(n_grid)) {
    n <- n_grid[ni]
    span_n <- min(0.9, n^(-1/5)) # shrinks with n
    errs <- replicate(n_rep, {
        xy_sim <- sim_xy(n)
        reg_lo <- loess(y_sim ~ x_sim, data=xy_sim, span=span_n, degree=1)
        y_pred <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=data.frame(x_sim=x_target))
        abs(y_pred - true_m(x_target))
    })
    avg_abs_err[ni] <- mean(errs, na.rm=TRUE)
}

plot(n_grid, avg_abs_err, type='b', pch=16,
    xlab='Sample size (n)',
    ylab='Mean Absolute Error',
    main=NA)












A similar result holds for OLS when the data come from a linear data generating process. Even with unlimited data, however, a misspecified model cannot recover the conditional expectation, as the linear fit to the pretend population shows.

title: 19  Classical Tests and Bias-Variance
text:
19.3 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Using the USArrests dataset, regress Murder on UrbanPop with lm. Extract the theoretical \(t\)-statistic and \(p\)-value for the slope from summary(). Then write a bootstrap loop with \(B = 399\) replicates to compute a bootstrap \(p\)-value and compare it to the theoretical one.
A linear regression has low variance but can have high bias when the true relationship is nonlinear. A loess regression with a small span has low bias but high variance. Explain why increasing the sample size \(n\) helps reduce the standard error for both models, but only helps reduce bias for loess (with an appropriate bandwidth rule).


Further Reading
Many introductory econometrics textbooks have a good appendix on probability and statistics. See also the further reading in Bivariate Theory.

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/5-htaciam.html – hypothesis testing, Type I and Type II errors, and power in a regression context.
https://learningstatisticswithr.com/book/regression.html#hypothesistestsforregressionmodels – testing regression slopes, interpreting p-values, and understanding standard errors.
https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability/significance-tests-one-sample/idea-of-significance-tests/v/simple-hypothesis-testing – video walkthrough of the logic behind hypothesis tests and p-values.
https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/computer-science/informationtheory/moderninfotheory/v/bias-variance – visual introduction to the bias-variance tradeoff that drives bandwidth choice.



Recall
This chapter tested two means with Welch’s \(t\)-test and a regression slope with the theoretical \(t_{n-2}\) distribution. It also used the large-sample \(z\)-statistic, which covers a difference in medians as well. It then decomposed prediction error into squared bias and variance. The bootstrap for wages and schooling showed that the histogram of \(\hat{t}\) roughly matched the theoretical \(t_{n-2}\) density. Treating Wages1 as a known population, the linear fit predicted a mean wage of \(5.96\) at \(12\) years of schooling against a population mean of \(5.67\), a bias that more data does not remove, while the LOESS error was mostly variance that shrank as \(n\) grew.




McGill, Robert, John W. Tukey, and Wayne A. Larsen. 1978. “Variations of Box Plots.” The American Statistician 32 (1): 12–16. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1978.10479236.


Satterthwaite, F. E. 1946. “An Approximate Distribution of Estimates of Variance Components.” Biometrics Bulletin 2 (6): 110–14. https://doi.org/10.2307/3002019.


Student. 1908. “The Probable Error of a Mean.” Biometrika 6 (1): 1–25. https://doi.org/10.2307/2331554.


Welch, B. L. 1947. “The Generalization of ‘Student’s’ Problem When Several Different Population Variances Are Involved.” Biometrika 34 (1-2): 28–35. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/34.1-2.28.

title: 19  Classical Tests and Bias-Variance
text:
One benefit of local linear regression is that it is theoretically motivated. Suppose that \(Y_{i}=m_{Y}(X_{i}) + \epsilon_{i}\), where \(m_{Y}(x)\) is the population average of \(Y_{i}\) among observations with \(X_{i}=x\), and \(\epsilon_{i}\) is an unobserved random error that averages zero at each value of \(X_{i}\). For \(X_{i}\) near \(x\), a Taylor approximation gives \[\begin{aligned}
m_{Y}(X_{i}) + \epsilon_{i} &\approx m_{Y}(x) + m_{Y}'(x)[X_{i}-x] + \epsilon_{i} \\
&= [m_{Y}(x) - m_{Y}'(x)x ] + m_{Y}'(x)X_{i} + \epsilon_{i} \\
&= b_{0}(x,h) + b_{1}(x,h) X_{i} + \epsilon_{i}.
\end{aligned}\] So near \(x\), the population relationship is approximately a line with slope \(b_{1}(x,h)=m_{Y}'(x)\), which is what a local linear regression fits.↩︎

title: 20  Communicating Results
text:
20.1 Outputs
Good analysis is only useful to others if its output is clear.
This chapter asks three questions.

title: 20  Communicating Results
text:
Interactive Figures
A single static plot fixes one view of the data, but readers often want to explore details the analyst did not pre-select.






ImportantKey Definition





An interactive figure is a plot whose viewer can change the display at runtime (hovering for point-level detail, panning, zooming, or filtering) without re-rendering on the analyst’s side.



Interactive figures are useful when the data have more structure than one static view can show. For example, hovering can reveal labels for many points, and the reader can toggle groups or zoom into a range. The plotly package wraps common plot types (notably histograms, boxplots, and scatterplots) into HTML widgets that work in any browser.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
library('plotly')            # install.packages('plotly')

# Lab data: 3294 US workers.
# wage is the hourly wage in 1980 dollars.
# school and exper are years of schooling and of work experience.
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')

# Scatter plot of wages vs schooling
fig <- plot_ly(
    Wages1, x = ~ school, y = ~ wage,
    mode='markers',
    type='scatter',
    hoverinfo='text',                              # use custom hover text
    marker=list(color=grey(0, .1)),                # transparent, as n is large
    text = ~ paste('<b>', sex, '</b>',             # one label per worker
        '<br>Schooling :', school,
        '<br>Wage :', round(wage, 2)))
fig <- layout(fig,
    showlegend=FALSE,
    title='Wages and Schooling in America',
    xaxis = list(title = 'Years of schooling'),
    yaxis = list(title = 'Hourly wage (1980 dollars)'))
fig






Code
# Only 52 wages are above 15 dollars.
# To see the rest in more detail, drag a box around them to zoom in.


Color and size can carry two more variables, and the hover text can list every variable for the observation under the cursor. See also https://plotly.com/r/bubble-charts/.


Code
# Bubble chart: color encodes sex and size encodes years of experience
fig <- plot_ly(
    Wages1, x = ~ school, y = ~ wage,
    mode='markers',
    type='scatter',
    hoverinfo='text',
    text = ~ paste('<b>', sex, '</b>',
        '<br>Schooling :', school,
        '<br>Experience :', exper,
        '<br>Wage :', round(wage, 2)),
    color= ~ sex,
    colors=c(rgb(.8, 0, 0), rgb(0, 0, .8)),        # one color per group
    marker=list(
        size= ~ exper,
        opacity=0.1))
fig <- layout(fig,
    title='Wages and Schooling in America',
    xaxis = list(title = 'Years of schooling'),
    yaxis = list(title = 'Hourly wage (1980 dollars)'))
fig






Code
# Click a legend entry to hide or show that group.
# The largest bubbles are at low schooling, where workers have more experience.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the bubble chart with USArrests, whose rows are named by state. The hover text can then show the name of the state under the cursor.


Code
# 50 US states, 1973: arrests per 100,000 people and percent urban population
xy2_hat <- USArrests
xy2_hat[, 'ID'] <- rownames(xy2_hat) # state name for hover text

# Bubble chart: color and size both encode the murder rate
fig <- plot_ly(
    xy2_hat, x = ~ UrbanPop, y = ~ Assault,
    mode='markers',
    type='scatter',
    hoverinfo='text',
    text = ~ paste('<b>', ID, '</b>',
        '<br>Urban  :', UrbanPop,
        '<br>Assault:', Assault,
        '<br>Murder :', Murder),
    color= ~ Murder,
    marker=list(
        size= ~ Murder,
        opacity=0.5,
        showscale=TRUE,
        colorbar = list(title='Murder Arrests (per 100,000)')))
fig <- layout(fig,
    showlegend=FALSE,
    title='Crime and Urbanization in America 1973',
    xaxis = list(title = 'Percent of People in an Urban Area'),
    yaxis = list(title = 'Assault Arrests per 100,000 People'))
fig









A second trace can add a fitted line, and the hover text can show each observation’s fitted value and residual. The figure below adds the line from a simple regression.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Wages and schooling, with the line from a simple regression
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)

# Copy the data and attach fitted values and residuals for hover text
xy_plot_hat <- xy_hat
xy_plot_hat[, 'y_fit'] <- predict(reg)
xy_plot_hat[, 'e_hat'] <- resid(reg)

# Plot Data
fig <- plot_ly(
    xy_plot_hat, x = ~ x_hat, y = ~ y_hat,
    mode='markers',
    type='scatter',
    hoverinfo='text',
    marker=list(color=grey(0, .1), size=10),
    text = ~ paste('Schooling :', x_hat,
        '<br>Wage :', round(y_hat, 2),
        '<br>Predicted Wage :', round(y_fit, 2),
        '<br>Residual :', round(e_hat, 2)))
fig <- layout(fig,
    showlegend=FALSE,
    title='Wages and Schooling in America',
    xaxis = list(title = 'Years of schooling'),
    yaxis = list(title = 'Hourly wage (1980 dollars)'))
# Plot Model Predictions as a second trace, with no hover text of its own
fig <- add_trace(fig, x = ~ x_hat, y = ~ y_fit,
    inherit=FALSE, hoverinfo='none',
    mode='lines', type='scatter',
    color=I(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)),
    line=list(width=2))
fig








Code
# Three schooling groups, as in Comparing Multiple Groups
school_g <- cut(Wages1[, 'school'], breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 16),
    labels=c('<12', '12', '>12'))

# Box Plot
fig <- plot_ly(Wages1,
    y= ~ wage, color= ~ school_g,
    colors=c(rgb(.8, 0, 0), rgb(0, .8, 0), rgb(0, 0, .8)), # one color per group
    alpha=0.6, type='box',
    pointpos=0, boxpoints = 'all',
    marker=list(opacity=0.1),    # transparent points, so the boxes show through
    hoverinfo='text',
    text = ~ paste('<b>', sex, '</b>',
        '<br>Schooling :', school,
        '<br>Experience :', exper,
        '<br>Wage :', round(wage, 2)))
fig <- layout(fig,
    showlegend=FALSE,
    title='Wages and Schooling in America',
    xaxis = list(title = 'Years of schooling',
        type='category'),        # 12 is a group label, not a number
    yaxis = list(title = 'Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', range=c(0, 20)))
fig






Code
# The 18 wages above 20 dollars start off screen.
# Double-click the figure to see them.
# Median wages rise across the groups, at about 4.59, 5.17, and 6.74 dollars.




Code
# Split workers at the mean schooling, about 11.6 years
m_x_hat <- mean(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
school_cut <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat'] < m_x_hat
y1_hat <- xy_hat[school_cut, 'y_hat']  # hourly wages, low schooling
y2_hat <- xy_hat[!school_cut, 'y_hat'] # hourly wages, high schooling

# Overlapping Histograms
fig <- plot_ly(alpha=0.6, hovertemplate='%{y}')
fig <- add_histogram(fig, y1_hat, name='Low (< Mean)',
    histnorm = 'probability density',
    xbins = list(start=0, size=1))
fig <- add_histogram(fig, y2_hat, name='High (>= Mean)',
    histnorm = 'probability density',
    xbins = list(start=0, size=1))
fig <- layout(fig,
    barmode='overlay',
    title='Wages and Schooling in America',
    xaxis = list(title='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', range=c(0, 20)),
    yaxis = list(title='Density'),
    legend=list(title=list(text='<b> Years of Schooling </b>')) )
fig






Code
# The 18 wages above 20 dollars start off screen.
# Both groups are right-skewed.
# The high group sits further right, with a median wage of about 5.73 vs 4.59.

# Possible, but less preferable, to stack histograms
# barmode='stack', histnorm='count'


Note that many plots can be made interactive via https://plotly.com/r/. For more details, see examples and then applications.
If you have many points, for example, you can make a 2D histogram.


Code
fig <- plot_ly(
    xy_hat, x = ~ x_hat, y = ~ y_hat)
fig <- add_histogram2d(fig, nbinsx=25, nbinsy=25)
fig




Interactive Tables
For raw data, a static table forces the analyst to pre-pick which rows the reader sees first.






ImportantKey Definition





An interactive table shows rows of data with built-in filtering, sorting, and search controls. The viewer chooses which rows to see; the analyst does not need to pre-aggregate.



Interactive tables are useful when the reader wants to look up specific records rather than a summary view: searching by row identifier, sorting on a particular column, or filtering down to a subset. The reactable package renders a data frame as an HTML widget with these controls already built in.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
library('reactable')                     # install.packages('reactable')

# Copy the data and round wages to the cent for display
xy_table_hat <- Wages1
xy_table_hat[, 'wage'] <- round(xy_table_hat[, 'wage'], 2)

reactable(xy_table_hat,
    filterable=TRUE,                        # one search box per column
    highlight=TRUE)                         # row highlighting on hover






Code
# The 3294 workers fill many pages, so the table shows ten rows at a time.


You can create an interactive table that summarizes the data too.


Code
# Compute summary statistics for the numeric columns, since sex is a factor
vars <- c('wage', 'school', 'exper')
stats_list <- vector('list', length(vars))
for (i in seq_along(vars)) {
  v <- vars[i]
  x_v_hat <- Wages1[[v]]
  stats_list[[i]] <- c(
    Variable = v,
    N       = sum(!is.na(x_v_hat)),
    Mean    = mean(x_v_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD      = sd(x_v_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min     = min(x_v_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1      = as.numeric(quantile(x_v_hat, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Median  = median(x_v_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q3      = as.numeric(quantile(x_v_hat, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Max     = max(x_v_hat, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

# Convert list to data frame with numeric columns 
stats_df <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, stats_list), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
num_cols <- setdiff(names(stats_df), 'Variable')
for (col in num_cols) {
    stats_df[[col]] <- round(as.numeric(stats_df[[col]]), 3)
}

# Display interactively
reactable(stats_df)








Polishing
A first-draft figure usually works for the analyst but not for anyone else. Polishing removes what is not data and adds what the reader needs, so the figure is readable at first glance.






ImportantKey Definition





The data-ink ratio is the share of ink in a figure devoted to displaying data: \[\text{data-ink ratio} = \frac{\text{ink used to display data}}{\text{total ink in the figure}}.\] Non-data ink is everything else: gridlines, borders, shading, redundant labels, and decoration.



The data-ink ratio is useful as a one-number guide for polishing. A low ratio means clutter is competing with the data. A high ratio means almost all the ink shows data. Tufte (2001) introduces it to push figures toward a single goal: every mark should help the reader see the data. So erase any element that, if removed, would not change what the reader learns. When polishing, you do two things:

Add details that are necessary.
Remove details that are not necessary.







NoteMust Know





Data-Ink Ratio numerical example. Consider a scatter plot of 50 points with a heavy gray background, a thick border, and three duplicate legends. Of all the pixels printed, only the 50 points are data ink. Suppose those points account for 200 pixels and the rest of the figure uses 1800 pixels. The data-ink ratio is \(200/(200 + 1800) = 0.10\). Strip the background, border, and duplicate legends, and the ratio for the same 200 data pixels might be \(200/250 = 0.80\). The figure carries the same information, and its ratio is eight times higher.



The two panels below show the same data. The left panel piles on non-data ink; the right strips it back. The extra ink on the left adds no information about the data.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(5, 4, 3, 1))

# Cluttered: oversized two-color markers, gridlines, redundant title
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat,
    pch=21, bg='red', col='blue', cex=1.5,
    main='Hourly Wage vs Schooling\n(US Workers)',
    sub='Source: Wages1',
    xlab='school (years)',
    ylab='Hourly Wage in 1980 Dollars (wage)')
grid(col='black', lwd=1)
box(lwd=2)
legend('topright', legend='Worker', pch=21, pt.bg='red', col='blue')
# The opaque markers merge into solid columns, hiding where workers pile up.

# Polished: light points, no grid, no redundant labels or legend
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat,
    pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),                     # transparent black points
    main=NA, xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)',
    bty='n')                                     # drop the surrounding box
title('US Workers', font.main=1, adj=0)









Code
# Schooling is in whole years, so the points form vertical stripes.
# The stripes are darkest where workers pile up, above all at 12 years.
# Wages tend to rise with schooling, though weakly (correlation about 0.28).


Removed: oversized two-color markers, grid, box, redundant title, subtitle, one-entry legend. Added: nothing; the cleaner panel reads faster because nothing competes with the points.






TipTest Yourself





Repeat the comparison with USArrests, a much smaller dataset. Does the cluttered panel still hide any points?


Code
# 50 US states, 1973
xy2_hat <- USArrests[, c('UrbanPop', 'Murder')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=urban population share, y_hat=murder arrests per 100K

par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(5, 4, 3, 1))

# Cluttered: oversized two-color markers, gridlines, redundant title
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat,
    pch=21, bg='red', col='blue', cex=1.5,
    main='Murder Arrests vs Urban Pop.\n(US, 1973)',
    sub='Source: USArrests',
    xlab='UrbanPop (%)',
    ylab='Murder Arrests per 100,000 People (Murder)')
grid(col='black', lwd=1)
box(lwd=2)
legend('topright', legend='State', pch=21, pt.bg='red', col='blue')

# Polished: light points, no grid, no redundant labels or legend
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat,
    pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),                     # transparent black points
    main=NA, xlab='Urban Population', ylab='Murder Arrests',
    bty='n')                                     # drop the surrounding box
title('US States, 1973', font.main=1, adj=0)









Code
# Both panels show a very weak positive relationship across the 50 states.
# With so few points, the markers barely overlap.
# So both panels carry the same information about the data.











TipTest Yourself





A colleague sends a scatterplot of monthly sales against advertising spend. It has a shaded background, a drop-shadow on every point, a 3D tilt, a legend that names the single series “Series 1”, and a company logo in the corner. Which elements should you remove, and what (if anything) should you add?
The shading, drop-shadows, 3D tilt, one-entry legend, and logo are all non-data ink: none of them help a reader read sales against spend, so all can go. Keep the points and clear axis labels. If a few months are special (say, a promotion), a short text label on those points is necessary ink worth adding.









NoteMust Know





Polishing a plot with many points. The simulated data below have tens of thousands of points, so a default first draft would be a solid black blob. The second draft standardizes both variables, uses small transparent points, and adds a 45 degree line for reference.


Code
# Random Data: 45,001 points
x_sim <- seq(1, 10, by=.0002)
e <- rnorm(length(x_sim), mean=0, sd=1)
y_sim <- .25*x_sim + e

# First Draft
# plot(x_sim, y_sim)

# Second Draft: Focus
# (In this example: relationship magnitude)
x_std_sim <- scale(x_sim)
y_std_sim <- scale(y_sim)
plot(x_std_sim, y_std_sim,
    xlab='', ylab='',
    pch=16, cex=.5, col=grey(0, .05),
    main=NA)
mtext(expression('['~X[i]-hat(m)[X]~'] /'~hat(s)[X]), 1, line=2.5)
mtext(expression('['~Y[i]-hat(m)[Y]~'] /'~hat(s)[Y]), 2, line=2.5)
# Add a 45 degree line
abline(a=0, b=1, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)
legend('topleft',
    legend=c('data point', '45 deg. line'),
    pch=c(16, NA), lty=c(NA, 2), col=c(grey(0, .05), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)),
    bty='n')
title('Standardized Relationship', font.main=1)









The next version of the same data has good features, but goes too far. The math in the axis labels, the outer legend, and the long title all add ink the reader does not need.


Code
# Another Example
xy_sim <- data.frame(x_sim=x_sim, y_sim=y_sim)
par(fig=c(0, 1, 0, 0.9), new=FALSE)
plot(y_sim ~ x_sim, xy_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .05), cex=.5,
    main=NA, xlab='', ylab='') # Format Axis Labels Separately
mtext( 'y=0.25 x + e\n e ~ standard-normal', 2, line=2.2)
mtext( expression(x%in%~'[1, 10]'), 1, line=2.2)
#abline( lm(y_sim ~ x_sim, data=xy_sim), lty=2)
title('Plot with good features, but too excessive in several ways',
    adj=0, font.main=1)

# Outer Legend (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3932038/)
outer_legend <- function(...) {
  opar <- par(fig=c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma=c(0, 0, 0, 0), 
    mar=c(0, 0, 0, 0), new=TRUE)
  on.exit(par(opar))
  plot(0, 0, type='n', bty='n', xaxt='n', yaxt='n')
  legend(...)
}
outer_legend('topright', legend='single data point',
    title='do you see the normal distribution?',
    pch=16, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .1), cex=1, bty='n')












Learn to edit your figures:

https://socviz.co/08-polishing.html – K. Healy’s chapter on refining a draft figure with color, annotation, and themes (its code uses ggplot2).
https://websites.umich.edu/~jpboyd/eng403_chap2_tuftegospel.pdf
https://jtr13.github.io/cc19/tuftes-principles-of-data-ink.html
https://github.com/cxli233/FriendsDontLetFriends
https://www.edwardtufte.com/notebook/chartjunk/
https://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman/topten_worstgraphs/
https://www.businessinsider.com/the-27-worst-charts-of-all-time-2013-6

Which features are most informative depends on what you want to show, and you can always mix and match. Be aware that each type has benefits and costs. E.g., see

https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveats.html
https://x.com/EdwardTufte/status/1092717905156993024/photo/1
Hintze and Nelson (1998) – why a boxplot alone can hide the distribution’s shape, and what to pair it with.

For small datasets, you can plot individual data points with a strip chart.






NoteMust Know





A strip chart shows every observation as a point along one axis, which works well when there are too few points to justify a histogram or boxplot.


Code
# Six workers: show each hourly wage directly
y_small_hat <- xy_hat[1:6, 'y_hat']
stripchart(y_small_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .6),
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')









With few values, a strip chart shows the data honestly; a boxplot would hide the individual points behind summary statistics.



For datasets with spatial information, a map is also helpful. Sometimes tables are better than graphs (see https://www.edwardtufte.com/notebook/boxplots-data-test). For useful tips, see C. Wilke (2019) “Fundamentals of Data Visualization: A Primer on Making Informative and Compelling Figures” https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/.
For plotting math, which should be done very sparingly, see https://astrostatistics.psu.edu/su07/R/html/grDevices/html/plotmath.html and https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/mathematical-annotation-in-r.


Static Publishing






NoteMust Know





You can export figures with specific dimensions


Code
pdf( 'Figures/plot_example.pdf', height=5, width=5)
# plot goes here
dev.off()


For exporting options, see ?pdf. For saving other types of files, see png("*.png"), tiff("*.tiff"), and jpeg("*.jpg")
You can also export tables in a variety of formats, including many that other software programs can easily read

library('stargazer')
# summary statistics
stargazer(Wages1,
    type='html',
    summary=TRUE,
    title='Summary Statistics for Wages1')

title: 20  Communicating Results
text:
20.2 Quarto Reports

Quarto Documents
A statistical analysis usually has code that produces numbers and prose that explains them. Keeping the two in sync by hand is the source of most reproducibility failures. A Quarto document (.qmd file) is a plain-text source that interleaves prose with executable R code chunks. Rendering produces a self-contained output (HTML, PDF, or Word) where the code, its results, and the surrounding text all stay in sync.
Quarto is useful as the format for any analysis that has both writing and computation: homework reports, technical notes, papers, slides, and the chapters of this book. R does the statistical computation and Quarto formats those computations into a polished document. Altogether, your project will use

R: does statistical computations
Quarto: formats statistical computations for sharing (.qmd files)
RStudio: graphical user interface that allows you to easily use both R and Quarto



Reproducible Reports
Quarto handles the mechanics of mixing code and prose, which is one step toward a reproducible report.






ImportantKey Definition





A reproducible report is one whose final figures, tables, and numbers can be regenerated from the source file alone, by anyone with the data and the listed software versions.



Reproducible reports are useful because they let collaborators (and your future self) re-run the analysis after data are updated, methods are corrected, or a coauthor wants to check a number. Published research applies the same idea with a public replication package (Peng 2011; Christensen and Miguel 2018). Homework reports are the smallest version of this: simple reproducible reports that are almost entirely self-contained (showing both code and output). To make them, you need Quarto installed on your computer.

RStudio (version 2022.07 or later) includes Quarto



Example
Start by opening RStudio, then

Click “File > New File > Quarto Document”
Add your name and a title
Save the file as “COURSEID_Template_Lastname.qmd”
Click “Render”
Notice how the code in the source document corresponds to formatting in the output document

Now try each of the following steps, re-rendering the document after each step

Basic Formatting:

Change the title to “My First Quarto Document”
Change the bold word Render to italics: Render
Create a new section header at the bottom called “Data Analysis”

Data Analysis:

Make a simple scatterplot for Murder vs. UrbanPop in the USArrests data
Change the simple scatterplot into a polished interactive scatterplot
Before the scatterplot add a reactable table for the raw data
Write your own description of a) the dataset and b) the relationship between Murder and UrbanPop

Polishing

Delete the default sections
clean up your analysis (make sure the table,figure, and writing are high quality)
Email the output, “COURSEID_Template_Lastname.html”, to yourself

title: 20  Communicating Results
text:
20.3 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
When polishing a figure, you must both add necessary details and remove unnecessary ones. Give one example of each for a scatterplot of Murder vs. UrbanPop in the USArrests dataset.
Using the USArrests dataset, compute summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, min, max) for all four variables. Present the results in a single data frame with one row per variable.
Using the USArrests dataset and the plotly library, write R code to create an interactive scatterplot of Murder (y-axis) vs. UrbanPop (x-axis). The hover text should display the state name, murder rate, and urban population percentage.


Further Reading

https://quarto.org/docs/guide/ – the official Quarto guide, covering document types, code cells, and output formats.
https://r4ds.hadley.nz/quarto – practical chapter on integrating Quarto into a data-analysis workflow.

A plotly scatterplot showed each worker’s sex, schooling, and wage as hover text, and a reactable table showed summary statistics. Side-by-side panels compared a cluttered and a polished scatterplot of wage vs. school.
