title: 24  Model Assessment
text:
24.1 Model Diagnostics
A fitted regression should be audited before its coefficients are reported.
This chapter asks two questions.
Before answering either question, look at the raw data with the scatterplot matrices and conditioning plots from Multivariate Distributions. Nonlinear patterns and outliers are often visible before any model is fit. So are explanatory variables that carry almost the same information.
There’s little sense in getting great standard errors for a terrible model. Plotting your regression object is a simple and easy step to help diagnose whether your model is in some way bad. Calling plot() on an lm object returns four standard plots: (1) residuals vs fitted, (2) Q-Q normal of residuals, (3) scale-location, and (4) residuals vs leverage with Cook’s distance contours. We next go through what each shows.
Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Fit a multiple regression and produce the four standard diagnostic plots.
# Lab data: 3294 US workers.
# wage is the hourly wage in 1980 dollars.
# school and exper are years of schooling and of work experience.
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1
reg <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat)
par(mfrow=c(2, 2))
plot(reg, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1))









Code
# The labels beside the most extreme points are row numbers.
# Residuals vs fitted: the smoother stays near 0, but a few residuals are huge.
# Q-Q: the upper tail bends far above the line, since a few wages are very high.
# Scale-location: the smoother rises slowly, so spread grows with the fit.
# Residuals vs leverage: no worker comes near the Cook's contour at 0.5.

title: 24  Model Assessment
text:
Outliers
Some observations sit far from the rest of the data. Eyeballing the plot will not tell us which ones actually move the fit, so we need quantitative tools.






ImportantKey Definition





For a regression with \(n\) observations and \(K\) explanatory variables (so \(K+1\) coefficients):
The leverage \(h_{i}~\text{in}~[0, 1]\) of observation \(i\) measures how unusual its predictor values \(\hat{x}_{i}\) are relative to the rest of the sample. It is small when \(\hat{x}_{i}\) sits near the centre of the predictor cloud and large when \(\hat{x}_{i}\) sits at the edges. Equivalently, \(h_{i}\) is the share of the fitted value \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\) that is determined by \(\hat{y}_{i}\) itself rather than by the other observations. Across the sample, the \(h_{i}\) sum to the number of coefficients \(K+1\).
The standardized residual \(r_{i} = \hat{e}_{i} / (\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\sqrt{1-h_{i}})\) rescales the raw residual by an estimate of its standard deviation, where \(\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}\) is the square root of the adjusted mean squared error of the regression.
Cook’s Distance (Cook 1977) sums all prediction changes when observation \(i\) is removed, scaled by the adjusted mean squared error: \[D_{i} = \frac{\sum_{j} \left( \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(\hat{x}_{j}) - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{j}) \right)^2 }{ (K+1) \hat{s}^2_{\text{adj}} } = \frac{\hat{e}_{i}^2}{(K+1) \hat{s}^2_{\text{adj}} } \frac{h_{i}}{(1-h_{i})^2}, \quad \hat{s}^2_{\text{adj}} = \frac{\sum_{i} \hat{e}_{i}^2}{n-K-1}.\] The adjusted mean squared error divides by \(n-K-1\) instead of the \(n\) in the mean squared error, an adjustment for degrees of freedom like the one in the adjusted \(\hat{R}^2\). In Cook’s distance, the argument \(\hat{x}_{j}\) identifies the prediction target and the superscript \((-i)\) identifies the observation omitted from the fit.



These three statistics are useful for finding observations that deserve a closer look. Leverage flags points whose \(\hat{x}_{i}\) is unusual, and the standardized residual flags points whose \(\hat{y}_{i}\) is far from its prediction. Cook’s Distance combines both into one number that says how much the overall fit depends on each observation. The first diagnostic plot (residuals vs fitted) shows outliers in the outcome. The fourth (residuals vs leverage with Cook’s contours) shows outliers in \(\hat{x}_{i}\). Both kinds of outliers can be problematic, but they do not have to be.


Code
N <- 40
x_sim <- c(25, runif(N-1, 3, 8))
e <- rnorm(N, 0, 0.4)
y_sim <- 3 + 0.6*sqrt(x_sim) + e
plot(y_sim ~ x_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5), main=NA)
points(x_sim[1], y_sim[1], pch=16, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .5))

abline(lm(y_sim ~ x_sim), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(lm(y_sim[-1] ~ x_sim[-1]), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=2)
legend('topleft', legend=c('All observations', 'Without the red point'),
    col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2, lty=c(1, 2), bty='n')















NoteMust Know





In the plot above, the red point is a high-leverage observation. How does removing it change the regression line? In your own data analysis, what steps would you take before deciding to remove an outlier?





Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Worker with the highest leverage, shown with its row number
xy_hat[which.max(hatvalues(reg)), ]
##      exper  sex school     wage
## 2102    18 male      3 5.516826
# Row 2102 has 3 years of schooling and 18 of experience, a rare mix.
# Worker with the largest standardized residual
xy_hat[which.max(rstandard(reg)), ]
##      exper  sex school     wage
## 1813     5 male     11 39.80892
# Row 1813 earns about 40 dollars, the highest wage in the data.
# The model predicts only about 5 dollars with 11 years of schooling.




Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Worker with the largest Cook's Distance
xy_hat[which.max(cooks.distance(reg)), ]
##      exper  sex school     wage
## 1813     5 male     11 39.80892
# Row 1813 again: a huge residual, though its leverage is about average.
max(cooks.distance(reg))
## [1] 0.040543
# Still only about 0.04, far below the contour at 0.5.
# So this one worker does not move the fit much.

# Influence plot: leverage vs. standardized residual,
# with point area proportional to Cook's Distance
h_i <- hatvalues(reg)
e_std_hat <- rstandard(reg)
d_i <- cooks.distance(reg)

plot(h_i, e_std_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    cex=1 + 4*d_i/max(d_i), main=NA,
    xlab='Leverage', ylab='Standardized residual')
abline(h=0, col=grey(.5), lty=3)

# Label the most influential observations by row number
inf_id <- order(d_i, decreasing=TRUE)[1:3]
text(h_i[inf_id], e_std_hat[inf_id],
    labels=inf_id, pos=3, cex=.7)









Code
# Row 1813 has a huge residual at ordinary leverage.
# Row 1986 has high leverage, with 4 years of schooling and 18 of experience.
# Row 2490 earns about 22 dollars, with about twice the average leverage.
# So a worker can be influential through the residual, the leverage, or both.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the outlier checks for lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop) on USArrests.


Code
# One row per state: arrests per 100,000 residents, and percent urban
# The row names identify the 50 states.
xy2_hat <- USArrests
reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat)

# State with the highest leverage
which.max(hatvalues(reg2))
## North Carolina 
##             33
# North Carolina has the highest assault rate and few urban residents.
# State with the largest standardized residual
which.max(rstandard(reg2))
## Georgia 
##      10
# Georgia sits about 3 standard deviations above its prediction.
# State with the largest Cook's Distance
which.max(cooks.distance(reg2))
## North Carolina 
##             33
# North Carolina again, through its leverage.
# Its standardized residual is only about -1.3.

# Influence plot: leverage vs. standardized residual,
# with point area proportional to Cook's Distance
h2_i <- hatvalues(reg2)
e2_std_hat <- rstandard(reg2)
d2_i <- cooks.distance(reg2)

plot(h2_i, e2_std_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    cex=1 + 4*d2_i/max(d2_i), main=NA,
    xlab='Leverage', ylab='Standardized residual')
abline(h=0, col=grey(.5), lty=3)

# Label the most influential observations
inf2_id <- order(d2_i, decreasing=TRUE)[1:3]
text(h2_i[inf2_id], e2_std_hat[inf2_id],
    labels=rownames(xy2_hat)[inf2_id], pos=3, cex=.7)












See https://www.r-bloggers.com/2016/06/leverage-and-influence-in-a-nutshell/ for a good interactive explanation, and https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat462/node/87/ for detail. See AEJ-leverage and NBER-leverage for examples of leverage in economics.


Collinearity
When two regressors carry nearly the same information, OLS cannot tell their separate effects apart.






ImportantKey Definition





Collinearity is when one explanatory variable can be closely predicted by a linear combination of the others. The Variance Inflation Factor for variable \(k\), \[\hat{\text{VIF}}_{k}=\frac{1}{1-\hat{R}^2_{k}},\] quantifies how much collinearity inflates the variance of \(\hat{b}_{k}\) compared to the no-collinearity case. Here \(\hat{R}^2_{k}\) comes from regressing \(\hat{x}_{k}\) on the other covariates \(\hat{x}_{-k}\), a regression that does not involve the response variable \(\hat{y}\).



The Variance Inflation Factor is useful as a quick diagnostic for overlapping information between regressors: a \(\hat{\text{VIF}}_{k}\) near \(1\) means \(\hat{x}_{k}\) is uncorrelated with the others, and a common rule of thumb flags \(\sqrt{\hat{\text{VIF}}_{k}} > 2\). Collinearity does not bias the coefficients; it only widens their standard errors so that coefficient estimates may change erratically in response to small changes in the model or the data. In the extreme case with more coefficients than observations (\(K+1>n\)), the linear model has infinitely many solutions.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Variance Inflation Factor from its definition: VIF_k = 1/(1 - R^2_k),
# where R^2_k comes from regressing covariate k on the other covariates.
R2_school <- summary(lm(school ~ exper, data=xy_hat))$r.squared
R2_exper  <- summary(lm(exper ~ school, data=xy_hat))$r.squared

vif <- c(school=1/(1-R2_school), exper=1/(1-R2_exper))
vif
##   school    exper 
## 1.038926 1.038926
# Both are about 1.04, as schooling and experience correlate at about -0.19.

# A common rule of thumb flags sqrt(VIF) > 2
sqrt(vif) > 2
## school  exper 
##  FALSE  FALSE
# Neither is flagged, so collinearity is mild in this model.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the Variance Inflation Factors for lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop) on USArrests.


Code
xy2_hat <- USArrests
R2_assault  <- summary(lm(Assault ~ UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat))$r.squared
R2_urbanpop <- summary(lm(UrbanPop ~ Assault, data=xy2_hat))$r.squared

vif2 <- c(Assault=1/(1-R2_assault), UrbanPop=1/(1-R2_urbanpop))
vif2
##  Assault UrbanPop 
## 1.071828 1.071828
# Both are about 1.07, as assault rates and urban share correlate at about 0.26.

# A common rule of thumb flags sqrt(VIF) > 2
sqrt(vif2) > 2
##  Assault UrbanPop 
##    FALSE    FALSE
# Neither is flagged.











NoteMust Know





A \(\hat{\text{VIF}}_{k}\) of \(1\) means covariate \(k\) is uncorrelated with the others. A \(\hat{\text{VIF}}_{k}\) of \(4\) means the variance of \(\hat{b}_{k}\) is \(4\) times larger than it would be with no collinearity, so its standard error is \(\sqrt{4}=2\) times larger. With only two covariates, \(\hat{R}^2_{1} = \hat{R}^2_{2}\) (it is just their squared correlation), so the two VIFs are equal. Collinearity does not bias the coefficients; it only makes them less precise.





Normality
The second diagnostic plot (Q-Q normal of residuals) examines whether the residuals are normally distributed. Your OLS coefficient estimates do not depend on the normality of the residuals. (Good thing, because there’s no reason the residuals of economic phenomena should be so well behaved.) Many hypothesis tests are, however, affected by the distribution of the residuals. For these reasons, you may be interested in assessing normality.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
# The axis keeps every residual, since the long tail is the point here.
hist(resid(reg), breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Residuals')
rug(resid(reg), col=grey(0, .1))
title('Histogram of Residuals', font.main=1)

qqnorm(resid(reg),
    main='Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals',
    font.main=1, col=grey(0, .1), pch=16)
qqline(resid(reg), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The residuals are right-skewed, with a long tail from a few very high wages.
# The Q-Q points rise far above the line in the upper tail.
# The lower tail is shorter than normal, since wages cannot fall below zero.
# So normality clearly fails here.

#shapiro.test(resid(reg))








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the normality checks for lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop) on USArrests. How do these residuals compare with the ones above?


Code
xy2_hat <- USArrests
reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(resid(reg2), breaks=15, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab='Residuals')
rug(resid(reg2), col=grey(0, .5))
title('Histogram of Residuals', font.main=1)

qqnorm(resid(reg2),
    main='Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals',
    font.main=1, col=grey(0, .5), pch=16)
qqline(resid(reg2), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The Q-Q points stay close to the line, apart from the largest few residuals.
# The largest, about 7.6, belongs to Georgia.







Heteroskedasticity
OLS treats the error variance as constant across observations, and when that assumption fails the coefficients are still fine but the standard errors are not.






ImportantKey Definition





Heteroskedasticity is when the variance of the residuals depends on the regressors.



Detecting heteroskedasticity is useful because the standard errors that R reports by default rely on a homoskedasticity assumption. If that assumption fails, every \(p\)-value and confidence interval based on those standard errors is wrong too, and typically too narrow. The third diagnostic plot (scale-location) is the visual check; the Breusch-Pagan test (Breusch and Pagan 1979) below is a numerical alternative, whose \(p\)-value comes from a chi-squared distribution.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Breusch-Pagan test for heteroskedasticity, by hand.
# Regress the squared residuals on the original regressors:
# a large n*R^2 signals non-constant variance.
e_sq_hat <- resid(reg)^2
aux <- lm(e_sq_hat ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat)
R2_aux <- summary(aux)$r.squared

# Test statistic n*R^2 ~ chi-squared with K degrees of freedom
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
K <- 2
BP <- n*R2_aux
c(statistic=BP, p.value=1-pchisq(BP, df=K))
##    statistic      p.value 
## 12.994415518  0.001507643
# The statistic is about 13 and the p-value about 0.0015, so the test rejects.
# With n this large, even an auxiliary R^2 of about 0.004 is enough to reject.








TipTest Yourself





Repeat the Breusch-Pagan test for lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop) on USArrests.


Code
xy2_hat <- USArrests
reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat)

# Breusch-Pagan test for heteroskedasticity, by hand.
e2_sq_hat <- resid(reg2)^2
aux2 <- lm(e2_sq_hat ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat)
R2_aux2 <- summary(aux2)$r.squared

# Test statistic n*R^2 ~ chi-squared with K degrees of freedom
n2 <- nrow(xy2_hat)
K2 <- 2
BP2 <- n2*R2_aux2
c(statistic=BP2, p.value=1-pchisq(BP2, df=K2))
## statistic   p.value 
## 1.9072736 0.3853371
# The statistic is about 1.9 and the p-value about 0.39, so no rejection.
# With only 50 states, that does not show the variance is constant.











TipTest Yourself





The Breusch-Pagan test asks whether the residual variance depends on the regressors. A small \(p\)-value is evidence of heteroskedasticity: the spread of the residuals changes with the regressors \(\hat{x}_{k}\). Why does heteroskedasticity leave the OLS coefficients unbiased, but make the usual standard errors unreliable?

title: 24  Model Assessment
text:
24.2 Data Transformations
Transforming variables can often improve your model fit while still estimating it via OLS. This is because OLS only requires the model to be “linear in the parameters”. Under the assumption that the model is correctly specified, the following table is how we can interpret the coefficients of the transformed data. (Note for small changes, \(\Delta \log(x) \approx \Delta x / x = \Delta x \% / 100\).)

Interpreting Coefficients in Log Specifications









Specification
Regressand
Regressor
Derivative
Interpretation (If True)




linear–linear
\(y\)
\(x\)
\(\Delta y = \beta_{1}\cdot\Delta x\)
Change \(x\) by one unit \(\rightarrow\) change \(y\) by \(\beta_{1}\) units.


log–linear
\(\log(y)\)
\(x\)
\(\Delta y \% / 100 \approx \beta_{1} \cdot \Delta x\)
Change \(x\) by one unit \(\rightarrow\) change \(y\) by \(100 \cdot \beta_{1}\) percent.


linear–log
\(y\)
\(\log(x)\)
\(\Delta y \approx  \frac{\beta_{1}}{100}\cdot \Delta x \%\)
Change \(x\) by one percent \(\rightarrow\) change \(y\) by \(\frac{\beta_{1}}{100}\) units


log–log
\(\log(y)\)
\(\log(x)\)
\(\Delta y \% \approx \beta_{1}\cdot \Delta x \%\)
Change \(x\) by one percent \(\rightarrow\) change \(y\) by \(\beta_{1}\) percent









TipTest Yourself





Suppose you estimate \(\log(y) = 2.1 + 0.08 \cdot x\). The coefficient \(0.08\) means that a one-unit increase in \(x\) is associated with an approximate \(100 \times 0.08 = 8\%\) increase in \(y\). If instead you estimate \(\log(y) = 1.5 + 0.6 \cdot \log(x)\), the coefficient \(0.6\) is an elasticity: a \(1\%\) increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(0.6\%\) increase in \(y\).



Now recall from micro theory that an additively separable and linear production function is referred to as “perfect substitutes”. With a linear model and untransformed data, you have implicitly modelled the different regressors \(X_{ik}\) as perfect substitutes. Further recall that the “perfect substitutes” model is a special case of the constant elasticity of substitution production function.

Box-Cox Transformation
When linear-linear, log-log, and other named specifications are all plausible, we want one estimation procedure that searches across them rather than committing to one ex ante.






ImportantKey Definition





The Box-Cox transformation (Box and Cox 1964) is a family of power transformations of the outcome (indexed by \(\lambda\)) and the regressors (indexed by \(\rho\)), fit to the regression \(Y^{(\lambda)}_{i} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_{k} X^{(\rho)}_{ik} + \epsilon_{i}\) where \[\begin{aligned}
Y^{(\lambda)}_{i} &= \begin{cases}
  \lambda^{-1}\left[ Y_{i}^{\lambda}- 1\right] & \lambda \neq 0 \\
  \log(Y_{i}) & \lambda=0 \end{cases}\\
X^{(\rho)}_{i} &= \begin{cases}
  \rho^{-1}\left[ X_{i}^{\rho}- 1\right] & \rho \neq 0 \\
  \log(X_{i}) & \rho=0 \end{cases}.
\end{aligned}\]



The Box-Cox family is useful when no single named specification is obviously right. It nests the above specifications as special cases.

linear-linear (\(\rho=\lambda=1\))
linear-log \((\lambda=1, \rho=0)\).
log-linear \((\lambda=0, \rho=1)\).
log-log (\(\rho=\lambda=0\))

We let the data choose between linear, log, and intermediate fits by minimizing prediction error on the original scale (Box and Cox 1964; Wooldridge 1992; Adamson 2025). When \(\rho=\lambda\) we get the CES production function, which spans the “perfect substitutes” linear-linear model and the “cobb-douglas” log-log model among others. In this CES case, \(\rho~\text{in}~(-\infty,1]\) controls the substitutability of explanatory variables (\(\rho<0\) is “complementary”). The returns to scale depend on the coefficients as well as on \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\), so \(\lambda\) alone does not set them. In the log-log case, the returns to scale equal \(\sum_{k} \beta_{k}\), and \(\sum_{k} \beta_{k}<1\) is “decreasing returns”.1
We compute the mean squared error in the original scale by inverting the predictions; \[
\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}} =
\begin{cases}
\left[ \lambda \cdot \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit},(\lambda)} + 1 \right]^{1/\lambda} & \lambda  \neq 0 \\
\exp\left( \hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit},(\lambda)} \right) &  \lambda=0
\end{cases}.
\]
It is easiest to optimize parameters in a 2-step procedure called concentrated optimization. We first solve for \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}(\rho,\lambda)\) and compute the mean squared error \(\text{MSE}(\rho,\lambda)\). We then find the \((\rho,\lambda)\) which minimizes \(\text{MSE}\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Box-Cox Transformation Function
bxcx <- function( xy, rho){
    if (rho == 0L) {
      log(xy)
    } else if(rho == 1L){
      xy
    } else {
      (xy^rho - 1)/rho
    }
}
bxcx_inv <- function( xy, rho){
    if (rho == 0L) {
      exp(xy)
    } else if(rho == 1L){
      xy
    } else {
     (xy * rho + 1)^(1/rho)
    }
}

# Which Variables
reg <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat)
X <- xy_hat[, c('school', 'exper')]
y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'wage']

# Simple Grid Search over potential (Rho, Lambda)
rl_df <- expand.grid(rho=seq(-2, 2, by=.5), lambda=seq(-2, 2, by=.5))

# Compute Mean Squared Error
# from OLS on Transformed Data
errors <- apply(rl_df, 1, function(rl){
    Xr <- bxcx(X, rl[[1]])
    y_trans_hat <- bxcx(y_hat, rl[[2]])
    xy_trans_hat <- cbind(wage=y_trans_hat, Xr)
    Regr <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_trans_hat)
    y_fit <- bxcx_inv(predict(Regr), rl[[2]])
    e_hat  <- (y_hat - y_fit)
    return(e_hat)
})
rl_df$mse <- colMeans(errors^2)

# Want Small MSE and Interpretable
layout(matrix(1:2, ncol=2), width=c(3, 1), height=c(1, 1))
par(mar=c(4, 4, 2, 0))
plot(lambda ~ rho, rl_df, cex=8, pch=15,
    xlab=expression(rho),
    ylab=expression(lambda),
    col=hcl.colors(25)[cut(1/rl_df$mse, 25)])
# Which min
rl0 <- rl_df[which.min(rl_df$mse), c('rho', 'lambda')]
points(rl0$rho, rl0$lambda, pch=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), cex=8, lwd=2)
# Legend
plot(c(0, 2), c(0, 1), type='n', axes=FALSE,
    xlab='', ylab='', cex.main=.8,
    main=expression(frac(1, 'Mean Square Error')))
rasterImage(as.raster(matrix(hcl.colors(25), ncol=1)), 0, 0, 1, 1)
text(x=1.5, y=seq(1, 0, l=10), cex=.5,
    labels=levels(cut(1/rl_df$mse, 10)))









Code
# The box marks the minimum, at rho=2 and lambda=1.
# So wages stay in dollars, and schooling and experience enter squared.
# This is the edge of the grid, but a wider grid finds nothing lower.
# The yellow cells near the box fit about equally well.
# Blank cells have no MSE, since some of their fits cannot be inverted.








NoteMust Know





The grid search finds the \((\rho, \lambda)\) that minimizes MSE. But simple values like \(-1, 0, 1, 2\) are easier to interpret. When might you choose an interpretable transformation over the MSE-minimizing one? What is the trade-off?



The parameters \(-1,0,1,2\) are easy to interpret and might be selected instead if there is only a small loss in fit. You can also plot the specific predictions to better understand the effect of data transformation beyond mean squared error.


Code
# Plot for Specific Comparisons
Xr <- bxcx(X, rl0[[1]])
y_trans_hat <- bxcx(y_hat, rl0[[2]])
xy_trans_hat <- cbind(wage=y_trans_hat, Xr)
Regr <- lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_trans_hat)
y_fit <- bxcx_inv(predict(Regr), rl0[[2]])

# Faint points, since each model has 3294 of them
pt_cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .1), rgb(0, 0, .8, .1))
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5)) # stronger, for the legend
# The axes stop just past 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn
plot(y_hat, y_fit, pch=16, col=pt_cols[1], ylab='Prediction',
    xlab='Observed hourly wage (1980 dollars)',
    main=NA, xlim=c(0, 20), ylim=c(0, 20))
points(y_hat, predict(reg), pch=16, col=pt_cols[2])
legend('topleft', pch=c(16), col=cols,
    title=expression(rho~', '~lambda),
    legend=c( paste0(rl0, collapse=', '), '1, 1') )
abline(a=0, b=1, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# Both models predict between about 2 and 9 dollars, while wages reach about 40.
# Their predictions differ by only about 0.12 dollars on average.


We can compare the fit on the original scale: the grid-search optimum versus the untransformed linear baseline.


Code
# Compare prediction MSE on the original wage scale
mse_linear <- mean(resid(reg)^2)
mse_boxcox <- min(rl_df$mse, na.rm=TRUE)
mse_loglog <- rl_df$mse[rl_df$rho == 0 & rl_df$lambda == 0]
c(rl0, mse_linear=round(mse_linear, 3), mse_boxcox=round(mse_boxcox, 3),
    mse_loglog=round(mse_loglog, 3))
## $rho
## [1] 2
## 
## $lambda
## [1] 1
## 
## $mse_linear
## [1] 9.707
## 
## $mse_boxcox
## [1] 9.686
## 
## $mse_loglog
## [1] 10.344
# The grid's best fit, 9.686, beats the linear model, 9.707, by only about 0.2%.
# So the linear model is the easier choice, at a small loss in fit.
# The log-log model, 10.344, fits about 6.6% worse than the linear model.
# On this measure the loss in fit is too large to choose it.
# Most of that gap is bias from undoing the log, since exp() predicts too low.


The grid contains the linear baseline, so its best MSE can only match or beat it. That gain comes at the cost of two extra parameters and a less direct interpretation of the coefficients.






TipTest Yourself





Repeat the grid search and the comparisons for lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop) on USArrests, using bxcx() and bxcx_inv() from above.


Code
# Which Variables
xy2_hat <- USArrests
reg2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_hat)
X2 <- xy2_hat[, c('Assault', 'UrbanPop')]
y2_hat <- xy2_hat[, 'Murder']

# Simple Grid Search over potential (Rho, Lambda)
rl2_df <- expand.grid(rho=seq(-2, 2, by=.5), lambda=seq(-2, 2, by=.5))

# Compute Mean Squared Error
# from OLS on Transformed Data
errors2 <- apply(rl2_df, 1, function(rl){
    Xr <- bxcx(X2, rl[[1]])
    y_trans_hat <- bxcx(y2_hat, rl[[2]])
    xy_trans_hat <- cbind(Murder=y_trans_hat, Xr)
    Regr <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy_trans_hat)
    y_fit <- bxcx_inv(predict(Regr), rl[[2]])
    e_hat  <- (y2_hat - y_fit)
    return(e_hat)
})
rl2_df$mse <- colMeans(errors2^2)

# Want Small MSE and Interpretable
layout(matrix(1:2, ncol=2), width=c(3, 1), height=c(1, 1))
par(mar=c(4, 4, 2, 0))
plot(lambda ~ rho, rl2_df, cex=8, pch=15,
    xlab=expression(rho),
    ylab=expression(lambda),
    col=hcl.colors(25)[cut(1/rl2_df$mse, 25)])
# Which min
rl2 <- rl2_df[which.min(rl2_df$mse), c('rho', 'lambda')]
points(rl2$rho, rl2$lambda, pch=0, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), cex=8, lwd=2)
# Legend
plot(c(0, 2), c(0, 1), type='n', axes=FALSE,
    xlab='', ylab='', cex.main=.8,
    main=expression(frac(1, 'Mean Square Error')))
rasterImage(as.raster(matrix(hcl.colors(25), ncol=1)), 0, 0, 1, 1)
text(x=1.5, y=seq(1, 0, l=10), cex=.5,
    labels=levels(cut(1/rl2_df$mse, 10)))









Code
# The box marks the minimum, at rho=0 and lambda=0.5, inside the grid.




Code
# Plot for Specific Comparisons
Xr2 <- bxcx(X2, rl2[[1]])
y2_trans_hat <- bxcx(y2_hat, rl2[[2]])
xy2_trans_hat <- cbind(Murder=y2_trans_hat, Xr2)
Regr2 <- lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=xy2_trans_hat)
y2_fit <- bxcx_inv(predict(Regr2), rl2[[2]])

cols2 <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
plot(y2_hat, y2_fit, pch=16, col=cols2[1], ylab='Prediction', xlab='Observed Murder',
    main=NA, ylim=range(y2_hat, y2_fit))
points(y2_hat, predict(reg2), pch=16, col=cols2[2])
legend('topleft', pch=c(16), col=cols2,
    title=expression(rho~', '~lambda),
    legend=c( paste0(rl2, collapse=', '), '1, 1') )
abline(a=0, b=1, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=2)









Code
# The two models' predictions differ by about 0.42 arrests on average.

# Compare prediction MSE on the original Murder scale
mse2_linear <- mean(resid(reg2)^2)
mse2_boxcox <- min(rl2_df$mse, na.rm=TRUE)
mse2_loglog <- rl2_df$mse[rl2_df$rho == 0 & rl2_df$lambda == 0]
c(rl2, mse_linear=round(mse2_linear, 3), mse_boxcox=round(mse2_boxcox, 3),
    mse_loglog=round(mse2_loglog, 3))
## $rho
## [1] 0
## 
## $lambda
## [1] 0.5
## 
## $mse_linear
## [1] 6.257
## 
## $mse_boxcox
## [1] 5.999
## 
## $mse_loglog
## [1] 6.446
# The grid's best fit, 5.999, beats the linear model, 6.257, by about 4%.
# The log-log model, 6.446, fits about 3% worse than the linear model.
# So the loss in fit is too large to choose it.





When explicitly transforming data according to \(\lambda\) and \(\rho\), these parameters increase the degrees of freedom by two. The default hypothesis testing procedures do not account for you trying out different transformations, and should be adjusted by the increased degrees of freedom. Specification searches deflate standard errors and are a major source for false discoveries.
Note that if you are ultimately interested in the outcome \(Y_{i}\), then transforming/untransforming \(Y_{i}\) can introduce a bias. To understand when you might be better off sticking with an untransformed outcome variable, see the literature on “smearing”.

title: 24  Model Assessment
text:
24.3 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
A regression has high \(\hat{R}^2\) but one observation has a very large Cook’s Distance. Should you automatically drop that observation? Explain what Cook’s Distance measures and describe a situation where keeping the outlier is the right choice.
Using the USArrests dataset, fit lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop). Produce the four standard diagnostic plots with plot(). Identify the state with the highest leverage (using hatvalues()) and the state with the largest standardized residual (using rstandard()). Are they the same state?
Fit the model lm(Murder ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=USArrests) and then fit a log-linear version lm(log(Murder) ~ Assault + UrbanPop, data=USArrests). Compare the two models by computing the mean squared prediction error in the original (untransformed) scale for each. Which specification fits better?


Further Reading

https://book.stat420.org/model-diagnostics.html – leverage, Cook’s distance, and residual diagnostics with R examples.
https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/6-rmwmr.html – interpreting coefficients, specification, and multicollinearity in multiple regression.
Fox (2020) – a short monograph on influence measures, outliers, and model misspecification.



Recall
This chapter checked a fitted regression with four diagnostic plots for outliers, leverage, normality, and scale. It measured collinearity with the Variance Inflation Factor and tested for heteroskedasticity with the Breusch-Pagan test. It then used Box-Cox transformations to try to rescue a misspecified linear model. The Box-Cox grid-search on wage ~ school + exper made the trade-off concrete: searching over \((\rho, \lambda)\) on \(\{-2, -1.5, \ldots, 2\}^2\) found a fit with MSE \(9.686\) on the original wage scale, barely below the untransformed baseline’s \(9.707\).




Adamson, Jordan. 2025. “Trade and the Rise of Ancient Greek City-States.” Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 235: 107035. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2025.107035.


Bellemare, Marc F., and Casey J. Wichman. 2020. “Elasticities and the Inverse Hyperbolic Sine Transformation.” Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics 82 (1): 50–61. https://doi.org/10.1111/obes.12325.


Box, G. E. P., and D. R. Cox. 1964. “An Analysis of Transformations.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological) 26 (2): 211–43. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1964.tb00553.x.


Breusch, T. S., and A. R. Pagan. 1979. “A Simple Test for Heteroscedasticity and Random Coefficient Variation.” Econometrica 47 (5): 1287–94. https://doi.org/10.2307/1911963.


Chen, Jiafeng, and Jonathan Roth. 2024. “Logs with Zeros? Some Problems and Solutions.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 139 (2): 891–936. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjad054.


Cook, R. Dennis. 1977. “Detection of Influential Observation in Linear Regression.” Technometrics 19 (1): 15–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1977.10489493.


Fox, John. 2020. Regression Diagnostics: An Introduction. 2nd ed. Quantitative Applications in the Social Sciences 79. SAGE Publications. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781071878651.


Wooldridge, Jeffrey M. 1992. “Some Alternatives to the Box-Cox Regression Model.” International Economic Review 33 (4): 935–55. https://doi.org/10.2307/2527151.

title: 24  Model Assessment
text: One can also use the “shifted” family of Box and Cox. Coefficients from such a regression depend on the units of the outcome, so they should not be read as percentage changes (Bellemare and Wichman 2020; Chen and Roth 2024).↩︎

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
25.1 Regressograms
In Local Regression, we estimated nonparametric models with a single explanatory variable. We now extend those tools to multiple explanatory variables. The ideas carry over directly: instead of binning one variable, we bin each variable, and instead of fitting a line in pieces, we fit a plane in pieces.
This chapter asks three questions.

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
Setup
We want a flexible estimate of \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i} \mid X_{i1}, X_{i2}]\) that does not commit to any functional form for either explanatory variable.






ImportantKey Definition





A multivariate regressogram cuts each explanatory variable into exclusive bins (each encoded as a dummy variable), then computes the prediction \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{K})\) within each bin combination using OLS on the full set of dummies. It is the multivariate generalization of the univariate regressogram from Local Regression.



The multivariate regressogram is useful for estimating a conditional mean without committing to linearity or any particular interaction structure, because every cell gets its own prediction. This flexibility is also its main drawback. As the number of explanatory variables grows, the cells empty out and predictions in sparse regions become noisy. The simulated data below uses two predictors so we can plot it.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## Simulate data: y_sim is a nonlinear function of x1_sim and x2_sim plus noise.
N <- 10000
e <- rnorm(N)
x1_sim <- seq(.1, 20, length.out=N)
x2_sim <- runif(N, 0, 1)
y_sim  <- 3*exp(-2*x2_sim + 1.5*x1_sim - .1*x1_sim^2)*x1_sim + e
xy_sim <- data.frame(x1_sim, x2_sim, y_sim)

## Create color palette (reused in later examples)
col_scale <- seq(min(y_sim)*1.1, max(y_sim)*1.1, length.out=401)
ycol_pal <- hcl.colors(length(col_scale), alpha=.5)
names(ycol_pal) <- sort(col_scale)

## Add legend (reused in later examples)
add_legend <- function(col_scale,
    yl=11,
    colfun=function(x){ hcl.colors(x, alpha=.5) },
    ...) {
  opar <- par(fig=c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma=c(0, 0, 0, 0), 
              mar=c(0, 0, 0, 0), new=TRUE)
  on.exit(par(opar))
  bin_mids <- hist(col_scale, plot=FALSE, breaks=yl-1)$mids
  plot(0, 0, type='n', bty='n', xaxt='n', yaxt='n')
  legend(...,
    legend=bin_mids,
    fill=colfun(length(bin_mids)),
    border=NA,
    bty='n')
}


## Plot Data
par(oma=c(0, 0, 0, 2))
plot(x1_sim ~ x2_sim, xy_sim,
    col=ycol_pal[cut(y_sim, col_scale)],
    pch=16, cex=.5,
    main=NA)
title('Raw Data', font.main=1)
add_legend(x='topright', col_scale=col_scale,
    yl=6, inset=c(0, .05), title='y')











OLS Baseline
We start with a global linear baseline, fitted without an interaction.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## OLS (without interaction; the additive baseline)
reg <- lm(y_sim ~ x1_sim+x2_sim, data=xy_sim)

## Grid Points for Prediction
# X1 bins
l1 <- 11
bks1 <- seq(0, 20, length.out=l1)
h1 <- diff(bks1)[1]/2
mids1 <- bks1[-1]-h1
# X2 bins
l2 <- 11
bks2 <- seq(0, 1, length.out=l2)
h2 <- diff(bks2)[1]/2
mids2 <- bks2[-1]-h2
# Grid
pred_x <- expand.grid(x1_sim=mids1, x2_sim=mids2)

## OLS Predictions
y_pred_ols <- predict(reg, newdata=pred_x)
pred_df_ols  <- cbind(y_pred_ols, pred_x)

## Plot Predictions
par(oma=c(0, 0, 0, 2))
plot(x1_sim ~ x2_sim, pred_df_ols,
    col=ycol_pal[cut(y_pred_ols, col_scale)],
    pch=15, cex=2,
    main=NA)
title('OLS Predictions', font.main=1)
add_legend(x='topright', col_scale=col_scale,
    yl=6, inset=c(0, .05), title='y')











Multivariate Bins


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
##################
# Multivariate Regressogram
##################

## Cut each variable into bins, then interact them: each (x1c_sim, x2c_sim) cell
## gets its own mean. With the `*` interaction the model is fully saturated.
xy_sim$x1c_sim <- cut(xy_sim$x1_sim, bks1)
xy_sim$x2c_sim <- cut(xy_sim$x2_sim, bks2)

## Regressogram (interacted bins -> one mean per (x1c_sim, x2c_sim) cell)
reg <- lm(y_sim ~ x1c_sim*x2c_sim, data=xy_sim)

## Predicted Values
## For Points in Middle of Each Bin
pred_df_rgrm <- expand.grid(
    x1c_sim=levels(xy_sim$x1c_sim),
    x2c_sim=levels(xy_sim$x2c_sim))
pred_df_rgrm$y_pred <- predict(reg, newdata=pred_df_rgrm)
pred_df_rgrm <- cbind(pred_df_rgrm, pred_x)

## Plot Predictions
par(oma=c(0, 0, 0, 2))
plot(x1_sim ~ x2_sim, pred_df_rgrm,
    col=ycol_pal[cut(pred_df_rgrm$y_pred, col_scale)],
    pch=15, cex=2,
    main=NA)
title('Regressogram Predictions', font.main=1)
add_legend(x='topright', col_scale=col_scale,
    yl=6, inset=c(0, .05), title='y')















TipTest Yourself





The regressogram divides the \((x_{1}, x_{2})\) space into a grid of bins and estimates the mean of \(y\) within each bin. Compared to OLS, the regressogram makes no assumption about functional form: it can capture nonlinear and interaction effects. The trade-off is that it requires more data to fill each bin, especially as the number of variables grows.









NoteMust Know





A regressogram prediction is just the average of \(\hat{y}_{i}\) within a bin. Consider six observations, with \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) each split into “low” and “high”.


Code
xy0_hat <- data.frame(
    y_hat  = c(2, 4, 5, 9, 8, 12),
    x1_hat = c('low', 'low', 'low', 'high', 'high', 'high'),
    x2_hat = c('low', 'low', 'high', 'low', 'high', 'high'))

# Regressogram prediction = mean of y_hat within each (x1_hat, x2_hat) cell
aggregate(y_hat ~ x1_hat + x2_hat, data=xy0_hat, FUN=mean)
##   x1_hat x2_hat y_hat
## 1   high   high    10
## 2    low   high     5
## 3   high    low     9
## 4    low    low     3


The fitted value for any point is its cell mean: \((2+4)/2 = 3\) for the (low, low) cell, \(5\) for (low, high), \(9\) for (high, low), and \((8+12)/2 = 10\) for (high, high).

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
25.2 Local Regressions

Piecewise Model
A regressogram is locally constant, so every point in a bin gets the same prediction. We sometimes want slopes within each bin instead of a flat shelf.






ImportantKey Definition





A multivariate piecewise regression bins one explanatory variable and fits a separate OLS plane on all the explanatory variables within each bin.



A piecewise regression is useful when you want something between the flat regressogram and the global OLS plane. It tracks gradients within each bin, so predictions vary smoothly within a bin and jump only at the bin edges. We bin one variable, then fit a full linear model of \(\hat{y}\) on the explanatory variables within each bin.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
##################
# Multivariate Piecewise Regression
##################

## Bin x1_sim, then fit a linear model of y_sim on (x1_sim, x2_sim) within each bin
xy_sim$x1c_sim <- cut(xy_sim$x1_sim, bks1)
preg <- lm(y_sim ~ x1c_sim/(x1_sim + x2_sim), data=xy_sim)

## Predicted Values
## For the same grid of points used above
pred_df_preg <- pred_x
pred_df_preg$x1c_sim <- cut(pred_df_preg$x1_sim, bks1)
pred_df_preg$y_pred <- predict(preg, newdata=pred_df_preg)

## Plot Predictions
par(oma=c(0, 0, 0, 2))
plot(x1_sim ~ x2_sim, pred_df_preg,
    col=ycol_pal[cut(pred_df_preg$y_pred, col_scale)],
    pch=15, cex=2,
    main=NA)
title('Piecewise Regression Predictions', font.main=1)
add_legend(x='topright', col_scale=col_scale,
    yl=6, inset=c(0, .05), title='y')









The formula y_sim ~ x1c_sim/(x1_sim + x2_sim) gives each x1_sim bin its own intercept and its own slopes on x1_sim and x2_sim. Running one regression per data subset with split() gives identical predictions, as shown for the bivariate case in Local Regression. A fully local linear regression generalizes this further, replacing hard bins with kernel weights and a separate bandwidth for each variable; see Local Regression for the bivariate version.






TipTest Yourself





Compare the three sets of predictions in this chapter (OLS, regressogram, and piecewise). Which captures the curvature in x1_sim? Which is smoothest? Refit the piecewise model with finer bins (bks1 <- seq(0, 20, length.out=21)) and describe how the prediction plot changes.





Break Points
Kinks and discontinuities in the relationship between \(\hat{y}\) and \(\hat{x}_{k}\) can be modeled with factor variables, just like any other transformation. We can then use \(F\)-tests to examine whether a break is statistically significant. Both the interaction-model \(F\)-test (anova) and the Chow test (Chow 1960) below test the same null of “no break”, and give the same answer.


Code
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)

# F-test for a break at school = 12
reg2 <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat*I(x_hat>12), data=xy_hat)
anova(reg, reg2)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: y_hat ~ x_hat
## Model 2: y_hat ~ x_hat * I(x_hat > 12)
##   Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
## 1   3292 32386                                  
## 2   3290 32146  2     239.8 12.271 4.902e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Chow test for the same break
data_splits <- split(xy_hat, xy_hat$x_hat <= 12)
resids <- sapply(data_splits, function(xy_sub){
    reg_sub <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_sub)
    sum(resid(reg_sub)^2)
})
Ns <- sapply(data_splits, function(xy_sub){ nrow(xy_sub) })

# Chow F-statistic: does splitting the sample reduce RSS enough?
Rt <- (sum(resid(reg)^2) - sum(resids))/sum(resids)
Rb <- (sum(Ns) - 2*reg$rank)/reg$rank
Ft <- Rt*Rb
pf(Ft, reg$rank, sum(Ns)-2*reg$rank, lower.tail=FALSE)
## [1] 4.901941e-06
# The p-value is about 5e-06, which is evidence of a break at 12 years.
# Twelve years is the end of secondary school.

# See also
# strucchange::sctest(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, type='Chow', point=.5)
# segmented::segmented(reg)


A small \(p\)-value is evidence that the line changes at the candidate break. The ratio Rt in the Chow test is the drop in the residual sum of squares, divided by the unrestricted residual sum of squares. This is the same loss-in-fit ratio as in Model Fit.






NoteMust Know





The Chow test checks whether a structural break exists at a specified point. What happens if you do not know where the break is? How does searching over many potential break points affect the validity of your test? (Hint: think about multiple testing.)

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
25.3 Model Selection

Leave-One-Out and K-Fold CV
A flexible model can fit the training data perfectly while predicting new observations badly, so we need a way to measure performance on data the model has not seen.






ImportantKey Definition





Cross-validation (CV) picks a model by minimizing out-of-sample prediction error. Leave-one-out CV drops one observation at a time, refits, and averages the squared prediction errors: \[
\min_{\mathbf{H}} \quad \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i},\mathbf{H}) \right]^2,
\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=[\hat{x}_{i1}, \ldots, \hat{x}_{iK}]\) collects the explanatory variables of observation \(i\), \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i},\mathbf{H})\) is the model’s prediction at \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\) from a fit that excluded observation \(i\), and \(\mathbf{H}\) is the bandwidth matrix. \(k\)-fold CV drops one of \(k\) random groups at a time instead of one observation.



Cross-validation is useful because it directly penalizes overfitting: a too-flexible model predicts held-out observations poorly even though it fits in-sample data tightly. With a weighted least squares regression on three explanatory variables, the bandwidth matrix has the form \[
\mathbf{H}=\begin{pmatrix}
h_{1} & 0 & 0  \\
0    & h_{2} & 0 \\
0    & 0 & h_{3} \\
\end{pmatrix},
\] where each \(h_{k}\) is the bandwidth for variable \(\hat{x}_{k}\). In the discrete-bin setting below, the role of the bandwidth is played by the number of bins \(L\): more bins means finer resolution (a smaller effective bandwidth) and fewer observations per bin.
There are many types of cross-validation (Arlot and Celisse 2010; Bates et al. 2023). Generalized cross-validation adjusts for the degrees of freedom, whereas the npreg function in R uses least-squares cross-validation (Racine 2019, 74) by default. You can refer to extensions on a case by case basis. In applied work, Adamson (2025) uses leave-one-out cross-validation (Allen 1974; Stone 1974; Hall and Racine 2015) to choose the bandwidth of geographically weighted regressions on ancient Greek city-states. These are local regressions whose kernel weights depend on the distance between locations (Brunsdon et al. 1996; Fotheringham et al. 2003).






TipTest Yourself





Cross-validation works by repeatedly holding out one observation, fitting the model on the rest, and measuring how well the model predicts the held-out point. A model that overfits (e.g., too many bins) will have low in-sample error but high cross-validation error. The bandwidth \(\mathbf{H}\) that minimizes cross-validation error balances flexibility against overfitting.



To make this concrete, we use cross-validation to choose the number of x1_sim bins for the piecewise regression above. We split the data into 5 folds, fit the model on 4 of them, and measure the squared prediction error on the held-out fold. With almost no noise, finer bins tend to keep lowering the error, so we first add more noise to y_sim (standard deviation \(2500\)).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
## 5-fold cross-validation for the number of x1_sim bins
n_folds <- 5
fold_id <- sample(rep(1:n_folds, length.out=nrow(xy_sim)))
bin_counts <- c(2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22)

## Noisier copy of the data, so that too many bins overfit
xy_cv_sim <- xy_sim
xy_cv_sim$y_sim <- xy_sim$y_sim + rnorm(nrow(xy_sim), sd=2500)
# The noise in y_sim alone is tiny compared to its curvature.
# Without more, the error would keep falling across all these bin counts.

cv_mse <- sapply(bin_counts, function(L){
    bks <- seq(0, 20, length.out=L+1)
    fold_mse <- sapply(1:n_folds, function(k){
        xy_train_sim <- xy_cv_sim[fold_id != k, ]
        xy_test_sim  <- xy_cv_sim[fold_id == k, ]
        xy_train_sim$x1c_sim <- cut(xy_train_sim$x1_sim, bks)
        xy_test_sim$x1c_sim  <- cut(xy_test_sim$x1_sim, bks)
        reg_k <- lm(y_sim ~ x1c_sim/(x1_sim + x2_sim), data=xy_train_sim)
        y_pred_k <- predict(reg_k, newdata=xy_test_sim)
        mean((xy_test_sim$y_sim - y_pred_k)^2, na.rm=TRUE)
    })
    mean(fold_mse)
})

## Plot CV error against model complexity
plot(bin_counts, cv_mse, type='o', pch=16,
    xlab='Number of x1 bins', ylab='5-fold CV mean squared error',
    main=NA)
L_star <- bin_counts[which.min(cv_mse)]
abline(v=L_star, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
title(paste0('CV-optimal: ', L_star, ' bins'), font.main=1)









Code
# The error is smallest at 10 bins, between too few and too many.


Too few bins cannot capture the curvature in x1_sim (high bias); too many bins split the data so finely that each local regression is noisy (high variance). The cross-validated error is usually smallest in between.






TipTest Yourself





The cross-validation above selects bins for the piecewise model. Adapt the code to instead select bins for the regressogram lm(y_sim ~ x1c_sim*x2c_sim), cutting both x1_sim and x2_sim into L bins. What happens to the cross-validated error once L is large enough that some grid cells are empty? (Hint: empty cells give NA predictions.)

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
25.4 Hypothesis Testing

Finite Differences
A gradient describes how \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}\) changes with each \(x_{k}\) at a point. We first summarize gradients, then test them.






ImportantKey Definition





A gradient of a fitted multivariate model is the partial derivative \(\partial \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}/\partial x_{k}\) evaluated at a point. For a regressogram with no slope coefficients, it must be approximated by a finite difference between adjacent bins, \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x}) &= \frac{ \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{1},...,x_{k}+ \frac{d}{2}...,x_{K})-\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{1},...,x_{k}-\frac{d}{2}...,x_{K})}{d},
\end{aligned}\] where the step \(d\) is the bin width and \(x_{k}\) is the edge between two bins, while a piecewise or local linear regression has within-bin slopes that are themselves gradient estimates.



The gradient is useful because, unlike the single OLS coefficient, it varies with \(\mathbf{x}\). This lets us see whether the marginal effect of \(\hat{x}_{k}\) is the same at small, medium, and large values of the other regressors. We can compute it two ways:

For regressograms, approximate the gradient with a small finite difference between adjacent bins (formula above).
For split-sample regressions or local linear regressions, read the within-bin slope coefficients \(\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x})\) directly as gradient estimates.

After computing gradients, you can summarize them in various plots: a histogram of \(\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x})\), a scatterplot of \(\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x})\) against \(x_{k}\), or the sorted gradients shown with their confidence intervals (Chaudhuri and Marron 1999; Henderson et al. 2012).
You may also be interested in a particular gradient or a single summary statistic. For example, a bivariate regressogram can estimate the marginal effect of \(\hat{x}_{1}\) at the means, \(\hat{b}_{1}(\mathbf{x}=[\hat{m}_{X_{1}}, \hat{m}_{X_{2}}])\), where \(\hat{m}_{X_{k}}\) is the mean of \(\hat{x}_{k}\). You may also be interested in the mean of the marginal effects (sometimes said simply as “average effect”), which averages the marginal effect over all datapoints in the dataset: \(1/n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{b}_{1}(\mathbf{x}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i})\), or the median marginal effect. Such statistics are single numbers that can be presented similar to an OLS regression table, where each row corresponds to a variable and each cell has two elements: “mean gradient (sd gradient)”. A single average can hide gradients that change sign (Henderson et al. 2012; Adamson 2021).
We illustrate both methods on the models fit earlier in this chapter. Method 1 differences the regressogram predictions; method 2 reads the slopes directly off the piecewise regression.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
##################
# Method 1: finite-difference gradients from the regressogram
##################

## Arrange the regressogram predictions into an x1_sim-by-x2_sim grid
grid_y_pred <- matrix(pred_df_rgrm$y_pred,
    nrow=length(mids1), ncol=length(mids2))

## Centered finite difference at each interior x1_sim bin edge, with d equal to the bin width
## The points x1 - d/2 and x1 + d/2 are the midpoints of the two adjacent bins
d1 <- diff(bks1)[1]
grad_x1 <- apply(grid_y_pred, 2, diff)/d1
x1_edges <- mids1[-1] - d1/2

## Summarize the gradient distribution
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(grad_x1, breaks=20, border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA, xlab=expression(hat(b)[1](x)))
title('Distribution of x1-gradients', font.main=1)
plot(rep(x1_edges, ncol(grad_x1)), grad_x1,
    pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    xlab=expression(x[1]), ylab=expression(hat(b)[1](x)),
    main=NA)
title('Gradient vs x1', font.main=1)











Slope Coefficients


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
##################
# Method 2: slope coefficients from the piecewise regression
##################

## The within-bin slope on x1_sim is itself a gradient estimate
coef_preg <- coef(preg)
slope_x1 <- coef_preg[grep(':x1_sim$', names(coef_preg))]

## Mean and standard deviation of the x1_sim-gradient
c(mean=mean(slope_x1, na.rm=TRUE), sd=sd(slope_x1, na.rm=TRUE))
##        mean          sd 
##   0.8222098 422.1854069


The mean gradient is a single-number summary, much like an OLS slope. The standard deviation across bins measures how much the gradient changes over the data, which a single OLS coefficient cannot show. To test whether a mean gradient differs from zero, bootstrap it exactly as in Gradients. To test whether all gradients equal zero, use Racine’s statistic instead.






NoteMust Know





Suppose the regressogram predicts \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{1}-1) = 8\) in one \(x_{1}\)-bin and \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x_{1}+1) = 14\) in the next, so the bin midpoints are \(2\) units apart. The estimated \(x_{1}\)-gradient at the edge \(x_{1}\) between the two bins is \((14 - 8)/2 = 3\): moving one unit in \(x_{1}\) raises the prediction by about \(3\).

title: 25  Local Relationships
text:
25.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
A regressogram bins each explanatory variable and estimates a separate mean within each bin combination. How does this differ from a standard OLS regression with the same variables? What advantage does it have when the true relationship is nonlinear, and what is its main drawback as the number of explanatory variables grows?
Using the simulated data from this chapter (x1_sim <- seq(.1, 20, length.out = 1000), x2_sim <- runif(1000, 0, 1), y_sim <- 3*exp(-2*x2_sim + 1.5*x1_sim - .1*x1_sim^2)*x1_sim + rnorm(1000)), build a regressogram by cutting x1_sim into 5 bins and x2_sim into 5 bins. Compute the mean of y_sim within each of the 25 bin combinations. Which bin combination has the highest predicted value?
Using lm(), fit two models to the mtcars dataset with mpg as the outcome: (a) a standard linear model mpg ~ wt + hp, and (b) a regressogram model where wt and hp are each cut into 4 bins using cut() and interacted (mpg ~ cut(wt,4) * cut(hp,4)). Compare the \(\hat{R}^2\) of each model. Plot the predicted values from both models against the observed mpg.


Further Reading

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/np/vignettes/np.pdf – the np package vignette for kernel and local-linear nonparametric regression in R.
https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/11-rwmad.html – nonparametric methods and their connection to regression, including bin-smoothers.



Recall
This chapter generalized regressograms, piecewise regression, and cross-validation to the multivariate setting, and showed two ways to summarize gradients: finite differences from the regressogram, and within-bin slopes from the piecewise model. The 5-fold CV exercise on y_sim ~ x1c_sim/(x1_sim + x2_sim) illustrated the bias-variance trade-off. We tried \(\{2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22\}\) bins for x1_sim. The cross-validated MSE fell to its minimum at the CV-optimal \(L^{*}\) and rose again as we kept adding bins.
