title: 26  Observational Data
text:
26.1 Temporal Interdependence
Most economic data are not generated by an experiment. They arrive with dependence across time, across space, and across the variables themselves. This dependence comes from market equilibrium, optimization, and selection. Each of those three forms of dependence violates the independence assumption of standard regression and complicates causal interpretation.
This chapter asks three questions.
Many observational datasets have temporal dependence, meaning that values at one point in time are related to past values. This violates the standard assumption of independence used in many statistical methods.
Stock prices are classic examples of temporally dependent processes. If Apple’s stock was high yesterday, it is more likely (but not guaranteed) to be high today.
Code
# Load a CSV of daily Apple stock prices and plot the daily high as a line.
library('plotly')
stock <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/finance-charts-apple.csv')
fig <- plot_ly(stock, type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines')%>%
  add_trace(x = ~ Date, y = ~ AAPL.High) %>%
  layout(showlegend = FALSE)
fig






Code
# Today's high is not independent of past highs.
A random walk is the simplest mathematical model of temporal dependence. Each new value is just the previous value plus a random shock (white noise).
Code
# Generate Random Walk
tN <- 200
y_rw_sim <- numeric(tN)
y_rw_sim[1] <- stock$AAPL.High[1]
for (ti in 2:tN) {
    y_rw_sim[ti] <- y_rw_sim[ti-1] + runif(1, -10, 10)
}
#x_sim <- runif(tN, -1, 1) White Noise

xy_rw_sim <- data.frame(Date=1:tN, RandomWalk=y_rw_sim)
fig <- plot_ly(xy_rw_sim, type = 'scatter', mode = 'lines') %>%
  add_trace(x= ~ Date, y= ~ RandomWalk) %>%
  layout(showlegend = FALSE)
fig






Code
# Today's value is not independent of past values.
In a temporally dependent series, today’s value is not independent of past values. In contrast to cross-sectional data (e.g. individual incomes), time series often require special methods to account for memory and nonstationarity.
It often helps to see the marginal distribution alongside the time path. A nonstationary series can disguise itself in a histogram because the histogram pools across \(t\).
Code
# Time path beside the marginal distribution
layout(matrix(c(1, 2), nrow = 1), widths = c(4, 1))

par(mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(1:tN, y_rw_sim, type='l', lwd=2,
    xlab='t', ylab=expression(y[t]))
title('Random walk: time path', font.main=1, adj=0)

par(mar=c(4, 1, 1, 2))
f_hat <- hist(y_rw_sim, breaks=20, plot=FALSE)
barplot(f_hat$counts, horiz=TRUE, space=0, border=NA,
    col=grey(.5, .5), axes=FALSE)
axis(1)
title('Marginal', font.main=1, adj=0)

title: 26  Observational Data
text:
NoteMust Know





Modify the random walk above by changing runif(1, -10, 10) to rnorm(1, 0, 5). How does the choice of shock distribution affect the path? Does it change whether the series is stationary or nonstationary?
Hint. Both choices produce zero-mean, finite-variance shocks, so each simulated path is still a random walk. The variance of \(Y_{t}\) grows linearly in \(t\), so the series is nonstationary whether the shocks are uniform or normal. The shape of individual paths looks slightly different but the long-run behavior is the same.







Stationary
The simplest time-series methods implicitly assume the data have a stable distribution over time; this assumption fails often enough that we need a name for it.






ImportantKey Definition





A time series is stationary if both its mean and variance do not depend on \(t\):

Stationary means: \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{t'}]\) for all time periods \(t, t'\).
Stationary variances: \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{t}]=\mathbb{V}[Y_{t'}]\) for all time periods \(t, t'\).




Stationarity is useful as a precondition for most classical time-series tools. Note that there is more than one way to be nonstationary. A series with a deterministic trend is mean-nonstationary, while a random walk is variance-nonstationary because \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{t}]\) grows linearly in \(t\).
For example, consider the data generating process \(Y_{t} = \beta t + \epsilon_{t}\), where \(\epsilon_{t}\) is Normal with \(\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{t}]=0\) and \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[\epsilon_{t}]}=\sigma+\alpha t>0\). Here \(\sigma\) is the baseline standard deviation in this Normal model. Then \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}]=\beta t\) and \(\mathbb{V}[Y_{t}]=(\sigma+\alpha t)^2\), so \(\beta\) affects mean stationarity and \(\alpha\) affects variance stationarity.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
tN <- 200
simulate_series <- function(beta, alpha, sigma=.2){
    y_sim <- numeric(tN)
    for (ti in 1:tN) {
        mean_ti <- beta*ti
        sd_ti <- (sigma + alpha*ti)
        y_sim[ti] <- mean_ti + rnorm(1, sd=sd_ti)
    }
    return(y_sim)
}

# Plotting Functions
plot_setup <- function(alpha, beta){
    plot.new()
    plot.window(xlim=c(1, tN), ylim=c(-5, 20))
    axis(1)
    axis(2)
    mtext(expression(y[t]), 2, line=2.5)
    mtext('Time (t)', 1, line=2.5)
}
plot_title <- function(alpha, beta){
    beta_name <- ifelse(beta==0, 'Mean Stationary', 'Mean Nonstationary')
    alpha_name <- ifelse(alpha==0, 'Var Stationary', 'Var Nonstationary')
    title(paste0(beta_name, ', ', alpha_name), font.main=1, adj=0)
}

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for(alpha in c(0, .015)){
for(beta in c(0, .05)){
    plot_setup(alpha=alpha, beta=beta)
    sim_cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
    for( sim in 1:2){
        y_sim <- simulate_series(beta=beta, alpha=alpha)
        lines(y_sim, col=sim_cols[sim], lwd=2)
    }
    plot_title(alpha=alpha, beta=beta)
}}















TipTest Yourself





In the top-left panel (\(\beta=0, \alpha=0\)), both the mean and variance are constant over time – this is stationary. In the top-right panel (\(\beta>0, \alpha=0\)), the mean drifts upward but the variance stays constant – mean nonstationary. In the bottom-left (\(\beta=0, \alpha>0\)), the mean is constant but the spread grows – variance nonstationary. The bottom-right has both problems.





Measures of temporal association
When values at one time depend on values at other times, we need correlation-based diagnostics across lags to characterize the dependence.






ImportantKey Definition





The autocorrelation function of \(Y_{t}\) at lag \(k\) is the correlation of \(Y_{t}\) with its own lagged value \(Y_{t-k}\), \[\text{ACF}_{Y}(k) = \frac{\mathbb{C}[Y_{t},Y_{t-k}]}{ \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[Y_{t}]\mathbb{V}[Y_{t-k}]}}.\] The cross-correlation function between \(Y_{t}\) and \(X_{t}\) at lag \(k\) is the corresponding correlation of \(Y_{t}\) with \(X_{t-k}\), \[\text{CCF}_{YX}(k) = \frac{\mathbb{C}[Y_{t},X_{t-k}]}{ \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[Y_{t}]\mathbb{V}[X_{t-k}]}}.\]



The ACF is useful for detecting temporal persistence (memory) within one series: for stationary processes it typically decays quickly, while nonstationary processes show ACFs that decay slowly or persist. The CCF is useful for detecting lagged relationships between two series, such as leading indicators or external drivers; if \(X_{t}\) is white noise, any visible structure in the CCF likely reflects nonstationarity in \(Y_{t}\).






NoteMust Know





Worked example: \(y=(2,4,6,8,10)\), with \(n=5\) and mean \(\bar{y}=6\). R’s acf() uses the biased estimator \[
\hat{\text{ACF}}(1) = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=2}^{n}(y_{t} - \bar{y})(y_{t-1}-\bar{y})}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_{t} - \bar{y})^2}.
\] Deviations are \((-4,-2,0,2,4)\); lag-1 cross-products are \((-4)(-2)=8\), \((-2)(0)=0\), \((0)(2)=0\), \((2)(4)=8\), summing to \(16\). Sum of squared deviations is \(16+4+0+4+16=40\). So \(\hat{\text{ACF}}(1) = 16/40 = 0.4\).


Code
y0_hat <- c(2,4,6,8,10)
acf(y0_hat, plot=FALSE)$acf[2]
## [1] 0.4







Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for(alpha in c(0, .015)){
for(beta in c(0, .05)){
    y_sim <- simulate_series(beta=beta, alpha=alpha)
    acf(y_sim, main=NA)
    plot_title(alpha=alpha, beta=beta)
}}









A cross-correlation plot diagnoses lagged dependence between two series at once:






NoteMust Know





Worked CCF example. Let \(y=(1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(x=(2,3,4,5,6)\), with \(\bar{y}=3, \bar{x}=4\). The lag-1 cross-correlation pairs \(y_{t}\) with \(x_{t-1}\), giving four cross-products \((2-3)(2-4) = 2\), \((3-3)(3-4) = 0\), \((4-3)(4-4) = 0\), \((5-3)(5-4) = 2\). With \(n=5\), the (biased) denominator is \(\sqrt{\sum_{t}(y_{t}-\bar y)^2 \sum_{t}(x_{t}-\bar x)^2}/n = \sqrt{10 \cdot 10}/5 = 2\), so \(\hat{\text{CCF}}(1) = (2+0+0+2)/5 / 2 = 0.4\).


Code
y0_hat <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
x0_hat <- c(2,3,4,5,6)
ccf(y0_hat, x0_hat, lag.max=1, plot=FALSE)$acf
## , , 1
## 
##      [,1]
## [1,]  0.4
## [2,]  1.0
## [3,]  0.4







Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
x_sim <- runif(tN, -1, 1) # White Noise
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for(alpha in c(0, .015)){
for(beta in c(0, .05)){
    y_sim <- simulate_series(beta=beta, alpha=alpha)
    ccf(y_sim, x_sim, main=NA)
    plot_title(alpha=alpha, beta=beta)
}}

title: 26  Observational Data
text:
26.2 Spatial Interdependence
Many observational datasets exhibit spatial dependence, meaning that values at one location tend to be related to values at nearby locations. This violates the standard assumption of independent observations used in many classical statistical methods.
For example, elevation is spatially dependent: if one location is at high elevation, nearby locations are also likely (though not guaranteed) to be high. Similarly, socioeconomic outcomes like disease rates or income often cluster geographically due to shared environmental or social factors.
Just as stock prices today depend on yesterday, spatial variables often depend on neighboring regions, creating a need for specialized statistical methods that account for spatial autocorrelation.

Raster vs. Vector Data
Spatial data typically comes in two formats, each suited to different types of information:

Vector data uses geometric shapes (points, lines, polygons) to store data. E.g., a census tract map that stores data on population demographics.
Raster data uses grid cells (typically squares, but sometimes hexagons) to store data. E.g., an image that stores data on elevation above seawater.



Code
# Vector Data
library('sf')
northcarolina_vector <- st_read(system.file('shape/nc.shp', package='sf'))
## Reading layer `nc' from data source `/home/jadamson/R-Libs/sf/shape/nc.shp' using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
## Simple feature collection with 100 features and 14 fields
## Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
## Dimension:     XY
## Bounding box:  xmin: -84.32385 ymin: 33.88199 xmax: -75.45698 ymax: 36.58965
## Geodetic CRS:  NAD27
plot(northcarolina_vector['BIR74'], main=NA)
title('Number of Live Births in 1974', font.main=1)









Code
# https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/articles/sids.html




Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Raster Data
library('terra')
luxembourg_elevation_raster <- rast(system.file('ex/elev.tif', package='terra'))
plot(luxembourg_elevation_raster)









The size and shape of the areal units used to aggregate spatial data are a choice, and results can depend on it (Gehlke and Biehl 1934; Openshaw 1984; Fotheringham and Wong 1991), including for econometric estimates (Briant et al. 2010). See Adamson (2022) for an econometric model of ethnic maps and the endogenous areal unit problem, where the same variables shape both the units and the outcomes. Earlier work in geography studied units that are grouped non-randomly, but not units that form endogenously (Holt et al. 1996).


Stationary
Just as with temporal data, stationarity in spatial data means that the statistical properties (like mean, variance, or spatial correlation) are roughly the same across space.

Stationary Means: \(\mathbb{E}[Y(s)]=\mathbb{E}[Y(s')]\) for all spatial locations \(s,s'\)
Stationary Vars: \(\mathbb{V}[Y(s)]=\mathbb{V}[Y(s')]\) for all spatial locations \(s,s'\)



Code
# Simulated 2D spatial fields
n <- 20
x <- y <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
grid <- expand.grid(x = x, y = y)

# 1. Stationary: Gaussian with constant mean and var
z_stationary <- matrix(rnorm(n^2, 0, 1), n, n)

# 2. Nonstationary: Mean increases with x and y
z_nonstationary <- outer(x, y, function(x, y) 3*x*y) + rnorm(n^2, 0, 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
# Stationary field
image(x, y, z_stationary,
      main = NA,
      col = terrain.colors(100),
      xlab = 'x', ylab = 'y')
title('Stationary Field', font.main = 1)
# Nonstationary field
image(x, y, z_nonstationary,
      main = NA,
      col = terrain.colors(100),
      xlab = 'x', ylab = 'y')
title('Nonstationary Field', font.main = 1)











Measures of spatial association
Just as temporal data can exhibit autocorrelation, so can spatial data. Nearby locations tend to be more (or less) similar than spatial independence would predict.






ImportantKey Definition





Moran’s I (Moran 1950) is an index of spatial autocorrelation ranging from \(-1\) to \(1\). Values near \(1\) indicate that nearby locations have similar values, \(-1\) that they have dissimilar values, and \(0\) that they are spatially independent.



Moran’s I is useful as the spatial analog of the ACF. It summarizes overall spatial dependence in one number. Large positive values signal that nearby observations share information, so we cannot treat them as independent. A two-variable analog measures spatial cross-correlation, computed like the CCF but with spatial rather than temporal lags.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Raster Data Example
autocor(luxembourg_elevation_raster, method='moran', global=TRUE)
## elevation 
## 0.8917057








TipTest Yourself





Moran’s I ranges from \(-1\) to \(1\). A value near \(1\) indicates strong positive spatial autocorrelation (nearby locations have similar values), near \(-1\) indicates negative spatial autocorrelation (nearby locations have dissimilar values), and near \(0\) indicates spatial independence. For elevation data, we expect strong positive autocorrelation because terrain changes gradually.



Cross-Correlation. We can also assess the relationship between two variables at varying distances.


Code
# Vector Data Example
xy_hat <- as.data.frame(northcarolina_vector)[, c('BIR74', 'SID74')]
column_means <- colMeans(xy_hat)

# Format Distances
dmat <- st_distance( st_centroid(northcarolina_vector) )
dmat <- units::set_units(dmat, 'km')

# At Which Distances to Compute CCF
# summary(dmat[, 1])
rdists <- c(-1, seq(0, 100, by=25)) # includes 0
rdists <- units::set_units(rdists , 'km')

# Compute Cross-Covariances
varXY <- prod( apply(xy_hat, 2, sd) )
CCF <- lapply( seq(2, length(rdists)), function(ri){
    # Which Observations are within (rmin, rmax] distance
    dmat_r <- dmat
    d_id <- (dmat_r > rdists[ri-1] & dmat_r <= rdists[ri]) 
    dmat_r[!d_id]  <- NA
    # Compute All Covariances (Stationary)
    covs_r <- lapply(1:nrow(dmat_r), function(i){
        pairsi <- which(!is.na(dmat_r[i, ]))        
        covXiYj <- sapply(pairsi, function(j) {
            dXi <- xy_hat[i, 1] - column_means[1]
            dYj <- xy_hat[j, 2] - column_means[2]
            return(dXi*dYj)
        })
        return(covXiYj)
    })
    corXY <- unlist(covs_r)/varXY
    return(corXY)
} )




Code
# Plot Cross-Covariance Function
x <- as.numeric(rdists[-1])

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))

# Distributional Summary
boxplot(CCF,
    outline=FALSE, whisklty=0, staplelty=0,
    ylim=c(-1, 1), #quantile(unlist(CCF), probs=c(.05, .95)),
    names=x,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Distance [km]',
    ylab='Cross-Correlation of BIR74 and SID74')
title('Binned Medians and IQRs', font.main=1, adj=0)
abline(h=0, col=grey(.5), lty=3)

# Inferential Summary
CCF_means <- sapply(CCF, mean)
plot(x, CCF_means,
    ylim=c(-1, 1),
    type='o', pch=16,
    main=NA,
    xlab='Distance [km]',
    ylab='Cross-Correlation of BIR74 and SID74')
title('Binned Means + 95% Confidence Band', font.main=1, adj=0)
abline(h=0, col=grey(.5), lty=3)
# Quick and Dirty Subsampling CI
CCF_meanCI <- sapply(CCF, function(corXY){
    ss_size <- floor(length(corXY)*3/4)
    corXY_boot <- sapply(1:200, function(b){
        corXY_b <- sample(corXY, ss_size, replace=FALSE)
        mean(corXY_b, na.rm=TRUE)
    })
    quantile(corXY_boot,  probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
})
polygon( c(x, rev(x)), 
    c(CCF_meanCI[1, ], rev(CCF_meanCI[2, ])), 
    col=grey(0, .25), border=NA)









Two variables can also be related locally, within a window around each location (Brunsdon et al. 2002; Adamson 2021, 2025). Neighbors’ values can also enter a regression directly: a spatially lagged X model regresses outcomes on each location’s own variables and the sum of its neighbors’ values (Anselin 1988; LeSage and Pace 2009; Halleck Vega and Elhorst 2015; Adamson 2025).
Spatial dependence also matters for standard errors (Conley 1999; Müller and Watson 2022; Conley and Kelly 2025). For example, Adamson (2025) uses a spatial subsampling procedure (Politis et al. 1999; Sherman 1996; Choi and Chue 2007) for strongly dependent data.

title: 26  Observational Data
text:
26.3 Economic Interdependence
In addition to spatial and temporal dependence, many observational datasets exhibit interdependence between variables for economic reasons.

Endogeneity
Economic outcomes are not free variables we can move at will. Many are jointly determined, affected by selection, or driven by variables we have not measured.






ImportantKey Definition





A regressor is endogenous if it is correlated with the error term in a regression. The three classic sources are

reverse causality: \(Y_{i} \to X_{i}\).
simultaneity: \(Y_{i} \to X_{i}\) and \(X_{i} \to Y_{i}\).
omitted variables: \(Z_{i}\to Y_{i}\) and either \(Z_{i}\to X_{i}\) or \(X_{i} \to Z_{i}\).




Endogeneity is a common reason that observational data are hard to interpret causally. In the linear model \(Y_{i}=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\beta_{k}X_{ik} + \epsilon_{i}\), endogeneity means \(\mathbb{E}[X_{ik}\epsilon_{i}] \neq 0\) for some \(k\). OLS is then biased away from the structural causal parameter.1






NoteMust Know





Consider the relationship between education and wages. Identify a potential source of (a) omitted variable bias, (b) reverse causality, and (c) measurement error. For each, explain the direction in which you expect the OLS estimate to be biased.





Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Simulate data with an endogeneity issue
n <- 300
z_sim <- rbinom(n, 1, .5)
xy_sim <- sapply(z_sim, function(zi){
    y_sim <- rnorm(1, zi, 1)
    x_sim <- rnorm(1, zi*2, 1)
    c(x_sim, y_sim)
})
xy_sim <- data.frame(x_sim=xy_sim[1, ], y_sim=xy_sim[2, ])
plot(y_sim ~ x_sim, data=xy_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA)
abline(lm(y_sim ~ x_sim, data=xy_sim), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









I will focus on the seminal economic example to provide some intuition.


Competitive Market Equilibrium
This model has three structural relationships. First, market supply is the sum of quantities supplied by individual firms at a given price. Second, market demand is the sum of quantities demanded by individual people at a given price. Third, market supply equals market demand in equilibrium. Assuming market supply and demand are linear, we can write these three relationships as \[\begin{aligned}
Q_{S}(P) &= \alpha_{S} + \beta_{S} P + E_{S}, \\
Q_{D}(P) &= \alpha_{D} - \beta_{D} P + E_{D}, \\
Q_{D} &= Q_{S} = Q.
%%  $Q_{D}(P) = \sum_{i} q_{D,i}(P)$,
\end{aligned}\]


Reduced Form
Neither variable is “exogenous” when the two are jointly determined in equilibrium, since we can only observe their joint outcomes.






ImportantKey Definition





The reduced form of a structural system writes each endogenous outcome (here \(P^{*}\) and \(Q^{*}\)) as a function of the exogenous variables (here the intercepts and shocks) only.



The reduced form is useful for seeing what observational data can identify. The reduced-form intercepts and shocks combine the structural parameters in known ways. Recovering the structural slopes \(\beta_{S}, \beta_{D}\) requires additional identifying variation. The equilibrium condition \(Q_{D} = Q_{S}\) in the structural equations above makes price and quantity jointly determined, so both are outcomes.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Demand Curve Simulator
qd_fun <- function(p, Ad=8, Bd=-.8, Ed_sigma=.25){
    Qd <- Ad + Bd*p + rnorm(1, 0, Ed_sigma)
    return(Qd)
}

# Supply Curve Simulator
qs_fun <- function(p, As=-8, Bs=1, Es_sigma=.25){
    Qs <- As + Bs*p + rnorm(1, 0, Es_sigma)
    return(Qs)
}

# Quantity Supplied and Demanded at 3 Prices
cbind(P=8:10, D=qd_fun(8:10), S=qs_fun(8:10))
##       P         D         S
## [1,]  8 1.8129598 0.1162905
## [2,]  9 1.0129598 1.1162905
## [3,] 10 0.2129598 2.1162905

# Market Equilibrium Finder
eq_fun <- function(demand, supply, P){
    # Compute EQ (what we observe)
    eq_id <- which.min( abs(demand-supply) )
    eq <- c(P=P[eq_id], Q=demand[eq_id]) 
    return(eq)
}




Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Simulations Parameters
N <- 300 # Number of Market Interactions
P <- seq(5, 10, by=.01) # Price Range to Consider

# Generate Data from Competitive Market  
# Plot Underlying Process
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim=c(0, 2), ylim=range(P))
EQ1 <- sapply(1:N, function(n){
    # Market Data Generating Process
    demand <- qd_fun(P)
    supply <- qs_fun(P)
    eq <- eq_fun(demand, supply, P)    
    # Plot Theoretical Supply and Demand
    lines(demand, P, col=grey(0, .01))
    lines(supply, P, col=grey(0, .01))
    points(eq[2], eq[1], col=grey(0, .05), pch=16)
    # Save Data
    return(eq)
})
axis(1)
axis(2)
mtext('Quantity', 1, line=2)
mtext('Price', 2, line=2)









Suppose we ask “what is the effect of price on quantity?” You can simply run a regression of quantity, \(\hat{y}\), on price, \(\hat{x}\), and get the slope coefficient \(\hat{b}_{1} = \hat{c}_{Q^{*} P^{*}} / \hat{v}_{P^{*}}\). You always get a number back, but it is hard to interpret meaningfully.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Analyze Market Data
xy1_sim <- data.frame(t(EQ1), cost='1', T=1:N)
reg1 <- lm(Q ~ P, data=xy1_sim)
summary(reg1)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Q ~ P, data = xy1_sim)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.47571 -0.12130 -0.00619  0.11426  0.48781 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept)  0.48931    0.43247   1.131    0.259
## P            0.04315    0.04867   0.887    0.376
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1715 on 298 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.002631,   Adjusted R-squared:  -0.0007155 
## F-statistic: 0.7862 on 1 and 298 DF,  p-value: 0.376


This simple example has a profound insight: price-quantity data does not generally tell you how price affects quantity (or vice-versa). The reason is simultaneity: price and quantity mutually cause one another in markets.2
Moreover, this example also clarifies that our initial question “what is the effect of price on quantity?” is misguided. We could more sensibly ask “what is the effect of price on quantity supplied?” or “what is the effect of price on quantity demanded?”


Contamination
With multiple linear regression, endogeneity biases are not just a problem for your main variable of interest. Suppose you are interested in how \(X_{i1}\) affects \(Y_{i}\), conditioning on \(X_{i2}\), and that the data generating process is linear: \(Y_{i}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}X_{i1}+\beta_{2}X_{i2}+\epsilon_{i}\). You paid special attention in your research design to find a case where \(X_{i1}\) is truly exogenous. Unfortunately, if \(X_{i2}\) is correlated with the error term, then there is also a bias for \(X_{i1}\). The magnitude of the bias for \(X_{i1}\) depends on the correlations between \(X_{i1}\) and \(X_{i2}\) as well as \(X_{i2}\) and \(\epsilon_{i}\).3

title: 26  Observational Data
text:
26.4 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain why simultaneity in a competitive market makes it difficult to interpret the OLS slope \(\hat{b}_{1}\) from a regression of quantity on price. In your answer, distinguish between the structural demand slope \(\beta_{D}\) and what OLS actually estimates.
Using the North Carolina births data (sf::st_read(system.file('shape/nc.shp', package='sf'))), compute Moran’s I for the variable SID74 (sudden infant deaths in 1974). Is there evidence of spatial autocorrelation? Briefly explain what a high value of Moran’s I would imply for standard OLS inference.
Simulate a random walk of length 200 in R (starting at 0, with increments drawn from runif(1, -1, 1)). Plot the series, compute the ACF using acf(), and describe how the ACF pattern differs from what you would expect for white noise.


Further Reading

Recall
This chapter introduced temporal, spatial, and economic dependence in observational data. It measured temporal dependence with the ACF and CCF, and spatial dependence with Moran’s I. For economic dependence, it listed the sources of endogeneity. The supply-demand simulation made the endogeneity bite concrete: we ran 300 market periods through qd_fun/qs_fun, fit lm(Q ~ P, data=xy1_sim), and got a slope that confuses the supply and demand sides because price and quantity are jointly determined.

title: 26  Observational Data
27  Experimental Data
text:
27.1 Design Basics
The previous chapter showed how observational data complicate causal inference. Experiments combine control, where the researcher fixes other factors, and randomization, where the researcher manipulates one factor independently of the others.
This chapter asks two questions.

title: 27  Experimental Data
text:
Control and Randomize
What separates an experiment from an observation is the researcher’s ability to set the value of one variable and hold the others fixed.






ImportantKey Definition





Control is the researcher’s ability to hold other factors constant; randomization is the assignment of treatment in a way that is statistically independent of every pre-treatment variable.



Together control and randomization are useful because they break the correlation between a regressor and the error term that produces endogeneity in observational data. They are the only fully reliable way to estimate causal effects. You manipulate one explanatory variable while ensuring no other factors change with it, so the manipulated variable is not systematically associated with anything else (Fisher 1935).
To be concrete, we will continue with our supply and demand example from the last chapter, and this time introduce a cost shock.


Competitive Equilibrium Example


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Demand Curve Simulator
qd_fun <- function(p, Ad=8, Bd=-.8, Ed_sigma=.25){
    Qd <- Ad + Bd*p + rnorm(1, 0, Ed_sigma)
    return(Qd)
}

# Supply Curve Simulator
qs_fun <- function(p, As=-8, Bs=1, Es_sigma=.25){
    Qs <- As + Bs*p + rnorm(1, 0, Es_sigma)
    return(Qs)
}

# Quantity Supplied and Demanded at 3 Prices
cbind(P=8:10, D=qd_fun(8:10), S=qs_fun(8:10))
##       P          D          S
## [1,]  8  1.4433865 0.04591083
## [2,]  9  0.6433865 1.04591083
## [3,] 10 -0.1566135 2.04591083

# Market Equilibrium Finder
eq_fun <- function(demand, supply, P){
    # Compute EQ (what we observe)
    eq_id <- which.min( abs(demand-supply) )
    eq <- c(P=P[eq_id], Q=demand[eq_id]) 
    return(eq)
}




Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
N <- 300 # Number of Market Interactions
P <- seq(5, 10, by=.01) # Price Range to Consider
EQ1 <- sapply(1:N, function(n){
    # Market Data Generating Process
    demand <- qd_fun(P)
    supply <- qs_fun(P)
    eq <- eq_fun(demand, supply, P)    
    return(eq)
})
xy1_sim <- data.frame(t(EQ1), cost='1', T=1:N)


If you have exogenous variation on one side of the market, you can get information on the other. For example, lower costs shift out supply (more is produced at given price), allowing you to trace out part of a demand curve.
To see this, consider an experiment where student subjects are recruited to a classroom and randomly assigned to be either buyers or sellers in a market for little red balls. In this case, the classroom environment allows the experimenter to control for various factors (e.g., the temperature of the room is constant for all subjects). The explicit randomization of subjects means that there are not typically systematic differences in different groups of students.
In the experiment, sellers are given linear “cost functions” that theoretically yield individual supplies like the supply equation from the previous chapter and are paid “price - cost”. Buyers are given linear “benefit functions” that theoretically yield individual demands like the demand equation from the previous chapter, and are paid “benefit - price”. The theoretical predictions are therefore given by the equilibrium of the supply and demand equations from the previous chapter. Moreover, experimental manipulation of \(\alpha_{S}\) leads to \[\begin{aligned}
\frac{d P^{*}}{d \alpha_{S}} &= \frac{-1}{\beta_{D}+\beta_{S}}, \\
\frac{d Q^{*}}{d \alpha_{S}} &= \frac{\beta_{D}}{\beta_{D}+\beta_{S}}.
\end{aligned}\] In this case, the supply shock has identified the demand slope: \(-\beta_{D}=d Q^{*}/d P^{*}\).






TipTest Yourself





With the parameters in the simulation (\(\beta_{D} = 0.8\), \(\beta_{S} = 1\)), the comparative statics predict \(dP^*/d\alpha_{S} = -1/(0.8+1) = -5/9 \approx -0.56\) and \(dQ^*/d\alpha_{S} = 0.8/1.8 = 4/9 \approx 0.44\). Shifting \(\alpha_{S}\) from \(-8\) to \(-6.5\) (a change of \(3/2\)) predicts a price decrease of \(3/2 \times 5/9 = 5/6 \approx 0.83\) and a quantity increase of \(3/2 \times 4/9 = 2/3 \approx 0.67\).





Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# New Observations After Cost Change
EQ2 <- sapply(1:N, function(n){
    demand <- qd_fun(P)
    supply2 <- qs_fun(P, As=-6.5) # More Supplied at Given Price
    eq <- eq_fun(demand, supply2, P)
    return(eq)
    # lines(supply2, P, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .01))
    #points(eq[2], eq[1], col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .05), pch=16)
})
xy2_sim <- data.frame(t(EQ2), cost='2', T=(1:N) + N)
xy2_sim <- rbind(xy1_sim, xy2_sim)

# Plot Simulated Market Data
cols <- ifelse(as.numeric(xy2_sim$cost)==2, rgb(0, 0, 1, .2), rgb(0, 0, 0, .2))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim=c(0, 2), ylim=range(P))
points(xy2_sim$Q, xy2_sim$P, col=cols, pch=16)
axis(1)
axis(2)
mtext('Quantity', 1, line=2)
mtext('Price', 2, line=2)









If the function forms for supply and demand are different from what we predicted, we can still measure how much the experimental manipulation of production costs affects the equilibrium quantity sold (and compare that to what was predicted).1

title: 27  Experimental Data
text:
27.2 Comparisons Over Time

Regression Discontinuities/Kinks
When a treatment switches on at a known cutoff in a running variable, observations just above and just below the threshold should look identical except for the treatment.






ImportantKey Definition





A regression discontinuity design (RDD) exploits a sharp change in treatment at a known cutoff in a running variable. The treatment effect is estimated as the jump in the outcome at the cutoff. A regression kink design (RKD) exploits a change in slope rather than in level.



RDD/RKD is useful when a policy rule or natural threshold supplies a sharp source of exogenous variation that we can verify graphically and exploit econometrically (see The Effect, Ch. Regression Discontinuity for a thorough introduction). In our canonical competitive market example, the RDD estimate is the difference between the lines at \(T=300\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Locally Linear Regression 
# (Compare means near break)

cols <- ifelse(as.numeric(xy2_sim$cost)==2, rgb(0, 0, 1, .5), rgb(0, 0, 0, .5))
plot(P ~ T, xy2_sim, main=NA, pch=16, col=cols)
title('Effect of Cost Shock on Price', font.main=1)
regP1 <- loess(P ~ T, xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==1, ])
x1_sim <- regP1$x
#lm(): x1_sim <- regP1$model$T
lines(x1_sim, predict(regP1), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
regP2 <- loess(P ~ T, xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==2, ])
x2_sim <- regP2$x #regP1$model$T
lines(x2_sim, predict(regP2), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)









Code

plot(Q ~ T, xy2_sim, main=NA, pch=16, col=cols)
title('Effect of Cost Shock on Quantity', font.main=1)
regQ1 <- loess(Q ~ T, xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==1, ])
lines(x1_sim, predict(regQ1), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
regQ2 <- loess(Q ~ T, xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==2, ])
lines(x2_sim, predict(regQ2), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)

# Keep 50 periods on each side of the break at T=300
sub_id <- (xy2_sim$cost==1 & xy2_sim$T > 250) | (xy2_sim$cost==2 & xy2_sim$T <= 350)
xy2_win_sim <- xy2_sim[sub_id,  ]
# Centering T at the break makes the cost2 coefficient the jump at T=300

Remember that this effect is local: different magnitudes of the cost shock or different demand curves generally yield different estimates.






NoteMust Know





The RDD estimate measures the effect at the discontinuity. Why might the effect differ for observations far from the cutoff? Give an economic example where a treatment effect varies with distance from the threshold.



Moreover, note that more than just costs have changed over time: subjects in the later periods have experience behind them while they do not in earlier periods. So hidden variables like “beliefs” are implicitly treated as well. This is one concrete reason to have an explicit control group. Another remedy is a crossover design, where some sessions switch from one treatment to another halfway through and other sessions switch in the opposite order. This allows comparisons across sessions as well as within them (Jones and Kenward 2014).


Difference in Differences
A pre/post comparison on the treated group alone confounds the treatment with anything else changing over time. We need a parallel comparison group to net it out.






ImportantKey Definition





Difference-in-differences (DID) compares the pre/post change in the outcome for a treated group to the pre/post change for a control group. The estimator is the interaction coefficient Post × Treated in a regression and relies on the parallel trends assumption: absent treatment, both groups would have followed the same trajectory.



DID is useful when a treatment hits one group but not another and we observe both before and after: the control group’s pre/post change estimates the counterfactual trend, and the treatment effect is what is left after subtracting it (see The Effect, Ch. Difference-in-Differences for more detail).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
EQ3 <- sapply(1:(2*N), function(n){

    # Market Mechanisms
    demand <- qd_fun(P)
    supply <- qs_fun(P)

    # Compute EQ (what we observe)
    eq_id <- which.min( abs(demand-supply) )
    eq <- c(P=P[eq_id], Q=demand[eq_id]) 

    # Return Equilibrium Observations
    return(eq)
})
xy3_sim <- data.frame(t(EQ3), cost='1', T=1:ncol(EQ3))
xy3_pre_sim  <- xy3_sim[xy3_sim$T <= N , ]
xy3_post_sim <- xy3_sim[xy3_sim$T > N , ]

# Plot Price Data
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(P ~ T, xy2_sim, main=NA, pch=16, col=cols, cex=.5)
title('Effect of Cost Shock on Price', font.main=1)
lines(x1_sim, predict(regP1), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
lines(x2_sim, predict(regP2), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
# W/ Control group
points(P ~ T, xy3_sim, pch=16, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .5), cex=.5)
regP3a <- loess(P ~ T, xy3_pre_sim)
x3a_sim <- regP3a$x
lines(x3a_sim, predict(regP3a), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
regP3b <- loess(P ~ T, xy3_post_sim)
x3b_sim <- regP3b$x
lines(x3b_sim, predict(regP3b), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)


# Plot Quantity Data
plot(Q ~ T, xy2_sim, main=NA, pch=17, col=cols, cex=.5)
title('Effect of Cost Shock on Quantity', font.main=1)

# W/ Control group
points(Q ~ T, xy3_sim, pch=16, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .5), cex=.5)

xy_pooled_sim <- rbind(

The DID estimate relies on the parallel trends assumption: absent treatment, the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trajectory. Look at the pre-treatment period in the plots above. Do the treated (black) and control (red) series appear to have parallel trends? What would violate this assumption?









TipTest Yourself: reading the DID table





The stargazer output for the DID model P ~ PostPeriod * EverTreated has four rows.

The intercept is the mean of \(P\) for the control group in the pre period.
PostPeriodTRUE is the change between pre and post in the control group.
EverTreated1 is the pre-period difference between treated and control.
PostPeriodTRUE:EverTreated1 is the DID estimate: the extra change in the treated group above the control trend. This is the coefficient to interpret as the treatment effect.

A statistically significant interaction term whose sign matches what theory predicts is the headline DID result. In the RDD table, cost2 is the jump at the discontinuity, and the I(T - 300):cost2 interaction captures the change in slope there.





Blocking and Clustering
When experimental units differ on a variable that also predicts the outcome, a fully random assignment can leave treatment and control unbalanced by chance.






ImportantKey Definition





Blocking partitions experimental units into homogeneous groups before randomly assigning treatment within each group.



Blocking is useful when the blocking variable predicts the outcome. Treatment and control groups then always have the same mix of the blocking variable. This removes one source of variation between the two groups, so the estimated treatment effect is more precise. A fully random (“completely randomized”) design works when units are homogeneous but does not protect against accidental imbalance otherwise.
Continuing with supply and demand example, we might manipulate costs (randomize high or low treatments) for companies in different industries (computer services, lumber harvesting). With a completely randomized design, industry composition can differ between treatment and control purely by chance; blocking by industry removes that source of imbalance.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Contrast completely randomized vs blocked assignment
industry <- rep(c('Computer', 'Lumber'), each=20)
n <- length(industry)

# Completely randomized: assign half to treatment, ignore industry
crd <- sample(rep(c('Treat','Control'), each=n/2))
table(industry, crd)
##           crd
## industry   Control Treat
##   Computer      11     9
##   Lumber         9    11

# Blocked: assign half within each industry
blocked <- character(n)
for(g in unique(industry)){
    idx <- which(industry == g)
    blocked[idx] <- sample(rep(c('Treat','Control'), each=length(idx)/2))
}
table(industry, blocked)
##           blocked
## industry   Control Treat
##   Computer      10    10
##   Lumber        10    10
# Every seed gives 10-10 in each industry.


Notice that the blocked design always returns an even split in each industry, whereas the completely randomized design can drift away from that balance from one realization to the next.
A within-subject design takes blocking to its limit, with each subject as its own block (Fisher 1935). Standard errors can then be clustered by session or by matched pair, using a cluster bootstrap or jackknife (Cameron et al. 2008; Cameron and Miller 2015; MacKinnon et al. 2023a, 2023b; Hansen 2026).

title: 27  Experimental Data
text:
27.3 Quasi Experiments
Quasi or natural experiments are historical case studies that have the second distinguishing feature of experiments (randomization) but not the first (control). This helps remedy the endogeneity issues in observational data. “Instrumental Variables”, “RDD”, “DID” methods discussed above are used in historical event studies. The elementary versions use linear regression, so I can cover them here using our competitive equilibrium example from before.

Two Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
When the regressor we care about is correlated with the error term, OLS is biased. A different variable that affects the outcome only through the endogenous regressor can still recover its causal effect.






ImportantKey Definition





Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) uses an instrumental variable (here, the cost shock) to recover the causal effect of an endogenous regressor on an outcome. The instrument must (i) be relevant, meaning it is correlated with the endogenous regressor, and (ii) satisfy the exclusion restriction, meaning it affects the outcome only through that regressor.



2SLS is useful when controlled experimentation is impossible but a natural source of exogenous variation in the endogenous regressor is available. For example, the cost shock supplies exogenous variation in price that lets us trace out the demand curve (see The Effect, Ch. Instrumental Variables for a broader treatment). Just running a second OLS regression on the pooled data would still be biased, as we will see below.


Code
# Not exactly right, but at least right sign
reg2 <- lm(Q ~ P, data=xy2_sim)
summary(reg2)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Q ~ P, data = xy2_sim)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.67144 -0.16935 -0.00056  0.17766  0.76115 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  6.43128    0.18773   34.26   <2e-16 ***
## P           -0.61555    0.02213  -27.82   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.2467 on 598 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5641, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5634 
## F-statistic: 773.8 on 1 and 598 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


It turns out that the noisiness of the process within each group affects our OLS estimate: \(\hat{b}=\hat{c}_{Q^{*}P^{*}} / \hat{v}_{P^{*}}\).






TipTest Yourself





You can experiment with the effect of different within-group variances on both OLS and IV in the code below. And note that if we had multiple supply shifts and recorded their magnitudes, then we could recover more information about demand, perhaps tracing it out entirely.


Code
library('fixest')

# Examine
Egrid <- expand.grid(Ed_sigma=c(.001, .25, 1), Es_sigma=c(.001, .25, 1))

Egrid_regs <- lapply(1:nrow(Egrid), function(i){
    Ed_sigma <- Egrid[i, 1]
    Es_sigma <- Egrid[i, 2]
    EQ1 <- sapply(1:N, function(n){
        demand <- qd_fun(P, Ed_sigma=Ed_sigma)
        supply <- qs_fun(P, Es_sigma=Es_sigma)
        return(eq_fun(demand, supply, P))
    })
    EQ2 <- sapply(1:N, function(n){
        demand <- qd_fun(P, Ed_sigma=Ed_sigma)
        supply2 <- qs_fun(P, As=-6.5, Es_sigma=Es_sigma)
        return(eq_fun(demand, supply2, P))
    })
    xy_sim_b <- rbind(
        data.frame(t(EQ1), cost='1'),
        data.frame(t(EQ2), cost='2'))
    return(xy_sim_b)
})
Egrid_OLS <- sapply(Egrid_regs, function(xy_sim_b) coef( lm(Q ~ P, data=xy_sim_b)))
Egrid_IV <- sapply(Egrid_regs, function(xy_sim_b) coef( feols(Q ~ 1|P ~ cost, data=xy_sim_b)))

#cbind(Egrid, coef_OLS=t(Egrid_OLS)[, 2], coef_IV=t(Egrid_IV)[, 2])
lapply( list(Egrid_OLS, Egrid_IV), function(ei){
    Emat <- matrix(ei[2, ], 3, 3)
    rownames(Emat) <- paste0('Ed_sigma.', c(.001, .25, 1))
    colnames(Emat) <- paste0('Es_sigma.', c(.001, .25, 1))
    return( round(Emat, 2))
})

To overcome this issue, we can compute the change in the expected values \(d \mathbb{E}[Q^{*}] / d \mathbb{E}[P^{*}] =-\beta_{D}\). Empirically, this is estimated via the change in average value.


Code
# Wald (1940) Estimate
xy_mean_sim <- rbind(
    colMeans(xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==1, 1:2]),
    colMeans(xy2_sim[xy2_sim$cost==2, 1:2]))
xy_mean_sim
##             P         Q
## [1,] 8.878567 0.8914761
## [2,] 8.064500 1.5417645
b_est <- diff(xy_mean_sim[, 2])/diff(xy_mean_sim[, 1])
round(b_est, 2)
## [1] -0.8


We can also separately recover \(d \mathbb{E}[Q^{*}] / d \mathbb{E}[\alpha_{S}]\) and \(d \mathbb{E}[P^{*}] / d \mathbb{E}[\alpha_{S}]\) from separate regressions.2


Code
# Heckman (2000, p.58) Estimate
ols_1 <- lm(P ~ cost, data=xy2_sim)
ols_2 <- lm(Q ~ cost, data=xy2_sim)
b_est2 <- coef(ols_2)/coef(ols_1)
round(b_est2[[2]], 2)
## [1] -0.8


Alternatively, we can recover the same estimate using a 2SLS regression with two equations: \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{p} &= b_{0p} + b_{1p} \alpha_{S} + \hat{e}_{p} \\
\hat{q} &= b_{0q} + b_{1q} \hat{p}^{\mathrm{fit}}  + \hat{e}_{q}.
\end{aligned}\] where \(\hat{p}^{\mathrm{fit}}\), the predicted value of \(\hat{p}\) from the first equation, is used to explain quantity in the second equation. In the first regression, we estimate how the cost shock affects prices, \(\hat{b}_{1p}\), and then predict prices \(\hat{p}^{\mathrm{fit}}\). In the second equation, we estimate the average effect of predicted prices (which are exogenous to demand) on quantity demanded.
To understand this theoretically, first substitute the equilibrium condition into the supply equation, \(Q_{D}=Q_{S}=\alpha_{S}+ \beta_{S} P + E_{S}\), which lets us rewrite \(P\) as a function of \(Q_{D}\). This yields two theoretical equations. We are using the cost shock to understand the theoretical demand curve. \[\begin{aligned}
P &= -\frac{\alpha_{S}}{{\beta_{S}}} + \frac{Q_{D}}{\beta_{S}} - \frac{E_{S}}{\beta_{S}} \\
Q_{D} &= \alpha_{D} - \beta_{D} P + E_{D}.
\end{aligned}\]


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Two Stage Least Squares Estimate
ols_1 <- lm(P ~ cost, data=xy2_sim)
xy2_new_sim  <- cbind(xy2_sim, p_fit=predict(ols_1))
reg_2sls <- lm(Q ~ p_fit, data=xy2_new_sim)
summary(reg_2sls)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Q ~ p_fit, data = xy2_new_sim)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -0.57706 -0.12815  0.00387  0.11967  0.59216 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  7.98381    0.15581   51.24   <2e-16 ***
## p_fit       -0.79881    0.01837  -43.48   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.1832 on 598 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.7597, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7593 
## F-statistic:  1891 on 1 and 598 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

# One Stage Instrumental Variables Estimate
library('fixest')
reg2_iv <- feols(Q ~ 1|P ~ cost, data=xy2_sim)
summary(reg2_iv)
## TSLS estimation: Second stage
## |- D.V.   : Q
## |- Endo.  : P
## |- Instr. : cost
## Dep. Var.: Q
## Observations: 600
## Standard-errors: IID 
##              Estimate Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  7.983806   0.221571  36.0327 < 2.2e-16 ***
## fit_P       -0.798815   0.026125 -30.5771 < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## RMSE: 0.260034   Adj. R2: 0.759305
## F-test (1st stage), P: stat = 2,387.65, p < 2.2e-16, on 1 and 598 DoF.
##            Wu-Hausman: stat =   504.45, p < 2.2e-16, on 1 and 597 DoF.


The Wald (Wald 1940), Heckman (Heckman 2000, 58), and 2SLS slopes are algebraically identical in this just-identified linear model: each one recovers \(-\beta_{D}\) by using the cost shock as the source of exogenous variation in price.






TipTest Yourself





The 2SLS procedure works in two steps. First, regress the endogenous variable (price) on the instrument (cost): this isolates the part of price variation driven by supply shifts. Second, regress quantity on the predicted prices from step 1. Because predicted prices reflect only supply-side variation, the second-stage coefficient estimates the demand slope. The key requirement is that cost shifts affect quantity only through price (the exclusion restriction).





Caveats
2SLS regression analysis can be very insightful, but I also want to stress some caveats about their practical application. Most of these stem directly from the absence of control that true experiments have.

Instrument exogeneity (Exclusion Restriction): The instrument must affect outcomes only through the treatment variable (e.g., only supply is affected directly, not demand).
Instrument relevance: The instrument must be strongly correlated with the endogenous regressor, implying the shock creates meaningful variation.
Functional form correctness: Supply and demand are assumed linear and additively separable.
Multiple hypothesis testing risks: We were not repeatedly testing different instruments, which can artificially produce significant findings by chance.
Exclusion restriction violations: Spatial or temporal spillovers may cause instruments to affect the outcome through unintended channels, undermining instrument exogeneity.
Weak instruments: Spatial clustering, serial correlation, or network interdependencies can reduce instrument variation, causing weak instruments.
Inference and standard errors: Spatial or temporal interdependence reduces the effective sample size, making conventional standard errors misleadingly small.

For example, Adamson and Stephenson (2026) note that geographic instruments for war plausibly affect productivity directly, which would violate the exclusion restriction (Angrist et al. 1996; Deaton 2010; Conley et al. 2012; Mellon 2025).
We always get coefficients back when running feols, and sometimes the computed p-values are very small. The interpretation of those numbers rests on many assumptions, and we are rarely sure that all of these assumptions hold. Researchers often also report their OLS results, but that is insufficient. A nonparametric estimator (e.g. loess) at each stage can help diagnose departures from linearity; other packages such as ivreg::ivreg provide alternative IV implementations.

27.4 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
In the competitive market simulation, a supply cost shock is used to identify the demand slope via 2SLS. Explain why simply regressing \(Q\) on \(P\) with both cost regimes pooled does not recover the demand slope \(-\beta_{D}\), and what role the exclusion restriction plays in the 2SLS approach.

Compare this to the 2SLS estimate from fixest::feols(Q ~ 1 | P ~ cost, data = xy2_sim). Are they the same? Why or why not?
Simulate a difference-in-differences setup in R. Generate two groups of 100 observations each over 200 time periods, where one group receives a treatment (a level shift of +2) at \(T = 100\). Estimate the DID coefficient using lm(y_sim ~ PostPeriod * EverTreated, data = xy_sim) and verify that it recovers the treatment effect.


Further Reading
The following resources discuss causal inference methods (IV, RDD, DID) in more detail.

Recall
This chapter introduced the experimental and quasi-experimental tools for recovering causal effects from data with limited control: RDD, DID, blocking, and 2SLS. The cost-shock experiment shifted \(\alpha_{S}\) from \(-8\) to \(-6.5\) in qs_fun. The Wald, Heckman, and 2SLS (feols(Q ~ 1 | P ~ cost, data=xy2_sim)) estimates of \(-\beta_{D}\) are algebraically identical. They recover the demand slope that pooled OLS confused.

Notice that even in this linear model, however, all effects are conditional: The effect of a cost change on quantity or price depends on the demand curve. A change in costs affects quantity supplied but not quantity demanded (which then affects equilibrium price) but the demand side of the market still matters! The change in price from a change in costs depends on the elasticity of demand.↩︎
Mathematically, we can also do this in a single step by exploiting linear algebra: \(\frac{\frac{ \mathbb{C}[Q^{*},\alpha_{S}]}{ \mathbb{V}[\alpha_{S}] } }{\frac{ \mathbb{C}[P^{*},\alpha_{S}]}{ \mathbb{V}[\alpha_{S}] }} = \frac{\mathbb{C}[Q^{*},\alpha_{S}]}{ \mathbb{C}[P^{*},\alpha_{S}]}.\)↩︎

title: 28  Data Scientism
text:
28.1 False Discoveries
In practice, it is hard to find a good natural experiment and easy to find a bad one. Paradoxically, natural experiments are something you are supposed to find but never search for. As you search for natural experiments, sometimes patterns will appear from random noise. In this age of big data, we are getting increasingly more data and, perhaps surprisingly, this makes it easier to make false discoveries.
This chapter asks two questions.
Although it is difficult to express numerically, searching for a good natural experiment can also lead you astray from important questions. Convenient measures can mislead as well (Campbell 1979). For example, Adamson and Rentschler (2025) show that the clearance rate, a police performance measure widely used in econometric studies, can suggest performance is better when it is unambiguously worse. There are good reasons to be excited about empirical social science, but we would be wise to recall some earlier wisdom from economists on the matter.

title: 28  Data Scientism
text:
False Discovery
Modern research generates so many statistical tests that some “significant” findings appear by chance alone, even when no real effect exists.






ImportantKey Definition





A false discovery is a statistically significant result that does not reflect a true effect in the population.



False discoveries are useful to track because classical hypothesis tests claim to control how often they happen. A 5% test promises a 5% false-positive rate on null data. Searching, dependence, and sloppy data can all push the actual rate above the stated 5%. The three engines surveyed below (data errors, \(p\)-hacking, and spurious regression) all generate false discoveries without anyone behaving fraudulently. The reverse mistake reads an insignificant result as evidence of no effect, ignoring the chance of a Type II error (Altman and Bland 1995; Abadie 2020).


Data Errors
A huge amount of data normally means a huge amount of data cleaning/merging/aggregating. This avoids many copy-paste errors, which are a recipe for disaster, but may also introduce other types of errors. Some spurious results are driven by honest errors in data cleaning. According to one estimate, this is responsible for around one fifth of all medical science retractions (there is even a whole book about this!). Although there are not similar meta-analysis in economics, there are some high-profile examples. This includes papers that are highly influential, like Lott, Levitt and Reinhart and Rogoff as well as others the top economics journals, like the RESTUD and AER. There are some reasons to think such errors are more widespread across the social sciences; e.g., in Census data and Aid data. So be careful!
Note: one reason to plot your data is to help spot such errors. Data errors are only one route to a spurious finding. The next one is searching the same dataset for any specification that “works”.


P-Hacking
Once you can run dozens of regressions in a single afternoon, the search for “significance” itself becomes a route to false discoveries that no single \(p\)-value can warn you about.






ImportantKey Definition





P-hacking is trying many models, transformations, or subsamples and then reporting a \(p\)-value that does not account for those searches. Such a \(p\)-value no longer reflects the true probability of seeing the result under the null.



P-hacking is useful to recognize because it can occur without any fraudulent intent: trying different variable transformations or sample windows to uncover patterns is itself a form of search. Its various synonyms (data dredging, star mining) name the same behavior across different disciplines. The practice is both pernicious and widespread, and applies equally to OLS and to more sophisticated tools like 2SLS, as the next two code blocks illustrate.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# P-hacking OLS with different explanatory vars
set.seed(123)
n <- 50
x1_sim <- runif(n)

# Regression Machine:
# repeatedly finds covariate, runs regression
# stops when statistically significant at .1%
p <- 1
i <- 0
while(p >= .001){ 
    # Get Random Covariate
    x2_sim_b <-  runif(n)
    # Merge and 'Analyze'
    xy_sim_b <- data.frame(x1_sim, x2_sim_b)
    reg_i <- lm(x1_sim ~ x2_sim_b, data=xy_sim_b)
    # update results in global environment
    p <- summary(reg_i)$coefficients[2, 4]
    i <- i+1
}
#summary(reg_i)

plot(x1_sim ~ x2_sim_b, data=xy_sim_b,
    pch=16, col=grey(0, .5), main=NA)
title(paste0('Random Dataset ', i, ':   p=',
    formatC(p, digits=2, format='fg')), font.main=1)
abline(reg_i, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)















TipTest Yourself





The loop ran through i random datasets before finding one with \(p < 0.001\). With truly random data, each regression has a \(0.1\%\) chance of producing \(p < 0.001\). After \(k\) independent tests, the probability of at least one false discovery is \(1-(1-\alpha)^k\). The probability climbs fast in \(k\):


Code
alpha <- 0.001
k <- c(1, 10, 100, 700, 5000)
round(1 - (1 - alpha)^k, 3)
## [1] 0.001 0.010 0.095 0.504 0.993


So at \(k=700\) tries the chance of at least one false discovery exceeds 50%, and by \(k=5000\) it is essentially 1. The more you search, the more likely you are to find a spurious result.





Code
# P-hacking 2SLS with different explanatory vars
# and different instrumental vars
library('fixest')
# No new seed: resetting to 123 would make the first x2_sim_b an exact copy of x1_sim
p <- 1
ii <- 0
while(p >= .05){
    # Get Random Covariates
    x2_sim_b <-  runif(n)
    x3_sim_b <-  runif(n)
    # Create Treatment Variable based on Cutoff
    cutoffs <- seq(0, 1, length.out=11)[-c(1, 11)]
    for(tau in cutoffs){
        T3 <- 1*(x3_sim_b > tau)
        # Merge and 'Analyze'
        xy_sim_b <- data.frame(x1_sim, x2_sim_b, T3)
        ivreg_i <- feols(x1_sim ~ 1|x2_sim_b ~ T3, data=xy_sim_b)
        # Update results in global environment
        ptab <- summary(ivreg_i)$coeftable
        if( nrow(ptab)==2){
            p <- ptab[2, 4]
            ii <- ii+1
        }
        # Stop at the first cutoff that reaches significance
        if(p < .05){ break }
    }
}
summary(ivreg_i)
## TSLS estimation: Second stage
## |- D.V.   : x1_sim
## |- Endo.  : x2_sim_b
## |- Instr. : T3
## Dep. Var.: x1_sim
## Observations: 50
## Standard-errors: IID 
##              Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  0.153326   0.186421 0.822473 0.414875    
## fit_x2_sim_b 0.792858   0.389610 2.035003 0.047393 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## RMSE: 0.330118   Adj. R2: 0.092253
## F-test (1st stage), x2_sim_b: stat = 8.4898, p = 0.005409, on 1 and 48 DoF.
##                   Wu-Hausman: stat = 3.3875, p = 0.072012, on 1 and 47 DoF.








NoteMust Know





The p-hacking example found a statistically significant IV result using random data. What safeguards could a researcher adopt to avoid this problem? Consider: (a) pre-registration of hypotheses, (b) adjusting for multiple testing, and (c) out-of-sample validation.

title: 28  Data Scientism
text:
28.2 Spurious Regression
Even without any coding errors or p-hacking, you can sometimes make a false discovery. We begin with a motivating empirical example of “US Gov’t Spending on Science”.

Trending Series
When two variables both drift upward over time, OLS can flag them as related even when nothing connects them.






ImportantKey Definition





Spurious regression arises when two unrelated time series share a common trend and so produce a large \(\hat{R}^2\) and a small \(p\)-value when one is regressed on the other.



Spurious regression is useful to know about because the resulting significance is not a property of any underlying relationship. It grows with the sample length, so longer time series make the problem worse rather than better. The problem is that trending series violate the OLS independence assumption. The standard errors assume independent observations. But trending series share so much information across periods that the effective sample size is far smaller than \(n\).
First, get and inspect some data.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Your data is not made up in the computer (hopefully!)
# Original source: https://tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations
vigen_csv <- read.csv(

)

TipTest Yourself





When two time series share a common trend, their correlation can be very high even if they are completely unrelated. This is why regression with trending time series requires special care (e.g., detrending or differencing).





Another Example
Now regress one of these series on another.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Drop Data before 1999
vigen_csv <- vigen_csv[vigen_csv$year >= 1999, ]

# Run OLS Regression of Cage's film count on science spending.
# The p-value on `science_spending` will be tiny, despite zero plausible causal link.
reg1 <-  lm(cage_films ~ -1 + science_spending, data=vigen_csv)
summary(reg1)

Next, plot science spending beside another series.

title: 28  Data Scientism
text:
28.3 Spurious Causal Impacts
Good natural experiments are hard to find. For example, suppose we asked “what is the effect of wages on police demanded?” and examined a policy which lowered the educational requirements from 4 years to 2 to become an officer. This increases the labour supply, but it also affects the demand curve through “general equilibrium”: as some of the new officers were potentially criminals and, with fewer criminals, the demand for police shifts down. Bad natural experiments, by contrast, are easier to find than you might imagine. The remainder of this section illustrates that risk: applying canonical causal-inference recipes (IV, RDD, DID) to data that is purely noise.

Spurious Instrument
The same search problem that produces spurious OLS results also produces spurious instruments. By chance, some candidate variable will satisfy the statistical tests for relevance and exogeneity.






ImportantKey Definition





A spurious instrument is a variable that satisfies the formal statistical criteria for an instrumental variable (relevance, exogeneity) by chance, despite having no plausible causal connection to the endogenous regressor.



A spurious instrument is useful to recognize because it is the IV analog of p-hacking. Search over enough candidate instruments and one will pass the formal tests by luck. The 2SLS estimate it produces has no causal interpretation. The risk grows with the number of candidates considered, which is the same multiple-testing problem as p-hacking applied to instrument selection. The Vigen IV exercise below runs this kind of search.


Example: Vigen IV’s
We now run IV regressions for different variable combinations in the dataset of spurious relationships


Code
knames <- names(vigen_csv)[2:11] # First 10 Variables
#knames <- names(vigen_csv)[-1] # Try All Variables
p <- 1
ii <- 1
ivreg_list <- vector('list', factorial(length(knames))/factorial(length(knames)-3))

# Choose 3 variable
for( k1 in knames){
for( k2 in setdiff(knames, k1)){
for( k3 in setdiff(knames, c(k1, k2)) ){   
    x1_hat <- vigen_csv[, k1]
    x2_hat <- vigen_csv[, k2]
    x3_hat <- vigen_csv[, k3]
    # Merge and 'Analyze'        
    xy_iv_hat <- na.omit(data.frame(x1_hat, x2_hat, x3_hat))
    ivreg_i <- feols(x1_hat ~ 1|x2_hat ~ x3_hat, data=xy_iv_hat)
    ivreg_list[[ii]] <- list(ivreg_i, c(k1, k2, k3))
    ii <- ii+1
}}}
pvals <- sapply(ivreg_list, function(ivreg_i){ivreg_i[[1]]$coeftable[2, 4]})

plot(ecdf(pvals), xlab='p-value', ylab='CDF', main=NA)
title('Frequency IV is Statistically Significant', font.main=1)
abline(v=c(.01, .05), col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)









Code

# Most Significant Spurious Combinations
pvars <- sapply(ivreg_list, function(ivreg_i){ivreg_i[[2]]})
pdat <- data.frame(t(pvars), pvals)
pdat <- pdat[order(pdat$pvals), ]
head(pdat)
##                     X1                 X2            X3        pvals
## 76    hanging_suicides   science_spending    bed_deaths 3.049883e-08
## 4     science_spending   hanging_suicides    bed_deaths 3.049883e-08
## 3     science_spending   hanging_suicides cheese_percap 3.344890e-08
## 75    hanging_suicides   science_spending cheese_percap 3.344890e-08
## 485 maine_divorce_rate   margarine_percap cheese_percap 3.997738e-08
## 557   margarine_percap maine_divorce_rate cheese_percap 3.997738e-08

# Fraction of all combinations significant at conventional levels
c(at_0.05 = mean(pvals < 0.05, na.rm=TRUE),
  at_0.01 = mean(pvals < 0.01, na.rm=TRUE))
##   at_0.05   at_0.01 
## 0.3166667 0.2194444
# About 32% of the triples are significant at 5%, and about 22% at 1%.
# That is far more than the rates a single hypothesis test would imply.


The share of “significant” results in such a search can far exceed the rates a single hypothesis test would imply.


Simulation Study
We do not have many theoretical results for these newer recipes yet, but a numerical example should make the issue clear. We apply the three major credible methods (IV, RDD, DID) to random walks. Each time, we find a result that fits the mold and add various extensions that make it appear robust. One could tell a story about how \(X_{i2}\) affects \(X_{i1}\) but \(X_{i1}\) might also affect \(X_{i2}\), and how they discovered an instrument \(X_{i3}\) to provide the first causal estimate of \(X_{i2}\) on \(X_{i1}\). The analysis looks scientific and the story sounds plausible, so you could probably be convinced if it were not just random noise.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
n <- 1000
n_index <- seq(n)

random_walk1 <- cumsum(runif(n, -1, 1))

random_walk2 <- cumsum(runif(n, -1, 1))

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(random_walk1, pch=16, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .25),
    xlab='Time', ylab='Random Value')
plot(random_walk2, pch=16, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .25),
    xlab='Time', ylab='Random Value')









IV. First, find an instrument that satisfies various statistical criteria to provide a causal estimate of \(X_{i2}\) on \(X_{i1}\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# 'Find' 'valid' ingredients
library('fixest')
random_walk3 <- cumsum(runif(n, -1, 1))
xy_iv_sim <- data.frame(
    x1_sim=random_walk1,
    x2_sim=random_walk2,
    x3_sim=random_walk3)
ivreg_i <- feols(x1_sim ~ 1|x2_sim ~ x3_sim, data=xy_iv_sim)
summary(ivreg_i)
## TSLS estimation: Second stage
## |- D.V.   : x1_sim
## |- Endo.  : x2_sim
## |- Instr. : x3_sim
## Dep. Var.: x1_sim
## Observations: 1,000
## Standard-errors: IID 
##              Estimate Std. Error   t value   Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -2.019742   0.360628  -5.60063 2.7608e-08 ***
## fit_x2_sim  -0.303747   0.018652 -16.28518  < 2.2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## RMSE: 5.16906   Adj. R2: 0.198148
## F-test (1st stage), x2_sim: stat = 1,434.504, p < 2.2e-16 , on 1 and 998 DoF.
##                 Wu-Hausman: stat =    10.690, p = 0.001114, on 1 and 997 DoF.
# The slope on x2_sim is significant, with no true relationship.

# After experimenting with different instruments
# you can find even stronger results!


RDD. Second, find a large discrete change in the data that you can associate with a policy. You can use this as an instrument too, also providing a causal estimate of \(X_{i2}\) on \(X_{i1}\).


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Let the data take shape
# (around the large differences before and after)
n1 <- 290
wind1 <- c(n1-300, n1+300)
xy1_sim <- data.frame(t=n_index, y_sim=random_walk1, d=1*(n_index > n1))
xy1_sub_sim <- xy1_sim[ n_index>wind1[1] & n_index < wind1[2], ]

# Then find your big break
reg0 <- lm(y_sim ~ t, data=xy1_sub_sim[xy1_sub_sim$d==0, ])
reg1 <- lm(y_sim ~ t, data=xy1_sub_sim[xy1_sub_sim$d==1, ])

# The evidence should show openly (it's just science)
plot(random_walk1, pch=16, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .25),
    xlim=wind1, xlab='Time', ylab='Random Value')
abline(v=n1, col=grey(.5), lty=3)
lines(reg0$model$t, reg0$fitted.values, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
lines(reg1$model$t, reg1$fitted.values, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

DID. Third, find a change in the data that you can associate with a policy where the control group has parallel trends. This also provides a causal estimate of \(X_{i2}\) on \(X_{i1}\).


Code

# Find a reversal of fortune
# (A good story always goes well with a nice pre-trend)
n2 <- 318

    xlim=wind2, ylim=c(-15, 15), xlab='Time', ylab='Random Value')

NoteMust Know





All three empirical recipes (IV, RDD, DID) can produce statistically significant results from random walks with no true relationship. What is the common thread? In your own empirical work, how would you distinguish a genuine causal finding from a spurious one?



A broader literature documents spurious results without any true effect, with instrumental variables especially problematic (Ioannidis et al. 2017; Young 2022; Christian and Barrett 2024). Adamson and Stephenson (2026) run a related simulation study (Hendry 1984; Morris et al. 2019) for the economics of war. They build a model where war is unambiguously harmful, simulate many panel datasets from it, and apply OLS and 2SLS regressions that mirror the published literature. These regressions routinely report a positive “effect” of past conflict on output, so the causal claims can be qualitatively backwards. The inference that war causes growth rests on assuming the regression model is correct.

title: 28  Data Scientism
text:
28.4 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain the difference between p-hacking and spurious regression. Both can produce statistically significant results from unrelated data, but the mechanisms differ. Give a concrete example of each using concepts from this chapter.
Using the tylervigen.csv dataset from the chapter, pick any two variables and run an OLS regression. Then pick a third variable as an instrument and run a 2SLS regression with fixest::feols. Report the p-values for both. Do these significant results reflect a real causal relationship? Why or why not?
Simulate two independent random walks of length 500 in R (each starting at 0, with increments from runif(1, -1, 1)). Regress one on the other using lm() and record the p-value on the slope. Repeat this 200 times and plot the distribution of p-values. What fraction are below 0.05, and how does this compare to what you would expect under independence?


Further Reading

https://www.econometrics-with-r.org/9-1-testing-joint-hypotheses.html – multiple testing and joint hypothesis testing in a regression context.
Athey and Imbens (2019) – a survey of when and how machine learning tools complement econometric inference.



Recall
This chapter showed how data errors, \(p\)-hacking, and spurious regression produce significant results from noise. It also showed that the IV, RDD, and DID recipes can produce statistically significant findings from purely random data. In the p-hacking loop, we used a strict cutoff of \(p < 0.001\). The while loop kept regenerating random x2_sim_b values until it hit a “significant” regression. The formula \(1-(1-\alpha)^k\) showed that the chance of at least one false discovery passes \(50\%\) by \(k=700\) tries.
