title: 29  Misc. Multivariate Topics
text:
29.1 Prediction
The remaining multivariate topics did not fit cleanly into the preceding chapters.
This chapter asks four questions.

title: 29  Misc. Multivariate Topics
text:
Describe vs. Explain vs. Predict
Understanding whether we aim to describe, explain, or predict is central to empirical analysis. The three distinct purposes are to accurately describe empirical patterns, explain why the empirical patterns exist, and predict what empirical patterns will exist.

Three Objectives of Empirical Analysis








Objective
Core Question
Goal
Methods




Describe
What is happening?
Characterize patterns & facts
Summary stats, visualizations, correlations


Explain
Why is it happening?
Establish causal relationships & mechanisms
Theoretical models; experimentation; counterfactual reasoning


Predict
What will happen?
Anticipate outcomes; support decisions that affect the future
Machine learning, treatment effect forecasting, policy simulations



Here is an example for minimum wages.

Describe: Studies document that following minimum-wage increases, overall low-wage employment may look roughly stable in the short run. But disaggregated data often show larger employment declines over longer horizons, especially among youths and racial minorities.
Explain: Studies investigate economic mechanisms. One question is whether lower productivity populations are more vulnerable and employers adjust along hiring margins (fewer openings, higher required skills). Another is whether effects are larger in sectors like retail/food service, where minimum wages bite hardest.
Predict: A policy simulation that raises the wage floor incorporates subgroup-specific elasticities to forecast different employment losses (e.g., unemployment for teenage or black workers and income gains for stayers)

The distinctions matter, as they help you recognize that predictive accuracy or good data visualization does not equal causal insight (Shmueli 2010). You can then better align statistical tools with questions. Try remembering this: Describe reality, Explain causes, Predict futures






NoteMust Know





Consider the relationship between class size and student test scores. Write one sentence for each: (a) a descriptive finding, (b) an explanatory hypothesis, and (c) a predictive statement. Which of the three requires the strongest assumptions?





Prediction Intervals
A confidence interval for the mean \(m_{Y}(x)\) does not by itself tell us how far a new observation at \(x\) might land.






ImportantKey Definition





A prediction interval for \(Y_{i}\) at \(X_{i} = x\) is a range that captures a stated probability (e.g., 95%) of new observations at that \(x\).



Prediction intervals are useful when the question is about individuals rather than averages. We ask what wage a new worker with 12 years of schooling might actually earn, not what the average wage of such workers is. Because they also include the residual variability of \(Y_{i}\) around the mean, they are generally wider than a confidence interval for \(m_{Y}(x)\) at the same level.
For a nice overview of different types of intervals, see https://www.jstor.org/stable/2685212. For an in-depth view, see “Statistical Intervals: A Guide for Practitioners and Researchers” or “Statistical Tolerance Regions: Theory, Applications, and Computation”. See https://robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/intervals/ for constructing intervals for future observations in a time-series context. See Davison and Hinkley, chapters 5 and 6 (also Efron and Tibshirani, or Wehrens et al.)


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE

## Data
# 3294 US workers, with hourly wages in 1980 dollars
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
xy_hat <- xy_hat[order(xy_hat[, 'x_hat']), ]


# Design Points
x_values <- unique(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
# Regression
reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, span=.8)
y_pred_lo <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_values))

# Bootstrap Residuals
n <- nrow(xy_hat)
res_lo <- lapply(1:399, function(i){
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[sample(n, replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot, span=.8)
    resids_b <- resid(reg_b)
    cbind(e_hat=resids_b, x_hat=xy_boot[, 'x_hat'])
})
res_lo <- do.call(rbind, res_lo)

## Smooth residuals
res_fun <- function(x0, h){
    # Include only residuals within h distance to x0
    ki0 <- abs(res_lo[, 'x_hat']-x0)/h
    ki0 <- dunif(ki0)/h
    e_local_hat <- res_lo[ki0 != 0, 'e_hat'] #subset estimates
    ## Local quantiles
    res_i <- quantile(e_local_hat, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
    res_i
}
res_ci <- sapply(x_values, res_fun, h=2)

## Prediction Interval
pi_lo1 <- y_pred_lo + res_ci[1, ]
pi_lo2 <- y_pred_lo + res_ci[2, ]

#Plot
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    data=xy_hat, ylim=c(0, 40), main=NA,
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
lines(x_values, y_pred_lo,
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lwd=2, type='o')
polygon( c(x_values, rev(x_values)),
    c(pi_lo1, rev(pi_lo2)),
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .3), border=NA)















TipTest Yourself





Consider also this example below with a linear model. Expand on it by using the Normal Approximation for the residuals (hint: use qnorm).


Code
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat)

# Bootstrap Prediction Interval
boot_resids <- lapply(1:399, function(b){
    b_id <- sample( nrow(xy_hat), replace=TRUE)
    xy_boot <- xy_hat[b_id, ]
    reg_b <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_boot)
    e_b_hat <- resid(reg_b)
    x_boot <- reg_b[['model']][['x_hat']]
    res_b <- cbind(e_b_hat, x_boot)
})
boot_resids <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, boot_resids))

# Errors do not vary with x_hat
q_e_hat <- quantile(boot_resids[, 'e_b_hat'], probs=c(.025, .975))

# PI
y_fit <- predict(reg)
boot_pi <- cbind(y_fit + q_e_hat[1], y_fit + q_e_hat[2])

# Plot Bootstrap PI
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1), main=NA,
    ylim=c(0, 40), xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
title('Prediction Intervals', font.main=1)
x_hat <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat']
lines(x_hat, y_fit, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
polygon( c(x_hat, rev(x_hat)),
    c(boot_pi[, 1], rev(boot_pi[, 2])),
    col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .3), border=NA)









Code

# Normal PI (Make by hand)
#pi <- predict(reg, interval='prediction')
#lines( x_hat, pi[, 'lwr'], lty=2)
#lines( x_hat, pi[, 'upr'], lty=2)











TipTest Yourself





Here is the same prediction interval for monthly earnings by years of education.


Code

## Data
# Monthly earnings of 935 US working men in 1980
data(wage2, package='wooldridge')
xy2_hat <- wage2[, c('educ', 'wage')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=monthly earnings
xy2_hat <- xy2_hat[order(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat']), ]


# Design Points
x_values <- unique(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'])
# Regression
reg_lo <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat, span=.8)
y_pred_lo <- predict(reg_lo, newdata=data.frame(x_hat=x_values))

# Bootstrap Residuals
n2 <- nrow(xy2_hat)
res_lo <- lapply(1:399, function(i){
    xy2_boot <- xy2_hat[sample(n2, replace=TRUE), ]
    reg_b <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_boot, span=.8)
    resids_b <- resid(reg_b)
    cbind(e_hat=resids_b, x_hat=xy2_boot[, 'x_hat'])
})
res_lo <- do.call(rbind, res_lo)

## Smooth residuals
res_fun <- function(x0, h){
    # Include only residuals within h distance to x0
    ki0 <- abs(res_lo[, 'x_hat']-x0)/h
    ki0 <- dunif(ki0)/h
    e_local_hat <- res_lo[ki0 != 0, 'e_hat'] #subset estimates
    ## Local quantiles
    res_i <- quantile(e_local_hat, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
    res_i
}
res_ci <- sapply(x_values, res_fun, h=2)

## Prediction Interval
pi_lo1 <- y_pred_lo + res_ci[1, ]
pi_lo2 <- y_pred_lo + res_ci[2, ]

#Plot
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25),
    data=xy2_hat, ylim=c(0, 3100), main=NA, xlab='educ', ylab='wage')
lines(x_values, y_pred_lo,
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lwd=2, type='o')
polygon( c(x_values, rev(x_values)),
    c(pi_lo1, rev(pi_lo2)),
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .3), border=NA)














Cross Validation
A model that fits the training data perfectly can still predict new observations badly, so we need a score that rewards out-of-sample accuracy rather than in-sample fit.






ImportantKey Definition





Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) fits the model \(n\) times, each time leaving one observation out and predicting it from the rest, then chooses the bandwidth \(h\) that minimizes the average squared prediction error, \[\min_{h} \quad \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i},h) \right]^2,\] where \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i},h)\) is the model’s predicted value at \(\hat{x}_{i}\) from a fit that excluded \(\hat{x}_{i}\) and \(h\) is the bandwidth (e.g., bin size in a regressogram).



Leave-one-out cross-validation is useful as the simplest computational way to choose bandwidths, and it directly addresses an issue that plagues observational studies in the social sciences: your model explains everything and predicts nothing. The score it minimizes is an out-of-sample average, so a too-flexible model that fits in-sample noise will be penalized. Minimizing prediction error is not objectively “best”, but it is a sensible choice when you have no better criterion.
In practice, compare models with cross-validation (below). The preferred model is the one with best out-of-sample performance, not the one with the most flexible in-sample fit (Stone 1974; Hastie et al. 2009; Mullainathan and Spiess 2017). The same idea selects bin counts and bandwidths in Local Relationships.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
# Crossvalidated bandwidth for regression
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage

## Grid Search
# The grid starts at 0.75.
# With a span of 0.5, only workers with exactly 12 years of schooling get weight at 12 years.
BWS <- c(0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
BWS_CV <- sapply(BWS, function(h){
    e_bw_hat <- sapply(1:nrow(xy_hat), function(i){
        llls <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat[-i, ], span=h,
            degree=1)
        y_pred_i <- predict(llls, newdata=xy_hat[i, ])
        e_i_hat <-  (y_pred_i- xy_hat[i, 'y_hat'])
        return(e_i_hat)
    })
    # LOESS does not extrapolate, so it cannot predict the only worker with 3 years of schooling
    return( mean(e_bw_hat^2, na.rm=TRUE) )
})

## Plot MSE
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(BWS, BWS_CV, ylab='CV error', pch=3,
    xlab='bandwidth (h)')
# The error is smallest at the smallest bandwidth.
# It rises toward that of a linear regression as the bandwidth grows.
# So a more flexible fit predicts hourly wages slightly better.

## Plot Optimal Predictions
h_star <- BWS[which.min(BWS_CV)]
llls <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat, span=h_star,
    degree=1)
plot(xy_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .1),
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', main=NA)

pred_id <- order(xy_hat[, 'x_hat'])
lines(xy_hat[pred_id, 'x_hat'], predict(llls)[pred_id],
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lwd=2)















TipTest Yourself





Here is the same bandwidth search for monthly earnings by years of education.


Code
# Monthly earnings of 935 US working men in 1980
data(wage2, package='wooldridge')
# Crossvalidated bandwidth for regression
xy2_hat <- wage2[, c('educ', 'wage')]
colnames(xy2_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=monthly earnings

## Grid Search
BWS <- c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
BWS_CV <- sapply(BWS, function(h){
    e_bw_hat <- sapply(1:nrow(xy2_hat), function(i){
        llls <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat[-i, ], span=h,
            degree=1, surface='direct')
        y_pred_i <- predict(llls, newdata=xy2_hat[i, ])
        e_i_hat <-  (y_pred_i- xy2_hat[i, 'y_hat'])
        return(e_i_hat)
    })
    return( mean(e_bw_hat^2) )
})

## Plot MSE
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(BWS, BWS_CV, ylab='CV error', pch=3,
    xlab='bandwidth (h)')
# The error falls as the bandwidth grows.
# It flattens toward that of a linear regression.
# So more flexibility does not improve predictions of monthly earnings.

## Plot Optimal Predictions
h_star <- BWS[which.min(BWS_CV)]
llls <- loess(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy2_hat, span=h_star,
    degree=1, surface='direct')
plot(xy2_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25),
    xlab='X', ylab='Predictions', main=NA)

pred_id <- order(xy2_hat[, 'x_hat'])
lines(xy2_hat[pred_id, 'x_hat'], predict(llls)[pred_id],
    col=rgb(0, .7, .7, .8), lwd=2)


















NoteMust Know





Leave-one-out cross-validation is just an average of out-of-sample errors. Suppose \(n=4\) and, for one bandwidth \(h\), leaving out each point in turn gives the predictions \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})\) below.

Leave-One-Out Prediction Errors








\(i\)
\(\hat{y}_{i}\)
\(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})\)
\(\hat{y}_{i} - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{i})\)




1
10
9
1


2
12
14
-2


3
15

The cross-validation score is the mean squared error: \((1^2 + (-2)^2 + 1^2 + 0^2)/4 = 6/4 = 1.5\). Repeating this for several bandwidths, the one with the smallest score is preferred.

title: 29  Misc. Multivariate Topics
text:
29.2 Filtering

Filtering
In some cases we want to estimate the level of a time series at \(t\) rather than forecast forward, and the relevant question is which neighbors we are allowed to use.






ImportantKey Definition





Filtering estimates the value of a time series at \(t\) using only past observations, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t} \mid X_{t-1}, X_{t-2}]\); smoothing uses both past and future, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t} \mid X_{t-1}, X_{t+1}]\).



Filtering is useful for forecasting, or any time the future is unknown at time \(t\). Smoothing gives lower-variance estimates, so use it to analyze the past when you have the full series. The two are otherwise built from the same kernel weights, so the only practical difference is which observations the weights are allowed to touch.
One example of filtering is Exponential Filtering (sometimes confusingly referred to as “Exponential Smoothing”) which weights only previous observations using an exponential kernel.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Time series data
## Underlying Trend
trend_sim <- cumsum(rnorm(500, 0, 1))
## Observed Datapoints
x_sim <- trend_sim + runif(length(trend_sim), -10, 10)
xy_sim <- data.frame(t=seq_along(x_sim), trend_sim=trend_sim, x_sim=x_sim)

## Asymmetric kernel (filtering: uses current and past only)
bw1 <- c(2/3, 1/3)
s1 <- filter(x_sim, bw1/sum(bw1), sides=1)

## Symmetric kernel (smoothing: also uses future)
bw2 <- c(1/6, 2/3, 1/6)
s2 <- filter(x_sim, bw2/sum(bw2), sides=2)

## Plot the series with both smoothers
plot(x_sim ~ t, data=xy_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25),
    main=NA, xlab='Time', ylab='x')
lines(xy_sim$t, s1, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
lines(xy_sim$t, s2, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
legend('topleft', lwd=2, bty='n',
    col=c(rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)),
    legend=c('Asymmetric (filtering)', 'Symmetric (smoothing)'))









There are several cross-validation procedures for filtering time series data (Opsomer et al. 2001). One is called time series cross-validation (TSCV), which is useful for temporally dependent data (Hart 1991; Haerdle and Vieu 1992; Bergmeir et al. 2018). Unlike ordinary cross-validation, TSCV only ever predicts a point from its past, never its future, which respects the time ordering of the data. We use it below to choose the window of a one-sided moving average.


Code
# Time series cross-validation for a one-sided moving average
# For each window h, predict each point from the previous h points
x_sim <- xy_sim$x_sim
ma_windows <- 2:20
tscv_mse <- sapply(ma_windows, function(h){
    ## Weight the previous h points equally, 0 weight on the current point
    ma_coefs <- c(0, rep(1/h, h))
    x_fit <- filter(x_sim, ma_coefs, sides=1)
    mean((x_sim - x_fit)^2, na.rm=TRUE)
})

## CV-optimal window
h_star <- ma_windows[which.min(tscv_mse)]

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
## Plot CV error against window size
plot(ma_windows, tscv_mse, type='o', pch=16, main=NA,
    xlab='Moving-average window (h)', ylab='TSCV mean squared error')
abline(v=h_star, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)

## Plot the series with the CV-optimal filter
x_smooth <- filter(x_sim, c(0, rep(1/h_star, h_star)), sides=1)
plot(x_sim ~ t, data=xy_sim, pch=16, col=grey(0, .25), main=NA,
    xlab='Time', ylab='x')
lines(xy_sim$t, x_smooth, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
title(paste0('One-sided MA, h = ', h_star), font.main=1)









Code

## See also https://robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/tscvexample/

text:
29.3 Inference

Arrays
Arrays are a generalization of matrices to multiple dimensions. They are a very efficient way to store well-formatted numeric data, and are often used in spatial econometrics and time series (often in the form of “data cubes”).


Code
# data square (matrix)
array(data = seq(1, 24), dim=c(3, 8))
##      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [,8]
## [1,]    1    4    7   10   13   16   19   22
## [2,]    2    5    8   11   14   17   20   23
## [3,]    3    6    9   12   15   18   21   24

# data cube
a <- array(data = seq(1, 24), dim=c(3, 2, 4))
a
## , , 1
## 
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]    1    4
## [2,]    2    5
## [3,]    3    6
## 
## , , 2
## 
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]    7   10
## [2,]    8   11
## [3,]    9   12
## 
## , , 3
## 
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]   13   16
## [2,]   14   17
## [3,]   15   18
## 
## , , 4
## 
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]   19   22
## [2,]   20   23
## [3,]   21   24




Code
a[1, , , drop = FALSE]  # Row 1
#a[, 1, , drop = FALSE]  # Column 1
#a[, , 1, drop = FALSE]  # Layer 1

a[ 1, 1,  ]  # Row 1, column 1
#a[ 1,  , 1]  # Row 1, 'layer' 1
#a[  , 1, 1]  # Column 1, 'layer' 1
a[1 , 1, 1]  # Row 1, column 1, 'layer' 1


Apply extends to arrays


Code
apply(a, 1, mean)    # Row means
## [1] 11.5 12.5 13.5
apply(a, 2, mean)    # Column means
## [1] 11 14
apply(a, 3, mean)    # 'Layer' means
## [1]  3.5  9.5 15.5 21.5
apply(a, c(1, 2), mean)  # Row/Column combination 
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]   10   13
## [2,]   11   14
## [3,]   12   15


The outer function produces an array by multiplying every element of one vector with every element of another.


Code
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
x_outer <- outer(x, x) # x %o% x
x_outer
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]    1    2    3
## [2,]    2    4    6
## [3,]    3    6    9
is.array(x_outer) # Matrices are arrays
## [1] TRUE

x_mat <- matrix( seq(6, 1), 2, 3)
outer(x_mat, x)
## , , 1
## 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]    6    4    2
## [2,]    5    3    1
## 
## , , 2
## 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]   12    8    4
## [2,]   10    6    2
## 
## , , 3
## 
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]   18   12    6
## [2,]   15    9    3
# outer(x_mat, matrix(x))
# outer(x_mat, t(x))
# outer(x_outer, x_mat)


Matrices are the two-dimensional case, and they carry the regression algebra that follows.


Matrix Calculations
First, note that you can use matrix algebra in R


Code
x_mat1 <- matrix( seq(2, 7), 2, 3)
x_mat1
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]    2    4    6
## [2,]    3    5    7

x_mat2 <- matrix( seq(4, -1), 2, 3)
x_mat2
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]    4    2    0
## [2,]    3    1   -1

x_mat1*x_mat2 #NOT classical matrix multiplication
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]    8    8    0
## [2,]    9    5   -7
x_mat1^x_mat2
##      [,1] [,2]      [,3]
## [1,]   16   16 1.0000000
## [2,]   27    5 0.1428571

tcrossprod(x_mat1, x_mat2) #x_mat1 %*% t(x_mat2)
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,]   16    4
## [2,]   22    7

crossprod(x_mat1, x_mat2)
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]   17    7   -3
## [2,]   31   13   -5
## [3,]   45   19   -7








TipTest Yourself





Matrix multiplication %*% follows the rule that element \((i,j)\) of the product equals the dot product of row \(i\) of the first matrix and column \(j\) of the second. For crossprod(A, B), R computes \(A'B\) efficiently without explicitly transposing. This is useful in OLS where we need \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}\) repeatedly.



Second, note that you can apply functions to matrices


Code
sum_squared <- function(x1, x2) {
    y <- (x1 + x2)^2
    return(y)
}
sum_squared(x_mat1, x_mat2)
##      [,1] [,2] [,3]
## [1,]   36   36   36
## [2,]   36   36   36


solve(x_mat1[1:2, 1:2])
##      [,1] [,2]
## [1,] -2.5    2
## [2,]  1.5   -1


Third, note that we can conduct OLS regressions efficiently using matrix algebra. Grouping the trial coefficients as a vector \(\mathbf{b}=(b_{0} ~~ b_{1} ~~... ~~ b_{K})\), we want to find coefficients that minimize the sum of squared errors. The linear model has a fairly simple solution for \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) if you know linear algebra. Denoting \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i} = [1~~  \hat{x}_{i1} ~~...~~ \hat{x}_{iK}]\) as a row vector, we can write the model as \(\hat{y}_{i} = \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{i}\mathbf{b} + \hat{e}_{i}\). The residuals \(\hat{e}_{i}\) depend on the trial coefficients but are computed from the observed sample. We can then write the model in matrix form \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{y} &= \hat{\textbf{X}}\mathbf{b} + \hat{\mathbf{e}} \\
\hat{y} &= \begin{pmatrix}
\hat{y}_{1} \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_{N}
\end{pmatrix} \quad
\hat{\textbf{X}} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \hat{x}_{11} & ... & \hat{x}_{1K} \\
& \vdots & & \\
1 & \hat{x}_{n1} & ... & \hat{x}_{nK}
\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}\] Minimizing the squared errors: \(\min_{\mathbf{b}} \hat{e}_{i}^2 = \min_{\mathbf{b}} (\hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}})\), yields coefficient estimates and predictions \[\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{b}} &= (\hat{\textbf{X}}'\hat{\textbf{X}})^{-1}\hat{\textbf{X}}'\hat{y} \\
\hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}} &= \hat{\textbf{X}} \hat{\mathbf{b}} \\
\hat{\mathbf{e}} &= \hat{y} - \hat{y}^{\mathrm{fit}}
\end{aligned}\]


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Multivariate data: all columns of Wages1, not only schooling and wage as above
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1
# Three-level schooling factor, as in Comparing Multiple Groups
xy_hat$school_g <- cut(xy_hat$school, breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 16), labels=c('<12', '12', '>12'))

# Manually compute b_hat = (X'X)^{-1} X'y_hat step by step.
y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'wage']
X <- xy_hat[, c('school', 'exper')]
X <- as.matrix(cbind(1, X))

XtX  <- t(X) %*% X         # K+1 by K+1 cross-product
XtXi <- solve(XtX)         # invert
XtY  <- t(X) %*% y_hat          # K+1 by 1 cross-product with y_hat
b_hat <- XtXi %*% XtY        # K+1 coefficient vector
c(b_hat)
## [1] -2.4766831  0.5992289  0.1572607

# Confirms the same answer as lm()
coef(lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat))
## (Intercept)      school       exper 
##  -2.4766831   0.5992289   0.1572607




Bias
With matrix notation, we can establish that OLS is an unbiased estimator for additively separable and linear relationships. Assume \[\begin{aligned}
Y_{i} = X_{i} \beta + \epsilon_{i} &\quad \mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i} | X_{i} ]=0,
\end{aligned}\] then, stacking the \(Y_{i}\) into the vector \(\mathbf{Y}\) and the rows \(X_{i}\) into the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), notice that \[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{B} &= (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'(\mathbf{X}\beta + \epsilon) = \beta + (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\epsilon \\
\mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbf{B} \right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[ (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y} \right] = \beta + (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbf{X}'\epsilon \right] = \beta
\end{aligned}\]
If we do not know that the data generating process is additively separable and linear, then we do not know how to interpret \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\). There is a very mathematical expression for it, which I do not cover here. If we run a local linear regression analysis, on the other hand, we get the estimator \[\begin{aligned}
\beta(\mathbf{x}) &= [\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{X}]^{-1} \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{Y} \\
\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x}) &= \begin{pmatrix}
k\left(\mathbf{X}_{1}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{H}\right) & ... & 0\\
\vdots & & \\
0 & ... & k\left(\mathbf{X}_{n}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{H}\right)
\end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}\] which is unbiased far more often.
The weight matrix \(\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x})\) is \(n \times n\) and diagonal, holding one weight per observation rather than one per variable. Each weight multiplies the univariate kernels across the \(K\) variables, \[\begin{aligned}
k\left(\mathbf{X}_{i}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{H}\right) &= \prod_{k=1}^{K} k\left(\frac{X_{ik}-x_{k}}{h_{k}}\right),
\end{aligned}\] where \(h_{k}\) is the \(k\)th diagonal element of the bandwidth matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) from Local Relationships. So observation \(i\) gets a large weight only when it is close to \(\mathbf{x}\) in every variable, and \(h_{k}\) sets how close it has to be in variable \(k\).

title: 29  Misc. Multivariate Topics
text:
29.4 Multiple Testing
When you test one hypothesis at the \(5\%\) level, there is a \(5\%\) chance of a false positive. When you test many hypotheses, those chances accumulate. This is the statistical engine behind much of Data Scientism: search long enough and something will look significant.

Family-Wise Error Rate
A single \(5\%\) test promises a \(5\%\) false-positive rate, but a researcher rarely stops at one test. The relevant question is the chance of any false positive across the whole batch.






ImportantKey Definition





The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of at least one false positive across a family of \(K\) tests. If the tests are independent and each has false-positive rate \(\alpha\), \[\text{FWER} = 1-(1-\alpha)^{K}.\]



The FWER is useful for any procedure that runs many hypothesis tests. It tells you how likely you are to declare something “significant” by chance even when every null is true. With \(\alpha=0.05\), one test has FWER \(0.05\), but \(K=10\) tests give \(1-0.95^{10}\approx 0.40\) and \(K=100\) tests give \(1-0.95^{100}\approx 0.99\). Almost any dataset will yield a “significant” result if you test it enough ways.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Family-wise error rate grows with the number of tests
alpha <- 0.05
K <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)
fwer <- 1 - (1-alpha)^K
cbind(K, fwer=round(fwer, 3))
##        K  fwer
## [1,]   1 0.050
## [2,]   5 0.226
## [3,]  10 0.401
## [4,]  20 0.642
## [5,]  50 0.923
## [6,] 100 0.994




Bonferroni and Holm Corrections
To hold the family-wise error rate down to \(\alpha\), we have to make each individual test stricter. Exactly how strict matters for whether real effects survive.






ImportantKey Definition





The Bonferroni correction (Bonferroni 1936; Dunn 1961) multiplies each \(p\)-value by the number of tests \(K\) (equivalently, lowers the threshold to \(\alpha/K\)). The Holm correction applies the same idea stepwise: sort the \(p\)-values from smallest to largest and compare the \(j\)th smallest to \(\alpha/(K-j+1)\).



The Bonferroni correction is useful as the simplest valid adjustment, since it guarantees \(\text{FWER} \leq \alpha\) under any dependence structure between tests. It is conservative, though, and with many tests it can miss real effects. The Holm correction (Holm 1979) is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni while still controlling the FWER, so it is generally preferred when only family-wise control is wanted.


Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Five p-values from five separate tests
pvals <- c(0.001, 0.013, 0.021, 0.04, 0.21)

# Adjust for multiple testing
cbind(
    raw        = pvals,
    bonferroni = p.adjust(pvals, method='bonferroni'),
    holm       = p.adjust(pvals, method='holm'))
##        raw bonferroni  holm
## [1,] 0.001      0.005 0.005
## [2,] 0.013      0.065 0.052
## [3,] 0.021      0.105 0.063
## [4,] 0.040      0.200 0.080
## [5,] 0.210      1.000 0.210








NoteMust Know





A researcher runs \(K=5\) tests and reports a \(p\)-value of \(0.013\). On its own, \(0.013 < 0.05\) looks significant. The Bonferroni-adjusted value is \(0.013 \times 5 = 0.065 > 0.05\), so it is not significant once we account for the five tests. The threshold view is equivalent: compare the raw \(p\)-value to \(\alpha/K = 0.05/5 = 0.01\).





Post-Hoc Pairwise Tests
A significant global test says some group differs, but the question we usually care about is which one. Asking each pair separately reintroduces the multiple-testing problem we just controlled at the global level.






ImportantKey Definition





A post-hoc test is a follow-up comparison conducted after a significant global test (like ANOVA). Because there are \(G(G-1)/2\) pairs to test, the per-pair significance threshold must be tightened to control the family-wise error rate; Tukey’s HSD (Tukey 1953) and Holm-adjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests are common choices.



Post-hoc tests are useful after a significant ANOVA \(F\)-test (see Comparing Multiple Groups). They find which group or groups differ without inflating the false-positive rate. The number of comparisons grows quadratically in \(G\), so the per-pair threshold gets noticeably stricter as soon as there are more than a handful of groups.


Code
# Global test: do hourly wages differ by schooling group?
summary(aov(wage ~ school_g, data=xy_hat))
##               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## school_g       2   2541  1270.3     128 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   3291  32654     9.9                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
# F is about 128, with a p-value far below 5%, so some group differs.




Code
## MAIN EXAMPLE
# Post-hoc: which schooling groups differ? (pairwise t-tests, Holm-adjusted)
pairwise.t.test(xy_hat$wage, xy_hat$school_g, p.adjust.method='holm')
## 
##  Pairwise comparisons using t tests with pooled SD 
## 
## data:  xy_hat$wage and xy_hat$school_g 
## 
##     <12     12     
## 12  6.8e-08 -      
## >12 < 2e-16 < 2e-16
## 
## P value adjustment method: holm
# All three pairs differ at the 5% level.




Code
# Tukey's Honest Significant Differences:
# pairwise confidence intervals that already account for all comparisons
TukeyHSD(aov(wage ~ school_g, data=xy_hat))
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = wage ~ school_g, data = xy_hat)
## 
## $school_g
##              diff       lwr       upr p adj
## 12-<12  0.6774177 0.3837567 0.9710787 2e-07
## >12-<12 2.2849502 1.9491477 2.6207526 0e+00
## >12-12  1.6075324 1.2634931 1.9515718 0e+00
# No interval contains 0, so all three pairs differ here too.
# The largest gap is about 2.28 dollars an hour, between >12 and <12 years.


To see what the adjustment does, the chunk below puts the raw and adjusted \(p\)-values side by side.


Code
# Raw p-values, one per pair of schooling groups
pair_tests <- pairwise.t.test(xy_hat$wage, xy_hat$school_g, p.adjust.method='none')
p_raw <- pair_tests[['p.value']]
p_raw <- p_raw[!is.na(p_raw)] # drop the empty cell of the table
names(p_raw) <- c('12 vs <12', '>12 vs <12', '>12 vs 12')

# Adjust for the three pairs
cbind(
    raw=p_raw,
    bonferroni=p.adjust(p_raw, method='bonferroni'),
    holm=p.adjust(p_raw, method='holm'))
##                     raw   bonferroni         holm
## 12 vs <12  6.794126e-08 2.038238e-07 6.794126e-08
## >12 vs <12 2.957116e-55 8.871348e-55 8.871348e-55
## >12 vs 12  1.843717e-27 5.531152e-27 3.687435e-27
# Bonferroni multiplies each raw p-value by 3.
# Holm multiplies the smallest by 3, the next by 2, and the largest by 1.
# All three stay far below 0.05, so the adjustment changes no conclusion here.


An adjustment never lowers a \(p\)-value. A raw \(p\)-value not far below the threshold, such as \(0.013\) in the five tests above, can lose its significance, while a much smaller one keeps it.






TipTest Yourself





Repeat the post-hoc tests with murder arrest rates across the four census regions.


Code
# Murder arrests per 100,000 in 50 US states in 1973, with Census region
xy3_hat <- USArrests
xy3_hat$Region <- state.region

# Global test: do murder rates differ by region?
summary(aov(Murder ~ Region, data=xy3_hat))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
## Region       3  391.2   130.4   11.14 1.28e-05 ***
## Residuals   46  538.3    11.7                     
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Post-hoc: which regions differ? (pairwise t-tests, Holm-adjusted)
pairwise.t.test(xy3_hat$Murder, xy3_hat$Region, p.adjust.method='holm')
## 
##  Pairwise comparisons using t tests with pooled SD 
## 
## data:  xy3_hat$Murder and xy3_hat$Region 
## 
##               Northeast South   North Central
## South         7e-05     -       -            
## North Central 0.67251   0.00017 -            
## West          0.36895   0.00259 0.67251      
## 
## P value adjustment method: holm

# Tukey's Honest Significant Differences:
# pairwise confidence intervals that already account for all comparisons
TukeyHSD(aov(Murder ~ Region, data=xy3_hat))
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = Murder ~ Region, data = xy3_hat)
## 
## $Region
##                              diff       lwr       upr     p adj
## South-Northeast          7.006250  3.206920 10.805580 0.0000673
## North Central-Northeast  1.000000 -3.020833  5.020833 0.9104265
## West-Northeast           2.330769 -1.623231  6.284769 0.4047789
## North Central-South     -6.006250 -9.488393 -2.524107 0.0001909
## West-South              -4.675481 -8.080233 -1.270728 0.0035034
## West-North Central       1.330769 -2.319509  4.981047 0.7660715


Rerun pairwise.t.test on the region data with p.adjust.method='none' and again with 'bonferroni'. How many pairs are significant at the \(5\%\) level under each? Why can the uncorrected version flag more differences than the corrected ones, and which version should you report?

title: 29  Misc. Multivariate Topics
text:
29.5 Exercises

Comment the script you wrote for this chapter, then restart R and check that it runs from a clean session, then check the script with AI as explained in Working with AI. Write three sentences from memory on the main statistical idea of this chapter, and ask the assistant what is wrong, vague, or missing. Finish with your own questions about whatever you found hardest.
Explain the distinction between description, explanation, and prediction using a concrete example other than minimum wages. For each objective, state what statistical tools you would use and what kind of evidence would be needed.
Using the USArrests dataset, regress Murder on Assault and UrbanPop. Compute \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) both with lm() and manually via \((\hat{\mathbf{X}}'\hat{\mathbf{X}})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{X}}'\hat{y}\) using matrix operations in R. Verify that the two approaches give the same coefficients.
Using the wage2 dataset from the wooldridge package, fit a loess regression of wage on educ for three different span values (e.g., 0.4, 0.6, 0.8). Use leave-one-out cross-validation to compute the mean squared prediction error for each span. Which span minimizes prediction error, and does a more flexible fit always predict better?
A researcher runs \(K=20\) independent tests, each at the \(5\%\) level. Compute the family-wise error rate \(1-(1-0.05)^{20}\), and find the per-test Bonferroni threshold \(\alpha/K\) that holds the family-wise rate at \(5\%\). Then create a vector of 20 \(p\)-values, apply p.adjust() with the 'bonferroni' and 'holm' methods, and report how many results remain significant under each.


Further Reading

https://otexts.com/fpp3/ – Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), covering time-series smoothing, cross-validation, and prediction in R.
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/np/vignettes/np.pdf – the np package vignette for nonparametric kernel estimation and bandwidth selection.
Shmueli (2010) – a clear discussion of the describe/explain/predict distinction in statistical modeling.
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/multcomp/vignettes/multcomp-examples.pdf – worked examples of multiple-comparison procedures and post-hoc tests in R.



Recall
This chapter wrapped up the multivariate part with the describe/explain/predict taxonomy, prediction intervals and cross-validation, time-series filtering, the matrix form of OLS, and multiple-testing corrections. The matrix-OLS sense-check on Wages1 made the algebra concrete: computing \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}=(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\hat{y}\) step by step with XtX <- t(X) %*% X, XtXi <- solve(XtX), and b_hat <- XtXi %*% XtY recovers exactly the coefficient vector that lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat) returns. These tools connect back to earlier chapters. Cross-validation chooses models, and multiple-testing corrections address the search problem from Data Scientism. The matrix form writes out the OLS algebra of Multiple Regression.

title: Appendix A — Working with AI
text:
A.1 Ground Rules
An AI assistant is now part of how most students write code, so this appendix suggests one way to use one while working through this book. The short version is that you attempt the task first, and the assistant then evaluates what you produced. That order matters because an assistant that writes your script leaves you unable to tell whether the output is right. Telling whether output is right is most of what this book teaches. The workflow below walks a script you already wrote through eight checks. The sections after it explain the ways an assistant will mislead you and how to catch that. Exercise 1 of every chapter points back here, so you may work through the checks many times.
Whatever your own course requires takes precedence over anything suggested here.
Asking for code you have not tried to write, or pasting an exercise prompt and submitting whatever comes back, skips the part where the learning happens. You stay the judge of every flag the assistant raises, which is what the eight steps are built around.

title: Appendix A — Working with AI
text:
What to Upload
The scripts in this book use datasets that come with R or its packages, which contain no personal data, so uploading them raises no issues. Other data is worth more thought. Data about identifiable people, licensed data you do not own, and another student’s work are best kept out of a chat window. If you are unsure whether a dataset is safe to paste, it is better to ask before pasting than after.


Disclosing What You Did
Step 8 suggests recording, inside the script itself, which flags you accepted and which you rejected. A course that asks you to disclose AI use is usually asking for something like this record, and it is the part that shows the judging was yours. A log with no rejections in it is worth a second look, since it usually means you accepted everything without checking.

title: Appendix A — Working with AI
text:
A.2 Reviewing Your Script

Step 1: Comment Your Code
Open the script you wrote while reading the chapter and comment it in the style shown in Comments. Each comment should say what the block does and why you ran it. Do this before you open an assistant, and a line you cannot describe in plain English is a line you do not yet understand.
Everything after this step happens in the copy, so that the difference between the two files is a record of what you changed.

Save your work as Script_01.R and do not edit it again.
Create a copy, Script_01_revised.R, saved next to the original in the same folder Desktop/ECON_XXXX/Code.

Update the names for later chapters. E.g., use Script_02.R for chapter 2.


Step 2: Predict, Then Run
Pick your two or three main results and write down, as comments, what you expect before you run anything. A number you write down after seeing the output is not a prediction.
Restart R with  Session > Restart R, and check that the Environment pane is empty. Then use the menu beside  Source to select Source with Echo, which runs the whole script and prints each command and result. Do not use  Run, which executes only the current line or selection.
If it errors, fix the error, then restart and Source again.
If you are stuck, upload the script and the error message.

Here is my R script and the error message it produces. What is causing the error, and what should I look at to fix it myself? Do not give me corrected code.

Once it runs from start to finish, compare each result against what you predicted.


Step 3: Ask Whether Your Comments Match Your Code
Ask whether your comments are accurate, but you stay the judge.

Here is an R script from an introductory statistics course, with my own comments. For each comment, tell me whether it accurately describes what that line of code actually does. Quote the comments that are wrong or incomplete, and explain the mismatch. Do not rewrite my comments or my code. Do not suggest replacing my method and keep to the notation used in my script.

The last line matters because this book builds inference from simulations, and an assistant left to itself steers you toward canned test functions and the notation of other textbooks. Settle each flag by running the line and doing a small hand-check. (Look at what comes back, since assistants write confidently when they are wrong.)


Step 4: Ask Whether You Estimated the Right Quantity
For each main result, write one sentence naming the quantity you meant to estimate, in words and in the notation of the chapter. Put those sentences under the script and ask.

Here is an R script, followed by one sentence per result naming the quantity I meant to estimate. For each, tell me whether the code computes that quantity or a different one, and name the difference. Do not rewrite my code.

You are the judge about what you want, and whether the code is doing what you want.


Step 5: Write Your Own Summary and Have It Critiqued
At the top of the script, write three sentences on the main statistical ideas. (This is what the chapter is about, not what the code does technically.)
Then start a new AI chat and ask

Here are three sentences I wrote from memory about a chapter in my introductory statistics course, followed by the chapter’s own summary. […] Tell me which of my statements are wrong, which are too vague to be useful, and what important idea I left out. Do not write a corrected summary for me.



Step 6: Ask Your Own Questions
Now ask the AI assistant about whatever you found hardest, in your own words. A vague question gets a vague answer, so name the specific idea, number, or line that lost you.

I do not follow X. Explain it a different way, then ask me three questions to check whether I understand it.

Questions about code work the same way, as long as they are specific.

Assuming Y already exists, why does Y < -43 not assign the value 43, when Y <- 43 does?

Finish by having the assistant quiz you, since answering a question tests your understanding better than reading an answer does.


Step 7 (Optional): Reorganizing Your Script
Once the revised script is saved, you can ask an assistant to reorganize it.

Help me reorganize the code into coherent blocks, for easy recall later.

Ask only when you already understand the script and want it tidier, since a long plain script is usually easier to learn from than a compact one built out of functions.


Step 8: Save Your Work
Just after your big-picture summary at the top of the revised script, record what you did with each flag. The rejections are useful to show that you did the judging.
# --- AI review ---
# Accepted:
#   ~ line 22: comment said "mean", code computed the median. Comment fixed.
#   ~ line 41: bootstrap resampled rows, not students. Now resamples by student.
# Rejected:
#   ~ line 12: claimed na.rm=TRUE hid a problem. Checked sum(is.na(x_hat)); there are none.
#   ~ line 58: suggested t.test over the permutation test. Not the method this chapter builds.

title: Appendix A — Working with AI
section: A.3 When the Assistant Is Wrong
text:
A.3 When the Assistant Is Wrong
An assistant produces text that is likely to follow your prompt, which is not the same as text that is true. It cannot run your code, check a number, or see what your data contain, so a wrong answer arrives in exactly the same confident tone as a right one. The fix is to check the few claims that matter, which is usually quick.

A Worked Check
Suppose you asked whether your comments match your code, and the assistant returned this flag.

Line 4 is wrong. sd() computes the population standard deviation, dividing the sum of squared deviations by \(n\). Your comment calls it the sample standard deviation.

That is a claim about arithmetic, so settle it with arithmetic.


Code
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
x_hat <- Wages1[, 'wage'] # lab data: hourly wages in 1980 dollars
n <- length(x_hat)

# The two candidate formulas, computed by hand
sqrt(sum((x_hat - mean(x_hat))^2) / n)        # divides by n
## [1] 3.26869
sqrt(sum((x_hat - mean(x_hat))^2) / (n - 1))  # divides by n-1
## [1] 3.269186

# What R actually does
sd(x_hat)
## [1] 3.269186


sd(x_hat) matches the second number, so R divides by \(n - 1\) and the flag is wrong. Your comment stays, and the rejection goes into the Step 8 log.
# Rejected:
#   ~ line 4: claimed sd() divides by n. Hand-checked both formulas; sd() matches n-1.
The check took three lines and one comparison, which is the general shape of it. Any claim about what a function computes can be settled by computing it both ways and looking.






TipTest Yourself





Ask an assistant whether var() divides by \(n\) or by \(n - 1\), then settle it by hand before accepting the answer.


Code
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
x_hat <- Wages1[, 'wage'] # lab data: hourly wages in 1980 dollars
n <- length(x_hat)

sum((x_hat - mean(x_hat))^2) / n        # divides by n
## [1] 10.68433
sum((x_hat - mean(x_hat))^2) / (n - 1)  # divides by n-1
## [1] 10.68758
var(x_hat)
## [1] 10.68758


Which line does var(x_hat) match, and is that consistent with what you found for sd(x_hat) above?





Failure Modes to Expect
Four patterns come up often enough to be worth naming.
Substituting the standard method. You build a bootstrap or a permutation test, and the assistant proposes t.test() instead. It is not wrong that t.test() exists, but it is wrong as a review of what you wrote, because this book builds inference from simulation on purpose. Tell the assistant which method the chapter uses, and reject the flag if it ignores you.
Switching notation. The assistant writes \(\bar{x}\) and \(s\) where this book writes \(\hat{m}\) and \(\hat{s}\), or renames your objects to match another textbook. Notation is the reference for what this book uses.
Inventing arguments. The assistant suggests plausible-looking arguments that do not exist, such as a bins= argument where hist() actually takes breaks=. Reading ?hist settles this immediately.
Misstating what a result means. The most common single error is describing a \(p\)-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is not, and Hypothesis Tests explains what it is instead.

title: Appendix A — Working with AI
text:
A.4 Writing Good Prompts
The prompts in the eight steps share four features, which you can reuse when writing your own.
Name the specific thing. “I do not follow the bootstrap” gets you a lecture, while “I do not follow why line 22 resamples rows instead of students” gets you an answer.
Say what you do not want. Every prompt above ends with a restriction, such as “Do not give me corrected code.” Without it you get a rewritten script and learn nothing.
State the method. Say that you are building inference from simulations, or the assistant will steer you toward canned test functions.
Ask to be tested. “Ask me three questions to check whether I understand it” is worth more than another paragraph of explanation.

Further Reading

Korinek (2023) – a survey of where these tools help and where they fail in economic research.
Data Scientism – how confident-looking results mislead, which is the same problem in a different form.





Korinek, Anton. 2023. “Generative AI for Economic Research: Use Cases and Implications for Economists.” Journal of Economic Literature 61 (4): 1281–317. https://doi.org/10.1257/jel.20231736.

title: Appendix B — Code Conventions
text:
B.1 Assignment and Naming
This is the house style used by every piece of R code in this book, not a standard that R enforces or that other R programmers follow. R will happily run code written any other way, and you will meet plenty of it: other books use = for assignment, load the tidyverse, and prefer double quotes. The conventions here are collected for two reasons. The first is practical: when your code looks like the book’s code, you can compare the two line by line and see where you diverged. The second is that most of these choices exist to prevent a specific mistake, and the notes below say which one. Where a convention is a matter of taste rather than safety, it says so. The code blocks on this page are shown for reference and are not run.
Always use <- for assignment, never =. The two are not interchangeable, because = also passes arguments to functions, and mixing the two makes it hard to see which is happening.
Use snake_case for multi-word names and _hat for generic names that hold observed values or sample summaries. Use y_fit for fitted values, y_pred for predictions at design points, and e_hat for residuals. Keep capitals where the mathematical notation uses them, such as the design matrix X and the empirical CDF F_hat.
Names that match the notation in Notation let you read a formula and the code that implements it side by side. For example, x_hat[i] corresponds to \(\hat{x}_{i}\), m_hat to \(\hat{m}\), y_fit[i] to \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}\), and y_pred to \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\). The sample median is med_hat in code and \(\tilde{m}\) in formulas. Use F_hat for an empirical cumulative distribution function and f_hat for a kernel density estimate or a stored histogram. The capital F distinguishes the cumulative distribution from the density. Add a group or variable label when needed, as in x1_hat, x2_hat, m_x_hat, and m_y_hat. For two distributions, use names such as F1_hat and F2_hat, or f_x_hat and f_y_hat. Descriptive names such as wage and region_means can stay descriptive, and existing dataset column names keep their spelling. Possible outcomes and evaluation points can use x or x_values, while known population quantities use names such as population_mean. These are different roles from the sample values in x_hat.
In the Part 1 labs, x_hat always holds hourly wages from Wages1. In Data & Visualization, Summary Statistics, and Advanced Empirics, it holds all 3294 of them, Wages1[, 'wage']. Each chapter defines it once, where the lab data first appears. Small hand-typed examples, such as c(3, 3.1, 0.02), use x0_hat, and simulated draws use x_sim, so neither overwrites the lab data. If you copy a lab chunk into a new session, run the definition of x_hat first. In Sampling & Resampling, Confidence Intervals, and Hypothesis Testing, the Wages1 hourly wages play the role of a known population. They are stored in population_wages, with population_wage_mean for the population mean, and x_hat holds one random sample of 50 workers drawn from them. Other samples drawn from them use x_sim. Estimation Theory uses the same population and draws its samples of 50 workers into x_sim.
In the Part 2 labs, xy_hat plays the same role for bivariate data. It holds Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')] with columns renamed x_hat and y_hat, so a regression reads lm(y_hat ~ x_hat, data=xy_hat). Small hand-typed examples use xy0_hat, and simulated data use xy_sim with columns x_sim and y_sim. A second dataset, such as USArrests in a Test Yourself, uses xy2_hat with the same column names.
In the Part 3 labs, xy_hat holds the multivariate data, usually Wages1, with a school_g factor added in chapters that compare groups. Here the columns keep their names, so a regression reads lm(wage ~ school + exper, data=xy_hat) and its output names each variable. Bootstrap resamples of the data use xy_boot, and simulated data use xy_sim with columns such as x1_sim, x2_sim, and y_sim.

title: Appendix B — Code Conventions
text:
B.2 Base R
This book uses base R throughout, with no tidyverse verbs (mutate, filter, select, arrange) and no pipes. Use aggregate(), subset(), merge(), and bracket indexing instead. The one exception is %>% where a package requires chaining, as plotly does.
Access a package with :: when you use it once or twice, and with library() only when a chapter uses it repeatedly.
car::vif(reg)      # used once
library('fixest')  # used throughout a chapter
Writing car::vif() rather than loading the package makes it obvious where a function came from, which matters when an assistant suggests a function and you cannot find it.
Load a dataset from a package with data(), naming the package, rather than with library().
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
This keeps the package name next to the dataset, for the same reason as ::. It also loads only the one dataset you asked for. By contrast, library('Ecdat') attaches every Ecdat dataset, and one of them hides the built-in Orange data.

Data Access
Use bracket notation with the column name for subsetting, the dollar sign for quick single-column access inline, and double brackets for pulling an element out of a list.
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xy_hat <- Wages1[, c('school', 'wage')]
colnames(xy_hat) <- c('x_hat', 'y_hat') # x_hat=years of schooling, y_hat=hourly wage
x_hat <- xy_hat[, 'x_hat']
y_hat <- xy_hat[, 'y_hat']

# also acceptable for single columns
exper_high <- Wages1$exper > median(Wages1$exper)
Naming the column, rather than its position, means your code keeps working when the column order changes.

title: Appendix B — Code Conventions
text:
B.3 Functions and Comments
Put the opening brace on the same line as function(), indent the body, end with an explicit return(), and close the brace on its own line.
skewness <- function(x_hat) {
    m_hat <- mean(x_hat)
    m3_hat <- mean((x_hat - m_hat)^3)
    s3_hat <- sd(x_hat)^3
    skew <- m3_hat / s3_hat
    return(skew)
}
R returns the last expression evaluated even without return(), so an explicit return() is for the reader rather than the interpreter. It makes the output of a function unambiguous at a glance.
Use # with a space after it, and let comments explain purpose rather than mechanics.
x_sim <- rnorm(1000)        # simulated sample values
m_hat <- mean(x_sim)        # sample mean
A comment that restates the code (# take the mean) adds nothing, while one that says why (# sample mean, to compare against the population mean) does. This is the style Working with AI asks you to comment in, and Step 3 there checks these comments against what the code actually does.

Spacing and Strings
Put spaces around binary operators and after commas, and no spaces inside parentheses. The one exception is = when it names a function argument, which takes no spaces. This is deliberate: x <- y + 1 is arithmetic and gets room to breathe, while col='red' is one argument and reads as a single unit.
x <- y + 1
c(1, 2, 3)
X[1, 2]
grey(0, .5)
mean(x_hat)                        # not mean( x_hat )
hist(x_hat, breaks=25, freq=FALSE)     # not breaks = 25
Use single quotes for all strings, including column names, package names, and axis labels. R treats 'a' and "a" as identical, so this one is purely for consistency.
Wages1[, 'wage']
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)'


Logical Values
Write logical values in full, as TRUE and FALSE.
hist(x_hat, freq=FALSE, border=NA)
x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
R also accepts the abbreviations T and F, and you will see them constantly in other people’s code, but they are not safe. TRUE and FALSE are reserved words that cannot be reassigned, while T and F are ordinary variables that merely start out holding those values. Someone who writes T <- 0 earlier in a script silently breaks every freq=T after it, and nothing warns you. The full words cost three or four extra characters and remove the possibility.

title: Appendix B — Code Conventions
text:
B.4 Simulation and Loops
Call set.seed() once at the top of the block that generates random numbers, and never reset it partway through. Resetting midway makes the results depend on where the reset happened, which is very hard to debug later.
Use replicate() for repeated simulations that return a vector or matrix, sapply() and lapply() for apply-style iteration, and an explicit for loop when the iteration itself is the point being taught. Pre-allocate with rep(NA, n).
set.seed(1)
n_boot <- 999
boot_means <- rep(NA, n_boot)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
    boot_means[b] <- mean(x_boot)
}
m_boot <- mean(boot_means)
Here boot_means[b] is one replicate mean, while m_boot averages all the replicate means. If a loop stores its current replicate mean separately, use m_b_hat. The corresponding jackknife collection and its average are jack_means and m_jack.
Pre-allocating with rep(NA, n) rather than numeric(n) matters because numeric(n) fills the vector with zeros. If a bug leaves some entries unfilled, zeros look like real results and NA does not.

seq and seq_along
These two are not interchangeable, and the book uses each for a different job.
for (b in seq(n_boot))        { ... }   # n_boot is a count, so seq(n_boot) gives 1, 2, ..., n_boot
for (i in seq_along(x_hat))   { ... }   # x_hat is a vector, so this gives 1, ..., length(x_hat)
Writing seq_along(n_boot) when n_boot is a single number is a silent bug: it returns just 1, so the loop runs once and the code appears to work. Writing seq(x_hat) when x_hat is a vector happens to work, but it reads as though x_hat were a count.
One edge case is worth knowing. seq(n_boot) returns c(1, 0) when n_boot is zero, so a loop that should not run at all runs twice. seq_len(n_boot) returns nothing in that case and is the safer form. The book uses seq() because its counts are never zero.


Formulas and Output
Use standard R formula syntax with spaces around ~.
reg <- lm(y_hat ~ x_hat)
y_fit <- fitted(reg)
e_hat <- y_hat - y_fit
plot(y_hat ~ x_hat, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5))
Round for display with round(value, 2), build label strings with paste0(), and rely on auto-printing rather than calling print() except inside a loop or conditional.
title(paste0('mean= ', round(m_hat, 2)), font.main=1)

title: Appendix B — Code Conventions
text:
B.5 Reference Card

<- for assignment, never =.
Base R only, no tidyverse and no pipes.
library() for repeated use, pkg::fun() for one-off calls, data(x, package='pkg') for datasets.
Bracket notation [,'Name'] for column subsetting.
Explicit return() in every function you write.
set.seed() once at the top of a random block, never reset.
Single quotes for all strings.
Spaces around operators, none around an argument’s =.
TRUE and FALSE in full, never T and F.
Pre-allocate with rep(NA, n), not numeric(n).
seq() for counts, seq_along() for vectors.
Comments explain purpose, not mechanics.
x_hat, y_hat, m_hat, v_hat, s_hat, and med_hat for generic sample quantities, and xy_hat for the Part 2 and Part 3 lab data. x0_hat and xy0_hat for small examples, and x_sim and xy_sim for simulated draws. y_fit for fitted values, y_pred for predictions at design points, and e_hat for residuals.
F_hat for ECDFs; f_hat for kernel density estimates and stored histograms.


Further Reading

https://style.tidyverse.org/ – a widely used R style guide. It assumes the tidyverse rather than base R, so read it for the general principles rather than the specific verbs.
Figures – the matching conventions for plots.

title: Appendix C — Figure Conventions
text:
C.1 Histograms of Data
A default R plot is rarely a good plot, and the gap between the two is mostly a handful of arguments. This appendix collects the choices the book makes and what each one is for, so you can apply them to figures the book never draws. They are house style, and the theme running through them is that ink should carry information, since borders, bold titles, and full-strength colors draw the eye without telling the reader anything.
A histogram of data summarizes the \(n\) observations you actually have. The two panels below plot the same data with R’s defaults and with the book’s conventions.
Code
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
x_hat <- Wages1[, 'wage'] # lab data: hourly wages in 1980 dollars
par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4, 4, 2, 1))

# Default settings
hist(x_hat)

# House style
hist(x_hat, breaks=25, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,   # more bins, since n is 3294
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')
rug(x_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
The bar borders are gone, so the distribution reads as one silhouette instead of twenty outlined boxes. The vertical axis is a density rather than a count, so a fitted curve can be drawn on the same axes. The axis label gives the variable and its units, and the rug along the bottom marks each of the observations that the bars summarize.

title: Appendix C — Figure Conventions
text:
C.2 Histograms of Resampled Data
A histogram of resampled data summarizes statistics rather than observations: hundreds or thousands of bootstrap, jackknife, or permutation draws, or repeated samples from a known population. It keeps the default grey fill, border=NA, and freq=FALSE, but differs from a histogram of data in three ways.









Data
Resampled data




breaks
15–25, fewer when \(n\) is small
25–100, since draws are plentiful


rug()
rug(x_hat, col=grey(0, .5))
None, since the draws would merge into a solid band


Vertical lines
A sample statistic in red, lwd=2
Interval bounds in black and, for null bootstrap or permutation distributions, the observed statistic in red, both lwd=2





Code
# Bootstrap distribution of the mean hourly wage
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
boot_means <- rep(NA, 999)
for (b in seq_along(boot_means)) {
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE)
    boot_means[b] <- mean(x_boot)
}
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975))

hist(boot_means, breaks=50, border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Bootstrap means of hourly wages (1980 dollars)')
abline(v=boot_ci, col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2) # 95% bootstrap interval









A bootstrap confidence interval does not need the observed statistic marked. A null bootstrap or permutation distribution does, since the observed statistic is the value being tested. A statistic’s distribution is filled with rgb(1, 0, 0, .5) only when introducing the idea, to make clear it is not a histogram of data.
The same line styles apply to any figure that marks a value, not only to histograms.

rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)
2

A hypothesized value, a null of 0, a true mean, a 45-degree line
rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)
1

Color says what a line is: red is the observed statistic, black is an interval, and blue is a hypothesized, true, or theoretical value. Thickness says where it comes from: thick is computed from this sample, and thin is assumed or known. Line type separates variants within a role, such as a second interval on the same figure. So a reader who has seen one figure in the book can read the next without a legend.
A 0 that is being tested uses the null style, and a 0 that is only a baseline uses the guide style. A significance level \(\alpha\) is chosen rather than computed, but it acts as a cutoff, so it uses the interval style. A density that is the subject of its own figure, rather than a comparison for a histogram, stays solid.
Draw a confidence band around a curve with polygon(..., border=NA), filled with the fit’s color at an alpha of .3, or with grey(0, .25) when the fit has no color. Coverage plots of many intervals are an exception: intervals that cover are rgb(0, 0, 0, .3) and intervals that miss are rgb(1, 0, 0, .5), and the title says so.

C.3 Boxplots
boxplot(x1_hat, x2_hat, names=c('A', 'B'), main=NA, xlab='Groups')
Use main=NA in boxplot() and add titles with title(..., font.main=1). Color grouped boxplots with the group colors from The Grey and RGB System, and set border='white' or border=NA when a fill color is specified.

Transparency is how a scatterplot survives a large sample, since transparent points darken where observations pile up instead of overplotting into a solid blob.

text:
C.5 Regression Lines
Each model keeps one color, so a reader can follow it from figure to figure.










Model
Includes
col
lwd
lty




Straight line
OLS, through the origin, piecewise, local line
rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)
2
1


Constant
A mean, regressogram, local constant
rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)
2
1


LOESS
Any span or degree
rgb(0, .7, .7, .8)
2
1



Every fit is thick, since it is computed from this sample. A population line keeps the population style from Histograms of Resampled Data, so a thick blue constant is a fit and a thin dashed blue line is a known value. Variants of one model in the same figure, such as two bandwidths or a fit through the origin, share the model’s color and differ by line type: lty=1, then 2, then 3. Fits drawn separately by group take the group’s color instead of the model’s.
Draw a straight line with abline(reg) and any other fit with lines(x_sorted, y_fit), rather than curve(). lines() takes the fitted values you actually computed, whereas curve() re-evaluates a function, which can quietly differ from the model you fit. Sort by the horizontal variable first, or lines() will zigzag back and forth across the plot.
Fitted values and predictions share the model’s color and width, and differ only in their markers. Fitted values y_fit are a plain line. Predictions y_pred at a few design points use type='o', whose open circles mark where the curve was actually computed. Predictions on a dense grid stay a plain line, since the circles would merge. When a legend shows circles on dashed lines, set seg.len=4, or the circle hides the dashes.

title: Appendix C — Figure Conventions
text:
C.6 Polishing
Use par(mfrow=c(1,2)) for two panels side by side, c(1,3) for three, and c(2,2) for a grid, with small top and right margins from par(mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1)). If you change par() inside a function, restore it on exit.
op <- par(no.readonly=TRUE)
on.exit(par(op), add=TRUE)
Position legends with a string such as 'topright' or 'topleft' rather than coordinates, so the legend moves with the data instead of landing on top of it. Add bty='n' to drop the box when it clutters the plot, keep entries to one to three words, and match lty, pch, and col to the plot symbols.
The figure below splits the workers by sex and shows the two groups in two panels, with one legend for both.


Code
female <- Wages1[, 'sex'] == 'female'
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4, 4, 1, 1), oma=c(0, 0, 2, 0))

# Scatterplot
# Both panels stop near 20 dollars, so the 16 largest wages are not drawn
# alpha.f=.2 fades cols from an alpha of .5 to .1, since n is 3294
plot(Wages1[, 'wage'] ~ Wages1[, 'school'], ylim=c(0, 20),
    pch=16, col=adjustcolor(ifelse(female, cols[1], cols[2]), alpha.f=.2),
    xlab='Years of schooling', ylab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)')

# ECDFs
F_female_hat <- ecdf(Wages1[female, 'wage'])
F_male_hat <- ecdf(Wages1[!female, 'wage'])
plot(F_female_hat, col=cols[1], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA,
    xlim=c(0, 20), main=NA,
    xlab='Hourly wage (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers')
plot(F_male_hat, add=TRUE, col=cols[2], lwd=2, verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)

# One legend for both panels, in the outer margin above them
par(fig=c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma=c(0, 0, 0, 0), mar=c(0, 0, 0, 0), new=TRUE)
plot.new()
legend('top', legend=c('Women', 'Men'),
    pch=16, lwd=2, col=cols, horiz=TRUE, bty='n',
    text.width=.2) # room between entries, which horiz=TRUE packs tightly









Both panels share one cols vector, so a group has the same color everywhere and a single legend can serve both panels. oma=c(0, 0, 2, 0) leaves two lines of outer margin above the panels. The last par() call then lays an empty plot over the whole figure, so that legend('top', ...) lands in that margin rather than inside either panel. The legend sets both pch=16 and lwd=2, so its symbols match the points in one panel and the lines in the other.
Add titles with title(..., font.main=1) after the plot call, rather than with main= inside it. R’s default title is bold, and a bold title competes with the data for attention. Keep the text short, usually a statistic or a single phrase, and use title('label', outer=TRUE) for a label spanning a multi-panel figure. For text annotations with text(), match the color to the element being labeled, use expression() or bquote() for math, and set adj=0 to left-align or adj=0.5 to center.

The Grey and RGB System
Scatterpoints and histogram fills use grey(0, alpha), varying only the transparency, while anything you want the reader to look at uses rgb() with an explicit alpha channel.








Code
Color
Use for




rgb(1, 0, 0, .8)
Red
Means, straight-line fits, key statistics


rgb(0, 0, 1, .8)
Blue
SD bounds, secondary reference lines, constant fits


rgb(0, .7, .7, .8)
Teal
LOESS fits


rgb(0, 0, 0, .8)
Black
Interval bounds, and horizontal and vertical reference lines



Avoid numeric codes such as col=2, which depend on the current palette, and names such as 'red', since neither form lets you set transparency. To compare groups, store one color per group in cols.







Groups
Colors




2
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))


3
cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, .8, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))


4 or more
cols <- hcl.colors(k, alpha=.45), where k is the number of groups



With four or more groups, hcl.colors() spaces the colors evenly in a perceptual space, so no one group looks louder than the others.

text:
C.7 Reference Card

border=NA and freq=FALSE for every histogram.
A rug under histograms of data; more bins and no rug for histograms of resampled data.
Interval bounds in black and, for null bootstrap or permutation distributions, the observed statistic in red, both lwd=2.
Null values, population values, and theoretical densities over a histogram in blue, with lwd=1 and lty=2.
pch=16 and grey(0, alpha) for scatterplots, with alpha matched to \(n\).
One color per model at lwd=2: red for straight lines, blue for constants, and teal for LOESS, with line type for variants and type='o' for predictions at design points.
font.main=1 for every title.
rgb() with alpha for emphasis colors, never col=2 or 'red'.
par(mfrow=...) for multi-panel layouts, not layout().


Further Reading

https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/ – Fundamentals of Data Visualization, free online, on which figures work and why.
Tufte (2001) – the source of the ink-per-unit-information argument above.
Communicating Results – applies these conventions to a full worked figure.

title: Appendix D — Notation
text:
D.1 Hats and No Hats
This appendix collects every symbol this book uses, so you have one place to look when a formula in a later chapter reuses a letter from an earlier one. It describes this book’s choices, since there is no universal standard. Statistics notation varies by field, by textbook, and sometimes by chapter within one textbook. Expect other sources to write the sample mean as \(\bar{x}\) where this book writes \(\hat{m}\), and to use \(P(\cdot)\) where this book uses \(\text{Prob}(\cdot)\). Throughout, a hat marks a quantity computed from data, and a bare letter marks the theoretical quantity it corresponds to. Once you have that, most formulas can be read before you know the details, because the decoration tells you whether you are looking at something you can compute or something you can only estimate. The tables below are grouped by topic in roughly the order the book introduces them.
The book distinguishes the sample (the data you observed) from the population (the theoretical quantity you want to know) using hats.
For example, \(M\) estimates the population mean \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\) and varies across samples, while \(\hat{m}\) is the one number from your sample data. We use lowercase letters under the hat for sample quantities, including the mean \(\hat{m}\), variance \(\hat{v}\), standard deviation \(\hat{s}\), proportion \(\hat{p}(x)\), covariance \(\hat{c}_{XY}\), and correlation \(\hat{r}_{XY}\). The mean, variance, and standard-deviation estimators are \(M\), \(V\), and \(S\) before the sample is observed. Observed values of the random variables \(X_{i}\) and \(Y_{i}\) are written \(\hat{x}_{i}\) and \(\hat{y}_{i}\). Without a subscript, \(\hat{x}=(\hat{x}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{x}_{n})\) and \(\hat{y}\) denote the whole vector of observed values, as in “the variance of \(\hat{x}\)”. The superscript \(\mathrm{pred}\) marks a model’s prediction: \(\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)\) is its prediction at a design point \(x\). The superscript \(\mathrm{fit}\) marks a fitted value: \(\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}=\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(\hat{x}_{i})\) is the model’s prediction for the observed outcome \(\hat{y}_{i}\). Uppercase variable labels in subscripts identify which variables a statistic describes: \(\hat{c}_{XY}\) is the sample covariance of \(\hat{x}\) and \(\hat{y}\). Conventional names retain their capitals: \(\hat{F}\) denotes an empirical CDF or an F-statistic, \(\hat{U}\) is the Mann–Whitney statistic, and \(\hat{R}^2\) is the coefficient of determination. Abbreviations such as \(\hat{\text{SE}}\), \(\hat{\text{IQR}}\), and \(\hat{\text{RSS}}\) also retain their capitals.
In R code, observed sample values use x_hat and y_hat (or xy_hat for a pair), and simulated draws use x_sim (or xy_sim). Their mean, variance, standard deviation, and median use m_hat, v_hat, s_hat, and med_hat. For example, x_hat[i] corresponds to \(\hat{x}_{i}\) and med_hat to \(\tilde{m}\). Fitted values use y_fit, predictions at design points use y_pred, and residuals use e_hat, so e_hat <- y_hat - y_fit matches the residual identity. Empirical CDFs use F_hat in code, while kernel density estimates and stored histograms use f_hat, matching \(\hat{F}(x)\) and \(\hat{f}(x)\). See Code Conventions for naming groups, bootstrap replicates, and matrices.
The table below pairs sample quantities with their population or theoretical counterparts.
Note that \(\mathbb{E}\), \(\mathbb{V}\), and \(\mathbb{C}\) are functions computed only on random variables. We write population means, variances, and standard deviations as \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]\), \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\), and \(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}\) throughout the book. The argument identifies the random variable: \(\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\) describes individual observations, while \(\mathbb{V}[M]\) describes the sample mean across samples. Distribution parameters keep their own names, such as \(\theta\) for a Bernoulli distribution and \(\lambda\) for a Poisson distribution (with \(\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=\lambda\)). Similarly, we reserve \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) for the Normal distribution.
